10084-kazan:
James Oliver Curwood's 1914 northern tale follows Kazan, a dog of the far north, opening with a miracle and a journey into the north. McCready pays the debt, Kazan is free from bonds, and a fight in the snow brings Joan, whose voice the frontispiece hears.

Out of the blizzard comes a great change, then tragedy on Sun Rock, days of fire, always two by two, the red death, the trail of hunger, and the right of fang. Curwood writes of the wild with feeling for animals. Readers get an animal adventure of loyalty, survival, and the law of the north.
10109-the-unspeakable-gentleman:
J. P. Marquand's 1922 novel centers on a son judging his father's reputation. The narrator sets out to explain what his father did in the French royalist plot of 1805. He worries his account could slide into a fanciful tale of a man who aimed to be a bad example only because a good one seemed out of reach.

Uncle Jason stood beside him, looking kindly worried, when news came that his father had returned to America. Marquand builds his tale from memory, plot, and family shame. Readers get a subtle novel of reputation, where a son must judge a father the world calls unspeakable.
1037-the-life-of-john-bunyan:
Edmund Venables tells the life of John Bunyan, the Bedford tinker who became England's most-read religious writer. Bunyan fought in the civil war, preached in barns and fields when the law barred him, spent twelve years in Bedford jail, and wrote The Pilgrim's Progress there. Venables follows him from youth to fame.

The biography draws on Bunyan's own Grace Abounding and on parish records, and it sets his dreams, fears, and plain speech in their Puritan age. Readers meet a man of low birth and high fire. The book suits those who want the life behind the allegory, told with care and warmth.
106-jungle-tales-of-tarzan:
Between the great adventures, Tarzan's youth holds smaller jungle stories. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Jungle Tales of Tarzan gathers twelve episodes from his early years among the apes. First love, capture, and fights over the young ape Teeka fill the chapters.

Tarzan meets a black boy, a witch-doctor seeking vengeance, and the lion who haunts his dreams. He rescues the moon in one comic tale and battles for Teeka in another. The stories show how the ape-man learned courage, pity, and law. They enrich the main Tarzan novels with quieter days.
10679-the-story-of-the-other-wise-man:
Henry Van Dyke's beloved Christmas tale, The Story of the Other Wise Man, imagines a fourth wise man who also saw the star rise. Artaban sets out for Bethlehem with gifts, but on the road he stops to help the sick, the poor, and the lost, and so misses the child he sought. His chapters carry him by the waters of Babylon, through hidden ways of sorrow, and toward a pearl of great price.

The story ends with the old man at last finding the King he sought, not in a palace but in the lives he served. Van Dyke writes in gentle, musical prose, with illustrations in the original. Readers return to it each Christmas for its simple claim: love shown to others is itself a way of reaching heaven.
10728-christie-the-king-s-servant-a-sequ:
Mrs. O. F. Walton wrote Christie, the King's Servant as a sequel to her popular Christie's Old Organ. The story returns to Runswick Bay, the Yorkshire fishing village Christie knew, with chapters on Little John, strange music, the Runswick sports, a tug of war, and a night of storm. Yellow ragwort in a dream brings the narrator back to the bay.

Walton writes a warm, Christian tale for young readers, in which service to the King means kindness, courage, and faith in daily life. Fishermen, cliffs, and sea air fill the scenes. Readers who loved the first Christie book will find this sequel a gentle continuation of its spirit.
10729-jack-s-ward-or-the-boy-guardian:
Horatio Alger Jr., the beloved American writer of boys' stories, tells Jack's Ward, or The Boy Guardian, in his familiar manner. Jack, a brave lad, takes charge of a younger ward and must guard him against schemers, as one illustration shows him thrusting an old man through a secret door. Alger himself, born in 1834 and a Harvard man, spent years among New York street boys.

The story rewards honesty, pluck, and kindness, as Alger's seventy-odd tales always did, selling over a million copies in his lifetime. Young readers get adventure with a moral spine. The book shows why Alger's name became shorthand for rising by merit and good character.
10761-essays-of-robert-louis-stevenson-s:
William Lyon Phelps selected and edited these Essays of Robert Louis Stevenson, with an introduction, notes, and a life of the author. The contents include "An Apology for Idlers," "Talk and Talkers," "A Gossip on Romance," "The Character of Dogs," "Books Which Have Influenced Me," and "Pulvis et Umbra." Phelps traces Stevenson from his Edinburgh birth in 1850, son and grandson of lighthouse engineers.

The essays show Stevenson's charm, wit, and moral sense in short form, on idleness, talk, dogs, and books. Notes help students follow his allusions. Readers get the best short road into Stevenson beyond his novels, edited for classroom and general use.
1079-the-life-and-opinions-of-tristram-s:
Laurence Sterne tells the life of Tristram Shandy, but Tristram cannot get born until hundreds of pages in. He is too busy with his father's theories, his uncle Toby's sieges, and endless digressions. The novel breaks every rule, with blank pages, black pages, chapters out of order, and jokes aimed straight at the reader.

Beneath the pranks lies a warm portrait of odd, kind men and their hobby-horses. Sterne mocks systems, doctors, and scholars while praising human folly. The book shocked and delighted its age, and it still reads as the first truly modern novel, playful and wise at once.
10857-my-native-land-the-united-states-i:
James Cox published My Native Land in 1903 as a profusely illustrated book on the United States: its wonders, beauties, and people, with notes, character sketches, folklore, traditions, and history. Written for the amusement of the old and the instruction of the young, it opens with the nation's birth, the Liberty Bell, and the shot heard around the world. The witch of Salem follows.

Cox ranges across regions and legends, mixing patriotic story with local lore. His style is hearty and popular, made for family reading. Readers get a turn-of-the-century celebration of America, in the voice of its boosters and storytellers.
1099-the-riverman:
Stewart Edward White sends his hero up a Michigan river with a crew of lumberjacks driving logs to the mill. The riverman must fight jams, rapids, and rival crews, and his skill with a peavey and his nerve in white water decide whether the drive pays or breaks. The novel draws on White's own time in the lumber camps.

Love, rivalry, and a feud with a crooked boss give the drive its plot, while the river itself steals the show. White writes the work, the food, and the talk of the camps with firsthand zest. The book stands as the classic novel of the old lumber days.
11057-the-wife-of-his-youth-and-other-st:
Charles W. Chesnutt collected nine stories of the color line in this 1899 volume, with three essays appended. The title story follows Mr. Ryder, dean of the Blue Veins, a society of light-skinned Black people in a northern city, who plans a ball and a new marriage, only to meet the wife of his youth.

Other stories include Her Virginia Mammy, The Sheriff's Children, The Passing of Grandison, and Uncle Wellington's Wives, each probing passing, family, and prejudice. Essays ask what is a white man, picture the future American, and analyse disfranchisement. Chesnutt writes with irony and restraint, and the book remains a landmark of African American literature on race and identity.
11115-frank-merriwell-at-yale-or-freshma:
Burt L. Standish published this 1903 boys' adventure, Frank Merriwell at Yale, in thirty-four chapters. Frank hears Yale men singing from his rooms on York Street, having passed his entrance examinations without a preparatory course at Phillips Academy.

Chapters follow trouble brewing, challenged and hazed, the blow, the fight, the roast at East Rock, the duel, Lambda Chi, freshman against sophomore, the rush, the ball field, breaking an enemy's wrist. Evan Hartwick confesses an almost irresistible desire to strike the cool freshman, while Browning, growing fat again out of training, warns that Merriwell is a bad man to hit. Standish's hero wins through sport, pluck, and fair play.
11309-the-booming-of-acre-hill-and-other:
John Kendrick Bangs's 1902 collection, The Booming of Acre Hill. gathers humorous reminiscences of urban and suburban life first printed in the Ladies' Home Journal, the Woman's Home Companion, and Harper publications, illustrated by C. Dana Gibson. The title story finds Acre Hill, once void of houses as a primeval forest, suddenly sold out by the Acre Hill Land Improvement Company, leaving old owners bewildered at losing their paradise.

Other stories include a strange organ's misadventures, a failed plot, the ingratitude of Barkis, M. D. , and the mayor's lamps. Bangs's humor targets speculation, suburbia, and middle-class pretension. The collection shows a popular American humorist at work just as suburbs began reshaping city life.
11328-the-hunted-woman:
James Oliver Curwood's 1915 northern novel, The Hunted Woman, follows a veiled woman traveling eighteen hours into a gold-rush horde pouring into the mountains, always in and never out. She watches toughened miners, singing and blaspheming, and a dark-eyed girl called a straying angel, while a bearded man explains the horde that beats trails ahead of civilization. Illustrations show MacDonald, a huge brown bear, and a closed tunnel with forty-five minutes to live.

Curwood, author of Kazan, builds the plot on gold, pursuit, and a grave calling MacDonald north. The woman's past drives the hunt, and the northern setting supplies danger at every turn. The novel is a brisk adventure romance, typical of Curwood's popular northland fiction.
11329-lands-of-the-slave-and-the-free-or:
Captain Henry A. Murray's Lands of the Slave and the Free, in a second cheap edition dated 1857, compares Cuba, the United States, and Canada through a British naval officer's travels. Epigraphs from Milton, Whittier, Dryden, and others frame the argument, and Murray cut passages from the first edition to reach a popular audience. Slavery, American institutions, and Canadian freedom supply the running contrast.

Murray writes as a traveler and moral observer, praising liberty while describing plantation life in Cuba and the American South. His dedication to friends and his London preface of 1855 set a personal tone. The book remains a vivid outsider's account of the Americas on the eve of the Civil War.
11424-the-trade-union-woman:
Alice Henry's Trade Union Woman, published in 1915 and dedicated to trade union women of the United States and Canada. traces women's labor organizing from early New England cotton mills to the Women's Trade Union League and huge strikes. Chapters cover the Knights of Labor, immigrant women, women organizers, vocations, vocational training, marriage, the vote, and union ideals, with appendices on hotel agreements and Hart, Schaffner and Marx contracts. Henry edited Life and Labor.

Henry begins with Deborah Skinner at Waltham's first power loom in 1814 and Fall River weavers in 1817, showing women as pioneers of factory labor. Her argument is that organization, not protection alone, secures women's wages and conditions. The book remains a foundational history of American women workers.
11654-confessions-of-a-young-man:
George Moore's Confessions of a Young Man opens with a soul like smooth wax, ready to take any impress. Moore says he might equally have been a Pharaoh, an ostler, a pimp, or an archbishop, and done each job with some success.

Impulses drive him from trail to trail, with weariness and despondency between, until a word, a book, or a yielding moment starts a new chase. Later pages bring Paris life, a Pierrotte dress for a cotillion, a marquise's ball, and a play called Maître-Forges. The book is a young artist's self-portrait, frank, restless, and fond of paradox.
11867-the-alaskan:
James Oliver Curwood's 1923 novel of the North, dedicated to the men and women of Alaska, opens aboard a steamship with the aging Captain Rifle still hungry for adventure. Alan Holt, a younger man bound for the tundra, meets Mary Standish under strange circumstances that neither fully understands.

As Alan puzzles over why Mary sought him out, played him against the villain Rossland. Then reached his northern home ahead of him, the story moves from shipboard encounters to open country and confrontation. Curwood uses the Alaskan landscape as more than scenery, making distance, weather, and isolation shape every choice his characters make.
11902-a-peep-into-toorkisthan:
Captain Rollo Burslem, of the Thirteenth Prince Albert's Light Infantry, published A Peep into Toorkisthan in 1846, an early English account of Central Asia. The edition's transcriber notes preserve macron vowels, a sign of the book's attempt to render Turkic sounds for English readers.

Burslem writes as a soldier-traveller, describing peoples, places, and customs of a region then barely mapped by Europeans. His peep is deliberately modest in title: a short, observant visit rather than a survey. It preserves details of dress, hospitality, and political life that later, fuller accounts would check, correct, and expand.
12096-bushido-the-soul-of-japan:
Inazo Nitobe wrote Bushido in English around 1900, during a long illness, to answer Western friends who asked about Japanese morals. The thirteenth edition of 1908, revised and enlarged, is the text preserved here.

Nitobe explains the samurai code through virtues he names rectitude, courage, benevolence, politeness, veracity, honor, and loyalty, with chapters on training in fencing, archery, horsemanship, letters, and self-control. He draws parallels with European chivalry and argues that feudal ethics still shaped modern Japan. The book shaped Western views of Japan for decades, and it remains a clear, personal statement of how one Japanese writer wished his country to be understood.
12238-science-in-the-kitchen-a-scientifi:
Mrs. E. E. Kellogg's Science in the Kitchen, a scientific treatise on food substances and their dietetic properties, teaches healthful cookery on chemical principles. The book explains what foods contain, how cooking changes them, and how to feed invalids, children, and workers.

Long sections cover grains, fruits, vegetables, milk, eggs, and meats, with practical recipes that apply the science: why bread rises, why milk sours, how heat treats starch. Kellogg writes for housekeepers who want reasons, not just rules, and the tone is earnest and reforming. As a record, the book shows late Victorian domestic science taking shape, when kitchens began to borrow the language of the laboratory.
12278-confessions-of-a-young-man:
George Moore published Confessions of a Young Man in 1886, revising and annotating it in 1904. Moore, an Irish novelist and art critic, wrote the book as a memoir of youth in Paris and London, dedicated to the painter Jacques Blanche.

Chapters recall art studios, cafes, and the struggle to become a writer, with frank talk of love, money, and aesthetic faith. Moore paints his past as an Egyptian soul might, preserving its spirit and form in art, and the French epigraph frames the book as memory made into portrait. The confessions influenced a generation of young writers who prized style and sensation over Victorian moral. It reads now as both memoir and manifesto.
12329-heart-of-man:
George Edward Woodberry published Heart of Man in 1899 with Macmillan, dedicating the book to his friend Eugene Montgomery. Woodberry, a poet and critic, writes essays on poetry, democracy, and the inner life.

Contents include Taormina, A New Defence of Poetry, Democracy, and The Ride. Woodberry opens with Wordsworth line deep in the general heart of man, and argues that poetry speaks universal feeling. A mid-book passage treats Virgil mood as both subjective in form and objective in content, felt universally. The essays are high-minded and literary, in the manner of late Victorian criticism. The book shows a scholar defending poetry against science and commerce.
12436-the-night-horseman:
Max Brand published The Night Horseman in 1920, a western novel of the Untamed series, following Dan Barry and the wild riders of the range. Brand, a prolific pulp western writer, fills the book with gunplay, mystery, and a haunting hero.

Chapters run from the scholar and words and bullets through the doctor rides, the chain, and the waiting, to Jerry Strann, the gift horse, battle light, and Sweet Adeline. A mid-book scene holds a man fascinated by a girl passing wearily upstairs and by a silent battle in the next room. The novel blends western action with psychological suspense. Brand hero, half wild himself, rides between law and outlawry.
12495-casey-ryan:
B. M. Bower's 1921 western introduces Casey Ryan as a man talked about from Denver to Spokane and El Paso to Fort Benton. Old men at pipes recall his tumultuous youth. He drove the six fastest horses in Colorado out of Cripple Creek and whooped past would-be holdups, bullets whining after him while passengers prayed and clung to their seats.

Casey, lanky, flat and fearless, meets trouble with a grin, and the novel follows his scrapes, jobs and romances across the West. Bower writes in a humorous, tall-tale manner, letting reputation run ahead of the man. The book is a light, fast western, built on stage driving, mining camps and the legend of a driver who never quite slowed down.
12513-a-classification-and-subject-index:
Melvil Dewey's 1876 classification and subject index for cataloguing and arranging library books and pamphlets, reprinted in facsimile for the decimal centennial, is the founding document of the Dewey system. Dewey developed the plan early in 1873, after months studying library economy in hundreds of books and pamphlets, and over fifty personal visits to American libraries.

Three years of practical use convinced him that libraries could serve far better without extra spending, with his aid. The scheme orders knowledge by number, so any book finds a place and any reader finds a book. The pamphlet remains a landmark in library science, modest in size and immense in effect on shelves worldwide.
12548-the-secret-memoirs-of-the-courts-o:
Madame la Marquise de Fontenoy's first volume of secret memoirs treats William II of Germany and Francis Joseph of Austria-Hungary. The publishers note that the author, sheltered under a pen name, claims actual acquaintance with the persons named, intimate knowledge of their daily lives and personal familiarity with court scenes.

Her work offers personal reminiscences and panoramic views of court life, its striking features and characteristic happenings, illustrated with portraits from life. Readers meet emperors at home, at ceremony and in private habit. The memoirs belong to popular court literature before the First World War, gossipy, admiring and fond of rank, and they capture how European courts wished to be seen.
12586-satan:
Lewis Sperry Chafer's 1909 study, Satan, with a foreword by C. I. Scofield, treats the devil as a vital subject for believers. Scofield wishes all believers, especially ministers and Christian workers, might read it, since Satan's existence, personality and power bear on the age and on personal conflict. Contents run from Satan's career and the ages to his motive, methods, the man of sin, modern devices and the believer's victory.

Chafer writes as a dispensational theologian, systematic and earnest, mapping a satanic system behind modern life. The book belongs to early fundamentalist publishing, confident in Scripture and urgent in tone. It remains a clear statement of that theology, and of why its readers took spiritual warfare literally.
12626-the-earlier-work-of-titian:
Claude Phillips, keeper of the Wallace Collection, published The Earlier Work of Titian in 1897, in the Portfolio Artistic Monographs, with many illustrations. Plates show Flora in the Uffizi as frontispiece, Sacred and Profane Love in the Borghese, Virgin and Child with saints in the Louvre, and Le Jeune Homme au Gant in the Louvre.

Colour plates add a design for a Holy Family at Chatsworth and a sketch for the Madonna di Casa Pesaro. Phillips traces Titian's early manner, from Giorgionesque youth to Venetian mastery. The book remains a handsome, scholarly monograph, written by a museum man who studied the pictures in their galleries.
12657-the-later-works-of-titian:
Claude Phillips, keeper of the Wallace Collection, published The Later Work of Titian in 1898, illustrated in copper plates, sepia and text. Plates show Titian's self-portrait in the Uffizi, La Bella di Tiziano in the Pitti, his daughter Lavinia in Berlin, and the Cornaro family of the Duke of Northumberland.

Sepia plates add a St. Jerome drawing and a landscape with stag, while text illustrations include a Madonna and Child with saints in the National Gallery. Phillips traces Titian's late manner, looser, darker and more profound. The book remains a handsome, scholarly study of a master in old age, written by a museum man who knew the pictures first-hand.
12679-a-trip-abroad-an-account-of-a-jour:
Don Carlos Janes wrote this 1905 travel book from a trip across Palestine and Egypt, the lands he calls the earthly Canaan and the land of the Pharaohs. He visits holy sites, towns, and ruins, and retells Bible stories where they took place, from Elijah on Carmel to scenes along the Jordan. A plain, devout voice guides the tour.

Added chapters give the geography and history of Palestine in outline, with help for readers using a map, and a final chapter on Churches of Christ in Great Britain. Janes aimed to help Bible readers see the land behind the text. The book works both as a travel record and as a simple guide for study.
12681-us-and-the-bottle-man:
Edith Ballinger Price's 1920 children's book starts on a picnic, when Jerry, Greg, and their sister turn an empty olive bottle into a shipwreck message. Thrown into the sea, the bottle leads them to the Bottle Man, an old sailor with a store of sea yarns. Summer days on the shore frame his tales.

His stories carry the children far from home: to ships off Peru, divers in strange suits, and treasure on the sea floor. Price tells it all in a child's voice, full of jokes and small family detail. The book charms as a seaside adventure and as a tribute to how a good story can widen a child's world.
12684-dorian:
Nephi Anderson's 1921 novel, Dorian, published in Salt Lake City, opens with a Brigham Young saying: keys of the holy priesthood unlock knowledge and let readers look into the palace of truth. Anderson, author of Added Upon, a story of past, present and future existence, and Romance of a Missionary, writes Mormon fiction for a Mormon audience.

Dorian, a young hero of faith, faces trials, love and duty, in a story shaped by Latter-day Saint teaching on spirit, family and eternity. Anderson writes plainly and earnestly, valuing testimony over literary display. The novel offers a window on early twentieth-century Mormon storytelling, where doctrine and romance walk together.
12846-the-first-white-man-of-the-west-li:
Timothy Flint's 1856 life of Daniel Boone calls him the first white settler of Kentucky and follows him from boyhood to frontier fame. School pranks, a first hunt, a panther encounter, and fire hunting open the tale, before Boone meets Finley and crosses into the green valleys of Kentucky. Marriage and family moves punctuate the wandering.

Later chapters bring captivity, escapes, and battles, including a near execution stopped by rifle fire from rescuers. Flint mixes Boone's story with early annals of the whole region. The book, written in the heroic style of its age, remains a classic early Boone narrative.
12851-folk-tales-from-the-russian:
Verra Xenophontovna Kalamatiano de Blumenthal retold these Russian folk tales for American children, with pictures to match. The Tsarevna Frog opens the set, followed by Seven Simeons, The Language of the Birds, Ivanoushka the Simpleton, Baba Yaga, Father Frost, and more. Each tale moves by magic, cunning, and brave deeds.

In one story a proud king rages when his daughter seems wedded to the deep sea, while the Simeon brothers sail their ship like a golden fish beneath the waves. The retellings keep the old wonder while smoothing the language for young readers. The book offers a friendly first taste of Russian story lore.
12916-the-secret-history-of-the-court-of:
Procopius's Secret History of the Court of Justinian, put into English from Greek for the Athenian Society in 1896, tells the seamy side of the Byzantine court. Its contents list Antonina's wedding to Belisarius, her love affairs, her help to Empress Theodora, her love for the Thracian Theodosius, and Belisarius's weak yielding to them.

A later passage traces Theodora from a low past to Justinian's lover, then to high rank, then to empress plundering the realm with her husband as a fellow Blue. Procopius writes with fierce, gossipy detail. The book remains a famed, hostile source on Justinian's reign.
12920-the-goldfish-being-the-confessions:
Edited by Arthur Train in 1921, The Goldfish presents the confessions of a successful man, a fifty-year-old looking back on house, affairs, ache, and religion. Chapters on myself, friends, children, mind, morals, and future frame a life of wealth and worry. Hastings's image gives the title: rich people like goldfish swimming round a bowl, seeing dimly out but unable to escape.

A William James passage quoted inside attacks the fear of poverty as the worst moral disease of educated life, praising the unbribed soul and manlier indifference. The narrator's Paris and New York scenes show wealth's pleasures and emptiness. The book offers a candid, period portrait of American success.
13015-tales-of-old-japan:
Lord Redesdale, formerly second secretary to the British legation in Japan, wrote Tales of Old Japan, first published in 1871 and long a standard source on Japanese folklore. Contents include the Forty-Seven Ronins, the loves of Gompachi and Komurasaki, Kazuma's revenge, the eta maiden and the hatamoto, and fairy tales like the Tongue-Cut Sparrow. Japanese artists drew and cut the illustrations.

A sea adventure shows Funakoshi Jiuyemon diving from a pirate ship, swimming to a lantern-lit vessel of the Osaka governor, and begging rescue as a man fallen among pirates. Redesdale writes with a diplomat's fondness for Japan. The book remains a classic doorway into old Japan.
13123-the-great-prince-shan:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's 1922 novel The Great Prince Shan opens in a London club for diplomats and gentlemen, where Prince Karschoff cannot find a fourth for bridge. Sir Daniel Harker, a retired plenipotentiary, declares diplomacy itself is passing, since every taxpayer now counts as a gentleman. Young Nigel Kingley, asked to ransack the club, becomes the tale's center.

Nigel suspects his uncle was murdered while decoding a report, after agents sent east were stabbed in Petrograd and poisoned in Berlin. A later scene follows a woman through a dim reception room hung with apple-green silk, past an ebony cabinet. Oppenheim mixes club talk, spies, and romance in a smooth thriller of post-war intrigue.
13204-sermons-to-the-natural-man:
William G. T. Shedd's 1871 Sermons to the Natural Man, published by Charles Scribner in New York, aims to anatomize the natural heart before offering the gospel. Shedd, author of a history of Christian doctrine, writes with solemn care, saying his words may prove life or death to hearers. His purpose is psychological: to show what man is by nature, before grace.

Sermons define sin as any want of conformity to God's law, so that falling short counts as fully as stepping over the line. Shedd quotes Tertullian and Calvin on the soul's witness to one God, heard in common phrases such as God sees and God grant. The sermons are stern, learned, and systematic, a window on nineteenth-century American Calvinist preaching.
13285-occasional-thoughts-in-reference-t:
Printed in London in 1705 for A. and J. Churchill at the Black Swan, Occasional Thoughts on a virtuous or Christian life lay unread for over two years before friends urged print. The author says the papers were written in leisure hours, with no set plan to publish, and that they claim nothing but obvious truths, often overlooked. The preface is modest, and the prose is plain for its age.

The discourse argues that pagans never fully knew nature's law, and that Christianity beat out gross immorality once honored by heathen gods. It also warns against one-sided faith, where zeal for doctrine crowds out good works, and against zeal for works that forgets justifying faith. The book is a quiet work of early eighteenth-century moral theology.
13300-the-doctrine-and-practice-of-yoga-:
Swami Mukerji, yogi of the South India Order, published The Doctrine and Practice of Yoga in 1922, covering concentration, mentation, Maya, guru worship, and will-force. His announcement warns that no sentence is useless, every word is condensed, and readers must think deeply. Speedy or miraculous results, he says, must not be expected.

Mukerji teaches that centers within great consciousness carry growth, and that since the seventeenth century, by the law of averages, mankind reached self-consciousness and must now direct its own progress. Full realization, he says, ends in bestowing freedom on others and feeling for all humanity, even animals. The book is a practical, earnest manual of early Western yoga teaching.
13377-a-tour-through-some-parts-of-franc:
Richard Boyle Bernard's 1815 Tour Through Some Parts of France, Switzerland, Savoy, Germany, and Belgium, during the summer and autumn of 1814, records a post-Napoleonic journey, dedicated to the Prince Regent. Bernard, a member of Parliament, thanks the prince for leave to inscribe pages that celebrate restored peace. The tour is a gentleman's travelogue of the Continent just after war.

In Paris, he copies a prospectus for Delacroix's gymnastic establishment for correcting defects of nature, with a mast for developing hips and chest and columns for setting the body straight. Later, in Switzerland, he notes lakes frozen fourteen degrees below freezing, the Bise wind ruffling summer waters, and a climate colder than surrounding countries. The book is a vivid record of Europe in 1814.
134-maria-or-the-wrongs-of-woman:
Mary Wollstonecraft died before finishing her novel of a woman locked away by her husband. Maria, or the Wrongs of Woman, published in 1798, follows Maria Venables from a madhouse to a friendship with her guard's wife. Her story exposes marriage law as a trap.

Maria tells her life in chapters written from prison, recalling seduction, betrayal, and a stolen child. An appendix and conclusion complete the fragment as far as it goes. Wollstonecraft's preface defends printing unfinished genius. The novel stands as an early feminist classic. Feminist scholars revived the novel in the twentieth century as a founding text.
13423-zarlah-the-martian:
R. Norman Grisewood's 1909 romance Zarlah the Martian sends its narrator from a London laboratory to Mars and back. A strange shadow, a voice from another world, and the story of Martian life open the tale. With a hazardous undertaking, a melody of flowers, and a hundred miles a minute in an aerenoid to follow.

Almos explains his virator, chloroform cone, and regenerating rays in super-radium, by which a spirit passes to an upper chamber. Zarlah confesses, warns of danger, and races with death, until the narrator is hurled from the Moon and wakes to traffic roar, unsure if the night was dream or journey. Early science fiction mixes wonder, love, and laboratory talk.
1344-the-secrets-of-the-princesse-de-cad:
After the July Revolution of 1830 wrecks many court fortunes, the Princesse de Cadignan keeps her place in Paris by wit and nerve. Balzac's short novel studies this famed beauty, whose past lovers and past scandals are the talk of every salon, and whose present life depends on managing what others believe about her.

Into her circle comes a serious writer, and the princess sets out to win his trust with a frank-seeming confession of her life. Readers must judge how much is truth and how much is art. The tale is a cool study of reputation, charm, and survival in high society.
13450-the-motor-maids-in-fair-japan:
Katherine Stokes sends her Motor Maids to Japan in this 1913 girls' adventure, a sequel to school days, palm and pine, and travel across the continent. Billie, Elinor, Nancy, and their friends sail off for Japan, then settle into gardens, shopping trips in jinrikshas, cherry blossom outings, and theatre parties.

A bad quarter of an hour, a compassionate god called Jizu, and a letter that came though never sent stir the plot. A storm king, a birthday party, and a visit of ceremony fill the time between. Generosity, quarrels, and a missing friend in the rain keep the girls busy. The book offers young readers Japan as a place of gardens, kindness, and lively mishap.
13576-the-poor-gentleman:
Hendrik Conscience's Poor Gentleman, translated expressly for its American edition, belongs to a series delineating grades of female character in trial. In The Village Innkeeper, Conscience showed a woman torn between propriety and ambition for high life, while in The Conscript his heroine shows nobler, uncorrupted virtue. The Poor Gentleman continues that study.

De Vlierbeck talks easily on all subjects for his guests, listening with good manners to Denecker on commercial matters, while. A young woman wonders in silence if her family are beggars and if that secret explains her father's depression. Her face brightens with resolution as she fights misfortune bravely, until wheels are heard outside. Conscience writes Flemish domestic life with moral warmth.
1373-study-of-a-woman:
Honoré de Balzac tells a short, sharp tale of Mme de Listomère, a virtuous provincial lady. She receives a love letter meant for another woman and, flattered and curious, answers it, only to find herself caught in a game of manners. The story turns on a single letter and its consequences.

Balzac writes the comedy of reputation with wit and precision, and the tale's irony is complete. The study is brief and brilliant. It suits readers who like Balzac in miniature, with society's rules as the plot. Balzac's brief study shows society's rules doing the work of plot.
1377-the-talisman:
Walter Scott sets this Crusader tale in the Holy Land, where Richard the Lionheart lies ill and the Scots knight Kenneth, in disguise, serves as his guard. The tale follows Kenneth's love for the Lady Edith, Saladin's chivalry, and the plots of the Crusader princes.

Scott writes the Crusades as romance, with tournaments, disguises, and a famous meeting between king and sultan. The novel, part of his Tales of the Crusaders, shows his gift for historical color. It suits readers who like Scott's chivalry at its most stirring. Scott's Crusader romance still stirs with tournaments and chivalry.
13842-the-story-of-manhattan:
Charles Hemstreet wrote this 1901 history of Manhattan for general readers. Chapters run from Henry Hudson's voyages to the English takeover and beyond. Peter Minuit, Walter Van Twiller, William Kieft, and Peter Stuyvesant each get a chapter. Illustrations help younger readers picture old New York.

Hemstreet tells how traders, governors, and Native peoples shaped the island. Hudson's river, first called by his name, anchors the opening. Wars, trade, and town growth follow in clear order. The prose stays simple and story-like throughout. The book works well as a first history of New York City.
1385-lin-mclean:
Owen Wister gathers stories of Lin McLean, a Wyoming cowboy of good heart and poor luck, who drifts through roundups, love affairs, and scrapes with the law. The tales follow Lin from a young rider to a man worn by the range, with humor and pathos.

Wister writes the cowboy West with affection and a novelist's eye, and Lin stands beside the Virginian as a classic figure. The stories are episodic and warm. The book suits readers who like Wister's West in short, vivid pieces. Wister's Lin stands beside the Virginian as a classic cowboy figure.
13865-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-41:
William and Robert Chambers edited this Edinburgh journal, and number 418 appeared on January 3, 1852. It opens with A Child's Toy, a gentle sketch of evening, hills, and a hidden city. Later pieces discuss kites, their colours, and an old Indian woman's memories of kite shops. Short tales and instructive notes fill the rest.

Chambers aimed at cheap, improving reading for a wide public. Each number mixed story, fact, and moral reflection at a low price. The journal's success helped build the Chambers publishing house. This issue shows Victorian popular journalism at its most domestic. It offers a quiet window on Edinburgh life in winter.
13870-a-summary-history-of-the-palazzo-d:
This short 1896 history traces the Palazzo Dandolo, now the Royal Hotel Danieli in Venice. In 1805, Dal Niel, surnamed Danieli, bought the second floor from the Michiel and Bernardo families. He turned it into a hotel bearing his own name. The palace, built in 1400 by the great Dandolo family, fronts the Riva degli Schiavoni.

The sketch follows the palace through inheritance and marriage into hotel use. It notes the building's place in Venetian glory and its magnificent exterior. Two palaces now form the hotel, pictured in the volume. The history suits travellers to Venice and lovers of old hotels. It packs centuries of ownership into a brief, elegant pamphlet.
14257-the-magician:
W. Somerset Maugham's 1908 novel The Magician centers on Oliver Haddo, a figure of occult power who dazzles and frightens a circle of artists and doctors. Arthur Burdon, Margaret, and Susie Boyd move through London studios and Paris rooms, while Haddo sends vast masses of chrysanthemums to Margaret's door, changing her austere studio with ephemeral brightness. Politeness frays as fascination grows.

A fragment of autobiography opens the volume. Maugham recalls qualifying in medicine in 1897 after five years at St Thomas's, publishing Liza of Lambeth as a student, and spending a year in Seville writing a bad novel. The magician's story then tests reason against appetite: a surgeon hero, a woman torn between lovers, and a villain who enjoys every scene. Dark, theatrical, and skeptical, the novel made Maugham's reputation for sinister romance.
14362-the-way-of-a-man:
Emerson Hough's 1907 novel follows Gordon Orme, a young easterner who heads west and learns the codes of ranch, trail, and frontier town. Grace Sheraton, the woman he loves, tests his honor at nearly every turn.

Cattle drives, river wrecks, horse races, and gunplay carry the plot across the plains, while Orme's rivals press him toward violence or retreat. Hough, a seasoned writer of western tales, keeps the action brisk and the scenery wide. A later photoplay version spread the story further. The novel celebrates courage, loyalty, and restraint as the marks of manhood on a closing frontier.
14367-when-a-man-s-a-man:
Harold Bell Wright's 1916 novel is set on Arizona ranches, where an eastern tenderfoot known as Phil Acton must prove himself among cowboys, foremen, and ranch owners. He takes hard work, long rides, and rough company in stride.

Kitty, a spirited ranch girl, watches his progress and challenges his pride, while rivals test his temper and courage. Wright drew on summers spent in the Williamson Valley, and the desert, corrals, and roundups feel closely observed. The story preaches honest labor and self-control, and it became one of the best-selling western novels of its era.
14472-showell-s-dictionary-of-birmingham:
Showell's Dictionary of Birmingham, arranged alphabetically, gathers thousands of dates and notes on the town's past and present. Its entries cover churches, chapels, clubs, schools, parks, theaters, trades, and manufactures, plus local worthies.

Readers can look up a street, a society, a factory, or a public building and find its history, population figures, and rates of progress. The volume also notes charitable gifts, such as collections for Trafalgar wounded in 1805. As a civic reference work it remains a treasure for local historians tracing Victorian Birmingham's growth. Genealogists still use its entries to place families and firms.
14502-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-41:
This January 10, 1852, number of Chambers' Edinburgh Journal, edited by William and Robert Chambers, offers the weekly miscellany at a penny halfpenny. The opening piece dreams of lost ages in the manner of Charles Lamb.

Other items include Catherine Crowe's story of Gaspar Mendez, an essay on railway influence, a chapter on cats, beggars in the Far East, a prison report, and notes on mangel-wurzel farming. The journal's improving, family tone runs throughout. The issue is a neat sample of cheap Victorian periodical reading, mixing fiction, fact, and moral reflection.
14603-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-42:
Chambers' Edinburgh Journal for January 17, 1852, edited by William and Robert Chambers, opens with an essay asking how the world uses us, and what we have done to deserve better use. The penny-halfpenny weekly mixed moral reflection with fact.

Other items include Sisters of Charity in Bohemia and adventures of an army physician who tore his shirt for bandages. A mysterious lady, a story of Rembrandt, and market reports on cash, corn, and coal follow. The issue shows the Chambers formula at work: improving, varied, and meant for family reading across Britain.
14612-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-42:
Chambers' Edinburgh Journal for January 24, 1852, edited by William and Robert Chambers, opens with The Wolf-Gathering, a Polish exile's tale of the failed revolution of 1831. The narrator sits round a fire with friends.

Other items cover false political economy and plans for paying the national debt. Sir Francis Head's Faggot of French Sticks, ivory and its uses, blighted flowers, notes from Australia, and a ground lizard of Jamaica follow. The journal's mix of story, science, and economy shows its improving mission. The issue is a typical mid-century number, varied and readable.
14613-the-foundations-of-japan:
This study of rural Japan, by J. W. Robertson Scott, who had written widely on farming and the Far East, examines the countryside behind the nation's modern rise. Illustrations show an agricultural school, jujitsu, and rifles side by side.

The writer travels by train through farming districts, notes rising prices pressing farmers, and weighs superstition, faith, and the invasion of rural life by factories run on commercial lines. The book argues that Japan's strength rests on its villages. It offers a thoughtful, if dated, portrait of Japanese country life before the Second World War.
1470-the-fall-of-the-moghul-empire-of-hi:
H. G. Keene writes a short history of the fall of the Moghul Empire in Hindustan, from its height under the great emperors to its collapse before British power. Keene, a colonial historian, keeps the narrative compact. Keene, a British civil servant in India, wrote short histories for English readers.

The book follows weak successors, Maratha and Sikh rivals, and the East India Company's rise, ending with Delhi under British rule. It serves as a clear introduction, though modern readers will weigh its imperial viewpoint. The Moghul fall, from Aurangzeb to Bahadur Shah, took a century of slow decline.
15099-the-hoosier-schoolmaster-a-story-o:
Edward Eggleston's 1871 novel of backwoods Indiana follows a young schoolmaster in a rough district school. Revised for a library edition with notes on the district and character sketches, the book draws on Eggleston's own early studies of American dialect. A dedication honors James Russell Lowell, who cheered that work.

Schoolhouse rows, spelling bees, and local rogues mix with a tender love story and a portrait of pioneer manners. Eggleston writes in dialect with warmth and humor, never mere mockery. The novel became a classic of American local color, and it still reads as a lively picture of frontier school life.
15186-folk-lore-and-legends-scandinavian:
Collected by C. J. Tibbitts and printed in London in 1890, this volume gathers Scandinavian folk lore and legends from Thiele, Asbjörnsen and Moe, Hylten-Cavallius, and Stephens. Tales include a wonderful plough from Rügen, a lad who stole a giant's treasure, tales of cats from Denmark, and a magician's daughter from Sweden.

A hill-man invited to a christening and other northern wonders fill the book, with only one or two tales from the Prose Edda for want of space. The editor aimed at a fair general view of northern folk life. Readers who love folk tales will find the collection charming, strange, and rich in old northern magic.
15189-when-buffalo-ran:
George Bird Grinnell's 1920 memoir recalls Plains Indian life seventy years earlier, when buffalo still ran and the prairie stretched to the sky. Chapters tell of an attack on camp, standing alone, lessons of the prairie, life on a buffalo horse, and time among enemy lodges. A marriage and a warrior's sacrifice close the arc.

Grinnell, who knew the Plains peoples well, writes from stories told by Native men and women, with respect for their customs. His prose is plain and vivid, full of lodges, hunts, and councils. The book offers a valuable, if outsider-told, record of a world that was already passing when he wrote.
15228-lady-good-for-nothing-a-man-s-port:
Arthur Quiller-Couch's 1910 novel, subtitled a man's portrait of a woman, reworks the tale of Sir Harry Frankland and Agnes Surriage, a poor Marblehead fisherman's daughter. Quiller-Couch notes that Holmes had versified the theme, but facts cramped his own story, so he changed place and people while keeping the loves and adventures.

The novel follows a colonial collector and a low-born girl through passion, rank, and reputation, in Q's polished, literary prose. First printed in the Times weekly edition, it now stands as a book. Readers who like historical romance with a wry, male narrator will find Lady Good-for-Nothing stylish and engaging.
15234-the-tale-of-the-pie-and-the-patty-:
Beatrix Potter's 1905 tale tells of Ribby the cat, who invites Duchess the dog to tea, with an old rhyme about pussy by the fire heading the book. Ribby urges her guest to come in good time, and the pair's manners, food, and small mishaps drive the comedy. Potter's pictures, absent here, add much charm.

A pie and a patty-pan sit at the heart of the plot, with a surprise about what each guest has really brought. Potter writes in neat, funny prose for small children. The tale pairs well with her other animal stories, and it rewards reading aloud with its crisp dialogue and gentle jokes.
15379-robert-moffat-the-missionary-hero-:
David J. Deane wrote this life of Robert Moffat, the South African missionary known as the hero of Kuruman, in a popular fifth edition. The preface promises a record of noble deeds and patient work: danger from lions on the plain, talks with chiefs whose warriors had slain thousands, and years of sickness, hunger, and thirst. Moffat's aim, as Deane tells it, was to win African peoples to the Gospel.

Chapters follow Moffat from childhood and youth to his sailing for the Cape, his marriage, and his arrival at Lattakoo. Later parts cover a Mantatee invasion, a visit to England, and his great labor, the translation of the Bible into Sechwana. The closing scenes round out a life of long service. The book is a Victorian hero tale, earnest and admiring, written to inspire young readers.
15406-the-little-red-chimney-being-the-l:
Mary Finley Leonard published this love story in New York in 1914, with silhouette pictures by Katharine Gassaway. The curtain rises on a candy wagon, where fate throws the leading characters together in a tidy, comic manner. A candy man, a girl named Virginia, and a little red chimney soon anchor the plot, though the chimney's meaning stays a mystery at first.

Later chapters play with mistaken identity: the candy man in citizen's clothes passes for a man of wealth and standing, and glimpses of high life depress him. A double life is explained, an alibi is proved, and talk by the fire sorts out Margaret Elizabeth's troubles. The novel is light romance with a fairy-tale touch, built on disguise, kind hearts, and a small landmark that means more than it seems.
15438-the-bells-of-san-juan:
Jackson Gregory published this western novel in New York in 1919, illustrated by Frank Tenney Johnson. A foreword called The Bells sets the scene, and chapters follow the sheriff of San Juan, a banker's home, a ride through the night, and a fight at La Casa Blanca. The frontispiece shows a horseman reining in, staring in surprise at a woman.

Jim Galloway's game, a bribe and a threat, a stack of gold pieces, and the strong hand of Galloway drive the plot toward a crisis and an open ending. Cliff-dwellers, a Mexican from Mexico, and a town full of watchers add color to the desert border country. Gregory writes a fast, clean western of law, gold, and loyalty, in the popular style that made his ranch novels sell widely.
15578-the-miracle-man:
Frank L. Packard published this novel in New York in 1914, with Grosset and Dunlap, dedicated to nearly everybody. Twenty-four chapters run from the Roost, a new cult, and Needley, through the patriarch, a strange conversation, and official endorsement, to a pilgrimage, a miracle, and its aftermath. Real money, a fly in the ointment, and a way out close the scheme.

The book opens in a dark Bowery alley, where a misshapen figure bulks as a black blotch in the night. The Flopper moves out onto the pavement, flopping knee to toe on one leg and dragging the other, limp and wobbling. Packard's tale is a con story with a religious mask: fake miracles, pilgrims, and cash, told with pace and a sharp eye for human greed. The miracle, overdone, at last turns on its makers.
15625-the-lookout-man:
B. M. Bower, author of Good Indian and The Gringos, saw this western printed in Boston in August 1917, from Little, Brown, with a frontispiece by H. Weston Taylor. A front picture shows a woman who was, after all, the goddess she looked, in the hero's whimsical thought. Twenty chapters or more run from some time and thanks for the car to the Feather River country and freedom.

Jack finds a job, sings of Tipperary, and meets Miss Rose Forward, guardian of the forests. A girl plays billiards on a mountain top, forests blaze, and Kate finds something to worry over. Jack should have a hide-out, Murphy turns humorous, and Mike spies on the spies. Hank Brown proves he can read tracks, and trouble rocks the pan looking for grains of gold. Bower writes a forest-ranger western of fire, spies, and romance in the Sierra country.
15662-an-historical-journal-of-the-trans:
John Hunter, post captain in His Majesty's Navy, compiled this historical journal of Port Jackson and Norfolk Island, published in London in 1793, printed for John Stockdale. Seventeen maps, charts, views, and embellishments, drawn on the spot by Hunter, Bradley, Dawes, and Governor King, illustrate the volume. It covers the voyages from the first sailing of the Sirius in 1787 to the return of that ship's company to England in 1792.

Chapter one follows ships bound for Botany Bay from the Mother Bank, through a convict insurrection attempt, Santa Cruz, and Rio de Janeiro. Later chapters anchor in Table Bay, leave the Cape of Good Hope, and record Governor Phillip's and King's journals and Lieutenant Ball's. The book is a first-hand record of Australia's founding years: convicts, sailors, and officials building a colony from official papers.
15743-bunker-bean:
A comic novel by Harry Leon Wilson, issued by Doubleday, Page and Company in Garden City in 1913. F. R. Gruger supplied the pictures, and Wilson dedicates the book to H. G. Wells. Bunker Bean, a shy clerk, is told by a fortune teller that he carries the soul of Napoleon. The news changes a timid life at once.

Bean straightens up, speaks out, and dares to love, borrowing courage from his supposed past. His new boldness brings laughter, trouble, and a real chance at happiness. Wilson keeps the comedy kind, siding with the small man against a hard world. The novel endures as a fable of confidence: belief, even a false one, can free a life.
15843-slippy-mcgee-sometimes-known-as-th:
A 1917 novel by Marie Conway Oemler, issued by the Century Company in New York and often reprinted. Slippy McGee, a crook on the run, finds shelter in the village of Appleboro. There a minister's kindness and the study of butterflies slowly change him. Oemler writes with warmth for small-town folk and second chances.

Neighbours, underwings, and the coming of Kerry fill the early chapters, as Slippy learns the names and habits of moths. A biblical challenge to fight the Philistine tests his new courage. The going of Slippy McGee closes the arc. The novel endures as a tale of reform: a man known for theft becomes known for beauty.
15906-a-good-samaritan:
A short tale by Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews, illustrated by Charlotte Harding, issued by McClure, Phillips and Company in New York in 1906, second impression. Pictures show a boy chuckling over Webster's Union charging two cents for soon, and a friend called Recky, the best friend he ever had. Andrews writes of kindness in plain, warm prose.

Billy, a boy with a quick tongue, meets a neighbour in need and learns what a good Samaritan does. Thank-yous, laughter, and small heroics fill the short tale. Andrews keeps the moral light and the feeling true. The story charms as a Sunday-school classic: a child who helps, and a friend who remembers.
15915-new-version-of-les-contes-d-hoffma:
A libretto for Offenbach's opera The Tales of Hoffmann, in a new version by Charles Alfred Byrne. Jules Barbier wrote the book, with music by Jacques Offenbach. The edition adds an original and novel first act and other important changes. It was performed for the first time in America at a Manhattan house. Both English and French texts appear in the file.

Hoffmann, a poet, tells of three lost loves: a doll, a singer, and a courtesan, each undone by a villain in turn. The prologue and epilogue frame the tales with wine, song, and regret. A transcriber's note warns that both texts carry many errors, left uncorrected. The libretto still serves opera lovers: a beloved fantasy, in words that sing.
15986-th-barrel-organ:
Edwin Waugh tells this Lancashire tale in the local dialect, with spellings that sound out how his people spoke. The plot turns on a simple mix-up. Carrier Robin brings a new barrel organ up from town in his cart on a Friday night. He also hauls a washing machine for Isaac Buckley at Hollins Farm. Warned to keep the organ upright and unshaken, Robin muddles the two loads.

The washing machine ends up at the church and the organ at the farm, and the comedy grows from that wrong delivery and the folk who try to set it right. Waugh's humor rests on character and speech, not on grand events. Readers get a warm, funny glimpse of village life, work, and talk in nineteenth-century Lancashire.
16-peter-pan:
All children grow up, except one boy who refuses to. J. M. Barrie's Peter Pan, the 1911 novel form of Peter and Wendy, follows Wendy Darling to Neverland. Peter breaks through her nursery window in search of his shadow.

Wendy, John, and Michael fly to an island of Lost Boys, mermaids, and pirates. Captain Hook hunts Peter while Tinker Bell guards him with fierce loyalty. The book ends with Wendy grown and Peter returning for her daughter. Its mix of play and loss made Neverland endure. Stage plays, films, and sequels have kept Peter's refusal to grow up in popular culture ever since.
16096-a-man-s-woman:
Frank Norris finished this novel in March 1899, and it reached print in 1904 under a title already claimed by a play, which Norris notes with regret. The story opens at four in the morning in a polar camp, where men lie spent after a terrible march over hummocky ice and pressure ridges. Men and dogs have hauled and tugged at heavy sledges since six the day before.

The novel follows an Arctic party led by a man named Bennett, testing nerve, leadership, and love against cold, hunger, and exhaustion. Norris writes the ice country in hard, physical detail, and the human strain matters as much as the miles. Readers of adventure fiction will find a stern, gripping tale of exploration at the edge of endurance.
16101-diane-of-the-green-van:
Leona Dalrymple's Diane of the Green Van, published in Chicago in 1914 with pictures by Reginald Birch, won a ten-thousand-dollar prize in a contest that drew over five hundred manuscripts. Its opening verse invites readers to linger in Arcadie, the land of heart's desire, where lovers play a sparkling comedy with fire while fate waits with her wand. Chapters promise a great white bird on a lake, an indoor tempest, a whim, and the voice of the open country.

Diane's green van, a traveling home, gives the romance its gypsy color and its freedom. Love, pride, and adventure follow a heroine who chooses the open road over convention. Readers of popular romance will enjoy its bright, prize-winning charm.
16143-a-man-and-a-woman:
Stanley Waterloo's novel opens at a party at the Laffins', where music, flowers, and clever talk fill the rooms. The narrator drifts through the crowd until he meets Miss Cornish, the woman his friend Harlson loves so hard. He admits he does not know how to describe a woman, and this one, whom he has known better than any other, is hardest of all to picture.

From that meeting grows a story of love, friendship, and pride, summed in its opening verse: a strong man battles so the woman he loves shall be proud of him. Waterloo writes in a plain, reflective voice about men and women testing each other. Readers of turn-of-the-century romance will find a quiet, thoughtful tale of devotion.
16228-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-42:
Number four hundred twenty-two of Chambers's Edinburgh Journal, new series, dated Saturday, January 31, 1852, leads with The Happy Jacks. Its narrator accepts a humble dinner invitation and rides a Kentish-town omnibus on a pleasant summer Saturday to visit Happy Jack, a man who called himself happy and believed it intensely. Friends shook their heads and added poor devil to his name, yet Jack, borrowing a half-sovereign while two children had measles, stayed in the highest spirits.

The journal, edited by William and Robert Chambers at a penny halfpenny, mixed stories, facts, and moral essays for a mass readership. This number shows its homely, humane style at its best. Readers of Victorian popular print will enjoy a warm, funny character sketch.
16257-the-turtles-of-tasman:
Jack London's Turtles of Tasman, published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1916 by arrangement with Macmillan, gathers seven stories and a coda. The title tale opens on Frederick Travers, whose face law, order, and restraint had carved into strong, firm lines, with healthy skin and honest lines from hard, devoted work. The Eternity of Forms, Told in the Drooling Ward, The Hobo and the Fairy, The Prodigal Father, and The First Poet follow.

London writes with his usual force about power, pity, and the human lot, from sick wards to fairy encounters. The collection shows his range beyond the Klondike and the sea. Readers who like London's short fiction will find a strong, varied volume.
16291-the-story-of-the-other-wise-man:
Henry Van Dyke's Story of the Other Wise Man, copyright 1895 and 1899 by Harper, imagines a fourth wise man who misses the goal yet finds it by another road. Its epigraph warns that one who seeks heaven only to save his soul may keep the path and miss the goal. One who walks in love may wander far yet be brought where the blessed are. The hero is Artaban, a Median of Ecbatana in the days of Augustus and Herod.

Artaban's house stands by the outermost of seven walls around the royal treasury, and his garden spreads with flowers and fruit beneath battlements of many colors. His search for a pearl of great price and a sign in the sky becomes a life of giving. Readers will find a beloved Christmas tale of love outlasting plans.
16298-historic-tales-the-romance-of-real:
Charles Morris built this first volume of his fifteen-volume set on one claim: real history often beats made-up romance for sheer color. The American tales run from Vineland and the Vikings through Frobisher, Champlain, and the Iroquois, then on to Franklin in Philadelphia, Daniel Boone, Paul Revere's ride, and the Green Mountain Boys.

Each piece is short and self-contained, meant to be read on its own. Sieges, escapes, traitors, and frontier fights fill the pages, with the Revolution taking up much of the second half. The book suits readers who want vivid scenes from early America without a long, dense history.
16453-the-measure-of-a-man:
Amelia E. Barr's 1915 novel opens on the great sea waters and follows a family through love, loss, and hard choice. Brothers John and Harry stand at the center, with Jane and the Harlow household close by. Chapter titles trace the path: love ventures in, shock and sorrow, profit and loss, and at last the love that never fails.

Barr writes in the full, earnest style of popular fiction of her day, with country scenes and domestic crises. The tale weighs what a man is worth by his deeds, not his wealth. Readers of old-fashioned family sagas will find it a satisfying, emotional read with a firm moral close.
16577-the-business-of-being-a-woman:
Ida M. Tarbell, famed for her Standard Oil history, turns to women's lives in this 1921 book. Chapters take up the uneasy woman, the imitation of man, and the socialization of the home. Woman and her raiment, woman and democracy, the homeless daughter, and the childless woman and the friendless child follow. A closing chapter ennobles the woman's business.

Tarbell writes with her usual clarity and moral seriousness, arguing that home-making is real work worthy of respect. The book speaks to women caught between old roles and new freedoms after suffrage. Readers of feminist history will find it a thoughtful, conservative voice in a fast-changing debate.
16587-historic-tales-the-romance-of-real:
Charles Morris turns to Germany in this fifth volume of his fifteen-volume Historical Tales. Hermann the hero of Germany opens the set, followed by Wittekind the Saxon patriot, sea-rovers, Bishop Hatto, Henry IV, Frederick Barbarossa at Milan, and the fall of the Ghibellines. William Tell, the Black Death, Morgarten, and Ziska the blind warrior follow.

Each tale is short and vivid, meant to show history's romance in single scenes. The volume runs from early German heroes to medieval war and plague. Readers who enjoyed the American volume will find the same lively, story-first history here, now on German ground.
16716-the-going-of-the-white-swan:
Gilbert Parker wrote this short 1912 tale of a father and his hurt son in a far northern camp. The boy waits for his mother, who has gone away, while the father tends him in silence and dread. A priest, a wildcat scare, and the cold wild land frame their wait.

Parker keeps the tale tight and stark, with few words and much left unsaid between father and son. Grief, guilt, and hope pull against each other as the boy asks plain questions the man cannot answer. The story is short enough to read in one sitting, yet it leaves a strong sense of loss and love in a harsh place.
16821-the-scarlet-gown-being-verses-by-a:
A St. Andrews man wrote this 1891 book of verses called The Scarlet Gown, issued at St. Andrews and in London by Simpkin, Marshall. An epigraph from Andrew Lang calls St. Andrews a haunted town, with its little town, drifting surf, wintry year, and college of the scarlet gown by the northern sea. Poems run from a voice that sings across the night to a best pipe and a cutty clay.

The verses mix student life, pipes, monks, and memory, in light, musical lines. They praise a small university town and its past with affection and wit. Readers who love university verse will find a charming, local book, best read for its St. Andrews scenes and its gentle, backward look.
17136-selected-official-documents-of-the:
Hugh Williams and Frederick Charles Hicks, both of the Library of Congress, gathered this set of papers on the causes of the war in South Africa. It opens with the London Convention of 1884 and the republic's 1889 constitution, then moves through franchise laws, joint inquiry plans, and the ultimatum of October 1899. The Orange Free State alliance papers close the run.

The editors chose papers a general reader could not else reach without a great library, and set them in date order with short heads. The result is a clean source book, not a polemic: both sides speak in their own words. Students of the Boer War will find it a useful first file of the dispute.
17137-some-mooted-questions-in-reinforce:
Edward Godfrey's paper for the American Society of Civil Engineers, number 1169, questions the rules of reinforced concrete design. He likens current rules to old bloodletting rules: once held as logic, now abandoned. If his case fails, he says, debate will at least give good reasons for the rules, which the literature then lacked. Discussion by seventeen engineers follows, from Wright and Russell to Thompson and Godfrey himself.

The paper suits engineers and historians of building, with plain argument over a new material's codes. Its tone is blunt and reforming, fond of logic over habit. Readers keen on how engineering rules are tested will find a sharp, period debate on concrete, steel, and safety.
1714-another-study-of-woman:
At any Paris ball, Balzac observes, two parties are always going on at once: the official dance, and the private talk in corners where reputations are made and unmade. The frame lets Balzac's narrator listen to de Marsay act out a woman's airs and graces, to the offense of the women watching. Then turn to other sketches of Parisian wives, widows, and girls.

The studies are less a single plot than a set of portraits, each asking how women live inside marriages, reputations, and money. Balzac's eye for dress, speech, and social rank is sharp throughout. The volume reads as a companion to La Grande Bretèche, which follows it in the same translation.
17147-theodicy-essays-on-the-goodness-of:
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz asks in this classic work how a good God and human freedom can stand beside evil in the world. Austin Farrer edited the volume, and E. M. Huggard translated it from Gerhardt's edition of Leibniz's collected works. The essays test pain, sin, and choice against reason, faith, and the idea of the best of all possible worlds.

Leibniz, a top mathematician and a keen mind in physics and moral thought, builds a system, not a set of stray remarks. The prose is dense and needs slow reading, but its core questions still drive debate today. Students of philosophy and faith will find here the fullest early modern defense of God's goodness in a world full of hurt.
17272-a-people-s-man:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's People's Man opens with a cry across Soho: Maraton has come. Aaron Thurnbrein pedals an ancient bicycle through narrow streets, past gibbering crowds and haltered horses, bearing great tidings eastward to the Commercial Road. His dusty cheeks, ragged clothes, and blazing eyes mark him as one of the submerged, still fighting with hands that beat the air.

From that messenger's ride grows a political novel of London's poor, power, and a people's champion. Oppenheim writes in rich, melodramatic prose, with Soho's streets and shops in sharp color. Readers who like Edwardian political romance will find a long, stirring tale of a leader raised from the streets.
1729-the-deserted-woman:
In the spring of 1822, doctors sent a young man to Lower Normandy to recover his health. There he met a woman living apart from the world in a quiet house. She is the Vicomtesse de Beauséant, once a leader of Paris society, now in retreat after a love affair that ended her standing.

The story follows their growing closeness and the question of whether she can return to life or must stay in exile. Balzac writes the provincial setting with care — candlelight, country doctors, and long evenings. And the tale's sadness comes from a woman who knows exactly what society took from her and refuses to beg for it back.
17292-the-new-frontiers-of-freedom-from-:
E. Alexander Powell published this travel account in New York in 1920, after a motor trip through southeast Europe in the summer and autumn of 1919. With officials and army officers as hosts and guides, he covered nearly three thousand miles from Italy through Dalmatia, Montenegro, Albania, Macedonia, Turkey, Rumania, Hungary, and Serbia. The book records lands redrawn just after the First World War.

Chapters cross redeemed border lands, a Slav and Latin border zone, and a region Powell calls a cemetery of four empires. They weigh the peace makers' work on the Danube and the making of new states. Readers get a reporter's view of new borders, old faiths, and peoples caught between empires, written while the settlements were still fresh.
17356-nobody-s-man:
E. Phillips Oppenheim published this novel in 1921. It opens in a Devonshire hamlet among the hills, where Andrew Tallente steps off a small train onto a flower-decked platform. He is met by a tall, ungainly figure with an unpleasant smile, a meeting that is plainly no accident. The man, Miller, greets him with a challenge, noting that Tallente is not the only great statesman who needs to step off the treadmill now and then.

From that meeting the story builds a tale of politics, intrigue, and personal danger, in Oppenheim's smooth, popular style. Readers get a post-war thriller of statesmen and shadows, set between country quiet and high affairs. Oppenheim's many readers will recognise his blend of romance, mystery, and the corridors of power.
17359-arms-and-the-woman:
Harold MacGrath's 1899 romance opens with a young reporter of twenty-two meeting a girl in short dresses in a walled garden of roses, poppies, and lilacs. Her October-brown hair, forest-pool eyes, and rose lips, with a pitcher of lemonade close at hand, leave the narrator tongue-tied. The book is dedicated to the hand that rocked the cradle.

From that garden meeting grows a romance of youth, arms, and love, told in MacGrath's lush, popular style. The heroine's calm gaze and the hero's diffidence set the tone for a tale of courtship and adventure. Fans of old romantic fiction will enjoy a warm, flowery novel from the age of magazine romance.
1738-statesman:
What does a ruler actually know that a general, a judge, or a merchant does not. That question drives this dialogue, in which the Eleatic Stranger takes up the inquiry with Socrates' friends. Socrates' friends take up the question with the Eleatic Stranger. He compares the king to a weaver, separating the threads of a city as a weaver separates wool and keeping the useful arts apart from rule itself.

The dialogue is a companion to the Sophist, and it is more a study of method than a manual for kings. Readers will find Plato sorting kinds of knowledge with care. The famous image of the statesman as weaver gives the book its lasting picture: ruling as a craft of binding a community together, not of forcing it.
17595-narrative-of-the-most-remarkable-e:
Frederic Shoberl compiled and translated this narrative of the most remarkable events in and near Leipzig. It covers the time before, during, and after the sanguinary series of engagements between the allied armies and the French, from October 14 to 19, 1813. Military maps showing the movements of the respective armies illustrate the volume. An eighth edition appeared in London in 1814, printed for R. Ackermann at five shillings.

Shoberl's preface notes that Britain, thanks to its island position, knew war's calamities chiefly from report, while fire and sword desolated towns elsewhere. Readers get a contemporary account of the Battle of the Nations, vivid and detailed. The book suits readers of Napoleonic history.
17645-arbor-day-leaves-a-complete-progra:
N. H. Egleston wrote this programme for Arbor Day observance. He worked in the Forestry Division of the Department of Agriculture in Washington and wrote a handbook of tree planting. The American Book Company published it in New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago. The book was supplied to superintendents, teachers, and school officers for their schools at ten cents for a single copy, postage paid, with cheaper rates for twenty-five copies.

Readers get readings, exercises, and suggestions for school Arbor Day ceremonies, built around planting and care for trees. The programme suits teachers, local historians, and readers of the conservation movement's schoolroom side. Its practical form shows how a national tree holiday reached the classroom.
17697-the-trumpeter-swan:
Temple Bailey, author of The Tin Soldier and Contrary Mary, published this novel in Philadelphia in 1920 with the Penn Publishing Company, with pictures by Alice Barber Stephens. Its Latin motto is translated in the book: a sound from the clouds shall call thee from this earth. Chapters open with a major and two minors, stuffed birds, and a wolf in the forest.

Rain and Randy's soul, little sister, Georgie-Porgie, and Mademoiselle Midas follow, with ancestors and a chapter called T. Branch ahead. Readers get a popular romance of family, music, and country life, in Bailey's warm, sentimental style. The book suits readers of early twentieth-century popular fiction.
177-the-american:
Christopher Newman, a rich American businessman, lounges in the Louvre in May 1868 and decides to conquer Paris. Henry James's American follows Newman through salons, business deals, and a courtship with Claire de Cintré. Her aristocratic family weighs his money against their pride.

Newman learns French manners, buys art, and befriends the painter Noémie. The Bellegardes accept him, then break the engagement for rank and revenge. James pits American energy against European tradition in a full-length novel. The American announced his international theme. Newman's blunt energy makes him James's most likable American hero abroad.
17756-the-submarine-boys-and-the-middies:
Victor G. Durham wrote this boys' tale of the Submarine Boys at Annapolis, where Jack Benson and his crew join a prize detail with the middies. The Saalfield firm printed it in Akron, as one more in a run of sea tales for young readers.

Chapters mix jest and peril: a flirt with science, a sulking rival, two kinds of voodoo, a young captain in rags, and a strange camel-elephant sight. Jack must explain, guess, and act fast to keep his crew in good stead. It is brisk, clean fun for boys who liked boats, brass, and pluck, with a mild rivalry to spice the cruise.
17826-memoir-of-old-elizabeth-a-coloured:
Old Elizabeth's memoir was printed in Philadelphia in 1863, taken mainly from her own lips in her ninety-seventh year. Born in Maryland in 1766 to enslaved parents, she grew up in a Methodist home where her father read the Bible aloud each Sunday morn.

At five she felt the stir of faith, at eleven she was sent to a farm miles from her kin, and she once walked twenty miles to find her mother. Her mother told her she had nobody in the wide world to look to but God. The memoir is short, plain, and moving, a rare voice of a Black woman who lived from slavery's early years to its last decade.
17844-ben-blair-the-story-of-a-plainsman:
Will Lillibridge, author of Where the Trail Divides, wrote this story of a plainsman, published in New York by A. L. Burt Company, copyright 1905 by A. C. McClurg and Company. The book appeared October 21, 1905, and ran through six editions by February 1907. Lillibridge dedicates it to his wife.

Chapters open in rude border land and desolation, then the Box R ranch and Ben's new home. The exotics, the soil and the seed, and the sanity of the wild follow, with the glitter of the unknown and a riffle of prairie ahead. Readers get a western novel of farming, character, and the open land.
17872-gifts-of-genius-a-miscellany-of-pr:
Printed in New York in 1859 for C. A. Davenport, this miscellany gathers short prose and verse by American writers of the day. The names on its contents page read like a roll of the young republic's letters: Longfellow, Lowell, Julia Ward Howe, Thomas Buchanan Read, and more.

Pieces range from a Paris notebook leaf to sea songs, church history, psalm essays, and tales of travel in South America. No one theme binds them; the joy is the mix, a parlor shelf of what bright Americans were writing just before the Civil War. Readers who like to browse old magazines will find much here to sample, quote, and enjoy in small bites.
17918-one-young-man:
Edited by Sir Ernest Hodder-Williams and printed in 1917, this short book tells the true story of a clerk who joined up in 1914. He fought on the Western Front for near two years, was badly hurt at the Somme, and was on his way back to his desk when the book appeared.

Chapters follow him from camp to Hill 60, through letters home and the long strain of trench war. The tale is plain and spare, with no hero talk, just a young man doing his duty. It stands as a quiet war memoir, and a moving note on one clerk's war, told for friends and kin.
18219-the-trumpeter-swan:
Temple Bailey, author of The Tin Soldier and Contrary Mary, published this novel in 1920, with pictures by Alice Barber Stephens. Its frontispiece asks, when I am married will you sound your trumpet high up near the moon. Its epigraph promises a sound from the clouds shall call thee from this earth. The book opens in a sleeper after a summer rain that began in Washington.

Chapters run from a major and two minors, stuffed birds, and a wolf in the forest. They pass through Rain and Randy's soul, little sister, and Georgie-Porgie. Later chapters give Mademoiselle Midas, ancestors, a gentleman's lie, the whistling Sally, the dancer on the moor, and the trumpeter swan itself. Readers get a romance of love, family, and second chances, with music and wild birds sounding through its close.
1823-the-make-believe-man:
Richard Harding Davis tells of a young man of twenty-five who has always wished for adventures and always gone halfway to meet them. He spends his vacation hunting for one in earnest. He finds it in the form of a young woman whose eyes measure him and his shoulders, as if wondering to what weight he could strip.

The story is a light romance of pretending: a holiday hero tries on courage, and the people he meets try it on him. Davis writes it with the ease of a man who knew both society and the field. The tale's charm lies in watching a make-believe man discover that real feeling was waiting behind the game.
18300-history-of-english-humour-vol-1-wi:
Rev. A. G. L'Estrange, author of a life of Rev. William Harness, wrote this history of English humour in two volumes, the first published in London by Hurst and Blackett in 1878.
