L'Estrange opens with preliminary observations on the ludicrous: its subjective character, the little study it has received, its evanescence, and the distinction between humour and the merely laughable.

An introduction then traces the origin of humour. Chapters on the Middle Ages follow, when civilization relapsed and books grew scarce. Religious writings, fantastic legends, crusade romances, and allegories filled the gap. Sir Bevis of Hamptoun and the prominence of lower animals mark the age. Readers get a Victorian attempt to give humour a history: theory first, then the slow growth of English laughter from medieval tale to modern wit.
18357-a-jacobite-exile-being-the-adventu:
G. A. Henty wrote this adventure of a young Englishman in the service of Charles XII of Sweden. The hero begins as a Jacobite exile, denounced and rescued after a spy is found in the household. From England he passes into Sweden, where war, prison, and exchange follow in quick order.

Chapters take him to Narva, across the Dwina, to Warsaw, among brigands, treed by wolves, and into the battle of Clissow. An old acquaintance, a return to England, the north coach, and a confession close the tale. Henty writes for lads, and the book mixes real campaigns of the Great Northern War with a invented hero who learns soldiering, loyalty, and nerve under a hard king.
1838-a-new-voyage-to-carolina-containing:
John Lawson, Surveyor-General of North Carolina, wrote this account of his travels in 1700, and it remains the classic early description of the Carolina country. Lawson gives the exact description and natural history of the land: its rivers, timber, grapevines, and the great tracts of good ground on the northwest side of the rivers.

A journal of a thousand miles' travel through Indian towns runs alongside the natural history. Lawson records the peoples he met, their customs, and their languages with unusual care for his time. The book is both a settler's guide and an early ethnography, and it is still read as a first-hand record of the Southeast before it changed.
18637-the-constitution-of-the-united-sta:
Prepared by the Legislative Reference Service of the Library of Congress under editor Edward S. Corwin, this volume is Senate Document 170 of the 82nd Congress, printed at Washington in 1953. It gives the Constitution with analysis and notes on cases decided by the Supreme Court to June 30, 1952, each ruling placed under the clause it construes.

Senator Alexander Wiley presented the work, noting that members treat the Constitution as a daily companion and counsellor. The volume revises and extends the 1938 annotated edition, which had gone out of print. Lawyers, students, and citizens will find it a standard reference for constitutional law of its era.
18684-a-certain-rich-man:
William Allen White's novel, issued at New York in 1909 by the Macmillan Company, opens in a lumber town's woods. Boys between seven and fourteen play at horse raids with hickory switches for steeds. They drink at Sycamore Creek, where local lore says a drinker turns horse thief at once.

Thirty chapters follow the hero from such boyhood games toward the life of a rich man, as the title promises. White, known for Stratagems and Spoils and The Court of Boyville, writes with Midwestern warmth and humor. The novel gives a vivid picture of small-town boyhood and ambition.
1877-a-mountain-woman:
Elia Wilkinson Peattie's Mountain Woman gathers tales of the West, dedicated to her best friend and kindest critic, her husband. The foreword notes that most of the tales have been printed before, and the stories that follow move through mining camps, ranches, and lonely houses.

One tale turns on a letter from a woman who will never come back. Writing to Jim, she says it is hopeless and that she would not mind standing still to be shot if there were any good in it. Peattie writes the mountain West from a woman's angle, with attention to the lives that hardship left behind. The collection is a strong sample of regional writing of its day.
18792-john-gabriel-borkman:
Henrik Ibsen's late play, in William Archer's translation, appeared in Copenhagen in December 1896 and reached stages across Scandinavia the next month. It centers on John Gabriel Borkman and the two sisters at his side, Gunhild, strong and masterful, and Ella, tender and devoted.

Around them stands Foldal, an old clerk who keeps touching up a play from his youth and lives on the hope that it will one day succeed. The play works through pride, old love, and hopes that have worn thin, in close, tense scenes rather than through action outdoors. Its swift spread through Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, and Germany shows how eagerly audiences took up Ibsen's late studies of lives shaped by the past.
18868-with-kitchener-in-the-soudan-a-sto:
G. A. Henty wrote this adventure novel about the Sudan campaign under Kitchener, centered on the battles of Atbara and Omdurman. His young hero, Gregory, is disinherited, caught in a rising in Alexandria, and then travels southward to serve with the army. Chapters follow him among the Dervishes, as a prisoner, afloat on the Nile, and through the final advance.

Atbara, Omdurman, and Khartoum appear in turn, mixed with escapes, a fugitive's flight, and a voice from the dead. Henty aimed to give boy readers a vivid picture of a recent war. Readers get a fast historical adventure, dated in its outlook, but useful as an introduction to a campaign that closed the nineteenth century in Africa.
18933-man-to-man:
Jackson Gregory published this western novel in 1920, with illustrations by J. G. Shepherd. Its hero is Steve Packard, a young man drawn into a hard fight in ranch and lumber country. Around him stand Terry, the mountain man Blenham, and the Temple family, whose quarrels drive much of the action. Chapter titles promise rides, stampedes, and confrontations at Red Creek and the lumber camp.

The novel moves between open range, town streets, and forest work sites as Packard faces rivals, old debts, and a family feud. Loyalty, courage under threat, and fair dealing are tested again and again. Readers get a fast, old-style western built on action scenes, strong villains, and a hero who settles matters face to face.
1897-the-seventh-man:
Max Brand's Seventh Man opens with a reflection on young men and silence: a man under thirty needs neighbors. To stop up the current of his life with a long silence is like damming a river, until the water sweeps the dam away or rises over it. The hero, a gunman turned outlaw, tests that truth when a sheriff's posse calls 'Halt, there. Up with your hands, or I'll drill you. '.

Brand writes the western as a story of character under pressure, with chases, posses, and a man learning what his solitude costs. The novel is fast, lean, and romantic, and it shows Brand, the most prolific of western writers, at the height of his early powers.
19012-the-two-gun-man:
Charles Alden Seltzer wrote this 1911 western about a stranger who rides into Dry Bottom. The town soon learns his skill when he tosses a tin can high and shoots it again and again before it can fall. Crowds gasp, and word of his gun spreads fast through the streets.

The stranger finds a cabin, an orphan, and a girl unlike the rest, while local bullies and ranch hands test his nerve. Each chapter tightens the feud around him. Readers get a classic range tale of fast guns, loyalty, and a man who must prove what kind of man he truly is.
19044-adrift-on-an-ice-pan:
Wilfred Thomason Grenfell wrote this short memoir of being adrift on an ice pan in the North. Grenfell was a doctor and missionary on the Labrador coast. He tells of a night and day on drifting ice with his dogs. Cold, hunger, and fear of being carried out to sea pressed on him. The tale is told in plain, brave prose.

An appendix keeps local dialect as spoken. A contents note lists his team of dogs. The story turns on endurance, quick thought, and faith under strain. Readers get a stirring true tale of survival in a harsh land, from a man who gave his life to its people.
19098-christmas-in-ritual-and-tradition-:
Clement A. Miles wrote this 1912 study of Christmas in ritual and tradition, Christian and pagan. It traces the feast from its origin and names through pagan survivals, Yule, the Kalends of January, and the feast of the Nativity on December 25. The plan divides the Christian feast from pagan survivals.

Chapters cover Christmas poetry, Latin hymns from Notker of St. Gall to Bernard of Clairvaux, and the shift from dogmatic verse to human, popular song under Franciscan influence. Readers get a learned, readable history of how Christmas customs grew, blending church rite with older winter festivals.
19148-the-henchman:
Mark Lee Luther wrote this 1902 novel, The Henchman, dedicated to George Rice Carpenter of Columbia. Its Tuscarora stories adapt Judge Arad Thomas's Pioneer History of Orleans County, while the main tale follows politics, salons, and small-town ambition in western New York. The opening likens states to a boot, a coffee pot, and a turkey.

Mrs. Hilliard's salon shines with new decorations, ices, and a paper on Shakespeare's anachronisms by Volney Sprague, yet she misses Bowers and Shelby, whose absence steals the club's spark. Editors polish glasses and trade sarcasm. Readers get a clever novel of society, politics, and the henchmen who serve power.
1935-the-tremendous-adventures-of-major-:
William Makepeace Thackeray's Tremendous Adventures of Major Gahagan presents a soldier of the Indian wars whose tales grow taller with every telling. Chapters on Allyghur and Laswaree, a peep into Spain, and the Ahmednuggar Irregulars carry Gahagan through battles he may or may not have fought.

Thackeray frames the book as a joke on military memoirs. Gahagan insists his facts are true and leaves his proofs at his publisher's office, beside an extract from the Bengal Hurkaru, for anyone to examine. The comedy lies in the major's perfect confidence, and the novel reads as a warm-up for the satire of Vanity Fair.
19405-confessions-of-an-etonian:
I. E. M. wrote this memoir of school life at Eton, told in the first person with humor and candor. Lessons, masters, games, and boyish scrapes fill the early chapters, while parties and country visits bring the schoolboy into wider society.

A young lady named Miss Curzon appears at a gathering, and the narrator's shy notice of her gives the book a thread of first love. The memoir charms by its honesty: it admits folly, fondness, and the slow growth from boy to young man. One remembered prank sends a young marquis out each evening to milk a quiet cow in the playing fields.
19486-irish-wonders-the-ghosts-giants-po:
D. R. McAnally Jr. collected these popular Irish tales as told by the people, under a New York imprint in the late eighteen hundreds. Ghosts, giants, pookas, demons, leprechauns, banshees, fairies, witches, widows, and old maids all crowd its pages, with a frontispiece blessing for a holy man.

One tale turns on a shillelagh quarrel, where blows struck by accident count or do not count as a wife and husband argue the rules. McAnally praises the Celtic gift for fancy, and his book remains a rich store of fireside marvels from the Emerald Isle.
19608-the-story-of-the-other-wise-man:
Henry Van Dyke wrote this Christmas tale of a fourth wise man, issued in New York in the mid eighteen nineties with pictures. The other wise man sees the same star as the three kings and sets out for Bethlehem, but his road keeps turning aside to help the sick, the poor, and the lost.

Chapters follow him by the waters of Babylon, for the sake of a little child, and at last to a pearl of great price. Van Dyke's moral is plain: he who walks in love may wander far, yet still reach the goal he sought.
1970-a-poor-wise-man:
Mary Roberts Rinehart's Poor Wise Man opens on a city turning its dreariest aspect toward the railway. Blackened walls, irregular and ill-paved streets, gloomy warehouses, and a gray, smoke-laden atmosphere give it mystery. Into that city comes Willy Cameron, a young man whose coming upsets the habits of an entire family.

Lily's father, sitting upright, demands to know who is coming to-night and why he should upset the household. The novel follows Willy's efforts to do good in a world of strikes, politics, and suspicion. Rinehart writes the postwar years with sympathy for both workers and owners, and the book's title names its hero: poor, wise, and out of step with his age.
19750-the-waif-woman:
Robert Louis Stevenson set The Waif Woman in old Norse Iceland. Finnward is a prosperous man who keeps open house. His wife Aud cares more for fine clothes and admiration. She is thought careless in her conduct for a married woman. Their children are Eyolf, a likely boy, and Asdis, a young daughter. Trouble is plainly gathering around the household.

Stevenson loved saga style: flat telling, heavy fate. A waif woman, a castaway stranger, brings the outside world into Finnward's hall. Stevenson's Norse tales show his range beyond Treasure Island. He retells northern material in spare, hard prose. The story stays little known, which makes it a find. It shows a master storyteller testing an ancient form.
19833-the-heroic-enthusiasts-gli-eroici-:
Part the second of Giordano Bruno's Heroic Enthusiasts continues his dialogues on heroic love. Its pages play with the number nine, ninth letter and ninth door. Fifty portals, it says, lead to the concealed mysteries of being. Od is named the pure life-giving light, or magnetic fluid. Bruno's text, in this edition, wears layers of mystical commentary. The result is heady and strange.

Victorian occult interest revived Bruno as a martyr of free thought. Editions like this one fed that revival. The commentary's talk of Od comes from Baron von Reichenbach's magnetism theories. Bruno's own sonnets and arguments sit beneath the gloss. Readers must dig for the philosopher under the mystic. Part two rewards that digging.
1986-life-and-death-of-mr-badman:
John Bunyan published this allegory in 1680, two years after the first part of The Pilgrim's Progress, as its dark mirror image. Where Christian walks toward heaven, Mr. Badman walks the other road, from a bad youth to a bad death. Bunyan wrote from prison experience and Puritan preaching, in language meant for plain readers of his day.

Told as a talk between two friends, the book follows Badman through lying, theft, loose living, and hard dealing, showing each step as a moral choice. Bunyan writes plainly and directly, aiming to warn readers rather than to entertain them with plot. The dialogue form lets a godly friend answer doubts, so the warning lands as talk, not as a sermon alone.
19863-the-old-masters-and-their-pictures:
Sarah Tytler wrote The Old Masters and Their Pictures for the use of schools. Her survey gives many records of Dutch painters in particular. Dutch art, she notes, proved specially popular in England. Some Dutch masters are better represented in England than at home. Flemish art also gets full treatment here. J. A. Crowe revised the art history for this edition.

School art history began with books like this one. Pupils learned painters' lives beside their famous pictures. The canon here is the Victorian canon: Raphael to Rembrandt. Tytler writes clearly for young students without flattening the art. Her selections shaped what schoolchildren thought great painting was. The book documents that teaching tradition well.
19988-little-maid-marian:
Amy E. Blanchard wrote Little Maid Marian in 1908, a story for girls. Marian talks often with her grandmother in its pages. Faith, both feel, is difficult to exercise completely. Marian has made numberless mighty efforts to believe as she should. Yet things did not come out as her efforts promised. The gap between effort and outcome troubles her young conscience. Blanchard writes that trouble gently.

Blanchard's girls' books often carry quiet religious feeling. Marian's doubts are treated as growth, not failure. Grandmother and granddaughter anchor the story's warmth. The setting is a modest, churchgoing American household. Young readers got companionship for their own questions. The book is a soft-spoken period piece for girls.
20132-the-wizard-of-the-sea-or-a-trip-un:
Roy Rockwood wrote The Wizard of the Sea, a trip under the ocean for boys. Young Mont hears he may join a nautical school with a sly grin. A town man calls him the worst boy in town for mischief. Mont takes the charge with more pride than shame, it seems.

Rockwood wrote many sea and adventure tales under that shared name. A school at sea leads, here, to a craft that dives below waves. Undersea travel was still a marvel when the book came out. Readers get boyish fun mixed with wonder at a new kind of ship.
20205-the-maya-chronicles-brinton-s-libr:
The Maya Chronicles gathers native Maya texts in Daniel Brinton's library series. Brinton sought true specimens of native literature for American scholars. Such works are rare and hard to reach, he warns readers. They sit in manuscript with a few collectors, or in costly society volumes.

This volume brings Maya chronicles from Yucatan into print for study. They record kings, wars, famines, and the coming of the Spanish. Brinton's series aimed to save aboriginal American literature from loss. Readers get primary Maya history in translation, with a scholar's care around it.
20279-the-veterinarian:
The Veterinarian is a reference book for those who treat sick and hurt animals. One entry defines creosote, a colorless to yellowish oily liquid. It holds phenols and comes from the destructive distillation of wood tar. Beech wood tar, in particular, yields much of the supply described.

Creosote once served as a medicine for chronic bronchitis in practice. Entries like this one give drugs, doses, and uses in plain order. Farmers and vets kept such books close in stable and surgery. Readers get a practical window on animal medicine of an earlier age.
20439-susan-b-anthony-rebel-crusader-hum:
Alma Lutz wrote this life of Susan B. Anthony, published by Beacon Press in 1959. Its subtitle calls Anthony a rebel, a crusader, and a humanitarian. Lutz had spent years gathering letters and records of the women's rights movement.

Anthony spent her long life fighting for women's right to vote. She spoke, organized, and faced arrest for casting a ballot in 1872. The biography follows her from her Quaker childhood to national fame. It remains a standard life of the leader who did more than any other to win American women the vote.
20555-what-is-and-what-might-be-a-study-:
What Is and What Might Be studies education in general and elementary education in particular. Its author was a school inspector who came to doubt the cramming system of his day. The book argues that schools crush the very powers they claim to train.

Our faculties grow by use, the book holds. Once they reach their fullest growth, we keep them at that level by exercising them. Mental and spiritual powers have no fixed limit, so the need for exercise is more urgent still. To neglect them is to stunt them. The study became a noted plea for freer, fuller schooling.
2070-to-the-last-man:
Zane Grey turns at last to the feud story he had long avoided, setting a tale of pioneer families whose old quarrel shapes a whole corner of the West. Love and loyalty pull against blood and revenge across the range. Grey had long avoided feud stories, fearing they would repeat the same bloodshed without purpose.

Grey argues in his foreword that the violence of the frontier cannot be left out of its history, and the novel follows that belief. The result is a full-blooded western, with gunfights, chases, and a stubborn fight for home. His foreword argues that pioneer history must face violence honestly, or it will tell a false tale.
20754-the-blunders-of-a-bashful-man:
Shyness is the curse of the man who tells The Blunders of a Bashful Man. He hopes no other soul must bear the mishaps his complaint has cost him. Smallpox and scarlet fever, he notes, strike once, but bashfulness strikes for life.

Comic scenes pile up as the poor man trips through calls, meals, and courtship. Each fresh crowd brings a fresh blunder to dread. The humor is gentle, built on pain most readers know at least a little. This slight, funny book shows how Victorian humor could turn a common flaw into a whole tale of woe.
21063-the-missing-merchantman:
Harry Collingwood worked as a ship designer and shipwright, and that trade knowledge runs through this sea novel. The crew of a merchant vessel decide that captains and officers are paid far too much. Convinced they have been robbed of fair wages for years, the deckhands seize the ship.

In taking the vessel the crew make themselves little better than pirates. The officers and passengers, though, are resourceful people who work their way out of the trap. At last they bring their ship home, where she has long been posted as missing. The tale mixes mutiny, seamanship, and a sharp argument about pay and skill.
21065-the-log-of-a-privateersman:
Early in the nineteenth century, with Britain at war against France, privateers worked as licensed sea raiders against enemy shipping. Harry Collingwood's novel opens with a bold French stroke in October 1804. French sailors slip into Weymouth harbour at night and carry off the trader Weymouth, loaded with rum, sugar, and tobacco.

From that capture the hero's career as a privateersman grows. He proves very good at preying on enemy ships and taking prizes. His success at last brings him an offer of a permanent commission in the Royal Navy. The log form keeps the action close to decks, watches, and pay-offs.
21331-the-adventures-of-hajji-baba-of-is:
James Morier's comic novel follows Hajji Baba, a Persian barber's son, through every trade and scrape his country offers. Chapter headings tell the pattern. He is captured by Turcomans, rescues his master's money and keeps it, and becomes a robber in self-defence. Later he works as a water carrier and an itinerant seller of smoke.

Morier had lived in Persia as a British diplomat, and the tale pokes fun at Persian manners and English ones alike. The poet Asker's history and the dervish Sefer's story fill side chapters. George Curzon introduced this 1895 edition. Hajji Baba remains the classic English comic novel of Persia, sharp, episodic, and often unfair in the way of good satire.
21415-the-young-visiters-or-mr-salteena-:
Daisy Ashford wrote The Young Visiters as a child, and it reached print in 1919 with a preface by J. M. Barrie. Mr Salteena, a man of forty-two, loves having guests to stay. His young guest Ethel Monticue, aged seventeen, joins him at the start.

Ashford keeps her child spelling and her grave, funny view of grown-up life. Visits, a trip to the Crystal Palace, grand calls, and a proposal fill the short tale. A wedding brings the plot to its close. The book became a famed curio, loved for the clear young voice that never slips.
21532-the-university-of-michigan:
Wilfred Shaw, the university's alumni chief, wrote The University of Michigan in 1920. Shaw edited the Michigan Alumnus and etched four of the book's pictures himself. Photographs crowd the rest of the volume, from University Hall onward.

Chapters run from the founding and early days to Presidents Angell and Hutchins. Schools of law, medicine, and letters get their own accounts. Student life, fraternities, athletics, and town and campus fill later pages. A chapter on the university in war, and one on its alumni, close the tale. The odd first name of the school, the Catholepistemiad, gets its due at the start.
21576-the-privateersman:
A cruise off Hispaniola in the privateer Revenge opens Captain Marryat's The Privateersman, published in 1846. The narrator hopes his tale, if ever made public, may bring profit to its readers. Privateering, as Marryat notes, is piracy made lawful by a government's licence.

The Revenge takes a French ship early, then holds her course for more prizes. Marryat's twenty-third book draws on the last great age of the privateer. Captures, fights, and the division of prize money fill the log-like tale. No writer knew this world better from the inside than a post-captain turned novelist.
21582-the-mightiest-man:
Patrick Fahy's tale The Mightiest Man, from Worlds of If in November 1961, opens after aliens have left Earth. A few shining metal huts in the Siberian tundra alone prove they came. Earth stood helpless while vast minds slithered over her fields and cities.

They caught up with the mightiest man in Belgrade, the blurb declares, and he feared nothing. A neural plague has spread to Zagreb, Albania, and Italy in the tale's grim reach. Twenty million lunatics fill the Balkans, and the Danube stands dammed into a lake. Fahy asks who betrayed mankind, and at what price, in a stark cold-war nightmare.
21700-don-juan:
Lord Byron turns the Don Juan legend inside out in Don Juan, his great comic epic in verse. The poem runs to seventeen cantos in the copy given here, with a sharp dedication. Juan is no bold seducer here, but a young man whom women pursue.

Byron opens fire on Southey, the poet laureate, and the Lake poets at Keswick. Their narrow circle, he charges, thinks poetry's wreaths belong to them alone. Shipwreck, a slave market, a sultan's court, and the siege of Ismail fill the cantos. Love affairs, war, and English society all take Byron's wit in ottava rima, the poem's dancing, rhyming measure.
21719-blue-lights-hot-work-in-the-soudan:
Miles Milton stands at a turning point in his life as this Ballantyne novel opens. Ballantyne compares him to water at a ridge, where one drop flows to the Atlantic and the next to Hudson's Bay. Miles leans the wrong way, and the book follows where that false step leads. His strong will and hot temper keep causing trouble at home.

The trail leads at last to the Soudan, where British troops fought in desert heat. Ballantyne mixes a young man's moral fall and recovery with scenes of real campaigning. The title's blue lights point to the Christian soldiers whose faith lights the darker parts of the tale.
21743-jeff-benson-or-the-young-coastguar:
Jeff Benson loses his father, a poor schoolmaster in the coastal town of Cranby, as this Ballantyne tale opens. Jeff is fifteen, tall, hearty, and sure he can do anything he sets his mind to. Fun has ruled his life so far, in school and on the playground. His uncle Jacob, a hard and grasping lawyer, cares little for the boy.

Work by the sea gives Jeff his chance, and the coastguard gives him his calling. Ballantyne follows the lad from schoolboy pranks to rescues on a dangerous coast. Smugglers, storms, and duty test the young coastguardsman in turn. It is a steady tale of a boy growing straight under hard knocks and salt air.
2184-unbeaten-tracks-in-japan:
Isabella L. Bird traveled where few Western visitors had gone, into the interior of Japan and among the Ainu people of Yezo. Unbeaten Tracks in Japan records that journey in letters full of hard roads, remote villages, shrines at Nikko, and the daily life of people far from the treaty ports. Bird writes as a keen, practical observer with little patience for easy praise.

Her account covers food, housing, customs, and the strain of travel itself, often on foot or horseback through rough country. The book still reads as a vivid firsthand record of a Japan that was changing fast. Anyone curious about travel before tourism will find it frank, detailed, and full of surprises.
2196-an-iceland-fisherman:
Pierre Loti's Iceland Fisherman follows Breton sailors who leave home each year to fish the cold waters off Iceland. At the center stands Yann, a strong, silent fisherman, and Gaud, the woman who waits and loves him through long absences. The sea gives and takes with indifference, and the village measures life by returns and losses.

Loti writes the Breton coast and the northern ocean with a painter's eye for light, weather, and ritual. The novel is quiet and sad, more elegy than adventure, and its power grows from small scenes of work, prayer, and parting. It remains a beloved portrait of a fishing world now gone.
21962-harvard-classics-volume-28-essays-:
Great essays in English fill this twenty-eighth volume of the Harvard Classics, Dr. Charles W. Eliot's famous five-foot shelf of books, issued in 1910. The frontispiece shows Thomas Huxley, whose Science and Culture stands inside. Swift and Thackeray open the prose line. Newman's lectures on the idea of a university follow, with his account of university life at Athens.

Matthew Arnold's Study of Poetry and Ruskin's Sesame and Lilies carry the Victorian center. Milton, Bagehot, Freeman on race and language, Pepys on truth of intercourse, and Stevenson close the range. Introductions and notes frame each author. The volume is a portable university of English prose, chosen to prove that a busy reader could self-educate from a single shelf.
21997-christie-s-old-organ:
An old barrel-organ man and a lost boy meet in O. F. Walton's Christie's Old Organ, also called Home, Sweet Home. Old Treffy sits alone in his attic in a dreary lodging house, turning his organ with a trembling hand. The tune it plays, Home Sweet Home, mocks every bare bench below. Yet the flowers of love still live in his withered heart, and he gives them all to his antiquated organ.

Walton wrote tales for Sunday school readers, and this is among her best known. Christie, the boy of the story, learns what home means from the old man who has none. The clergyman pictured with Christie carries the tale's gentle preaching. Sentimental in the Victorian way, the little book moved generations of young readers.
22072-folk-lore-and-legends-north-americ:
Folk-Lore and Legends: North American Indian gathers tales told by Native peoples across the continent. The volume belongs to a popular series that sorted old stories by the peoples who told them. One tale concerns a village belle admired by every hunter and warrior. Her suitor, the Beau-Man, trusts his secrets to a friend, and trouble follows.

Other stories tell of spirits, animals, courtship, and revenge in the woods and villages. The tellers' names and tribes stand behind many of the pieces. Such collections preserved tales that might otherwise have stayed only in oral tradition. They also show how nineteenth-century readers liked their folklore: romantic, brief, and framed as a window on a vanishing world.
22073-the-repairman:
Harry Harrison wrote The Repairman, a short science fiction tale from the early days of his career. Harrison later became famous for the Stainless Steel Rat books and Make Room! Make Room! His repairman narrator has fixed hyperspace beacons across the whole Galaxy. He boasts that he has worked on every type or model ever made.

Then a call names a kind of beacon he has never heard of. The job takes him somewhere stranger than his long experience prepared him for. Harrison builds the joke and the puzzle out of one man's professional pride. The story is quick, dry, and typical of the clever short fiction that filled the science fiction magazines of the 1950s.
22140-the-wrong-woman:
Charles D. Stewart published The Wrong Woman in 1912, a novel of the American West. The frontispiece shows a woman who must continue her journey afoot. Stewart opens on ranch matters: a horse that swells itself out when saddled, then lets the girths hang loose. Such stable talk sets the scene among people who live by horses.

A case of mistaken identity drives the plot, as the title promises. The wrong woman arrives where another was expected, and ranch life must sort out the error. Stewart writes comedy and courtship in a Western setting. His books were known for shrewd humour about human nature, and this one keeps that reputation.
22182-the-best-of-the-world-s-classics-v:
Volume V of The Best of the World's Classics turns to Great Britain and presents its prose masters. The set was a standard home library of its day, ten volumes strong. Each author arrives with a short life. Boswell's sketch, for example, runs from his birth in 1740 to his Life of Johnson in 1791 in a few brisk lines.

Essays, speeches, and passages from the great prose writers fill the volume. The editors chose what a general reader was expected to know. Such collections built the canon for homes without a scholar's library. This volume shows Edwardian taste in British prose: Johnson's circle, the essayists, and the historians, all in one thick book.
22331-the-chocolate-soldier-or-heroism-t:
C. T. Studd wrote The Chocolate Soldier, a sharp call for braver Christians. Its full title calls heroism the lost chord of Christianity. Studd mocks soft believers with his chocolate soldier figure.

The Chocolate Christian, he writes, shakes at the very thought of war. The call to battle always finds him with the palsy. Such a man says he cannot move, only sing. Studd quotes the man's favorite lines without mercy. The pamphlet argues that faith should produce courage and sacrifice. It still reads as a brisk, stinging challenge. Studd wanted soldiers for Christ, not sweets that melt when heat comes.
22371-the-chief-end-of-man:
The Chief End of Man, dated 1897, takes up life's largest question directly. Its title echoes the old catechism answer about man's purpose. The passage preserved shows a man in deep perplexity, near dismay.

At such a time, the writer counsels looking backward attentively. A guided life can review the steps by which it advanced. Past crises, once recalled, show how they were met. Light may then break on the path ahead. Or the reader may simply take fresh heart and hope. The book offers that counsel at length. It treats purpose as something proved by a whole life's road.
22532-mary-louise-and-josie-o-gorman:
Edith Van Dyne wrote Mary Louise and Josie O'Gorman, published in 1922. Van Dyne was a pen name used for popular girls' series books. Hard news opens this volume for Mary Louise and her friends.

Hope of Danny Dexter's survival was finally abandoned by everyone. His sorrowing little wife and many friends gave up that hope. Colonel Hathaway's comfortable fortune had also mysteriously disappeared by then. Mary Louise thus faced a future of poverty without warning. With native pluck, she rose to the sad occasion bravely. In spite of her sad heart, she showed cheerful spirit. Josie O'Gorman, girl detective, helps drive the mystery plot. Readers get series fiction with courage under loss.
22664-the-severed-hand-from-german-tales:
Wilhelm Hauff wrote The Severed Hand, a dark tale from his fairy-tale almanacs, here taken from German Tales as published for American readers. The catalog record gives no year. Hauff, who died young, filled his brief career with stories of the East, of students, and of quiet horror.

The sample opens in farewell: a father embraces his son and gives him clothes for the journey, plus the weapons his grandfather hung on the father when he went abroad. Use them only when attacked, the father counsels, but then defend yourself bravely. Such blessings arm the hero for a tale of murder, disguise, and a hand that will not rest. Hauff mixes the storyteller's ease with real dread, and this is among his most gripping tales.
22840-honor-o-callaghan:
Schoolgirl rank is serious business in Honor O'Callaghan, a story by Mary Russell Mitford. The excerpt looks inside a fashionable house of education, where a newcomer's place turns on odd details. One mother calls on her daughter attended by only one footman, and the slight is noted. A father's town address and a mother's milliner also weigh in the scale.

Mitford watches this small world with amused precision. Honor, the Irish girl of the title, must make her way among classmates quick to judge surfaces. The story turns school etiquette into a study of class itself. Beneath the manners sits a real question about worth. The tale answers it the Mitford way, through character shown in daily behavior.
22844-miss-philly-firkin-the-china-woman:
A crowded London street opens Miss Philly Firkin, the China Woman, by Mary Russell Mitford. Houses in the best streets let for double their value, goods sell at nearly the same rate, and horse traffic and foot traffic jostle on the pavement. Coaches and phaetons run against each other in the road.

Philly Firkin keeps her china shop inside that crush of commerce. Mitford follows the small tradeswoman through the risks and pleasures of city shopkeeping, where a fragile stock meets a rough crowd. The portrait mixes sympathy with sharp observation of London manners. Village readers of Mitford's sketches got a capital-city counterpart here. Philly's counter becomes a fine post from which to watch the whole town go by.
23152-the-mcbrides-a-romance-of-arran:
John Sillars lays out his chapters in The McBrides, a romance of Arran. Chapter titles promise the Urie's foot as a resting place, a halflin's message, and another ride to McAllan's locker. A doorstep wedding, a kiss from Margaret McBride, Betty's growing pains, and a raking black schooner fill out the list.

Arran, the Firth of Clyde island called Scotland in miniature, frames the McBrides' fortunes. Smuggling schooners, weddings, and messages cross the island's hills in Sillars's Highland manner. The chapter heads alone tell a family saga's rhythm, rest, errands, weddings, and sails on the horizon. Readers who enjoy Scottish regional romance, dialect and all, will find a whole island community between these covers, arranged around one family's name.
23191-count-ulrich-of-lindburg-a-tale-of:
Count Ulrich of Lindburg is a tale of the Reformation in Germany. Its scene is the Castle of Lindburg, on the banks of the river Saal at Merseburg in Saxony. The land then answered to the aged Elector Frederick, praised in the tale as an excellent ruler.

The castle is drawn as a feudal pile from the Middle Ages, proof against the siege tools of older war. Yet such strongholds were bound to crumble before cannon fire. The tale links that fall to a wider change: the old order giving way before the light of Gospel truth.
23194-the-common-man: Guy McCord's The Common Man opens on a small, telling gesture. A man named Braun lets a sentence trail off, then stuffs a paper into a coat pocket that has clearly served as a waste bin for years. He leads the way up a cement walk, with his younger companions close behind him.
23245-ancient-ballads-and-legends-of-hin:
Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan gathers poems retelling old Indian stories. Its introduction tells a sad, striking story about the poet herself. Within four years of her death, it says, her genius had been revealed to the world in many forms and recognised across France and England.

At her death she had published only one book. That book had found only two reviewers in Europe. The gap between those two facts gives the volume its charge. Readers get ballads and legends from a young Indian poet whose name, the editor insists, no well-read person should fail to know.
23269-the-heir-of-kilfinnan-a-tale-of-th:
The Heir of Kilfinnan is a tale of the shore and ocean, told here through a later summary of its plot. After several exciting events, an earl dies. To everyone's surprise, the young hero Denham is revealed as Dermot, a young man met much earlier in the tale.

A lawyer then states that Dermot's father stood in line to the earldom. That makes Dermot the new earl, and the room erupts in cheers. One catch remains: who wants a ruined castle and a bankrupt estate? Readers get inheritance, hidden identity, and sea adventure in a cheerfully spoiled package.
23270-on-the-indian-trail-stories-of-mis:
On the Indian Trail gathers stories of missionary work among Cree and other Indigenous peoples. Its author explains the book's shape at the start. Unlike some of his other books, it is not one continuous narrative of missionary life, but a set of distinct chapters.

Some chapters were written just for this volume. Others had already seen print, in whole or in part, and are gathered here at the request of friends, with the publishers' courtesy. Readers get first-hand period accounts of travel, teaching, and mission stations, told as separate episodes rather than one long story.
23481-the-perfect-gentleman:
Ralph Bergengren wrote this nineteen nineteen book of essays on what it means to be a perfect gentleman, printed by the Atlantic Monthly Press. In the back of every man's mind, he says, dwells a wistful wish to be thought such a figure, a high ideal of conduct. In narrower eyes, the same figure may look a perfect ass.

Essays follow on dress, the barber's chair, shining shoes, making calls, the liar in bed, boring or not boring, tailors, shaving thoughts, and afternoon tea. Bergengren writes with wit and a light, civilised touch, praising courtesy while mocking its excesses. Readers who enjoy manners, dress, and social comedy will find a charming, slightly arch guide to behaving well without becoming a prig.
2351-john-halifax-gentleman:
Dinah Maria Mulock Craik's John Halifax, Gentleman follows a penniless orphan who rises by honesty and hard work to become a respected manufacturer and family man. The novel's narrator, a disabled friend, watches Halifax's long life unfold: his labors, his marriage, his children, and his quiet heroism in business and in private sorrow. Craik makes goodness itself the plot.

Victorian readers loved the book for its moral earnestness, and it stayed popular for generations. Its view of industry is humane and hopeful. Readers of classic domestic fiction will find a long, satisfying chronicle.
2354-note-on-the-resemblances-and-differ:
Thomas Henry Huxley, Darwin's great defender, compares the brains of humans and apes in this famous scientific note. The essay, printed with Darwin's Descent of Man, argues from anatomy that the differences between human and ape brains are smaller than those between ape species themselves. Huxley writes with clarity and combativeness.

The note became a landmark in the evolution debate, giving Darwin's case its anatomical backbone. Its Victorian science has since been refined, but its logic still impresses. Readers of science history will find a concise classic. Huxley earned the nickname of Darwin's bulldog for defenses like this one.
24024-ups-and-downs-in-the-life-of-a-dis:
William L. Stone, author of Tales and Sketches, Such as They Are, published Ups and Downs in the Life of a Distressed Gentleman in New York in 1836. Its dedication addresses all doating parents who imagine wisdom will die with their own children, and inscribes to them this little record of the life and misfortunes of a genius.

Stone's motto states the theme: when fortune smiles, friends crowd like flies round honey, but when fortune frowns and casts thee down, thou mayest lie and rot. Chapters discourse on cycles, pedigree, and the birth of the hero, in a section of country described as beautiful. For readers of early American humor, it is a satire of genius, fortune, and the parents who mistake one for the other.
24073-general-john-regan:
George A. Birmingham published General John Regan in 1913, dedicating it to Charles H. Hawtrey in memory of times that were very pleasant to him. Birmingham, who also wrote Lalage's Lovers, sets his comedy in Ireland, where a town invents a hero and must live with the invention.

The book opens in an Irish police barrack, invariably clean, occasionally picturesque, but never comfortable. Its living room holds tables and benches with iron legs, for iron is harder than wood. Men who rub their legs against it at meals are likely to gain a stern, martial spirit. On the walls stand short carbines, with which, in dire emergencies, police fire on their fellow Irish, and handcuffs hang unobtrusively nearby. Nineteen chapters of blarney and bureaucracy follow.
24135-the-measure-of-a-man:
Randall Garrett wrote this science fiction story for Astounding Science Fiction in April 1960, with pictures by Martinez. Alfred Pendray makes his way down a corridor aboard the battleship Shane, flashlight in hand, steadying himself with his good leg and one hand. A thousand light-years from home, the wrecked ship has lost its false gravity, and a sprained ankle slams the wall as he turns.

Garrett states his theme up front: the desirable is not always necessary, while the necessary may be most undesirable. The measure of a man, he suggests, is telling one from the other and acting on it. Readers get a tense tale of duty and endurance aboard a blasted ship, far from help.
24379-the-admiral-s-caravan:
Charles E. Carryl, author of Davy and the Goblin, wrote this children's fantasy, with pictures by Reginald B. Birch, published by Houghton, Mifflin and Company in Boston and New York. Its copyrights run from 1891 and 1892 to 1919 and 1920, and its frontispiece shows the Admiral making a desperate attempt to view his legs through his spy-glass. It is dedicated to Constance, sweet chatterbox, whose gentle ways and small remarks the verse says the tale itself has wrought.

Chapters run from Dorothy and the Admiral and the ferry to nowhere through the cruise of the sideboard and tree-top country to Bob Scarlet's garden and the toy-shop. The song in the dell, something about the camel, and the camel's complaint follow, with the sizing tower, the dancing animals, and the caravan coming home. Readers get a child's caravan of wonders.
24435-four-americans-roosevelt-hawthorne:
Henry A. Beers, author of studies in American literature, gathered four essays reprinted from the Yale Review into this 1919 volume, published by Yale University Press. Each essay takes one American writer as its subject: Theodore Roosevelt as a man of letters, Nathaniel Hawthorne fifty years on, Ralph Waldo Emerson as a pilgrim in Concord, and Walt Whitman.

Beers weighs each man's books against his public life, asking what Roosevelt's writing reveals beyond politics, how Hawthorne's tales have lasted, what Emerson meant to Concord, and where Whitman's verse stands. The essays are short, clear, and opinionated, offering a compact guide to four very different American voices for readers new to any of them.
24529-the-unnecessary-man:
Randall Garrett wrote this short science-fiction story, illustrated by Martinez. Its frame opens with a businessman and a philosopher arguing over an old saying: if two colleagues always agree, one adds nothing. The philosopher answers that the spare man may still serve as a scapegoat.

The tale itself moves to an emperor's court, where a colonel reports that a boy named Senesin sits in jail, and the emperor raises an eyebrow at news he did not order. Garrett's joke turns serious: in a settled system, which man is truly needless? Readers get a clever, short tale about organisations, tradition, and the uses of a spare man.
24792-the-alternate-plan:
Gerry Maddren wrote this short science fiction story for Amazing Science Fiction Stories. Bart Neely, a psychologist, faces a grave throat operation under Dr. Jonas Morton. He refuses full sleep for the surgery, fearing he would wake voiceless and helpless, and he insists on staying awake so he can decide for himself.

Neely's alternate plan rests on his own field: mind over body, a switch in the brain that can call up vast stores of energy. As his body fails on the table, his will fights to pull him back. The tale turns on a stark question: can a trained mind refuse to die when the body gives out?
24910-the-last-woman:
Ross Beeckman published The Last Woman in New York in 1909, with a frontispiece by Howard Chandler Christy. Its theme verse asks for one treasure above all: you. The romance turns on Beatrice Brunswick's plot, a strange betrothal, a box at the opera, and Patricia's cowboy lover, with Monday the thirteenth bringing trouble.

Duncan, the hero, presses Jack Gardner, a young copper king, over a marriage-ceremony story Beatrice is said to have planted. Did Radnor question him, and did he concoct the tale at her bidding? Jealousy, pride, and sudden meetings drive the plot. Beeckman writes a high-society romance with Western color, in the popular style of its day.
24959-working-with-the-working-woman:
Cornelia Stratton Parker spent months taking factory jobs herself, and this 1922 Harper volume reports what she found from inside the work. She packs chocolates as No. 1075, works brass as 286, irons 'family' pieces as 195, sews in a dress factory, tickets pillow cases as No. 536, and serves as pantry girl No. 1470. The numbers replace names, and the pace, pay, and foremen's tempers become daily facts.

Irma, one of her fellow workers, earns thirteen dollars a week, a figure Parker sets against rent, food, and the cost of keeping respectable. The book's strength is its plain testimony: no theory, just the ache, the noise, and the small solidarities of the shop floor. It remains a vivid record of women's industrial work in the early 1920s.
25103-historic-tales-the-romance-of-real:
Charles Morris's Historic Tales, volume two, American, published by Lippincott in 1904, retells episodes from American history as short, stirring stories. It is one of fifteen volumes in Morris's popular series, written to make the past vivid for general readers and younger audiences.

Tales run from Ponce de Leon and the Fountain of Youth through De Soto on the Mississippi and the lost colony of Roanoke. Later tales cover Captain John Smith, La Salle, Patrick Henry, King's Mountain, and Eli Whitney's cotton gin. Later stories reach the Alamo and Houston's fight for Texas. Each tale stands alone, and together they form a brisk pageant of American adventure.
2520-the-man:
Bram Stoker, best known for Dracula, published this novel in 1897, and it opens in a quiet English churchyard where two children argue about angels and God. From that small scene grows the life story of Stephen Norman, a headstrong young woman raised with unusual freedom by her guardian.

Stephen loves, chooses, and suffers through the rules her world sets for women, while Leonard Everard and her circle test her resolve. Stoker writes with warmth about loyalty, pride, and forgiveness, and the book ends as a plea for judging people by their hearts rather than by custom. It is a gentler, more domestic Stoker than horror readers may expect.
25295-pharaoh-s-broker-being-the-very-re:
Pharaoh's Broker, edited by Ellsworth Douglass and published in London in 1899, presents the remarkable experiences in another world of Isidor Werner, written by himself. Werner's guide is Dr. Hermann Anderwelt, the Heidelberg professor who once failed Werner's physics examinations and kept him a year longer at the university.

Anderwelt builds a gravity projectile to carry them to Mars, through terrors of light, twilight of space, space fever, and the mystery of a minus weight. On Mars they face terror birds, armies, and Zaphnath, ruler of the Kemi, plus iron men from a blue star. The book mixes adventure with cosmic speculation.
25345-the-goose-man:
Jacob Wassermann's Goose Man, in Allen W. Porterfield's authorized translation, was published in 1922. Its title refers to the famous Goose Man statue in Nuremberg, and its first chapter and part of its second were translated by Ludwig Lewisohn.

Chapters follow a mother seeking her son, foes and brothers, a friend and a mask, Inspector Jordan and his children, and Daniel and Gertrude. A scene with Marian and a pregnant girl named Meta shows Wassermann's tender attention to women in trouble. The novel is a rich German story of art, family, and fate.
25438-the-airlords-of-han:
Philip Francis Nowlan continues the adventures of Anthony Rogers in this 1929 Amazing Stories serial. Rogers, overcome by radioactive gas in a Scranton mine in 1927, slept nearly five hundred years. He wakes to an America crushed under the Han Airlords, who rule from the air and call themselves a race of destiny. Rogers joins the forest men who plot to throw off Han rule.

The serial's chapters move from besieged airlords and ground ships to electrono-ray science, hypnotic torture, and the fall of Nu-Yok. Life in Lo-Tan, air balls, escape, and a counter-attack lead to victory. Nowlan mocks Han pride: centuries of killing weaklings, he notes, only forged stronger foes.
25504-khartoum-campaign-1898-or-the-re-c:
Bennet Burleigh served as a war correspondent for the Daily Telegraph. He recounts the 1898 Sudan campaign from his own day-by-day notes and dispatches. His account runs from the victory at Omdurman on 2 September 1898 through later moves to Fashoda and Sobat. It closes with the withdrawal of Major Marchand and his French mission.

Maps, battle plans, and many pictures support the narrative. Burleigh treats the fall of Mahdist rule as the opening of the Upper Nile to new rule from Khartoum. He writes as a witness on the ground, not as a later historian. Marches, river moves, and fighting fill the foreground. Questions about who should govern the region stay open in his preface.
25625-historic-tales-the-romance-of-real:
Charles Morris writes the Russian volume, eighth in his fifteen-volume Historical Tales, subtitled The Romance of Reality, published by Lippincott in 1898. The Kremlin fronts the book, marking Russia's historic heart.

The ancient Scythians, Oleg the Varangian, the vengeance of Queen Olga, and Vladimir the Great open the tales. The yoke of the Tartars, the victory of the Don, Ivan the first of the czars, and Ivan the Terrible follow. The conquest of Siberia, the era of impostors, and the boyhood of Peter the Great close a sweep from early tribes to empire.
25673-historic-tales-the-romance-of-real:
Charles Morris writes the Roman volume, eleventh in his fifteen-volume Historical Tales, subtitled The Romance of Reality, published by Lippincott in 1896. Castle St. Angelo fronts the book, a Roman landmark for a Roman history.

How Rome was founded opens the tales, with the Sabine virgins, the Horatii and Curiatii, and the dynasty of the Tarquins following. The books of the Sibyl, the story of Lucretia, and brave Horatius keeping the bridge lead onward. The battle of Lake Regillus, the revolt of the people, and the revenge of Coriolanus carry Rome from kings toward republic.
25779-drag-harlan:
Charles Alden Seltzer, author of The Boss of the Lazy Y and Firebrand Trevison, writes Drag Harlan, published by Grosset and Dunlap in May 1921 with a front picture by P. V. E. Ivory. A woman lays her head on Harlan's shoulder, sobbing and talking incoherently, in that picture.

Chapters open with a desert rider emerging from shimmering haze, a man's reputation, and a girl waiting. His shadow before, a prison, and chain lightning follow, as Harlan, a gunman with a past, rides into Purgatory, where wariness, love, and vengeance test whether a hard man can change.
25877-the-little-gingerbread-man:
G. H. P. tells a picture tale of a gingerbread man who runs from his makers, printed by Putnam in 1910 with pictures and decorations by Robert Gaston Herbert. The cook mixes flour, water, treacle, ginger, salt, and spice into a smooth dark yellow dough, cuts square cakes for little boys, and shapes one small man. Once baked, the little fellow takes to his heels, and the chase is on.

The fun runs through farmyard mix ups, with Towser the dog leaping after the cat at the cook's call, and beast, dog, and cook tumbling together in a fizzing heap. The gingerbread man dodges, teases, and scampers on, too quick for hands that would hold him. Herbert's pictures mark each turn, from the kitchen to the walk, in a tale made for reading aloud.
25916-prescott-of-saskatchewan:
Harold Bindloss sets a prairie tale of a wastrel, a land deal, and a promise, printed in 1913 and called The Wastrel in England. Jernyngham's happy thought opens the book, and Muriel soon sees the West, feels regret, and faces the mystery of the muskeg. A deal in land, a search, a day on the prairie, and a new clue lead to a revelation and a vow from Prescott.

The frontispiece shows folk putting long distance between themselves and the settlement, and the plot turns on shelter, quiet, and privacy. Jernyngham begs Prescott to take in his party, saying no one else near can house them and terms are no concern. Prescott holds his peace while the plea grows urgent. Bindloss writes of Saskatchewan farms, muskeg, and hard bargains with his usual outdoor drive.
2605-noto-an-unexplored-corner-of-japan:
Percival Lowell wrote this travel book about Noto, a remote corner of Japan he calls unexplored. He addressed it to his friend Basil Hall Chamberlain, the confidant of his hopes for the trip. Lowell's chapters run from first arrivals through the Usui Pass and the temple town of Zenkoji.

He notes new cornice roads, local shrines, and villages few foreign travelers had reached, with the curiosity of a man who loved Japan deeply. The book mixes road narrative with notes on custom and landscape. It reads as a gentle expedition into a Japan already changing, written before the age of mass travel.
26146-charles-frohman-manager-and-man:
Isaac F. Marcosson and Daniel Frohman published this life of theatrical manager Charles Frohman in 1916, opening with an appreciation by James M. Barrie. Its chapters trace Frohman from a child amid the theater. They follow hard years on the road and a spell as a minstrel manager. Then comes the New York whirlpool of booking, producing, and star-making.

Later chapters cover his stock company and the Empire Theatre. They also cover stars such as Maude Adams, John Drew, and Ethel Barrymore. The rise of the theatrical syndicate and his conquest of the London stage follow. Appendices add his letters and a full dated list of his productions, making the book both a life story and a record of American theater in his era.
26240-the-clansman-an-historical-romance:
Thomas Dixon's 1905 romance, the second book in his series on the race conflict, tells what Dixon calls the true story of the Ku Klux Klan conspiracy against Reconstruction rule. Dixon says the Klan, run by a Grand Wizard at Memphis with state and county officers below him, overturned the Reconstruction regime. His book is dedicated to his uncle, Colonel Leroy McAfee, whom he names a Grand Titan.

This edition adds pictures from the photo-play The Birth of a Nation. Opening pages show ragged soldiers in captured blue coats streaming home after surrender, while a doctor praises Lincoln's offers of peace and mercy. The novel presents Dixon's partisan view of the post-war South, and modern readers meet it as a historical document of its author's cause, not as a neutral history.
26427-cardinal-newman-as-a-musician:
Edward Bellasis, author of a life of Cherubini, wrote this 1892 study of Cardinal Newman's musical side, reprinted with additions and musical examples from The Month of September 1891. Bellasis quotes Newman on music as the expression of ideas greater and more profound than any in the visible world, ideas centered in God as the seat of beauty, order, and perfection. For Newman, music was no mere trick of art or fashion of the day.

The study also records Newman's modesty about his own gifts. He counted himself only ordinary folk in music, called his verses ephemeral effusions, and doubted he could match a classical Jesuit in Latin plays. The book thus pairs high doctrine about music's power to stir noble emotion with a humble portrait of the cardinal as amateur.
26719-an-anarchist-woman:
Hutchins Hapgood published this novel with Duffield and Company at New York in 1909, with a Goethe epigraph: the government that makes itself superfluous is best. Hapgood, author of The Autobiography of a Thief and The Spirit of Labor, tells the life of Marie. He first met her at twenty-three, a factory hand and servant girl who had translated her life into thought.

Marie was born in a Chicago slum; the year was 1884, to a cruel mother, half French and half German, and a drunken machinist father of German extraction. Both parents beat her, and authorities forced her to school for only two years. Chapters run from school and factory through domestic service to Terry, the meeting, the rogues' gallery, and the salon. Marie's attempt, failure, and revolt close a life shaped by vice, misery, and books.
26882-omega-the-man:
Lowell Howard Morrow wrote this story for Amazing Stories in January 1933, illustrated by Morey. A silver airship cuts through hot, thin air above a dead desert earth and settles on a salt-encrusted plain at the bottom of an ancient sea. From it float down Omega and Thalma, man and wife, the sole survivors of all earth's children. They are hairless and toothless, with huge heads, enormous chests, slender fleshless legs, and feet reduced to toeless stubs.

Millions of years of sun and wind have drunk the seas dry. One shallow brackish lake of scarcely a hundred acres remains, rimmed with yellow-green grass and faded flowers. That lake holds the last of earth's waters, and the couple's last hope clings to it. Yet one form of life still stands between them and the water: a beast that may or may not leave the lake at night to hunt.
26909-historical-introductions-to-the-sy:
F. Bente's historical introductions explain the Symbolical Books of the Evangelical Lutheran Church, the set of confessions gathered as the Book of Concord. He traces the word symbol from the Greek sumbolon, a token or watchword, to its use as a short rule of faith.

The volume then works through the three ecumenical creeds, the Augsburg Confession, Melanchthon's changes to it, the Roman reply, and the Apology. Readers get the history behind each document: who wrote it, what dispute forced it, and why Lutherans still treat the whole set as their agreed statement of belief.
26910-stories-of-authors-british-and-ame:
Edwin Watts Chubb, professor of English literature at Ohio University, published this illustrated volume with Sturgis and Walton of New York in 1910. Forty-five chapters tell stories of British writers. They run from the ancient Tabard Inn and Sir Philip Sidney at Zutphen through Shakspere, Milton, Lamb, and Johnson. They continue through Gray writing the Elegy and Gibbon's visit to Rome to Burns, Coleridge, Byron, Shelley, Keats, Scott, Dickens, the Brownings, and Kipling in India.

Fifteen more chapters cover American writers. They run from Benjamin Franklin running away and Washington Irving through Cooper and The Spy. They continue through Hawthorne and The Scarlet Letter, Longfellow the universal poet, Thoreau, and the last days of Edgar Allan Poe. Anecdotes carry the book's charm. Pope got $45,000 for his Homer against Milton's $25 for Paradise Lost. Chaucer, two years before his death, petitioned the king for a hogshead of wine a year.
27068-the-dead-command-from-the-spanish-:
Vicente Blasco Ibáñez's The Dead Command, translated by Frances Douglas from Los Muertos Mandan and published in 1919, opens in a Majorcan palace. Jaime Febrer rises at nine, roused by old Antonia, the servant who cherishes the past glories of his family.

Jaime, invited to breakfast at Valldemosa, lives among worm-eaten blinds and a lordly couch where generations of Febrers were born and died. The novel turns on the dead commanding the living, as a proud house faces marriage with Catalina Valls, offspring of the executed Jew, and old wives' tales stir.
27260-east-of-suez-ceylon-india-china-an:
Frederic Courtland Penfield's East of Suez, Ceylon, India, China and Japan, illustrated from drawings and photographs, continues his Present-Day Egypt. Penfield, former American diplomatic agent and consul-general to Egypt, received the Khedive's thanks for the earlier book, the only one on Egypt of today by an author long resident there.

The frontispiece shows a Gulf of Manar pearling boat with divers resting in the water. Chapters follow pearl fisheries, breadfruit, sensitive plants, kola trees, cardamom bushes, and aloe plants yielding sisal. Camphor and cinnamon shrubs fill a travel book of the East's coasts, gardens, and trades at the century's turn.
27280-the-praise-of-a-godly-woman:
Hanniball Gamon's The Praise of a Godly Woman is a sermon preached at the solemn funeral of Lady Frances Roberts at Lanhide-rock Church in Cornwall on August 10, 1626. It was printed at London in 1627. Gamon, minister at St. Maugan, takes his texts from First Corinthians and Galatians.

Judge nothing before the time, and neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free, male nor female, for all are one in Christ Jesus, frame the praise. Dedicated to John Roberts, son and heir, the sermon holds Lady Frances as a rare phoenix among women fearing the Lord.
27324-where-deep-seas-moan:
E. Gallienne-Robin set this novel on the rocky island of Guernsey, and Frederick Clarke printed it there in 1907. The story opens at Colomberie Farm, a comfortable house with a brown-thatched roof and a wide hearth. There pretty young Blaisette, the farmer's daughter, sets out into a great autumn wind that rattles the leafless trees.

From that stormy opening, the tale moves between farmhouse warmth and a stern granite house sheltered under a rocky cliff, in valleys of bracken and heather. Gallienne-Robin writes the island itself almost as a character, with its lanes, winds, and seas. Readers who enjoy regional novels will find Guernsey life drawn close and vivid.
2733-romano-lavo-lil-word-book-of-the-ro:
This word book of the Romany, or English Gypsy, language opens with a challenge. It asks the reader, in Romany and in English, whether he can speak the tongue, play the fiddle, eat prison loaf, and cut and whittle. The 1905 John Murray edition pairs vocabulary with specimens of Gypsy poetry.

An account of Gypsy life and speech accompanies the lists, giving the words a human setting. The book serves students of language, folklore, and the traveling people of Britain. It remains a pioneering record of a language once passed only by mouth, now fixed in print.
27423-elkan-lubliner-american:
Montague Glass, author of Potash and Perlmutter, published this set of stories with Doubleday, Page at Garden City, New York, in 1912. Its hero Elkan Lubliner moves through a world of Jewish immigrant businessmen in America, and the stories take their humor from showrooms, accounts, matches, and family obligations.

The opening story finds partners Marcus Polatkin and Philip Scheikowitz conserving the honour of their families. Marcus complains of a cousin in Minsk whose every letter brings a death and a plea for funeral expenses. Further stories include Appenweier's Account, A Match for Elkan Lubliner, and A Tale of Two Jacobean Chairs. Glass writes warm, dialect comedy with affection.
27431-the-adventures-of-daniel-boone-the:
The author of Uncle Philip's Conversations wrote this life of Daniel Boone, the Kentucky rifleman, published by D. Appleton in New York and Philadelphia, entered for copyright in 1843. Uncle Philip dedicates it warmly to young Americans everywhere, and above all to the lads of Kentucky.

Boone's own saying stands at the front, that he felt too crowded and wanted more elbow-room, spoken on his way to Missouri. The first chapter finds him born in Bucks County, Pennsylvania, and the story follows the frontiersman westward. Young readers get a stirring, old-fashioned hero tale of the American frontier.
27448-the-indian-to-day-the-past-and-fut:
Charles A. Eastman, called Ohiyesa, author of Old Indian Days and Indian Boyhood, published this book with Doubleday, Page at Garden City, New York, in 1915. It appeared in the American Books series, a library of good citizenship offering authoritative manuals on problems of interest in America today.

Eastman was born near Redwood Falls, Minnesota, in the winter of 1858, in a teepee of buffalo hide. He was the son of a full-blooded Sioux father, and he writes as a Native American about the past and future of the first Americans. The book weighs what had happened to Indian peoples and what might come next. It remains a valuable Native voice on policy and identity.
27494-the-patriotic-poems-of-walt-whitma:
Doubleday, Page published this selection of Walt Whitman's patriotic poems at Garden City, New York, in 1918, drawing on copyrights from 1855 to 1891 and on the work of his literary executors. The opening poem, America, hails a grand, sane, towering Mother, seated in Time's adamant, centre of equal daughters and equal sons.

Poems of War follow, including Thick-Sprinkled Bunting, Beat! Beat! Drums!, City of Ships, and A March in the Ranks Hard-Prest, and the Road Unknown. Whitman's democratic voice, ample and direct, runs through the set. The volume gathers his public, national verse in one compact book.
27499-folk-lore-and-legends-german:
W. W. Gibbings published this little volume of German folk-lore and legends in London in 1892, as the first of a series. Companion volumes were planned for Oriental, Scottish, and Irish lore, with a second series for England, Scandinavia, Russia, and North American Indian tales.

The prefatory note argues that a nation's legendary history recites the elements that formed its character. Legends hold early attempts to explain natural phenomena, traditions of early history, and moral rules of reward and punishment. German tales here mix charming simplicity with weird, fantastic matter, fit for a land of broad rivers, mountains, and deep forests.
27730-the-doomsman:
Van Tassel Sutphen's 1906 novel The Doomsman opens on a beach where a boy watches the sea, and builds toward a tale of terror, a new world, and a man on horseback. Published by Harper and Brothers with illustrations, it carries chapter titles such as The Night of the Terror and The Hedge of Arrows.

The story mixes romance, adventure, and fate, with a hero named Constans and a villain in Quinton Edge, moving toward a doomsday climax. Sutphen, author of The Cardinal's Rose, wrote for readers who liked their historical romance shadowed by doom.
2774-the-patrician:
John Galsworthy wrote this novel in two parts, following an English patrician through love, politics, and family duty. The hero, born to rank and wealth, must choose between a brilliant match and a woman the world calls unsuitable.

Galsworthy writes with restraint about the codes that bind the upper class, and the costs of breaking them. The novel moves from country houses to London drawing rooms, with his usual moral clarity. It stands as a study of privilege, and of a man learning its price. Galsworthy's patrician learns that rank cannot buy love.
27849-th-history-o-haworth-railway-fra-t:
Bill o'th' Hoylus End wrote this dialect pamphlet on the history of the Haworth railway, from its beginning to its end, with an account of the opening ceremony. The tenth edition was printed at Keighley in 1902 and sold for a single penny.

Written in Yorkshire dialect, the pamphlet jokes about Haworth, its founders, and the railway scheme that gave the author ample food for his pen. Its many editions show its local popularity, and it preserves a comic, vernacular voice from the West Riding at the turn of the century.
27950-the-rhodesian:
Gertrude Page, author of The Edge o' Beyond and The Silent Rancher, wrote The Rhodesian, published in London by Hurst and Blackett. The novel opens at night in Southern Rhodesia, among the grey walls of the Zimbabwe ruins, which baffle ingenuity and ravish curiosity.

Thirty-two chapters follow a police station and a mission station, two heiresses, a Rhodesian project, a mining camp, ancient ruins, and decisions by Meryl, Carew, Diana, and Ailsa. Page writes colonial romance with the landscape and social codes of early Rhodesia at its center, and the book is dedicated to the pathfinders.
27968-tulan:
C. C. MacApp wrote Tulan, a science-fiction novella about a space admiral of the old school who must disobey the Council of Four if his people are to live. The story opens with Admiral Tulan of the fleets of Sennech storming down stone steps after the council refuses to listen, even his ally Grefen.

The council orders full crews taken to Coar and surrendered with the ships. Tulan sees that Coar's new weapon has lost accuracy behind the sun and that he could pound her into surrender. The tale turns on duty, independent judgment, and a commander's refusal to accept a cowardly peace.
28060-the-fight-for-the-argonne-personal:
William Benjamin West published The Fight for the Argonne, personal experiences of a Y man, with the Abingdon Press in 1919, with an introduction by Burges Johnson. West dedicates the book to the boys of the 37th Division, American Expeditionary Forces, with whom he served on the Alsatian border and in the Argonne.

The front matter lists the division's units and commanders on September 5, 1918, from Major General C. S. Farnsworth to the 112th Trench Mortar Battery. West drove a Ford camionette for the YMCA, and his memoir gives a noncombatant's close view of the Meuse-Argonne fighting.
28216-respiration-calorimeters-for-study:
Francis G. Benedict and Thorne M. Carpenter wrote Respiration Calorimeters in 1910 for the Carnegie Institution of Washington, publication number 123. The volume describes chambers built to measure the heat and gases of the human body at rest and at work, so that doctors could study food, energy, and metabolism. The Nutrition Laboratory in Boston built and tested the apparatus.

Preface notes credit mechanicians and chemists who built steel frames, heating, and cooling devices, and who ran early trials. New features, the authors say, will keep coming as accuracy grows. The book gives a detailed record of early scientific instruments for the study of human energy.
28242-an-appeal-in-favor-of-that-class-o:
Lydia Maria Child wrote An Appeal in Favor of That Class of Americans Called Africans, New York, 1836, as one of the first American books against slavery by a woman. Child begs readers not to drop the book at its title. They should read for truth's sake, for her sake, or even from curiosity at what a woman will say on such a subject. Coleridge's lines on offence open the volume.

Child argues that Americans have offended grievously and been tyrannous to their Black brethren, sons of God. Her appeal mixes history, law, and moral argument, aimed at northern readers. The book stands as a landmark of abolitionist writing, brave and plain-spoken.
28301-the-beloved-woman:
Kathleen Norris wrote The Beloved Woman in 1921, copyright 1920 to 1921, as a novel of New York in a great snowstorm. For forty-eight hours snow raged over the city, banking in dirty blocks, while clean flakes powdered ledges and capped hydrants. Norris, author of Harriet and the Piper, dedicates the book to Mary O'Sullivan Sutro, for gifts beyond counting.

The story follows a beloved woman through love, family, and city life, in Norris's warm, popular style. A. L. Burt published the book by arrangement with Doubleday, Page. Readers of early twentieth-century domestic fiction will enjoy its snowbound opening and heartfelt plot.
28323-travels-in-north-america-from-mode:
Rev. William Bingley wrote Travels in North America, from Modern Writers, London, 1821, for young persons, with remarks and observations. Bingley, late of Peterhouse, Cambridge, gathers modern writers on the geography and present state of North America, from Washington and the pyramid of Cholula to New York. Harvey and Darton published the volume, with a frontispiece of American scenes.

Bingley frames the travels as daily lessons from a parent to children, aiming to lure young readers to geography through anecdotes of adventure. His earlier volumes treated Europe, South America, and Africa. The book offers a connected, schoolroom view of America in 1821.
28495-scally-the-story-of-a-perfect-gent:
Ian Hay's Scally, published in November 1915, tells how a family came to buy a dog. The narrator and his wife ride a Battersea tram while debating breed, sex, and age. His wife is torn between a bloodhound and a Pekinese, her sister urges an Old English sheepdog, and their three-year-old son asks for twelve tigers in a box.

They settle on an Aberdeen terrier, and the small, wet, shivering puppy of the frontispiece becomes Scally. Hay's short, humorous story follows the dog's life with his people, and its title says what the family learns: Scally is a perfect gentleman. The book is light, affectionate, and very British in its comedy.
28583-the-calm-man:
Frank Belknap Long's science-fiction story The Calm Man centers on Sally Anders, a shy woman whose ordinary life is upended. The tale opens with Sally watching molten gold in the sky, certain she will not see her son and husband again on Earth. It then rewinds to Sally primping for a party, with Uncle Ben near and dancing couples around her.

A corned beef and cabbage dinner anchors the homely scene before stranger events take hold. The contrast between the party and the sky gives the story its tension, as domestic detail meets a fate beyond Earth. Readers get a short, sharp tale of loss, wonder, and a life split in two.
28598-religion-in-japan:
George A. Cobbold's Religion in Japan, published by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge in 1905, treats Shintoism, Buddhism, and Christianity. Cobbold opens with Japan's transformation in a single generation, from a terra incognita more exclusive than China to a nation remade. New criminal codes, courts, police, posts, telegraphs, schools, army and navy, railways, harbours, and parliament replaced monarchical absolutism.

The Mikado drives a carriage fit for London or Paris, European dress rules at court, and English authors fill university reading. Chapters then take Shintoism, Buddhism in Japan, Buddhism and Christianity, and Christianity in Japan in turn. Readers get a missionary-era survey of faith amid rapid change.
28852-seventeen-species-of-bats-recorded:
E. Raymond Hall and William B. Jackson wrote this 1953 natural history paper listing seventeen species of bats found on Barro Colorado Island in the Panama Canal Zone. The paper updates earlier lists with fieldwork from April and May 1952. Researchers stretched a silk net thirty feet long and seven feet high across clearings and trails to catch bats on eight evenings.

Jackson, working with a group from the American Museum of Natural History, also set nets across Allee Creek in May. The paper gives a careful, dated record of which kinds were actually caught and where, a small but solid contribution to Panama's mammal survey. Readers interested in tropical biology get a precise snapshot of island bat life in the early 1950s.
29000-the-macdermots-of-ballycloran:
Anthony Trollope wrote this 1866 novel about the Macdermots of Ballycloran, in a fourth edition from Chapman and Hall. The story opens in the autumn of 184-. Business takes the narrator to Drumsna, a quiet village in Leitrim, seventy-two miles west-northwest of Dublin on the mail-coach road toward Sligo. Ballycloran House, its family, and its tenantry fill the early chapters, with Father John, Myles Ussher, and Mr. Keegan.

Later chapters bring a wedding, a coroner's inquest, escapes, a duel, and Thady's trial at the assizes in Carrick-on-Shannon. Trollope writes of Irish landlords, priests, and tenants with his usual care for character and money. Readers get an early Trollope novel of Ireland before the famine's shadow, tragic in its close and humane throughout.
29056-almost-a-man:
Mary Wood-Allen, a doctor, wrote this 1895 book, Almost a Man, published by her own Wood-Allen company in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The book opens with a prelude in which two lads, having crossed the sunny meadow land of childhood, stand at the gate to youth's rougher paths. An angel brings each a gift, not for himself but for others, and bids them listen.
