One lad hears only entrancing music for himself, while the other hears, deeper than pleasure, a holier strain. The chapters that follow, A Gateway and a Gift and The White Cross, draw the moral out. Wood-Allen writes for boys on the edge of manhood, in the earnest, improving style of her Teaching Truth. Readers get a short moral allegory about selfish pleasure and service to others.
29057-address-delivered-by-hon-henry-h-c:
Michigan governor Henry H. Crapo gave this address on May 24, 1866, to the Central Michigan Agricultural Society at its sheep-shearing exhibition on the Agricultural College Farm. Speaking just after the Civil War, Crapo notes that Michigan, far from the fighting, had kept its peaceful pursuits largely undisturbed while other states bore the war's direct costs.

Crapo turns from that contrast to farming itself: the work of the state's farmers, the role of the agricultural college, and the value of societies that spread better methods. Readers get a postwar governor's case for agriculture as Michigan's steady engine, delivered to the farmers gathered for a working exhibition rather than a formal ceremony.
29172-ferdinand-de-soto-the-discoverer-o:
John S. C. Abbott published this life of Ferdinand de Soto in New York in 1873, in the American Pioneers and Patriots series, illustrated and issued by Dodd and Mead. Abbott draws on Theodore Irving's history of the conquest of Florida, which praised de Soto's enterprise for hardihood and variety of incident above all Spanish ventures of the age.

De Soto, a Spanish cavalier of the early sixteenth century, led an expedition through Florida and the southeast and reached the Mississippi River. Abbott tells the march, its battles, and its hardships in the brisk style of the series. Readers get a nineteenth-century biography of a conquistador, heroic in tone and dated in view, but clear about the expedition's route and cost.
2924-the-perpetuation-of-living-beings-h:
Thomas Henry Huxley gave this lecture on the perpetuation of living beings, hereditary transmission, and variation as part of his working-men series on Darwin. He frames two questions, whether we know anything of the origin of living beings, and whether, granting an origin, we know anything about how forms persist and change. His answer to the first is altogether negative, and the lecture builds from there.

Huxley illustrates spontaneous variation with a man born with an unusual number of fingers and toes on each hand and foot, a case carefully observed at the time. Nobody knows why the variation appeared, he notes, which is why it earns the name spontaneous. The lecture shows Darwin's chief defender explaining heredity to a popular audience with examples rather than jargon.
29265-the-story-of-the-great-war-volume-:
Francis J. Reynolds edited this third volume of The Story of the Great War, a history of the European war drawn from official sources, with drawings, maps, and photographs. Prefaces come from Major General Leonard Wood, Rear Admiral Austin Knight, Frederick Palmer, Frank Simonds, and Arthur Ruhl. The volume gathers complete historical records of events to date.

Part one covers the Russian and Turkish campaign, including the Caucasus. Later parts treat Japan and the Far East, the war in Africa, and the western front. Naval operations, the eastern front, and the Balkans follow. Italy enters the war, and the Dardanelles, Arabia, Mesopotamia, and Egypt close the volume. Readers get a contemporary, richly illustrated history of the First World War's middle years.
29270-the-story-of-the-great-war-volume-:
Francis J. Reynolds edited this second volume of The Story of the Great War, a history of the European war drawn from official sources, illustrated with drawings, maps, and photographs. Like its companions, it carries prefaces by Major General Leonard Wood, Rear Admiral Austin Knight, Frederick Palmer, Frank Simonds, and Arthur Ruhl.

Part one covers the great battles of the western armies, from the attack on Belgium through the Battle of the Marne. Later parts treat naval operations, the eastern front, the Austro-Serbian campaign, the Austro-Russian and Russo-German campaigns, and Turkey and the Dardanelles. Readers get a contemporary illustrated history of the war's opening campaigns, written while the outcome was still unknown.
29300-rodney-the-partisan:
Harry Castlemon published this Civil War boys' novel in Philadelphia in 1890, in his War Series, with illustrations by George White. Rodney, the young partisan of the title, bids his mother farewell on the frontispiece and joins the rangers. Chapters follow the rangers electing officers, drills and parades, a scheme that fails, and a warning.

Later chapters bring suspicion, emergency men, a trade, and service with Price's men, through Bull Run to a full-fledged partisan and the Conscription Act. Castlemon, a veteran writer of boys' adventure, mixes camp life with action. Readers get a brisk Civil War story for young readers, told from the Confederate partisan side, in the popular series style of the day.
2933-on-some-fossil-remains-of-man:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote On Some Fossil Remains of Man to ask whether ancient human bones close the gap between humans and apes. He argues that the Anthropini, or man family, form a well-defined group of primates, with no transitional form linking them to the Catarhini in the existing world. Fossil evidence, he suggests, might diminish or even erase those intervals.

Huxley tests that hope against bones found in a thin mud deposit without stalagmite cover, which still kept much of their organic substance. Such preservation argues against great geological age, he warns, and warns against calling a skull the most savage primitive type when living peoples show similar forms. The essay remains a model of cautious reasoning about human origins.
29337-japanese-fairy-world-stories-from-:
William Elliot Griffis, author of The Mikado's Empire, published this collection in London in 1887 with Trubner and Company, illustrated by Ozawa of Tokio. Griffis gathers thirty-four stories from Japan's wonder-lore, chosen, his preface says, without the bloody, revengeful, or licentious elements found in some collections. A front illustration shows the sun-goddess enticed out of her cave.

Stories include The Meeting of the Star-Lovers, The Travels of Two Frogs, The Child of the Thunder, and The Tongue-Cut Sparrow. The Fire-Fly's Lovers, The Battle of the Ape and the Crab, The Wonderful Tea-Kettle, and Peach-Prince and the Treasure Island follow. Readers get a classic English collection of Japanese fairy tales, gentle in selection and rich in wonder.
29379-the-new-york-stock-exchange-and-pu:
Otto H. Kahn delivered these remarks at the annual dinner of the Association of Stock Exchange Brokers. The dinner was held at the Astor Hotel in New York on January 24, 1917. The New York Stock Exchange published the remarks. Kahn opens with a personal matter: a couple of weeks earlier he went to Washington to contradict under oath a gross calumny about his name, based on anonymous and irresponsible gossip.

On the train, Kahn rehearsed questions a committee might ask within its inquiry's scope, turning the ride into mental preparation. His remarks then take up the Exchange and public opinion, defending the market's role while answering its critics. Readers get a banker's public self-defense at a moment of scrutiny, frank about reputation and about the Exchange's place in American life.
29385-the-story-of-the-great-war-volume-:
This sixth volume of The Story of the Great War is a history of the European war from official sources. It covers the revolution in Russia and the United States at war among its themes. Edited by Francis J. Reynolds, it is illustrated with drawings, maps, and photographs, with an index at page 495. The volume gathers complete historical records of events to date.

Parts cover the western front at the Somme and Verdun, the eastern front, the Balkans, and the Austro-Italian front. Later parts treat war in the air and on the sea, the United States and the belligerents, the United States and Germany, and the Russian Revolution. Readers get a contemporary illustrated history of the war's turning years, written from official sources as events unfolded.
29581-the-bondwoman:
Marah Ellis Ryan, author of Told in the Hills and A Pagan of the Alleghanies, set The Bondwoman in France and America. It was printed in 1899 by Rand, McNally of Chicago and New York. Near Moret, where the Seine gathers and runs northward, lives Madame Blanc, an old lady who knows much of the history told here. She once served in the Caron household when Judithe first joined the family.

Madame Blanc now keeps a home for aged ladies of education whose means will not allow them to provide for themselves. A picture in the book shows a woman giving back a wedding ring. Readers of historical romance will find a tale of bonds, duty, and women's lives stretched between two countries.
29643-death-of-a-spaceman:
Walter M. Miller, Jr.'s short tale follows old man Donegal, dying as his family watches: his haggard wife, his daughter, and his grandson, back from the pre-astronautics academy on emergency leave. Donegal spent most of his adult life digging a tunnel through space to learn what lay on the other side. He knows he is dying, having lost control of his legs and taken to a cane.

Miller's tag line says the way a man has lived often explains the way he will die. Martha can bear his death, Donegal thinks, and can bear foreknowledge of it, but not the thought that he might take it calmly. Fans of Miller will enjoy a grave, humane tale of age, space, and a death faced head-on.
29646-once-to-every-man:
Larry Evans's 1913 novel was printed by Grosset and Dunlap of New York with pictures by Anton Otto Fischer. It opens in late afternoon giving way to nightfall, a long twilight heavy with spring scent despite patches of wet snow. Its frontispiece cries that it was for me you went, and only because of you that I desired them at all. Later pictures plead to be held tight, for they forgot me too.

Evans writes a romance of love, war, and memory, where once, to every man, comes a chance that defines a life. The novel's pictures carry its emotional peaks. Readers of early twentieth-century romance will find a heartfelt, period tale of longing and loyalty.
29759-architecture-classic-and-early-chr:
T. Roger Smith and John Slater wrote this handbook for the Illustrated Handbooks of Art History series, printed in London in 1882. Its aim is an outline of the architecture of the ancient world and of Christendom down to the Crusades. The authors do not try to give the minute detail a professional student needs. They aim to give a general idea of the works of the great building nations.

The Parthenon at Athens, as it stood in the time of Pericles around 438 BC, fronts the book. An atrium of a Roman mansion shows the domestic side. Technical words that cannot be avoided are explained in the text or in the glossary. The book suits readers of literary or artistic taste who want to know buildings without first learning a trade.
29764-kid-scanlan:
H. C. Witwer tells these eight linked yarns in the voice of a fight fan who trusts his eyes more than books. The narrator, who calls himself Kid Scanlan, sizes up school, work, and the ring with blunt jokes. A teacher earns fifteen dollars a week, a janitor thirty. A good light weight can take five thousand dollars for one fight. Brains, he insists, are fine things, but they are not the only road to a good living.

Each tale turns on a scrap, a bluff, or a bout gone wrong, told in slang that keeps the pace fast. Witwer, known for his fight tales, keeps the humor broad and the morals plain. The book reads as a set of ringside stories about luck, nerve, and getting by when school learning has let a boy down.
29786-raiding-with-morgan:
Byron A. Dunn published this boys' Civil War tale in Chicago in 1903, in his Young Kentuckians series. It follows Calhoun, a young Kentuckian who works in secret for the Knights of the Golden Circle, a hidden Southern society. General John H. Morgan raids through Kentucky and Tennessee meanwhile. Dunn's preface praises Morgan as a peerless raider who took and paroled at least ten thousand Federal soldiers.

The chapters run from Shiloh and Morgan's first raid to Gallatin, Hartsville, a duel, a spy scare, arrest, and a flight south. Calhoun moves through the lines, recruits, is caught, and escapes, with Morgan's horsemen always near. The book is brisk, loyal to the Southern side, and built for young readers who like raids and close calls.
29791-the-most-sentimental-man:
Evelyn E. Smith, praised for bitter-sweet stories of the worlds of tomorrow, wrote this short tale of a farewell. Johnson goes to see the others off at Idlewild, as duty demands, since it will be the last conventional gesture he must make. For centuries the climate has grown hotter, and even before June the day is uncomfortably warm. Sun glints off the bright metal flanks of the ship, and sweat sticks Johnson's shirt to his back.

Clifford, anxious to be off, still will not let inclination rule his acts. He asks Johnson once more if he will change his mind and come. Johnson shakes his head, and the younger man, who lives by the Colonial Officer's Manual, shows hatred through a film of politeness. Once these irritating farewells end, Johnson can live as he wished and dreamed. The tale is wistful, dry, and strange.
29794-tree-spare-that-woodman:
Dave Dryfoos opens this science fiction tale on an alien planet, where settlers farm in a place called the First Group. Naomi Heckscher walks to the one-room cabin of her old neighbor Cappy with her husband Ted and her small son. She expects a visit, a sip of home brew, and a birthday gift for Richard, who has just turned five. Instead she finds Cappy dead in bed, alone.

The tale turns on fear itself, which its epigraph calls ghastly and walking. Naomi weighs guilt, grief, and the shock of a death no one saw coming. Dryfoos keeps the cast small and the planet strange, so one quiet cabin becomes the whole stage. The story asks what fear does to people who must still live and work beside it.
29798-japan:
David Murray, late advisor to the Japanese Minister of Education, wrote this history of Japan, in a third edition dated 1896. Murray states his object plainly: to trace the story of Japan from its beginnings to the establishment of constitutional government. The task is not easy, he admits, since the story runs from vague, legendary antiquity through medieval disorder and centuries of seclusion.

Fifteen chapters carry the tale from the Japanese archipelago and the original races, through myths, the founding of the empire, and the middle ages, to emperor and shogun. Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the Tokugawa shogunate, and Commodore Perry follow, with revolutionary preludes and the restored empire. Lists of emperors, year periods, shoguns, and the laws of Shotoku Taishi close a trustworthy, connected account.
2992-the-middle-class-gentleman:
Moliere wrote Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme, here as The Middle Class Gentleman, translated by Philip Dwight Jones. The comedy-ballet was presented at Chambord for the king in October 1670 and in Paris at the Palais-Royal Theatre on November 23, 1670. Monsieur Jourdain, a bourgeois, hires masters of music, dancing, fencing, and philosophy to remake himself as a gentleman.

Madame Jourdain, their daughter Lucile, her suitor Cleonte, and the scheming Dorante and Dorimene fill the cast. The famous lesson has Jourdain discover, to his delight, what prose is, as his wife calls his conduct scarcely sensible. The play remains the classic comedy of social climbing, with music, dance, and philosophy all pressed into one man's vanity.
29929-bunyan:
James Anthony Froude wrote Bunyan for the English Men of Letters series, edited by John Morley, printed in London in 1880. Froude opens with Bunyan's own account of his birth: of a low and inconsiderable generation, his father's house of the meanest rank in the land. He never went to school to Aristotle or Plato, but grew up among poor countrymen in his father's house at Elstow, near Bedford, in 1628.

Ten chapters follow conviction of sin, Grace Abounding, and a call to the ministry. Arrest and trial lead to the Bedford gaol, then to The Life and Death of Mr. Badman and The Holy War. The Pilgrim's Progress gets its own chapter, with last days and death to close. Froude holds that no books save the Bible have shaped English spiritual opinion more. The life is short, vivid, and warm.
29963-goodbye-dead-man:
Tom W. Harris wrote Goodbye, Dead Man. Its headnote sets its logic: Mattup had killed a man, so it was logical he should be punished, and Danny came up with leaving him with a prophecy. At Bayless, Kentucky, the reactor installation employed the narrator and his friend Danny Hern when the Outsiders took everything over, and Orley Mattup served there as a guard. Mattup, the narrator insists, was an authentic human, not an Outsider.

Mattup, Danny, and the narrator played high-low-jack on the night Uncle Pete was killed, on the widewalk where Mattup could watch his part of the station. Danny had learned the back-country card game in northern Pennsylvania. Mattup, on a week's losing streak and in a foul humor, called for a new deck twice and walked around his seat four times. Danny advises him to endure the streak of misfortune rather than resist it.
29981-the-truth-about-woman:
C. Gasquoine Hartley, also known as Mrs. Walter M. Gallichan, published The Truth about Woman in New York in 1914, with Dodd, Mead and Company. Hartley was known for books on art and Spain, from A Record of Spanish Painting to Moorish Cities in Spain. She dedicates this book to Leslie, her little adopted son, and states the truth that forced itself upon her in writing it.

The mother, she says, is the main stream of the racial life, and all hope of the future rests upon faith in motherhood. Three parts carry the argument: a biological section, a historical section, and a modern section on present-day aspects of the woman problem. Hartley writes with earnest conviction, joining science, history, and social comment in a period study of woman's place and power.
30057-the-pirate-woman:
Captain Dingle tells a pirate adventure first serialized in All-Story Weekly in four installments, from November 2 to November 23, 1918. Dolores receives a diadem in a cave of terrible things, pirates hold a barbecue, and a party from a yacht stumbles into the grove of mystery. An attack on the vessel Feu Follette, a judgment by Dolores, and a treasure cave keep the plot moving through the second and third installments.

Dingle, author of The Coolie Ship and other sea tales, writes in the brisk pulp style of the weekly magazines, with short chapters and sharp turns. Milo sights a sail, Sancho settles his account, and Yellow Rufe meets his finish before the tale closes. Readers who like old sea yarns, hidden treasure, and a bold heroine at the center will enjoy this fast, colorful serial novel.
30111-a-noble-woman:
Mrs. Ann S. Stephens, author of Palaces and Prisons, Fashion and Famine, and many other popular novels, offers a thrilling domestic story in A Noble Woman. Peterson and Brothers entered the volume in 1871, and its publisher presents it as a tale of leading characters carried through exciting adventures from first page to last. Stephens, the puff says, avoids tangled metaphysics and gives a story pure and simple, sensational if need be.

Readers of her earlier successes, from The Heiress to The Rejected Wife and The Soldier's Orphans, will know the mode: strong feeling, sharp turns, and heroines tested by fortune. The book stands as a sample of mid-Victorian popular fiction, written to hold attention without pause. Modern readers can judge for themselves whether its pace still carries its old charm.
30200-ancient-and-modern-celebrated-free:
Edited by Iconoclast, the pen name of Charles Bradlaugh, with A. Collins and J. Watts, this Boston volume reprints lives and doctrines from Half-Hours with the Freethinkers. Hobbes, Bolingbroke, Condorcet, Spinoza, Collins, Descartes, and Voltaire open the set, followed by Toland, Volney, Blount, Shelley, Helvetius, Epicurus, Zeno the Stoic, Tindal, Hume, Burnet, Paine, Mirabaud, Holbach, Taylor, and Barker.

J. P. Mendum published the book in 1877, and its preface states its aim plainly: to put knowledge of freethought writers, otherwise out of reach, into the hands of the poorest of the party. Each sketch abstracts a life and a doctrine in readable form, from ancient Greece to modern France and England. As a period source, it shows freethought presenting its own heroes to its own readers.
30299-the-romance-of-a-plain-man:
Ellen Glasgow tells The Romance of a Plain Man, published by the Macmillan Company in New York in 1909. Published in May, it was reprinted in May, July, August, September, and October. Glasgow, author of The Deliverance and The Voice of the People, opens with a narrator appearing with few pretensions. Then an enchanted garden, a pair of red shoes, and play in the enchanted garden follow, before he starts in life.

Concerning carrots, mounting the rung of the ladder, and the beginning of his education follow. A little Latin and a deal of life, growing up, entering society and getting a fall, and walking into the country for an adventure follow. Running against traditions, testing his strength, a meeting in the enchanted garden, and Sally speaking her mind follow. Rising fortunes carry the romance toward the principles of Miss Matoaca and the triumph of love.
30364-an-account-of-the-kingdom-of-nepal:
Francis Buchanan Hamilton, M.D., gives an account of the kingdom of Nepal and of the territories annexed to that dominion by the house of Gorkha. The book is illustrated with engravings and inscribed to Richard Marquis Wellesley as a mark of esteem, respect, and gratitude. An opening picture shows the temple of Bouddhama. The first chapter treats the tribes inhabiting the territories of Gorkha, from original inhabitants and Hindu colonies to Brahmans, Rajputs, and low tribes.

Colonies from Chitaur and Asanti, Hindu tribes east and west from the river Kali, language, diet, festivals, and offspring receive attention. Customs of mountain Hindus follow, with Magars, Gurungs, Jariyas, Newars, Murmis, Kiratas, Limbus, Lapchas, and Bhotiyas named. The second chapter turns to the nature of the country, divided into four regions by elevation, beginning with the plain region, or Tariyani, its soil, productions, cultivation, climate, and rivers.
30378-the-merriweather-girls-and-the-mys:
Lizette M. Edholm tells The Merriweather Girls and the Mystery of the Queen's Fan, published by the Goldsmith Publishing Company in Chicago in 1932. Edholm, author of The Merriweather Girls series, opens with private property and a picnic. Then Merriweather Manor, the Queen's fan, across the Hudson, and a rescue follow, with Lady Betty's adventure and a thorn in the flesh.

Late summer sunshine glints on the broad Hudson while three girls sit silent on a hillside high above the bank, each lost in her own thoughts. Bet Baxter tracks a seagull as it rises, wheels, soars, and settles back on the water, her blue eyes following the sweep of its flight and the angle of its wings. Joy Evans watches the gull differently, and the fan, lost and under suspicion, drives the mystery onward.
30601-how-to-analyze-people-on-sight-thr:
Elsie Lincoln Benedict and Ralph Paine Benedict write How to Analyze People on Sight. Subtitled The Five Human Types, it was copyrighted in 1921 and printed by the Roycrofters in East Aurora, New York. Each person, an illustration says, acts according to his type.

The Benedicts thank many men and women for shares in producing the book, opening with thanks to many helpers. Their system sorts people into five types, reading face, body, and manner as clues to character and vocation. The book serves readers curious about personality, hiring, and social life, in the popular psychology of the 1920s.
30623-the-missourian:
Eugene Lyle writes The Missourian, published in New York in August 1905 by Doubleday, Page, with illustrations by Ernest Haskell. An illustration calls Jacqueline the spirit of the enigma, the very personification of the Napoleonic sphinx, and an Omar epigraph opens the book.

The novel is dedicated to the author's father and mother. Its first part, The Thorn in the Land of Roses, opens with a wilful maid arriving and a Fra Diavolo in the land of roses. Lyle blends romance, adventure, and Napoleonic intrigue, with a heroine at its center. The Missourian offers a colorful historical romance for readers of swashbuckling tales.
30705-the-happy-man:
Gerald W. Page writes The Happy Man, a science fiction story from Analog, March 1963, illustrated by George Schelling. It opens with a note that More's Utopia stood apart, sealed off from a bleak world outside, as all utopias do. Nelson rounds an outcropping of rock ten miles from the East Coast Mausoleum and meets a girl at the same moment she sees him.

Facing each other defensively, eyes alert, about twenty feet apart, they pause. She is blond and lean with outdoor conditioning, almost thin, attractive and young, probably not yet twenty, with even features and wild hair. Page turns a chance meeting near a mausoleum into a tale of utopia, outsiders, and what happiness costs.
30761-the-minus-woman:
Russ Winterbotham wrote this science fiction story about a tiny asteroid whose weight will not stay still, and a girl who, the story says, could not exist. On an asteroid three hundred million miles from Earth, Jay Hayling tries to fix balance scales that have gone wrong. A ten-gram weight will not balance two five-gram weights, and then the readings flip, with the two small weights weighing seven and a half grams and the slug weighing true.

Red Brewer, good with machines and a camera and good company on a lonely rock, jokes about shaving less often on the asteroid, but Hayling faces a tougher puzzle. The mass of the rock itself seems to shift against all known laws, and a girl appears where no girl should be. Winterbotham turns a lab fault into a mystery about matter, mind, and the impossible made real.
30817-the-beggar-man:
Ruby M. Ayres wrote this romance for Hodder and Stoughton in London, following her books The One Who Forgot and The Master Man. Its heroine first appears small and slight, with timid brown eyes, soft fair hair, and a daintiness that sets her apart despite shabby clothes. On her first morning at the factory, the other girls mark her as different: less rough, more refined, and ready to shrink quickly from jest and laughter.

Questions greet her from all sides, with interest mixed with faint suspicion, as she tries to hold her own among harder factory girls. Ayres builds the tale from that contrast, between a gentle girl and a rough working world, and from the title figure who will change her fortunes. Readers who enjoy early twentieth-century popular romance will find a sympathetic heroine and a warm, old-fashioned story.
30853-mrs-raffles-being-the-adventures-o:
Edited by John Kendrick Bangs and narrated by Bunny, this 1905 Harper book tells the adventures of Mrs. Raffles, an amateur crackswoman. Its frontispiece shows Mrs. Raffles in fine spirits, calling out to Bunny, and its twelve chapters run as a set of linked capers rather than one long novel. Bangs, known for light humor, turns the gentleman thief tale on its head with a woman at its center.

Chapters include the Herald Personal, the Newport villa, Mrs. Gaster's maid, the pearl rope of Mrs. Gushington-Andrews, steel bonds, the Fresh-Air Fund, Mrs. Rockerbilt's tiara, the Carnegie Library, a hold-up, Mrs. Shadd's musicale, and Mrs. Innitt's cook, closing with a last adventure. Readers who enjoy Raffles-style crime stories with a comic twist will find a witty, old-fashioned entertainment.
30855-the-wife-of-sir-isaac-harman:
H. G. Wells wrote this 1914 novel for the Macmillan Company in New York, published in September 1914. Its twelve chapters run from introducing Lady Harman and the personality of Sir Isaac through Lady Harman at home and her beginnings. They continue with the world according to Sir Isaac, an adventurous afternoon, and Lady Harman learning about herself. Later chapters give Sir Isaac as Petruchio, Mr. Brumley troubled by difficult ideas, and a last crisis.

The book opens with a motor-car at a little white gate, under a porch thick with jasmine. There a tall young woman with masses of blue-black hair surveys a small house with keen appreciation and gentle fear. Wells follows Lady Harman as she moves from a sheltered home into a larger, harder world, and as she learns to stand on her own. It is a novel of marriage, money, and a woman's growth.
30867-what-need-of-man:
Harold Calin wrote this science fiction story, printed in Amazing Stories in February 1961, about a rocket scientist named Bannister. Bannister began with a plan to test how people react to space probes under real conditions. Now, the story says, he is just testing space probes, and man has become a necessary evil to contend with, rather than the point of the test.

The tale opens with a summer night sky that looks warm and friendly, a moon like a big pleasant place, lighter than anything seen before. Lying on grass and looking up long enough, the narrator says, can feel like lying on a ceiling by a reverse pull of gravity. In winter, by contrast, the sky looks cold and unfriendly. Calin uses that shift in mood to ask what space is for, if not for people.
30959-george-eliot-centenary-november-19:
Held here is the catalogue of relics, manuscripts, prints, paintings, photographs, and books relating to George Eliot, exhibited in St. Mary's Hall, Coventry, for the George Eliot centenary in November 1919, issued by the Coventry Libraries Committee. The exhibition has special reference to Eliot's residence in Coventry and to the local Coventry circle.

Visitors were asked not to touch the exhibits, and copying, sketching, or photographing any exhibit was prohibited. Case one holds a portrait of Robert Evans, father of George Eliot and prototype of Adam Bede, lent by Canon Evans of Bedworth, with Evans's diaries. Case two holds a portrait of Isaac P. Evans, her brother and the original of Tom Tulliver. Case three holds a portrait of Eliot with her father, drawn in 1842 by Mrs. Charles Bray. It is a valuable record of a centenary exhibition.
30983-knots-bends-splices-with-tables-of:
Captain Jutsum of Cardiff wrote this revised and enlarged manual of knots, bends, and splices, published in Glasgow by James Brown and Son, the Nautical Press, in 1914. Its full title adds tables of strengths of ropes and wire rigging. Jutsum, signing himself J. Netherclift Jutsum, aims to present in compact, systematic order a complete list of the most useful workings connected with cordage, with clear explanations of how each is formed.

Elementary knots are explained in minute detail, since the book is meant for beginners as well as seamen of short experience. Diagrams appear at every stage to be followed step by step with the text. Jutsum warns that proficiency in this skilled workmanship, almost an art, comes only with much practice and with advice from more experienced shipmates. It remains a practical handbook for sailors, climbers, and anyone who works with rope.
31043-letters-from-china-and-japan:
John Dewey, professor of philosophy at Columbia University, and Alice Chipman Dewey wrote these letters from China and Japan, edited by Evelyn Dewey and published by E. P. Dutton in New York in 1920. The first letter, from Tokyo on a Monday in February, calls the city a muddy masquerade. Dewey is so amused that he wants to call from the housetops for everyone in all the world.

Cast-off clothing, he jokes, seems misdirected to Japan instead of Belgium, queer in cut as in material. It includes kimonos of all colors, patterns, and sizes, men's hats like nothing ever seen, and muddy streets. The ricksha men, in tight trousers and puttees, run all day through mud, snow, and wet in cotton cloth that is neither stockings nor shoes but both. It is a record of East Asia in 1920.
31099-jena-or-sedan:
Franz Adam Beyerlein's novel, translated from the German and published in London by William Heinemann in 1905, asks in its title whether Germany faces another Jena or another Sedan. Its hero, Franz Vogt, walks home from town with new linen and boots. He thinks over the two years of military service now before him, service he must perform whether he likes it or not.

The sons of the village's two richest peasants have been called to the Uhlans, while Vogt goes to the field artillery. Talk of hard words and harder usage from men on leave makes him nervous, though he trusts his strength and athletic skill. The novel follows a young German into uniform, and through him examines duty, class, and the army's hold on village life.
31139-the-plow-woman:
Eleanor Gates's 1906 novel, published by McClure, Phillips in New York, opens on the Dakota prairie. There, a scarlet coulée cuts the brown level and a plowed strip widens with each slow circuit of the team near the Lancasters' new cottonwood shack. Forty-one chapters follow Dallas and her neighbors through trips, misunderstandings, winter camps, awakenings, warnings, fires, flights, and a final settling of ends and beginnings.

The book is a prairie story of work, weather, and stubborn endurance, with a heroine who labors in the furrow herself. Gates, already known for The Biography of a Prairie Girl, writes the frontier as a place of hard choices and close communities. The novel still reads as a vivid picture of Dakota settlement life.
31179-fulton-s-steam-battery-blockship-a:
Howard I. Chapelle, curator of transportation at the Smithsonian, wrote this paper on Robert Fulton's Steam Battery, a catamaran-type blockship, as paper 39 of Bulletin 240 of the United States National Museum. It was published in 1966. Fulton designed the steam warship to defend harbors, joining two hulls in a single floating battery, and Chapelle traces its design, construction, and place in naval history.

Scale models, figures, and index entries support a careful technical account, aimed at historians of ships and technology. The paper shows Fulton beyond the steamboat, as a naval inventor wrestling with how steam power could change war at sea.
31322-alexander-crummell-an-apostle-of-n:
William H. Ferris's 1920 paper, number twenty in the American Negro Academy's Occasional Papers, honors Alexander Crummell as an apostle of Negro culture. Ferris opens twenty years and three months after Crummell's soul took flight from its bodily partner. He argues, like the scientists he cites, that a personality's influence lives on in lives inspired, examples set, and thoughts thrown out.

Two sections follow: The Negro Apostle of Culture, and a history of the American Negro Academy that Crummell founded. The paper is both eulogy and institutional history, preserving the Academy's memory of its guiding spirit.
31331-the-ballotless-victim-of-one-party:
Archibald H. Grimke delivered this address to the American Negro Academy in Washington, D.C., where it was published as Occasional Paper number 16 in 1913. Its subject is the Black citizen who, on paper, holds the rights of an American citizen, including the vote. In practice he receives nothing like those rights in parts of the republic. Grimke calls such a man the ballotless victim of one-party governments.

The argument turns on the gap between written law and daily life. The vote exists to let a citizen defend himself against bad laws and bad administration. Its loss leaves him exposed. Grimke's address is a sharp, early-twentieth-century protest against disfranchisement, and a clear statement of why the ballot mattered as protection, not merely as a symbol.
31362-the-weans-at-rowallan:
Kathleen Fitzpatrick's The Weans at Rowallan, first published in 1905 with four illustrations by A. Guy Smith, is a book of stories about children. Its chapters include Mrs. M'Rea's return to the faith of her fathers, Jane's conversion, the child Samuel, a stocking full of gold, a bantam hen, and a Dorcas society. The title word "weans" is Scots for small children, and the tales center on their doings at Rowallan.

Fitzpatrick writes with warmth for young readers, mixing everyday incidents with moral growth. A day of growth, a best finder, and a society meeting each become small dramas of character. The book belongs to the Edwardian tradition of children's stories rooted in a particular place and its people, and it still reads as a gentle portrait of childhood.
31387-betty-wales-freshman:
Margaret Warde's Betty Wales, Freshman, published by the Penn Publishing Company with copyright in 1904, follows Betty Wales through her first year at college. Warde had already written other Betty Wales books, from Sophomore and Junior to Senior and Betty Wales and Company, and this volume returns to the beginning of the story. An early illustration shows Betty declaring, in the caption, "I'm in a dreadful fix."

The novel belongs to the girls' college-story tradition, where friendships, studies, and small crises fill the year. Betty's freshman troubles are comic and earnest by turns, and the book's appeal lies in campus life itself. Readers who enjoy school stories will find a cheerful, old-fashioned account of a young woman finding her place among new friends.
31493-the-daughter-of-a-republican:
Bernie Babcock's The Daughter of a Republican was published in Chicago by the New Voice Press in 1900, with copyright by Dickie and Woolley in 1899. It is a novel dedicated by the author to her mother, for the loving interest she always took in every first attempt. The book opens by introducing the reader to the Crowley family, and an illustration shows a boy whining that he is cold. Babcock's preface notes that the world pays little heed to human effort until it reaches full, robust maturity.

The novel follows the Crowleys, and the daughter of the title, through family life and public questions, as the dedication's encouragement suggests. Babcock writes of obscure toilers and their bud of promise, in the reform-minded fiction of her day. Readers will find a period novel of family, politics, and aspiration, told with sympathy for ordinary effort.
315-rhymes-of-a-red-cross-man:
Robert W. Service, poet of the Yukon, turned to the trenches of France in this wartime book. Rhymes of a Red Cross Man, from a New York edition of 1916, is dedicated to his brother Albert, killed in action that August. The foreword and contents promise soldiers' verse.

Poems like The Call, The Volunteer, and The Man from Athabaska mix humor with mud and grief. The Haggis of Private McPhee, Fleurette, and Bill's Grave follow. Service wrote as a stretcher bearer, close to the wounded. The book brought the war home in plain rhyme.
31501-the-sensitive-man:
Poul Anderson's short novel of the future opens in an underwater world. Its headnote frames the tale as a story of conspiracy, a theme as old as Guy Fawkes and the Gunpowder Plot, now grown to a human conspiracy against conspirators. One man blocks a cabal's bid for world mastery, and his gifts are unusual.

The scene is set at the Mermaid Tavern, decked with coral pillars and booths, sea creatures on the walls, and murals of Neptune and his court. Broad quartz windows show only shifting greenish-blue seawater, and the only live fish in sight swim in an aquarium across from the bar. The Pacific Colony lacks the loveliness of Florida and Cuba, and the tale follows its sensitive man through a plot against the plotters.
31561-cupid-s-middleman:
Edward B. Lent's Cupid's Middleman, published in New York by Cupples and Leon with copyright in 1906 and illustrations by H. B. Matthews, is a romance of love letters written by proxy. Lent, author of Being Done Good, opens with Ben teasing his friend Jim, who has not asked him to help out in a love affair for years. Ben wishes he were paid by the ton for all the letters he has written for Jim. Jim admits what a fool he was to let Ben trifle with his fair friends in that way.

The middleman of the title is Ben himself, the friend who writes the words that win the girls. Readers of Edwardian romance will find a light, amusing novel, dedicated to Herbert F. Gunnison of the Brooklyn Eagle.
31701-noble-redman:
J. F. Bone's short story, printed in Amazing Science Fiction Stories in July 1960, plays a joke on a name. Its narrator says he detests the words noble and redman together, an ancient colloquialism for a race of aborigines on the American land mass. The tale turns on a father with a sense of humor who gave his son a fitting name.

The twist is that the narrator's people now rule a good-sized segment of the galaxy, yet nobody likes to be reminded that their ancestors came from Earth. Readers get a wry science-fiction comedy about ancestry, pride, and the names a spacefaring people would rather forget.
31781-the-bibliography-of-walt-whitman:
Frank Shay's Bibliography of Walt Whitman was published in New York by Friedmans' in 1920 in a limited edition of five hundred numbered copies. It lists Whitman's works in chronological order, the only practicable method, as Shay notes. He follows the typography and punctuation of the originals, marking his own interpolations with brackets.

Entries run from an 1898 introduction by Oscar Lovell Triggs and Whitman's own Walt Whitman at Home to Notes and Fragments edited by Dr. Richard Maurice Bucke and the 1900 Leaves of Grass with facsimile autobiography. Readers get a collector's and scholar's tool, precise about editions, bindings, and printings of America's most famous poet.
31861-almost-a-woman:
Mary Wood-Allen's Almost a Woman, in the Teaching Truth series and published at Cooperstown in 1911 with copyright in 1907, follows a girl on the edge of womanhood. Its first chapter opens with a clear girlish voice calling for mother through the house, answered not by mother but by father, Mr. Wayne, coming up the steps.

Helen, the daughter, has special things she wanted to ask her mother that evening, and her father, drawing her to his knee, offers what mother cannot: a man's view of things. Readers get an early twentieth-century guidance book in story form, written by a physician to help girls and parents talk about growing up.
31942-a-christian-but-a-roman:
Maurus Jókai's 1900 novel A Christian but a Roman was published in New York by Doubleday and McClure. It begins in Caesar-era days, when the land around Rome rivaled the capital itself for splendour and luxury. Villas of Roman patricians, where every artist from sculptor to cook had done his utmost, dotted the whole region.

Its central figure is Mesembrius Vio, the oldest senator. After Probus died, he never returned to Rome, staying on his estate at the Tiber's mouth and citing gout and cataracts. Readers get a historical novel of late Rome, where patricians avoid the imperial city from weariness, wounded vanity, and distrust of the Caesar.
32021-island-life-or-the-phenomena-and-c:
Alfred Russel Wallace's Island Life, or the Phenomena and Causes of Insular Faunas and Floras, appeared in its second and revised edition of 1895. It includes a revision and attempted solution of the problem of geological climates. Wallace, author of The Malay Archipelago and Darwinism, dedicates the volume to Sir Joseph Dalton Hooker.

Part one, on the dispersal of organisms, contrasts Britain and Japan, Australia and New Zealand, and Bali and Lombok. It also contrasts Florida and the Bahamas, arguing that islands offer the best subjects for studying distribution. Readers get a classic of biogeography, in which Wallace shows why islands, with their peculiar animals and plants, unlock the history of life on Earth.
32124-to-choke-an-ocean:
J. F. Bone's short story, printed in If in September 1960, opens in a detention room on an alien world. A commercial traveller, held in a Niobian quarantine station, welcomes a visit from Lanceford, the Consul General of the Terran Confederation. The traveller complains that he has never been checked so thoroughly, and that a thirty-day quarantine seems harsh for a man carrying only a sample case. Lanceford replies that the Confederation takes an interest in all its citizens' welfare.

The story's humour turns on food: its sidenote theme is that oysters beat even a star-spanning navy in a gourmet's ranking. The traveller's sample case, the quarantine, and the natives' toughness with visitors all point toward a trade dispute with high stakes. Readers get a comic science-fiction tale of commerce, quarantine, and an ocean that may hold more than oysters.
32152-the-widow-to-say-nothing-of-the-ma:
Helen Rowland's The Widow, subtitled To Say Nothing of the Man, was published in New York by Dodge in 1908, with drawings by Esther P. Hill. Its contents run from The Widow and The Winning Card through The Widow's Rival, Money and Matrimony, and Signs and Countersigns of Love. Later chapters cover Her Way, Marriage, and The Widow's Deal. New Year's Irresolutions closes the book. The chapters read as witty scenes and reflections on courtship after widowhood.

The opening chapter sets the pattern. A widow, settling her skirts and leaning back on bright pillows, asks a bachelor a question. What would he say, she asks, if she had found the very girl to make him a model wife? The bachelor dips his paddle lazily and asks what model she means. Readers get an Edwardian comedy of manners, where a widow's schemes, money, and matrimony provide the running joke.
32154-the-variable-man:
Philip K. Dick's short story, printed in Space Science Fiction in September 1953, centres on a man who fixes things: clocks, refrigerators, vidsenders, and destinies. The cover line warns that this man does not fit the age ahead, that its machines cannot reckon with him, and that Earth may rest yet fail on him. The story opens with Security Commissioner Reinhart climbing the Council steps, past guards, into a place of great whirring machines.

Reinhart gazes at the central SRB computer and studies its reading, while Kaplan, the lab organiser, reports a straight gain for the last quarter. They are catching up to their rivals, Reinhart says, but too slowly, and they must finally go over soon. Both sides design new weapons and counter-defences, yet nothing is actually made. Readers get a story about prediction, war, and one unpredictable man.
32229-high-man:
Jay Clarke's short story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in June 1954, is told through letters from a fiancee in London to a man rising in New York. Its sidenote says Roger got his chance to rise in the world, and wound up with his head in the clouds. Anne writes from London to Roger Brisby in New York. Her April 3 letter asks whether he is well, since she has not heard from him.

On April 11 she writes again. She reminds him she is his fiancee, and asks for at least a postal card, even on a business trip, after three weeks. On April 16 she refuses to stand for it any longer. She suspects him of running around with American women and spending her money. Readers get a joke told in letters. Rising in the world turns literal, and a fiancee waits overseas.
32281-first-man:
Clyde Brown's story, illustrated by Wood and printed in Galaxy in April 1958, tells how the first Moon man was chosen. Its sidenote says he wanted no part in the goal of generations, but the goal wanted all of him. The story opens, Orville Close took the first Moon trip, Harold Ferguson the second, and they never speak of it.

The tale begins on an October morning when the piece appeared in the Parkville News. Harold grumbled they had the story wrong, calling his craft a rocket ship and treating him as a flagpole sitter or a man shooting Niagara Falls in a barrel. His wife moved their thin little girl to her brother's house. Police blocked Elm Street to all but residents, and neighbors got up a petition. Orville stayed calm, while his wife Polly left for her sister's. Readers get a small-town Moon story.
32479-the-intelligence-of-woman:
W. L. George's Intelligence of Woman, published in Boston in 1916, argues against denying women intellect. George notes that men have credited women with instinct and intuition. They likened her linking of cause and effect to a dog linking a collar with a walk, while denying her the capacity to plan consecutively and execute steadfastly. Days are less dark, he writes, since woman has a place in the state, even a place under man's, yet men still call her illogical, petty, jealous, and vain.

Later chapters treat feminist intentions, uniforms for women, woman and the paint pot, the downfall of the home, the break-up of the family, and notes on marriage. George writes as a male feminist of his time, praising women's minds while repeating some of the charges he criticises. The book offers a period view of suffrage-era debate about intellect, work, and domestic life.
32579-micro-man:
Weaver Wright tells of a college student who spots a tiny man on a streetcar ledge during a dull morning ride. The small figure wears a blouse, shorts, and sandals. He has a silver head covering with knobs on it. The student slips him into a matchbox to keep him safe.

At home the student dreams of fame, wealth, and a newspaper scoop, and plans to show the find to the world. The tiny man has his own aims, though. He speaks of a temple where his gods may know and guard him. So the student's prize turns out to be a person with a life of his own, not a mere curiosity.
32623-geographic-variation-in-the-pocket:
Robert J. Russell and Rollin H. Baker study the plateau pocket gopher Cratogeomys castanops in Coahuila, Mexico, in a University of Kansas Museum paper dated March 15, 1955. Earlier workers had just thirty-five specimens from seven places; the authors had two hundred and thirty-four from sixty-three.

From that larger haul they describe four subspecies new to science, drop two wrongly listed for the state, and confirm three more from nearby states, making eleven known in Coahuila. Soil, dissected hills, and the Rio Grande, they argue, split the gophers into local forms.
32636-the-salesman:
Waldo T. Boyd sets this comedy in Tracy's department store in 1995, in the Roboid Department. Salesman Trevor Anson greets a first-time customer, a red-tied man with a fearful wife named Millicent. The pair want to see a robot on sale, though the husband dreads machines that might run wild.

Anson works by his Salesman's Guide, with rules for marked-down goods, for finding the deciding voice, and for never arguing with a buyer. His goods are Plasti-Cast Roboids, grown like crystals in vats in New Chicago. The tale turns on whether a smooth pitch can sell a machine to a man who fears it.
32652-the-chameleon-man:
William P. McGivern tells of a theatrical agent who meets a tall young man able to blend with his surroundings until he seems to vanish. The gift is real, not a trick, and it leaves the agent half sure his nerves have failed him.

The agent soon sees a use for the man, whose name is Horatio, in a stage magic act with a magician and his partner Alice. Horatio's unseen help makes the act shine, yet a gift that hides its owner brings its own risks, both on stage and off.
32655-the-last-gentleman:
Rory Magill opens on a warm summer night, when Jim and Myra Peters wake to an explosion. Neighbors gather in the dark, and the radio reports five bombs in a straight north-south line, with the town of Calas, Utah, wiped out. Jim takes pride in his brother Hugh, a nuclear scientist who would know the truth.

Hugh does know, and his account upends the war scare: there were no bombs at all. Five pieces of a dead white dwarf star, flung through space long before Earth formed, kept a rendezvous with our world. The tale turns on panic, science, and what a gentleman owes the truth.
32658-the-standardized-man:
Stephen Bartholomew imagines a world where firms sell just six suits, three for men and three for women. In that world every face is made to one standard. A worker is known only by a name tag worn at the neck, listing name, address, and number.

Charles, a lab man, learns that his firm's profit margin has slipped by three tenths of a percent in three weeks. A computer says only a drastic change in output can fix it. The tale follows Charles as the smooth, uniform order around him starts to fail.
3271-the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-:
Charles Farrar Browne, writing as Artemus Ward, opens his complete works with essays, sketches, and letters. Preliminary notes by John Camden Hotten, a biographical sketch by Melville D Landon, and an introduction by T W Robertson frame the set. A prefatory note by Edward P Hingston joins them. Then Ward himself takes over.

Business letters, a piece on forts, and the Shakers lead the contents, with a high-handed outrage at Utica and a celebration at Baldinsville. Among the spirits, on the wing, and the octoroon follow, with experience as an editor and a visit to Brigham Young. Wax figures versus Shakespeare shows Ward's comic method: misspelled wisdom aimed straight at American humbug.
32730-the-heart-of-a-woman:
Baroness Orczy, author of The Scarlet Pimpernel, tells this novel of a woman fighting for the thing she loved, published by Hodder and Stoughton and George H. Doran Company in 1911. Forty-two chapters move from commonplace incidents to a hand of death and one human life set against another.

The tale opens with Louisa alone in a hotel room, among red velvet furniture and an ormolu clock that no longer marks time. A death, a foggy night, and a visit to Grosvenor Square draw in Luke, Travers, and Uncle Rad. Police, witnesses, and a crowded inquest follow, as Orczy tests what a woman will risk and what the truth will cost.
32737-uniform-of-a-man:
Dave Dryfoos tells of Chet Barfield, a prisoner of the Agvars on the planet Hedlot, in this story from IF Worlds of Science Fiction of March 1954, illustrated by Rudolph Palais. For three years Chet has lived chained, starved, and tormented by village boys under a diffuse red sun.

He has learned to eat whatever he can get and to breathe the local air in its special rhythm. When a rescue ship's roar fills the sky, his first thought is revenge: the bestial Agvars must be taught a lesson. His rescuers, Commander Seymour and Dr. Pine, disagree. Chet must learn that revenge is not the lesson he needs.
3276-the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-:
Part six of Artemus Ward's complete works preserves his Panorama, the lecture that crowned his fame. A prefatory note by Melville D Landon introduces the Egyptian Hall lecture, with a Times notice and the programme of that lecture. An announcement and programme for the Dodworth Hall lecture join them. The panorama itself was illustrated as delivered at Egyptian Hall in London.

Landon notes that Ward's fame peaked in those last lectures at Egyptian Hall, Piccadilly. The final one broke off abruptly on the evening of 23 January 1867, and that night the humorist bade farewell to the public and retired to die. This part is thus both a comic text and a farewell: Ward's last stage, kept in print.
32845-international-short-stories-americ:
William Patten edits this collection of famous American short stories, published by P. F. Collier and Son in 1910. The use of copyrighted stories was authorized by their authors or representatives in each case, and a frontispiece shows Anna Katharine Green.

Contents range from Hawthorne's Prophetic Pictures and Irving's Legend of Sleepy Hollow to Poe's Gold-Bug and Cooper's Corporal Flint's Murder. Harte, Longfellow, Stockton, O. Henry, Bangs, and George Ade follow, with Freeman's Shadows on the Wall, Simms, Taylor, and Dunne's Mr. Dooley. Later stories include a Kentucky Cinderella, Crawford's By the Waters of Paradise, and Green's Memorable Night, a sampler of American fiction at its most famous.
32906-thy-name-is-woman:
Kenneth O'Hara sends Eddie Bowren as a stowaway to a Mars ruled by women, in a story from IF Worlds of Science Fiction of March 1953. Bowren hides in a steel cubicle in a cargo bin at the New Chicago Port, letting a doctor alter him so his body can survive acceleration. Male organisms, the story holds, cannot stand the rigors of the voyage unaided.

On Mars he meets Gloria Munsel, president of the city, who has no precedent and no laws for his case. The council must decide what to do with him. Bowren tells the investigation committee on Earth what he saw and heard, and his impressions of a world without men. The story turns on whether a man who escaped Earth can return, and what his report will cost both worlds.
3293-chronicle-of-the-conquest-of-granad:
Washington Irving tells the fall of Granada from the supposed papers of Fray Antonio Agapida, in this author's revised edition. The kingdom of Granada and its tribute to the Castilian crown open the chronicle. An embassy of Don Juan de Vera demands arrears of tribute from the Moorish monarch, and the tale of war begins.

Domestic feuds in the Alhambra follow, with rival sultanas and predictions about Boabdil, heir to the throne. Ferdinand's campaigns close the Moorish kingdom in the end. Irving writes history as romance, with Agapida as his grave, credulous guide. Readers get the last crusade of Spain as a story: sieges, chivalry, and a kingdom falling in slow, splendid ruin.
3301-the-naturewoman:
Upton Sinclair pits a nature cult against Boston society in this play. Oceana, the naturewoman, leads the cast, against Mrs Sophronia Masterson of Beacon Street and her husband Quincy, a doctor. Freddy, their son, and Ethel, their younger daughter, join Letitia, the elder daughter, and her husband Henry Selden. Remson, a butler, keeps order.

Act one sits in the Masterson drawing room on a winter afternoon, and act two returns the next afternoon to the same room. Nature worship meets drawing-room manners there, and neither side yields gracefully. Sinclair uses the clash to mock both camps: the cult's earnestness and society's polish. The play is short, witty, and very much of its reforming age.
3302-the-second-story-man:
Upton Sinclair builds this one-act play around a midnight burglary. Jim Faraday, the second-story man, meets Harvey Austin, a lawyer, and Helen Austin, his wife, in the library of the Austin home at two in the morning. A lamp burns on a center table, the front door shows through the hall entrance, and a cabinet of curios stands in the corner.

Faraday came through a window, but the play turns on talk rather than theft. Lawyer, wife, and burglar argue morals, law, and need across the lamplit room. Sinclair, best known for The Jungle, uses the stage to put class face to face. The piece is short, tense, and pointed: a crime play that asks who the real criminal is.
33039-the-orphan:
Clarence E. Mulford's Orphan, copyrighted in 1908 and illustrated in color by Allen True, follows a western sheriff and a boy found alone. Its chapters run from the sheriff rides to war and concerning an arrow through the sheriff finds the orphan and the second offense. They go on to Bill justifies his creation and the orphan obeys an impulse. Later chapters bring an outfit hunting strays, a timber wolf in his own country, and the Cross Bar-8 losing sleep.

Mulford, author of Bar-20, writes the range with humor and toughness. A sheriff, a ranch crew, and a boy without family test each other and grow into a kind of kinship. An illustration shows a girl unfastening a gold breast-pin to pin a bandage into place, a small act of care in a hard country. The novel remains a lively western, fond of its characters and their code.
33082-jack-hinton-the-guardsman:
Charles James Lever's Jack Hinton, the Guardsman, published in London in 1857 with illustrations by Browne, follows a young Englishman in Ireland. Lever's preface says he meant to depict, in Jack's early experiences, the almost inevitable mistakes of such a character, after hearing absurd and exaggerated opinions on Irish character formed on slight acquaintance. He soon strayed from that plan, he admits, and let Jack take his chance amongst the natives, with too much occupation to reflect on their peculiarities.

The novel that follows is a high-spirited Irish tale of a guardsman, soldiers, society, and the misunderstandings between English and Irish. Lever, himself Irish, writes with humor and affection for a country he knew well, even when his hero blunders. The book remains a lively example of the Irish novel of manners and adventure, and a good entry to Lever's long, popular career.
33088-putnam-s-handy-law-book-for-the-la:
Albert Sidney Bolles's Putnam's Handy Law Book for the Layman, published in 1921, explains the modern law of banking for readers without legal training. Bolles covers banks and their depositors, bank officers, bank collections, and the National Bank Act with its judicial interpretation. He was formerly professor of commercial law and banking at the University of Pennsylvania and lecturer at Haverford College. The book was reprinted several times through 1923, a sign of its use.

Written in plain terms, the volume aims to help ordinary depositors, business people, and students understand their rights and duties when dealing with banks. It treats checks, collections, and officers' responsibilities with the clarity of a textbook. As a legal guide of its day, it captures American banking law just after the First World War. It remains a useful historical source for how banking was explained to the public.
33131-the-spirit-of-japan:
Rabindranath Tagore's Spirit of Japan opens with a frank admission. It is a lecture delivered for students of Tokyo's private colleges and members of the Indo-Japanese Association at Keio Gijuku University and published in Tokyo on July 2, 1916. Tagore is glad to speak once more before leaving Japan. His stay has been so short that one might think he has not earned the right to speak about the country. He expects to be told he idealizes some aspects.

Tagore refuses to be browbeaten by long experience. He suggests it may be blindness carried through long years, even when foreigners doubt Japan's moral qualifications or its efficiency in modern progress. The lecture that follows offers an Indian poet's view of Japan's spirit, its discipline, and its place in Asia. It remains a thoughtful document of East Asian exchange, and of Tagore's effort to see a nation beyond its machines and armies.
33242-an-amateur-fireman:
James Otis's boys' book follows an amateur fireman through life-saving work in a city fire corps. Copyrighted in 1898, its chapters move from the amateur himself and 'Lish Davis to Jip's revenge, Sam the detective, and tardy repentance. Otis, author of Toby Tyler, writes with a fireman's eye for alarms, ladders, and the quick courage that saves lives.

The story blends adventure with moral lessons, as its hero learns duty, teamwork, and the cost of delay. Its frontispiece shows the life-saving corps at work, and its scenes of fire and rescue stay vivid. For young readers who love tales of brave deeds, An Amateur Fireman offers a brisk, wholesome story of a boy who learns to serve his city.
33285-her-royal-highness-woman:
Max O'Rell's book takes woman herself as its royal subject, offering witty notes on her ways, her talk, and her place in daily life. O'Rell, known for genial, good-humored observation, writes as a keen watcher of manners, refusing to take anything too solemnly. The press praised him as a delightful companion whose shrewd, reflective pages find humor in half the small problems that make up life.

The volume suits readers who enjoy light essays on society, full of anecdote and sharp comment. Its tone is friendly rather than severe, and its aim is to amuse while it observes. For fans of late Victorian humor, Her Royal Highness Woman is a pleasant, easy read, best taken in short sittings, like talk with a witty friend.
33496-scenes-and-adventures-in-affghanis:
William Taylor, late troop sergeant-major of the Fourth Light Dragoons, recounts his service in the campaign in Afghanistan in this 1842 memoir. The narrative follows British troops from embarkation at Bombay through mishaps at sea, reviews, and the advance through Scinde, with stops at towns, tombs, and river crossings along the way. Taylor records marches, desertions, accidents, and the daily frictions of an army on the move.

Beyond battle, the book preserves scenes of local life: mosques and Hindu customs, jugglers, native troopers, camel drivers, and the consternation caused by a steamer on the Indus. Dedicated to Florentine Lady Sale for her heroism in the campaign, the memoir offers a soldier's-eye view of a difficult expedition, frank about hardship and alert to unfamiliar sights.
3351-letters-to-his-son-1746-47-on-the-f:
The Earl of Chesterfield begins his famous correspondence in this volume covering 1746 and 1747. An editor's note opens the book, explaining old style and new style dates. On consultation with specialists, the editor learned that the abbreviations mark the Julian calendar used in England against the Gregorian calendar standard in Europe. In the mid eighteenth century the gap amounted to eleven days.

That note matters, because Chesterfield dated letters across the two systems as his son traveled. The letters themselves open the education: study, manners, and the world, taught by a father who writes as a statesman and a wit. Readers starting the correspondence here get its foundation, with the calendar key supplied before the first lesson.
33549-underground-man:
Gabriel Tarde imagines a future after catastrophe in this short philosophical romance, translated by Cloudesley Brereton with a preface by H. G. Wells and published in 1905. The narrator, writing long after the twentieth century of the old Christian era ended, relates a universal cataclysm that drove civilization underground. He also relates the redemption achieved within a few centuries of heroic effort. Prosperity, catastrophe, struggle, rescue, and regeneration structure the tale.

Tarde uses the underground world to reflect on art, love, and social life, arguing that a smaller, sheltered society might recover values the surface world had lost. Wells's preface praises the book's genial depth and its charming fancy. Readers of early science fiction and social theory will find a compact, thoughtful daydream rather than a thriller.
3357-letters-to-his-son-1753-54-on-the-f:
New Year's Day 1753 finds Chesterfield waiting for a letter, and content to wait, while his son works in Paris. Letter one hundred and eighty-five, dated New Year's Day 1753, opens on a fortnight's silence. It is above a fortnight since the earl received a letter, he writes, but he hopes the boy is well. The boy is likely engrossed by Lord Albemarle's bureau in the mornings, and by business of a genteeler nature in the evenings.

Chesterfield willingly gives up his own claim on the boy's time to that double business: diplomacy by day and society by night. The volume follows a young diplomat finding his footing in Paris. Readers get the earl as a patient correspondent, content to wait for letters and to teach through the waiting itself.
3358-letters-to-his-son-1756-58-on-the-f:
The Seven Years' War reaches the Chesterfield letters in 1756, and the old statesman reads its dispatches like lessons for his son. Letter two hundred and three, dated 15 November 1756, answers a packet received the day before. With it came the Prussian papers, read with great attention. If courts could blush, Chesterfield writes, those of Vienna and Dresden ought to, for their falsehoods stand publicly and undeniably exposed.

The Seven Years' War frames the letters that follow, as father and son track alliances, battles, and diplomacy. Chesterfield, an old statesman, teaches statecraft from the news itself. Readers get the war as a family correspondence saw it: dispatches judged, courts mocked, and a young diplomat learning to read Europe's moves as they happened.
3359-letters-to-his-son-1759-65-on-the-f:
Italian greetings for the New Year open the 1759 letters, and behind the joke stands a father's worry about his son's health. Letter two hundred and thirty-seven, dated New Year's Day 1759, opens with the season's greeting in Italian: many and happy returns. The earl has done with that subject, he jokes, one truth being fair on the most lying day of the year. Before him lies the boy's last letter, of 21 December.

That letter proves a bill of health, which pleases the father, though he warns against presuming on it. Obey and honor your physician, he advises, that your days may be long in the land. The volume follows the correspondence through war, travel, and middle age, with a father's care turning increasingly to health and to time itself.
3360-letters-to-his-son-1766-71-on-the-f:
The Earl of Chesterfield writes to his son from London in this final span of letters, 1766 to 1771. Letter two hundred and eighty-four, dated 11 February 1766, apologizes for delay with weather. The earl received one letter two days earlier and another only ten days earlier, though both were older. Bad weather and bad roads explain the gap, he writes, and he hardly remembers so severe a winter.

The volume's letters grow shorter and more personal as the earl ages. Advice gives way to news, health, and affection, with the tutor's voice softening into a father's. Readers closing the long correspondence here will find its end fitting: a great letter writer, still writing, against winter, distance, and failing strength.
33614-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This volume of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica covers the slice from Bohemia to Borgia, Francis, as volume four, slice two. Its article list runs alphabetically from Bohemia, Bohmund, and Böhmer through Boiardo, Boieldieu, Boileau-Despréaux, boiler, boiling to death, and Bonaparte's world, to Bonfire, Bonghi, Bonham, Bonheur, Boniface, and Borgia. Each entry reflects the scholarship and viewpoint of the great eleventh edition.

Readers will find compact, authoritative articles on history, geography, biography, science, and art, with the edition's characteristic cross-references and bibliographies. The slice is a reminder of how the Britannica organized knowledge before the digital age: dense, confident, and comprehensive. Researchers still consult these volumes for period detail and for the history of ideas themselves.
33651-the-shadow-of-a-man:
E. W. Hornung sets this 1901 novel in the Australian Riverina. It opens with the belle of Toorak and a courtship among log huts with galvanized iron roofs, pine trees, and salt-bush plains burning into blue sky. The fifteen chapters move through injury, insult, a red herring, a cavalier, and a case styled Bethune against Bethune, as reputations and relationships are tested.

Hornung writes about honor, truth told by inches, escapades, and a man facing the consequences of his own coin. The Australian setting gives the story its heat, distance, and rough domesticity, while the plot turns on social judgment and private reckoning. Readers who enjoy Hornung's Raffles-era fiction will find here a more domestic but still suspenseful tale of character under pressure.
33674-sonnets-from-the-patagonian:
Donald Evans published this limited 1918 edition of sonnets, in an edition of 750 copies from Nicholas L. Brown in Philadelphia. A special edition on Italian handmade paper was limited to 28 numbered, signed copies. An advertisement letter to Cornwall Hollis frames the book as a wartime aesthetic gesture, written while the Allied cause seemed to crumble and Mitteleuropa seemed a fact. Evans suggests that aesthetics, not only strategy, deserve thought in dark hours.

The sonnets themselves belong to Evans's earlier, half-forgotten work, now reissued with a plea for a new preface. Readers of modernist poetry will find a slim, self-consciously literary volume, shaped by wartime pessimism and by a belief that art endures when empires falter. The book's rarity and its framing letter make it a curiosity of American small-press publishing.
33912-the-engineering-contributions-of-w:
Robert M. Vogel wrote this Smithsonian paper on Wendel Bollman, a self-taught Baltimore civil engineer. Bollman, born in Baltimore in 1814 to German parents, rose on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad to master of road. His iron truss, first built in 1850, was the first iron system used steadily on an American railroad.

Vogel traces Bollman's work from Harpers Ferry spans to the Winchester span of 1851, and sets him beside Whipple and Fink. The paper explains how iron replaced timber in bridge building. It gives engineers and rail fans a clear account of a pioneer whose name now lives on in the Bollman truss.
3394-the-white-mr-longfellow-from-litera:
William Dean Howells remembers the white Mr Longfellow in this memoir from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. The Howellses planned only a short Boston stay until a house in Old Cambridge turned up. That proved less straightforward than it sounds, since the old town had not yet sped its academic tempo up to modern speed.

Howells writes that in spring 1866 no stir of expansion showed itself anywhere yet, and the huge material growth of later years lay still ahead. Into that quiet Cambridge steps Longfellow, white-haired and kind, the poet as neighbor. A famous man at home, before fame hardened into monument: Longfellow white-haired, kind, and neighborly.
33943-woman:
Magdeleine Marx wrote this novel, translated by Adele Szold Seltzer and published in New York in 1920, with a preface by Henri Barbusse. Its three books are called Being Born, Being, and Becoming. The story opens with a narrator walking in a forest, spent and full-fed by air and space, facing herself for an hour, step by step.

Marx follows a woman from birth through being to becoming, in a voice both intimate and searching. The novel treats sincerity, the body, and the self with frankness rare for its day. It remains a striking early feminist novel of a woman's inner life.
33979-miscellaneous-aphorisms-the-soul-o:
Oscar Wilde, writing as Sebastian Melmoth, left this set of aphorisms and his essay The Soul of Man, published in London in 1911. The aphorisms turn in short, sharp lines on love, beauty, women, reading, culture, and human nature. Wilde praises beauty, mocks fixed rules, and notes how hard it is to rejoice in a friend's success.

The Soul of Man carries the same wit into a longer argument about the self and society. Together the pieces show Wilde at his most quotable, after his fame and before his name faded. Readers meet a master of the short, stinging sentence.
34035-the-hillman:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote this novel, published in New York in January 1917 by A. L. Burt, by arrangement with Little, Brown. A frontispiece by George Avison shows a moment that came like a thunder-clap. The story opens with Louise leaning back among cushions in a motionless car, eyes traveling past a dim hillside of wall-enclosed fields to cloud and unseen heights.

Moonlight has not yet risen, but a faint glow halos the topmost peak, and a distant sheep-bell sounds. Louise, self-engrossed and detached, savors a beauty seldom found in her town life. Oppenheim writes of love, hills, and hidden pasts. The novel offers a romantic tale with a dramatic turn.
34071-the-evolution-of-an-empire-a-brief:
Mary Parmele wrote this brief historical sketch of France, published in New York in 1894 by William Beverley Harison. Parmele, author of the Evolution of Empire series on Germany, aims to tell a great nation's story in about one hundred pages, keeping only essential facts. To readers who know the subject, the sketch is a reminder of sequence; to students, a framework for later reading.

Contents run from the Aryan family, the Keltic race, and ancient Gaul through Roman conquest under Julius Caesar. They continue to the birth of Christianity, its spread, and persecution at Lyons by order of Marcus Aurelius. Parmele writes with order and clarity. The book offers a compact history of France.
34194-higgins-a-man-s-christian:
Norman Duncan's 1909 book tells of F. E. Higgins, a missionary known in the Minnesota lumber country as the Sky Pilot. Duncan learned the tales on two visits with Higgins, first in the winter lumber camps and towns, then again at the time of the spring drive.

Sixteen short chapters follow Higgins among rough crews, in camps and timber drives, where his plain talk and steady nerve win hard men over. The Rev. Thomas D. Whittles, Higgins's friend, shared the longer account from which Duncan drew, and the book reads as a set of camp stories drawn from life.
3466-the-foreigner-a-tale-of-saskatchewa:
Ralph Connor sets this novel on the Saskatchewan prairie, where a new nation is being made from many peoples. Saxon and Slav, Teuton, Celt, and Gaul meet on snow swept winter plains and flower decked summer fields, drawn by railways to Winnipeg, Empress of the Prairies. The book's foreigner is an immigrant who must find a place among neighbors of other tongues and faiths.

Connor, a Canadian minister and novelist, argues that justice and charity must bind these peoples together, or old lines of race will break the new country. The story mixes frontier hardship, romance, and moral appeal. It gives a vivid view of western Canada at settlement time, when farms, schools, and churches rose beside the railway lines.
3477-the-verse-book-of-a-homely-woman:
Fay Inchfawn, the pen name of Elizabeth Rebecca Ward, writes poems about the daily life of a housewife in this verse book. Contents move from The Housewife and The Little House to A Woman in Hospital, Homesick on Washing Day, When Baby Strayed, and To an Old Teapot. A second part steps outdoors for Early Spring and other country pieces.

The poems find feeling in small things: a carpet that rucks, a tap across the yard, a musty smell in rainy weather, and work made hard by a cramped house. Inchfawn writes in plain, rhymed verse that speaks for women whose labor rarely reached print. The book suits readers who like domestic poetry with humor, tenderness, and a clear eye.
3529-letters-written-during-a-short-resi:
Mary Wollstonecraft writes letters from a trip across Sweden, Norway, and Denmark in the 1790s, after the fame of her Vindication of the Rights of Woman. The letters mix travel notes with reflections on trade, law, manners, and the lives of women. An introduction sketches her early life, including her father, a quick tempered man, and her mother, a rigorous Irishwoman.

Wollstonecraft observes harbors, farms, and towns with a reformer's eye, asking how laws and customs shape ordinary people. She also writes about friendship, including Frances Blood, a gifted young artist who supported her family by drawing. The book suits readers who want early feminist travel writing and a vivid view of Scandinavia before modern industry.
3548-the-pharisee-and-the-publican:
John Bunyan expounds the parable of the Pharisee and the Publican in this Puritan sermon treatise. The text opens with two men who went up to the temple to pray. A Pharisee thanks God he is not like other men, extortioners, unjust persons, or adulterers. Beside him stands a publican who will not lift his eyes to heaven.

Bunyan contrasts proud, self satisfied religion with humble repentance. He warns readers against trusting in fasting, tithing, and outward duties while despising others.
