The treatise also comforts those who feel their sins deeply, since the publican went home justified. It suits readers interested in Bunyan beyond Pilgrim's Progress, in his plain, searching preaching voice.
3618-arms-and-the-man:
George Bernard Shaw writes a comedy about war and romance set during the Serbo-Bulgarian War. Raina Petkoff, a young Bulgarian woman, shelters a fleeing Swiss mercenary, Captain Bluntschli, who carries chocolate rather than cartridges in his bag. Bluntschli, a professional soldier, mocks the romantic view of battle that Raina learned from operas and novels.

The play follows Raina's engagement to the dashing Sergius, her growing regard for Bluntschli, and the clash between heroic talk and real soldiering. Shaw turns a war comedy into an argument about courage, love, and common sense. The play suits readers who enjoy Shaw at his lightest, with wit that still cuts through fine phrases.
3627-life-of-bunyan:
James Hamilton writes a life of John Bunyan for the 1845 edition of the Works of the Puritan Divines. Hamilton notes the graceful sketches by Southey and Montgomery and the elaborate biography by Philip, whose researches left few gaps, as well as Bunyan's own graphic narrative of his life. His task, he says, is to tell the story once more for readers of Bunyan's collected works.

The life follows Bunyan from a wild youth, when his energy ran to idle play and mischief, through conversion, preaching, prison, and the writing of Pilgrim's Progress. Hamilton writes as a minister admiring a fellow preacher. The book suits readers who want a short, sympathetic life of Bunyan beside his own writings.
3629-the-titan:
Theodore Dreiser continues the story of Frank Cowperwood in this second novel of his trilogy, following The Financier. Cowperwood, now in Chicago, builds a new city life, a new home, and a new empire in gas and street railways. Chapters trace a Chicago evening, a new queen of the home, the fight for franchises, and a declaration of love, ending with the quest for fifty year franchises.

Dreiser follows Cowperwood's ambition, his wife, and his mistresses through boardrooms and bedrooms, showing how money and desire drive the same man. The novel's scale matches its hero's hunger for power. Readers who enjoy large American novels of business and appetite will find Dreiser at his most detailed and relentless.
3741-the-writings-of-thomas-paine-volume:
Moncure Daniel Conway collected this first volume of Thomas Paine's writings from the opening years of the American Revolution. Its heart is the American Crisis papers, a run of pamphlets that urged the colonies to hold firm through defeat and doubt. Crisis papers addressed to Lord Howe, to General Howe, to the people of England, and to the people of America follow one another in order. Notes on taxation, the king's speech, and the coming peace fill the gaps between them.

Paine's prose hits hard and plain, with short sentences and direct appeals that still stir a reader. The volume shows a working pamphleteer at full stretch, answering each new British move as it came. Readers who know Common Sense will find here the longer argument behind it, written week by week while the war hung in the balance.
3804-pierre-and-jean:
Guy de Maupassant sets this short novel among a fishing family at Le Havre, where old Roland, his wife, and their two sons pass idle days on the water. Pierre, dark and restless, and Jean, fair and easy, seem a matched pair until a family friend dies and leaves his whole fortune to Jean alone. The will cracks the household open, since no honest reason explains such a preference.

Pierre turns the facts over in torment, recalling how the dead man first grew close to his parents through his own scarlet fever. Logic points one way, and affection points another, as he weighs whether Jean is truly his brother. Maupassant writes with cold precision, and the novel's power lies in what Pierre cannot bring himself to say aloud.
4008-count-julian:
A verse drama in the old manner tells of Count Julian, the lord whose wrongs and vengeance open Spain to invasion. In the sampled scenes, lovers speak of suspicion planted like a demon whisper, of hope argued back into the heart, and of parting made final by death.

Mountains and seas, the speakers say, are not true separation, since only death divides. The play moves in high, formal speech, with honor, betrayal, and fate as its ruling themes. Readers who enjoy early nineteenth-century verse tragedy will find a stern, grave work, closer to a stage poem than to a modern novel of action.
4011-epicoene-or-the-silent-woman:
Ben Jonson's comedy centers on Morose, a man who hates noise and seeks a silent wife, and on the young wife who turns out to be anything but silent. In the sampled scenes, a household of mutes makes legs and waits in silence, while talk praises the Turk's mute court as a model of order.

Jonson builds the joke through talk, disguise, and a wedding that upends every plan. The play moves at a brisk, farcical pace, with London wits and gallants crowding the stage. Readers who like sharp city comedy will enjoy a work that turns the dream of a quiet wife into a loud, funny defeat.
4026-the-first-man:
A play in four acts centers on a household in Bridgetown, where Martha, Jayson, and Sheffield argue over a woman's place and work. Talk of law as a career, of small-town air, and of catty remarks shows a family testing new ideas against old habits.

Martha presses for a life beyond the home, while the men around her answer with teasing, concern, and pride. The play moves through drawing-room debate toward a hard choice about marriage and freedom. Readers who like serious domestic drama will find a thoughtful, plain-spoken work about a woman asking for more room in her own life.
4036-essays-from-the-guardian:
Walter Horatio Pater's Guardian essays gather literary criticism first written for a newspaper readership. A sampled essay praises a study of Browning that points readers to the best, most solid parts of the poet's work, treating each book or group of poems as a distinct study.

Pater's own essays move with the same care, weighing writers and works in fine, balanced prose. The volume suits readers who like criticism as an art, where judgment grows from close reading rather than from praise or blame. It offers a window on Victorian taste and on Pater's quiet, exact mind.
4285-the-master-christian:
Marie Corelli set this novel in Rouen, where bells of old grey towers ring the Angelus at dusk. Market women, bargemen, and schoolchildren hear the chime over the city. News comes of a cardinal-archbishop from a small French cathedral town. The story grows into a romance about faith and the churches.

Corelli dedicated the book to all those churches who quarrel in the name of Christ. That purpose shapes the plot: a search for a truer Christianity amid ritual, ambition, and division. Readers of Corelli's popular romances will recognize her blend of sentiment, pageantry, and moral argument, set against a richly described French city.
4304-our-friend-the-charlatan:
George Gissing wrote this novel around Mr. Lashmar, a clergyman waiting for a late breakfast at Alverholme Vicarage. He drums on the window and watches a blackbird on the lawn, while his mind runs on human follies. Gissing calls him a man in mild, ceaseless indignation at the tenor of the age.

The charlatan of the title is a figure who trades in fine talk and borrowed ideas, and the novel tests him against honest folk. Gissing uses the vicarage, its parish, and London talk to ask how people judge sincerity. It is a satire with a serious edge, about belief, ambition, and the art of seeming.
4318-reproduction-of-copyrighted-works-b:
The United States Copyright Office issued this circular, number 21, for educators and librarians who ask about fair use and photocopying. It states plainly that the office cannot give legal advice or opinions on what is permitted. Instead it sets out the basic legislative provisions on reproduction by libraries and schools.

The circular covers fair use under section 107 and library copying under section 108, with related documents and the 1983 report of the Register of Copyrights. Teachers and librarians use it as a starting guide to classroom and reserve copying. For a specific case, readers must still seek counsel, but the rules themselves are laid out here.
4585-god-s-country-and-the-woman:
James Oliver Curwood opens God's Country and the Woman with Philip Weyman in the far north, where water flows north and a man can feel like several people at once. Philip laughs and sings, talks to himself, and tries to sing Radisson's La Belle Marie in a heavy bass, even though he has lately looked on Radisson's unpleasant death. Two years along the rim of the Arctic have taught him how a man becomes acquainted with himself.

From that lonely, buoyant start grows a northern romance in which a woman enters Philip's wilderness world and changes its terms. Curwood writes the cold, the rivers, and the long light with his usual vigour, while loyalty, love, and survival are tested. Readers get a popular Canadian adventure with a strong romantic thread, in which the north itself acts as both danger and judge.
4748-baree-son-of-kazan:
James Oliver Curwood wrote Baree, Son of Kazan, as his third animal book, after Kazan, the Wolf Dog, and The Grizzly King. His preface says hundreds of letters from friends of wild animal life asked questions about his earlier books. Those letters encouraged him to say more about his hope in writing of wild life, and about the foundation of fact beneath this book and its companions.

Curwood says he has always disliked preaching sermons in romance, comparing it to placing a halter about a reader's neck and dragging him down paths he may not like. If fact and truth produce a message in the reader's mind, then a work has been done, and that is what he hopes for in his nature books. He adds bluntly that Americans have gone after Nature with a gun. Readers get an animal story grounded in observed wild life, not a sermon.
4786-zone-policeman-88-a-close-range-stu:
Harry A. Franck, author of A Vagabond Journey Around the World, wrote Zone Policeman 88 as a close-range study of the Panama Canal and its workers. He dedicates it to a host of good fellows, the Zone Police, opening from Quito, December 31, 1912. His first chapter follows the Thousand Stairs up to the red-roofed Administration Building, where Panama and its bay lie below.

Underneath, tight-packed roofs and plazas with three tops nestle in a bright curve of Pacific water, with tree-covered peaks reaching toward distant Taboga. Behind, low, uneven, jungle-clad hills fade hazily toward South America. At the third-floor landing he stops to mop perspiration from his brow and hatband, then enters through the screen door into police headquarters. Inside, the Captain glances up from a letter and asks what military service he has seen. Readers get Franck's firsthand account of joining the Zone Police.
4943-the-river-war-an-account-of-the-rec:
Winston S. Churchill's River War recounts the reconquest of the Sudan, beginning with the Mahdi's rebellion and the Nile country that made it possible. The Egyptian Sudan lies five hundred miles from the sea on every side, divided by mountain, swamp, and desert, and the great river alone carries its commerce and lets European civilization penetrate.

Churchill, who rode in the campaign, describes the provinces along the Nile's headstreams and the forces that clashed over them. The narrative combines geography, history, and battle with a young officer's eye. Readers get a classic of imperial war writing, vivid on the ground and frank about the costs of reconquest.
4961-our-mr-wrenn-the-romantic-adventure:
Sinclair Lewis's Our Mr. Wrenn follows a gentle, lonely clerk who walks with Miss Theresa, starts for the land of elsewhere, and becomes the great little Bill Wrenn. Chapters trace his quaint English flavor, his orphanhood, his meetings with temperaments and intellectuals, and his gipsying, orange tie, and discovery of America.

Wrenn enters society, studies five hundred and savoir faire, grows mildly religious, and finally becomes our Mr. Wrenn, a man transformed by travel and company. Lewis writes with affectionate irony about a nobody finding a self. Readers get an early Lewis novel, comic and tender, about ordinariness turning romantic.
5068-on-being-human:
Woodrow Wilson's On Being Human argues that reading should open up a narrow, shut-in inner life rather than simply increase the knowledge a person holds. Books may instruct, inform, startle, arouse, reform, provoke, or amuse, Wilson concedes, but true readers take pleasure rather than laboriously seeking instruction.

What readers seek is companionship, a renewed spirit, richer thought, and complete mental adventure, enjoyed in congenial company and in a broader world where all of these can be found. Lovers of the masters, Wilson insists, understand this at once. Readers get a short meditation on reading itself, by a scholar-president who believed books enlarge the self.
5336-stories-by-foreign-authors-scandina:
Stories by Foreign Authors: Scandinavian gathers short stories from the North, translated for American readers. Its contents include The Father and The Railroad and the Churchyard by Bjornstjerne Bjornson, When Father Brought Home the Lamp by Juhani Aho, The Flying Mail by M. Goldschmidt, Two Friends by Alexander Kielland, and Hopes by Frederika Bremer.

The Father, from Bjornson's Bridal March and translated by R. B. Anderson, opens the book with the story of the wealthiest and most influential person in his district. Readers get a compact anthology of Scandinavian realism, in which fathers, friends, railroads, and churchyards carry the weight of ordinary lives.
5397-dr-jonathan:
Winston Churchill, the American novelist, wrote Dr. Jonathan as a play in three acts during the First World War. Managers declined to stage it at the time, so Churchill published it instead, believing its theme would grow more timely once the fighting ended. That theme is self-determination, the right of peoples to choose their own government, which he saw as the true issue of the war.

The preface argues the point directly, drawing on American ideals and on Churchill's own return from abroad late in 1917. Readers get a wartime drama of ideas rather than battles: a playwright using the stage to argue what the war was really about, and what peace should honor.
5637-literary-and-philosophical-essays-f:
Literary and Philosophical Essays, volume thirty-two of the Harvard Classics, gathers French, German, and Italian essays in translation. Montaigne leads with pieces on judging happiness only after death, philosophizing as learning how to die, the education of children, friendship, and books. Sainte-Beuve asks what a classic is, and Renan writes on the poetry of the Celtic races.

Lessing contributes The Education of the Human Race, Schiller his Letters upon the Aesthetic Education of Man, and Kant his Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals. Readers get a compact library of European thought, from Renaissance essay to German philosophy.
5659-stories-by-foreign-authors-polish-g:
Stories by Foreign Authors gathers Polish, Greek, Belgian, and Hungarian tales in translation. It opens with Henryk Sienkiewicz's The Light-House Keeper of Aspinwall, from Yanko the Musician and Other Stories, translated by Jeremiah Curtin and published by Little, Brown in 1893. It begins when a lighthouse keeper in Aspinwall, near Panama, vanishes without trace during a storm, his boat missing from its rocky niche.

Demetrios Bikelas's The Plain Sister, Maurice Maeterlinck's The Massacre of the Innocents, Camille Lemonnier's Saint Nicholas Eve, and Maurice Jokai's In Love with the Czarina complete the set. Readers get five short masterpieces from four literatures, in one slim volume.
5728-stories-by-foreign-authors-italian:
Stories by Foreign Authors: Italian gathers short fiction in English translation by leading Italian writers. Its contents include A Great Day by Edmondo de Amicis, Pereat Rochus by Antonio Fogazzaro, San Pantaleone by Gabriele D'Annunzio, It Snows by Enrico Castelnuovo, and College Friends again by de Amicis. Each story offers a distinct Italian scene, from school and church to village life.

Readers meet Italian realism, irony, and lyric feeling in compact form, without needing to commit to a full novel. The collection suits readers sampling European short fiction, and students of translation who want to compare national styles. Together the stories show a literature of strong feeling and sharp observation, rooted in towns, families, and faith.
5741-stories-by-foreign-authors-russian:
Stories by Foreign Authors: Russian gathers short fiction in English translation, opening with an officer's garrison life in a small town. Mornings bring drill and the riding school. Dinners come with the colonel or at a Jewish restaurant. Evenings bring punch and cards, in a town with no open house and no marriageable girl. The catalog title points to Turgenev's Mumu among the tales collected here.

Readers get Russian short fiction in compact, accessible form, with army routine, village life, and strong feeling rendered plainly. The collection suits readers sampling Russian literature beyond the great novels, and students who want to compare translators' English. Together the stories show a tradition of close observation, moral pressure, and sudden reversals of fortune.
5745-she-and-allan:
Rider Haggard reunites Allan Quatermain with the mysterious She in She and Allan, a romance of Africa and ancient power. Chapters open with a talisman and messengers, then bring Umslopogaas of the axe, a lion and an axe, Inez, a sea-cow hunt, an oath, pursuit, a swamp, and an attack. Through a mountain wall waits the White Witch, and Allan hears a strange tale before missing his opportunity.

Readers get Haggard's signature mix of adventure, lost kingdoms, and supernatural dread, with Quatermain's plain narration grounding the marvels. The novel appeals to fans of imperial romance and fantasy adventure, and to readers tracing Haggard's long saga of She. Its pace is brisk, its dangers are vivid, and its central mystery keeps the quest moving from camp to mountain.
5793-stories-of-red-hanrahan:
Yeats gathers the stories of Red Hanrahan, a schoolmaster and poet wandering the Irish countryside. Contents include Red Hanrahan, The Twisting of the Rope, Hanrahan and Cathleen the Daughter of Hoolihan, Red Hanrahan's Curse, Hanrahan's Vision, and The Death of Hanrahan. Yeats thanks Lady Gregory for helping him rewrite the stories, which blend folklore, love, and fate.

This introduces a hero tempted by fairy women, bound by curses, and haunted by visions, in prose that reads like poetry. The tales favor mood and myth over realistic plot, with the Irish landscape as a living presence. Lovers of Yeats, Irish folklore, and lyric short fiction will find a small, powerful collection that shows the poet as storyteller.
5983-the-institutes-of-justinian:
The Institutes of Justinian present Roman law in the emperor's own address to youth desirous of studying law. Justinian, conqueror of Goths, Franks, Vandals, and many more peoples, declares that imperial majesty should be armed with laws as well as glorified with arms, for good government in war and peace.

This English version by J. B. Moyle follows the fifth edition of 1913. The work sets out the foundations of Roman law as a teaching text, meant to train students in justice as surely as armies win victories. Its proem frames law as the ruler's second weapon, equal to the sword.
6056-the-desired-woman:
Will N. Harben opens in Atlanta, inside a gray-stone bank on a narrow asphalt street sloping toward the old passenger depot, warehouses, and hotels. Clerks and accountants bend over ponderous ledgers before opening hour, while locomotive bells clang, steam escapes, and newsboys cry the morning papers.

Jarvis Saunders, of Mostyn, Saunders and Company, bankers and brokers, comes in and hangs up his straw hat. Harben sets a southern business romance amid banks, railways, and city noise. The desired woman of the title moves through a world of ledgers, deals, and reputations, where money and longing meet.
6057-fran:
John Breckenridge Ellis opens with Fran knocking at a front door too dark for finding the bell, though she would have knocked anyway. Nobody answers at first, which surprises no one, since everybody is supposed to be at the Union Camp-meeting advertised for two months in Littleburg.

Chapters promise a disturbing laugh, a foot-bridge, the woman who was not Mrs. Gregory, war declared, skirmishing, an ambuscade, and a new bridge at midnight. Grace captures outposts, alliances form, and a tamer of lions appears. Ellis turns a small town's secrets into a lively campaign of wit and feeling.
6125-the-making-of-an-american:
Jacob A. Riis, author of How the Other Half Lives, tells his own making as an American, insisting his papers are not made-up stories. Originally published in The Outlook, with one chapter in The Churchman and parts in Century Magazine, they trace a Danish immigrant's American life.

Chapters run from a meeting on the Long Bridge and landing in New York to going to war at last. Working and wandering follow, then going into business headlong, and becoming an editor who receives his first love letter. Elizabeth tells her story, early married life follows, and Riis writes with pride at having been in it all.
6137-the-home-of-the-blizzard-being-the-:
Douglas Mawson tells the story of the Australasian Antarctic Expedition of 1911 to 1914 in The Home of the Blizzard. It is illustrated in color and black and white with maps, 260 pictures, photogravure frontispieces, and plates from Dr. Wilson's sketches. He dedicates it to subscribers, comrades, and those who waited.

Mawson's preface aims at a connected narrative from a popular and general point of view, admitting the record is inadequate to the expedition's endeavors. Lasting reputation, he says, rests on scientific volumes to come, while Antarctic exploration history is kept to a minimum. The book brings blizzard country home.
6159-vicky-van:
Carolyn Wells introduces Vicky Van, whose full name Victoria Van Allen appears on letters and cheques, while Vicky Van signs her whole captivating personality, from dainty tossing head to dainty dancing feet. The narrator likes her from the first, though her small and earlies puzzle guests.

Chapters follow Mr. Somers, a waiter's story, Somers's real name, the Schuyler household, Vicky's ways, Ruth Schuyler, a letter box, and a social secretary. An inquest, notes from Vicky, Fleming Stone, walls with tongues, and proofs lead to truth from Ruth. Wells mixes society mystery with bright comedy.
6395-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
Long disturbance ends when the Flavian family restores empire to peace and security, Suetonius says, though its descent was obscure and boasted no ancestral honours. The public had no cause to regret the elevation, except that Domitian later met the just reward of avarice and cruelty. Titus Flavius Petro of Reate, centurion or evocatus of Pompey's party, fled Pharsalia and went home, founding the line that would rule.

Vespasian himself reforms army discipline with a sharp tongue. Telling a perfumed young officer seeking thanks for a horse command that he would rather he had smelt of garlic, he revokes the commission. Fleet men travelling from Ostia and Puteoli to Rome petition late for gratuities, and the emperor answers with law and delay. Suetonius gives a plain, thrifty ruler, whose jokes and firmness steadied Rome after three violent reigns.
6397-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
Born on October 24, when his father was consul elect, in Rome's sixth region at the Pomegranate, Domitian grew up in want and infamy. Suetonius says he owned not one piece of plate. Clodius Pollio, a praetorian, kept a note in Domitian's handwriting and sometimes produced it, a small evidence of a youth spent borrowing and promising. The house of his birth later became a temple of the Flavian family.

As emperor, Domitian turns savage after civil war success. He puts Helvidius the younger to death for a farce on Paris and Oenone that mocked his divorce. Flavius Sabinus, his cousin, dies because a crier blundered and proclaimed him emperor instead of consul at election. He hunts the adverse party with industry. Suetonius writes the last Flavian as a reign where a slip of the tongue could kill, and fear governed Rome.
6451-the-rover-boys-on-the-great-lakes-o:
Arthur M. Winfield, the pen name of Edward Stratemeyer, sends the Rover boys to the Great Lakes in the fifth volume of their series, subtitled The Secret of the Island Cave. A storm on Lake Erie opens it: Dick, Sam, and Tom Rover watch wind freshening ten minutes and wonder if they should turn back, three miles from shore. Talk turns to the Baxters, buried alive in a Colorado mountain landslide, a terrible fate the brothers are glad to be rid of.

Later, Sam and Tom insist Captain Langless hides the Baxters and Dick aboard his boat, while the captain, asked about stowaways, hears his mate answer that none were found below. It is all a riddle to him, he says. The volume is a complete story in itself, the introduction promises, with sailing, storms, and a search for a hidden cave on island waters.
646-the-coral-island-a-tale-of-the-pacif:
Robert Michael Ballantyne writes a boys' adventure in this 1884 tale of the Pacific, with illustrations by Dalziel. Ralph Rover, born at sea to a line of captains, thirsts for adventure and sails abroad, only to be wrecked on a coral island with two companions. The preface speaks straight to boys, promising pleasure, profit, and amusement.

Ballantyne writes with brisk, hearty prose, full of reefs, canoes, and island perils. The tale taught generations of boys to dream of the South Seas. It endures as a classic castaway story, where three lads learn courage, friendship, and faith on a coral shore.
6474-the-iron-woman:
Margaret Deland's The Iron Woman, dated August 12, 1911, opens with Elizabeth Ferguson commanding children to climb an apple tree and play house in the Maitland orchard. She sits on the lowest branch, swinging white stockinged legs so recklessly that the summoned children back away for safety. If you do not, she warns, looking down, perhaps, maybe, I will get mad, her foreboding tempered by a giggle and a deepening dimple.

The others know well what Elizabeth mad means, and Nannie Maitland, oldest of the group, answers helplessly, well. Nannie is always helpless with Elizabeth, as with her half brother Blair. A mid passage shows Robert Ferguson complaining of a love sick girl on his hands, trowel under arm, thinning peonies in the fall. Deland writes a strong willed heroine and the family that bends around her.
6481-personal-experience-of-a-physician:
John Ellis, M.D., writes Personal Experience of a Physician with an appeal to the medical and clerical professions, plus a review of Christ and the Temperance Question in the Christian Union. Every physician, he opens, should strive for the best education medical schools afford, since physicians hold not simply property or money but the very lives of their fellows. His chapters argue why every physician should examine homoeopathy, and warn of dangers from allopathic treatment of diseases.

Personal religious experience follows, with dawn of a new dispensation, a new day for earth, wants of the Christian church, and restraining and curing spiritual and natural diseases. A mid passage quotes Galatians: whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap, urging practical doctrines uniting religion and life. Ellis writes a doctor's testimony, where medicine, faith, and temperance meet.
6609-myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-v:
Puritan New England takes center stage in Skinner's fourth volume, from Evangeline to Salem witchcraft. A snoring hermit, a dead ship at Harpswell, a partridge witch, and Peter Rugg, the missing man, all pass in turn. The White Mountains, Mount Katahdin, and the Saco river give the tales their stern, pine-dark ground.

Witch lore, lost loves, and grim portraits, like that of Edward Randolph, show a people who feared both devil and neighbor. Skinner tells each story briefly, letting the place and the dread do the work. Tales of Puritan Land is a dark, rich slice of New England folk memory.
663-the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-d:
This section of Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary, published in 1913 by Merriam under Noah Porter, covers words from F through G. Entries give spelling, pronunciation, part of speech, etymology, and numbered senses, from F, the sixth letter, through Fa, the fourth tone in solmization, and Fabaceous, like a bean, and onward. Notes trace Latin, Greek, and Phoenician forms.

Here the dictionary moves from music and fable into the thick of G: fables, fabrics, and feudal terms yield to gardens, gems, and ghosts. The two-letter span shows how much of English sits in ordinary work and play. It is a handy shelf for settling a spelling or tracing a word's kin.
665-the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-d:
This section of Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary, published in 1913 by Merriam under Noah Porter, covers words from M through N. Entries give spelling, pronunciation, part of speech, etymology, and numbered senses, from M, the labio-nasal letter, through Ma, a child's word for mother, and onward through hundreds of headwords. Guide references aid pronunciation.

Spanning two letters, this slice is a wide field for browsing: mammal names, manners, and measures sit beside nautical and legal terms. A reader can watch meanings shift as M gives way to N. It keeps 1913 English in view, a useful check for anyone reading old books or tracing a word's past.
6687-from-the-caves-and-jungles-of-hindo:
Helena Blavatsky's letters from India, first sent to the Russian Messenger, were written in leisure moments more for fun than for science. She warns readers herself that facts and incidents are broadly true. Yet she grouped, colored, and dramatized them for artistic effect. She would rather be judged as a romance of travel than as a serious work. Her translator adds a like caution.

Caves, jungles, temples, and strange folk fill the letters, with wonder and wit in equal parts. Blavatsky's voice is bold, curious, and never dull. From the Caves and Jungles of Hindostan is a vivid, period travel romance, best read for its color rather than as a guidebook.
6730-observations-of-a-retired-veteran:
Henry Tinsley, writing as P. Boyzy in the Staunton Vindicator, offers essays chosen from years of weekly columns. His editor praises a winning humor joined to pathos, humor's most exquisite companion, and a shrewd, homely wit joined to deep knowledge of the human heart. Tinsley, a political journalist in his strenuous years, turns here to gentler themes.

The essays that follow mix laughter and feeling, with a Virginian's eye for character. They read like talk from a wise old friend, not like lectures. Observations of a Retired Veteran is a warm, small book of newspaper wisdom, still pleasant to dip into.
6741-memoirs-of-the-life-of-the-rt-hon-r:
Thomas Moore writes the memoirs of Richard Brinsley Sheridan, playwright and statesman, in two volumes, the first inscribed to George Bryan. Moore notes that his first four chapters were written seven years before, then set aside during a long absence from England, and only finished in the last year. Charles Sheridan, the subject's son, supplied most of the materials.

Moore thanks Charles for trust and for restraint, since, though deeply concerned, he never meddled with the work. The memoirs that follow trace Sheridan from stage triumphs to parliament and ruin. Volume one is a rich, friendly life of a wit who ruled both theatre and Commons.
7016-adventures-in-the-land-of-canaan:
Robert Lee Berry writes Adventures in the Land of Canaan from the heart, hoping to reach the hearts of others. Some lessons came through long and bitter experience, and the adventures were very real, though he hopes readers may never face some of them. The real battles, he writes, are fought within, and the struggle for mastery goes on in the soul, hidden in the mysterious depths of the spirit.

Such battles are often fought alone, while others nearby sense nothing of moment happening. Berry disclaims interest in pleasing super critical minds, writing only to bless the hearts and lives of common men and women. The book blends travel, trial, and faith into a plain spiritual memoir, grateful for help received in the writing.
7040-paula-the-waldensian:
Eva Lecomte's Paula the Waldensian, adapted and translated from the Spanish by W M Strong, hopes young readers will share the joy its author found in writing it. Paula's Saviour, Lecomte writes, wishes to be the reader's Saviour too. Paula had her faults, yet she gave God her whole heart and cared for others as for herself: an unspoiled village girl, youthful and sturdy, gentle and selfless.

Lecomte compares her to a sparkling stream in the country she loved, clean and bright, gliding silently past forget-me-nots along its flowered banks. It was by love that Paula conquered, as the tale will show. The author, living at Villar at the valley's foot, invites any reader who visits her country to call. The book is a gentle tale of Waldensian faith.
706-the-amateur-cracksman:
E. W. Hornung introduced A. J. Raffles in this first set of tales, told by his school friend Bunny Manders. Raffles is a star cricketer and a darling of London clubs by day, and a bold burglar by night. Bunny, broke and in debt, is drawn into the game and narrates each job with awe and dread.

Eight stories follow, from the Ides of March to the Gift of the Emperor, with jewel thefts, disguise, and narrow escapes. Hornung plays the crime tale as a sport: skill, nerve, and honour among thieves count for more than brute force. The book set the model for the gentleman thief, and it still reads as brisk, witty adventure.
707-raffles-further-adventures-of-the-am:
E. W. Hornung continues the tales of A. J. Raffles, the gentleman cricketer who steals by night, told by his friend Bunny Manders. In these eight stories Raffles takes a sinecure, steals a jubilee gift, chases a thief, and meets old flames, all with cool nerve and charm. The year 1897 frames the action, and London's clubs and streets form the stage.

Bunny's voice gives the tales their pull: he admires Raffles, fears the law, and cannot quit the game. Hornung keeps the plots brisk, with disguise, wit, and close escapes. The book fixed the gentleman thief in popular fiction, and it still charms readers who enjoy crime told from the thief's side, with style rather than gore.
7072-tramping-through-mexico-guatemala-a:
Harry Franck tramps through Mexico, Guatemala, and Honduras in random notes of an incurable vagabond, illustrated with his own photographs. He dedicates the book to the Mexican peon, with sincere wishes for his ultimate emancipation. His foreword says the simple story of a journey southward grew up of itself, as he chose a less monotonous route than a steamship track toward a planned exploration of South America.

The narrative gives day by day rambles over bad roads into worse lodgings, the lot of all who venture afield south of the Rio Grande. It joins his five months on the Canal Zone, already published, and clears the stage for a larger South America volume to come. Franck writes a vagabond's plain, observant travel book.
7124-the-coral-island-a-tale-of-the-paci:
R M Ballantyne's Coral Island, a tale of the Pacific Ocean, opens with Ralph Rover recalling he was a boy when he lived the wonderful adventures set down. With boyish feelings strong in memory, he presents the book specially to boys, hoping they gain information, pleasure, profit, and unbounded amusement. Any boy or man who loves melancholy and cannot share kindly in fun, he warns, should shut the book and put it away, since it is not meant for him.

Contents promise early life and character, departure and a dreadful storm, the coral island itself, curious discoveries, and enchanting excursions among coral groves. An excursion inland and a horrible encounter with a shark wait beyond. Ballantyne writes a boys classic of shipwreck, island life, and high spirits.
7251-sweet-cicely-or-josiah-allen-as-a-p:
Marietta Holley, writing as Josiah Allen's Wife, dedicates Sweet Cicely to sad-eyed mothers who, like Cicely, look across the cradle of their boys into a great world of temptation and danger. Her preface opens in Josiah's voice, debating whether one child may be loved more than another. Her answer, that she loves them all yet feels a special sorrow for one, sets the book's tender, comic tone.

Josiah Allen as a politician gives the tale its public frame, while Cicely gives it a mother's heart. Holley writes in the wife's own homely dialect, mixing humour with moral warning about drink and danger. The novel pleads for boys at risk through a mother's eyes, plain and warm.
7279-the-shopkeeper-turned-gentleman:
Moliere's Shopkeeper Turned Gentleman, Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme in Charles Heron Wall's English prose translation, first played before the king at Chambord on October 14, 1670, and at the Palais Royal that November. Louis XIV told Moliere he had never written anything that amused him more, and Paris agreed, as the bourgeois good-humouredly laughed at what they took for their neighbours' weaknesses.

Wall notes that the first three acts are the best, since the king hurried Moliere over the last. Yet the comedy's heart stays clear: a tradesman aping gentility, taught by masters, dressed by tailors, and fooled by flattery. The play's laughter cuts both ways, at snobbery and at those who feed it. This translation keeps its prose brisk for stage and study.
7305-memoir-and-letters-of-francis-w-new:
I. Giberne Sieveking's Memoir and Letters of Francis W. Newman follows its subject from ancestors and two brothers at school and college through a missionary journey to the East, marriage, his mother's death, and a classical tutorship at Bristol in 1834. Friendship with Dr Martineau and Newman's work as a teacher carry the story onward, with letters giving the man's voice throughout.

Sieveking dedicates the book to her mother and fronts it with a Greek motto on praising one who dares to renew the state of the many. Newman emerges as a restless, principled scholar, brother to a cardinal yet on his own road. The memoir lets letters do much of the telling, plain and intimate.
7424-the-wishing-ring-man:
Margaret Widdemer, a Pulitzer-winning poet, wrote this romantic fantasy for young readers. Its heroine is Joy, first seen in amber satin. Its chapters promise the stuff of fairy tales: a wishing ring, a princess rescued, a fountain in fairyland, and pirate cousins coming to the rescue. Phyllis rides through the story, and a shadow named Gail falls across the bright scenes.

The book mixes the everyday with the enchanted, as a ring's grace turns ordinary girls' lives toward adventure and romance. Rose gardens and men, a very charming gentleman, and the serious business of staging Iolanthe fill out the tale. Widdemer dedicated it to her grandfather, one of the dearest and kindliest of men. It reads as a gentle fantasy of wishes, friendship, and first love.
744-the-golden-mean:
An electronic text gives the golden ratio, (1 + sqrt(5)) / 2, to one million digits, opening 1.6180339887 and running on in long blocks of figures. It rests on a computation of the square root of five by Robert Nemiroff and Jerry Bonnell. There is no essay or story here: the file is the number itself, laid out for reference.

Readers use such a file to check calculations, to test programs, or to feed art and design work that draws on the ratio. Its length is its point, since a million digits far pass any need of hand reckoning. The text stands as a plain, exact record of a famous constant, kept in full for anyone who wants it at hand.
7440-the-koran-al-qur-an:
George Sale's translation of the Koran, first published in 1734, was for two centuries the English Koran most readers knew. Sale worked from the original Arabic and added explanatory notes drawn from the most approved commentators of Islam. Before the text itself he placed a long Preliminary Discourse, explaining the history, teachings, and divisions of the Muslim faith to English readers.

The translation's plain, readable English and its wealth of notes made it the standard scholarly version of its age, and later translators measured themselves against it. Modern readers should know its eighteenth-century framing, which reflects its time. As a historical document, however, it remains important: the version through which the English-speaking world first met the Koran at length.
7562-quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-m:
Madame de Montespan, Louis XIV's famous mistress, tells her life in memoirs gathered here in quotations and images. All the death-in-life of a convent opens the entries, beside ambition putting a thick bandage over the eyes, and beauty armed with sarcasm. The memoirs show a woman who rose by charm and fell by intrigue, watching herself as she goes.

Conduct of the sort which cements and revives attachments appears, with console me on the morrow for what troubled me today. Cuddlings and caresses of decrepitude appear too, with domestics that included two nurses, a waiting-maid, and a physician. Depicting other figures, Montespan really portrays her own. The volume is a court memoir in fragments, extravagant, as its heroine admits, without the means to be so.
7775-memoirs-of-the-life-of-the-rt-hon-r:
Thomas Moore's Memoirs of Richard Brinsley Sheridan, volume two, follows the playwright and statesman through his middle years. Contents run from the impeachment of Hastings and his father's death to the king's illness, the regency, and the French Revolution, with parliament at the center.

Later chapters cover Burke's break with Sheridan, the death of Mrs. Sheridan, Drury Lane Theatre, the Friends of the People, war with France, and speeches in Parliament. Through letters and talk, Moore paints a brilliant, debt-ridden wit at the heart of Georgian politics and stage, loved for charm and blamed for excess.
7848-last-poems-by-a-e-housman:
A. E. Housman's Last Poems, published in September 1922, gathers verse mostly from 1895 to 1910, with a quarter from that April. Housman says he prints them because he no longer expects the sustained excitement that produced most of his first book in early 1895, and wishes to control spelling himself.

The opening poem bids farewell to woods where laurels are cut and bowers bare of bay. Later pieces look west beyond moor and mountain crest, where sun drinks day away and a lone pine guards the line. Spare, stoic, and musical, the book closes a small, lasting body of lyric work.
7857-the-way-of-an-indian:
Frederic Remington's The Way of an Indian, first published in February 1906 and pictured by the author, follows White Otter of the Chis-Chis-Chash. His heart is bad as he sits alone on rim-rocks above a sunlit valley, watching lodges, pony herds, and prismatic mountains in a rare day of peace.

Contents run from White Otter's own shadow and a brown bat's mischief through a new lodge, kites and crows, a fire-eater's bad medicine, pony soldiers, and a medicine fight. Through a Native hero's eyes, Remington tells of war, craft, and honor on the western plains.
7866-an-ambitious-man:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox's An Ambitious Man, first issued in 1908 and reprinted in 1914 by Gay and Hancock, opens with Preston Cheney waving farewell. He leaves a handsome Boulevard house, where Mabel Lawrence stands at a lace-curtained window. He has just asked her to marry him, yet her pale blue eyes show only satisfaction.

Mabel, the novel says, is moved by no passion stronger than worldly ambition, jealousy, or anger. Her meager nature matches a face that belies a siren's form. Through courtship, wealth, and social climbing, Wilcox traces ambition's cold bargain and its cost to love.
790-lady-windermere-s-fan:
Oscar Wilde wrote this play about a good woman, Lady Windermere, whose birthday fan becomes the token of a scandal. Mrs Erlynne, a woman with a past, enters London society and seems bent on stealing Lord Windermere, while Lady Windermere plans to flee with Lord Darlington. Secrets, letters, and a fan left in a man's rooms drive the plot.

Wilde's wit sparkles in every scene, yet the play turns serious on a mother's sacrifice: Mrs Erlynne is, in truth, Lady Windermere's mother, shielding her daughter at her own cost. First staged in 1892, the play made Wilde a West End force. It remains his most tender comedy of manners.
7936-peeps-at-many-lands-japan:
John Finnemore wrote this children's introduction to Japan for the Peeps at Many Lands series, with twelve colour illustrations by Ella Du Cane. Its short chapters cover the land itself, Japanese boys and girls, home life, a Japanese day, games. The Feast of Dolls and the Feast of Flags, kite-flying, fairy stories, tea-houses and temples, the rickshaw-man, the countryside, and police and soldiers.

The book explains everyday Japan in simple terms for young readers, with pictures to match each subject. It reflects the Edwardian taste for friendly, illustrated geography, and it now also reads as a period piece: Japan seen through British eyes a century ago. For families and collectors of old travel books for children, it is a gentle, vivid first look.
7937-journal-of-an-african-cruiser-compr:
Horatio Bridge, an officer of the United States Navy, kept the Journal of an African Cruiser, edited by Nathaniel Hawthorne and published in London in 1845. Sketches cover the Canaries, Cape Verds, Liberia, Madeira, Sierra Leone, and other west African coasts visited on cruise.

Bridge says idle hours in a region little seductive might have been wasted or embittered, so he wrote daily, keeping his journal form despite lack of literary practice. Notes from commonplace books join the entries. Through a sailor's plain record, the book shows Africa's coast as Americans met it.
808-the-complete-plays-of-gilbert-and-su:
William S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan wrote fourteen comic operas together between 1871 and 1896, and this volume gathers their libretti. The Gondoliers, The Grand Duke, H.M.S. Pinafore, Iolanthe, The Mikado, and The Pirates of Penzance head the set, with eight more in full acts.

Gilbert's topsy-turvy plots and witty verse meet Sullivan's graceful music, though only the words appear here. Each opera turns rank, law, or love upside down, with choruses of sailors, peers, or fairies. The collection is the core library for Savoy fans, and a fine way to read the jokes that made the pair famous.
81-the-return-of-tarzan:
Tarzan sails for Europe still torn between jungle and civilization. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Return of Tarzan, second in the series, opens with intrigue aboard a liner and a duel in Paris. Countess Olga explains a plot that binds Tarzan to old enemies.

Desert fights, a dancing girl, and the valley of the Waziri follow. Tarzan becomes white chief of the Waziri and finds the lost city of Opar, with its gold vaults and priestess La. The novel ends with Tarzan choosing the wild over London. Its mix of adventure and identity made the series grow.
8118-redburn-his-first-voyage-being-the-:
Herman Melville wrote Redburn from his own youth, following Wellingborough Redburn, son of a gentleman, on his first voyage in the merchant navy. The chapters trace how his taste for the sea was born, his departure from home, his arrival in town, the sale of his fowling-piece, and the purchase of his sea wardrobe. Once aboard, he cleans the pig-pen, slushes the top-mast, joins the larboard watch, and suffers seasickness.

Redburn is a young man's education in hard work, low pay, and the gap between romantic dreams of the sea and its reality. Melville, who had shipped before the mast himself, writes with humour and bitterness in equal measure. The book stands as a companion to his later sea fiction, and as a vivid picture of a sailor boy's Liverpool voyage.
8128-in-ghostly-japan:
Lafcadio Hearn's In Ghostly Japan gathers fragments, stories, and notes on Japanese ghost lore and Buddhism. Its contents include Furisode, Incense, A Story of Divination, Silkworms, A Passional Karma, Footprints of the Buddha, Ululation, Bits of Poetry, Japanese Buddhist Proverbs, and a Story of a Tengu at Yaidzu. Illustrations show the Mountain of Skulls, the Magical Incense, the Peony Lantern, and the Lights of the Dead.

Hearn retells ghost stories with atmosphere and respect, explaining the beliefs behind them rather than merely thrilling the reader. The opening fragment, at sunset at the foot of a desolate mountain, sets the book's mood. For lovers of ghost stories and Japanese culture, it is Hearn at his most evocative, and a classic of supernatural writing.
8388-poems-by-walt-whitman:
William Michael Rossetti selected and edited these poems by Walt Whitman for English readers, in a new edition that helped carry Leaves of Grass across the Atlantic. Whitman's free verse, catalogues of American life, and celebrations of the self, the body, and democracy appear here. Rossetti judged this selection fit to introduce a foreign audience to a startling new poet.

Rossetti's edition mattered: it gave Whitman his first serious English hearing, among readers who would champion him. The poems themselves need little introduction, from songs of the open road to elegies for Lincoln. Readers new to Whitman get a shaped introduction; readers who know him get a historic selection, made by a friend of the Pre-Raphaelites.
8429-the-ancestral-footstep-fragment-out:
Nathaniel Hawthorne left this volume's materials unfinished, and it gathers them together: The Dolliver Romance, Fanshawe, and Septimius Felton, with an appendix containing The Ancestral Footstep. An introductory note explains that Septimius Felton grew from Hawthorne's plan, formed while living in England, for a romance set there, and the Footstep outlines that English romance.

Readers meet Hawthorne's late experiments: a New England tale of elixirs and guilt, an early college novel, and fragments of a story about an American claiming an English estate. The volume suits Hawthorne devotees, who will find his themes, sin, inheritance, and the past's grip, in draft and outline. It is a book of beginnings, fascinating precisely because they stop short.
85-the-beasts-of-tarzan:
Tarzan's wife and child are stolen, and his revenge runs through jungle and sea. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Beasts of Tarzan, third in the series, opens with kidnapping and marooning off Africa. Tarzan escapes with the help of apes, panthers, and other beasts.

Mugambi the chieftain joins him, and the trail leads down the Ugambi River to the Kincaid. Paulvitch plots revenge while Tarzan rallies the law of the jungle. The novel pits beast loyalty against human treachery. Its pace and animal allies made it a series favorite. The beasts' loyalty contrasts with the villains' greed in nearly every chapter.
850-tom-grogan:
F. Hopkinson Smith wrote this novel about Tom Grogan, a stevedore boss on the New York waterfront. Babcock, a businessman waiting for a ferry, first senses trouble in the air, and the tale unfolds around the docks, where work, rivals, and loyalties clash. Tom runs a tough crew in a tough trade.

Smith, who knew the waterfront world, writes with vigour for its labour, its bargains, and its codes of honour. The novel turns on fair dealing against sharp practice, and on the respect Tom earns from men and rivals alike. It remains a sturdy, old-fashioned tale of American working life, told with sympathy and pace.
8539-in-those-days-the-story-of-an-old-m:
Jehudah Steinberg wrote In Those Days, the story of an old man, translated from Hebrew by George Jeshurun in 1915. It opens as the time draws near for Samuel the Beadle to let his son begin military service. The old man goes to market, buys a regulation shirt, a knapsack, and other things a soldier needs, not forgetting the main item, fetched in haste.

Steinberg writes of Jewish life in Eastern Europe, where a father's preparations for a son's army service carry a whole world of custom, fear, and love. Readers get a short, moving tale, told in an old man's voice, about generations and duty. The translation brings a Hebrew classic to English readers, plain and poignant.
8549-the-woman-with-the-fan:
Robert Hichens wrote The Woman with the Fan, opening in a large, cool London drawing room, where a few people listen to a soprano singing to piano accompaniment from an inner room. Most look earnestly toward the singer, while one or two seem indifferent to her fascination, including a little woman with oily black hair, whose presence hints at the story's tensions.

Hichens, a popular novelist of society and the exotic, writes of London life, music, and desire, with the fan as a symbol of coquetry and concealment. Readers get an Edwardian society novel, elegant and slightly scandalous. The book suits readers of Hichens's world, where drawing rooms hide as much as they display.
8644-the-story-of-ab-a-tale-of-the-time-:
Stanley Waterloo sets this 1905 novel in the Stone Age, following Ab, a cave man who loves and fights well in a world without fixed dates or written records. Waterloo says scholars of prehistoric life on two continents helped him shape the story, and the introduction stresses that Ab's age can only be guessed at. The tale moves through hunting, danger, and tribal struggle.

Ab's strength, loyalty, and temper carry the plot, while details of tools, shelters, and wild beasts fill out daily life before farming and metal. The book belongs to an era fascinated by early humans, when novelists turned new science into adventure. Readers today get both a rattling old story and a window onto how 1905 imagined the deep past, with all its confidence and its guesswork on show.
8661-an-algonquin-maiden-a-romance-of-th:
G. Mercer Adam and A. Ethelwynn Wetherald wrote this romance of early Upper Canada, entered for copyright in Ottawa in 1886. The story is set among the settlements, forests, and waterways of the young colony, where an Algonquin maiden stands at the meeting point of Native life and incoming settlers. Its dedication to Montreal publisher John Lovell presents it modestly as a Canadian fiction effort.

Love, loyalty, and cultural distance drive the plot, as characters from different worlds must judge one another across language and custom. The novel belongs to a generation of Canadian writers trying to give their country its own stories, rooted in its landscape and early history. Modern readers will find period views of Native people that need care, alongside a sincere attempt to imagine Canada's beginnings as romance.
8700-the-evolution-of-man:
Ernst Haeckel, the German biologist, sets out his popular study of human evolution in this 1912 English version, translated by Joseph McCabe from the fifth enlarged edition. Issued for the Rationalist Press Association, the book walks readers through embryology and phylogeny, the older and newer sciences of development and descent. Chapters cover the ovum, conception, the gastraea theory, and the gastrulation of vertebrates, with a glossary and a table classifying the animal world.

Haeckel's fundamental law, that the embryo repeats the history of its species, organizes the whole argument, illustrated with plates from the book's famous drawings. Some of his claims have been revised by later science, and readers should treat the book as history of science as much as science itself. Even so, it remains a powerful statement of Darwinian thought at its most confident, and a key to how evolution was popularized.
876-life-in-the-iron-mills-or-the-korl-w:
Rebecca Harding Davis wrote this novella of life in an iron-mill town, where the sky sinks muddy and flat before dawn and the air is thick with the breath of crowded workers. Hugh Wolfe, a mill hand, sculpts a strange figure from korl, the waste of the furnaces, a woman with a hungry, pleading face.

Davis uses Hugh's art to ask what becomes of souls crushed by labour, and whether beauty can plead for the poor. Her realism was new and shocking in its day, and the tale helped launch American social fiction. The book remains a powerful, short classic, read for its pity and its moral force.
90-the-son-of-tarzan:
Tarzan's son Jack grows up in London hearing tales of his father's jungle life. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Son of Tarzan follows Jack as he runs away to Africa and takes the ape name Korak. A strange white man on the Ugambi River sets the plot in motion.

Korak learns the jungle, befriends apes, and meets Meriem, a girl held by Arab raiders. Their youth, danger, and first love fill the novel's middle chapters. Tarzan himself returns to the story as father and judge. The book passes the series torch to a new generation.
9298-life-and-death-of-harriett-frean:
May Sinclair published this short novel in 1922, tracing one woman from babyhood to death. It opens with Baby Harriett laughing at Pussycat and the Queen, a rhyme her mother says three times. Her parents kiss her in turn, puzzled and charmed by what the child sees that they cannot.

From that bright start, Harriett grows into a woman shaped by duty, self-denial, and the claims of family. Sinclair follows her choices with cool, exact prose, showing how goodness can curdle into waste. The novel remains a sharp, modern study of a life lived for others.
938-good-indian:
B. M. Bower wrote this western about the Peaceful Hart Ranch and its folk, with a character called Good Indian at its heart. Chapters on old wives' tales, a Christmas angel who plays ghost, and Miss Georgie Howard, the telephone operator, mix ranch work with humour and romance. Pepajee Jim and midnight prowlers add trouble.

Bower writes the West with a light, knowing touch, praising ranch loyalty and poking fun at greenhorns and gossips. Her dialogue is brisk, and her people feel real. The book charms readers who like westerns with humour and heart, where the ranch, not the gunfight, is the centre of the tale.
9401-the-leopard-woman:
Stewart Edward White wrote this African novel in 1916, illustrated by W. H. D. Koerner. Its chapters march from camp and rhinoceros to a stranger, an encounter, and the leopard woman herself. A water hole, thirst, and a plateau follow, with an ivory stockade, a tropic moon, and ranges crossed. Kingozi, M'tela, and Winkleman's safari crowd the tale.

The leopard woman changes her spots, faces trial, and hears Kingozi's ultimatum, as councils of war gather. White writes of Africa with a hunter's eye and a novelist's pace. The book remains a rousing adventure of the dark continent, in the manner of its age.
946-lady-susan:
Jane Austen wrote this short novel in letters about Lady Susan Vernon, a beautiful, scheming widow who charms her way through society. In forty-one letters and a conclusion, Lady Susan writes to her brother, her friend, and her victims, plotting marriages for herself and her daughter Frederica, while hiding her true aims.

Austen's irony is sharp: Lady Susan's own letters betray her, even as she flatters her readers. The novella, written early and published after Austen's death, shows her wit at its most biting. Lady Susan remains a favourite among Austen fans, as a portrait of a villainess who almost wins.
9476-ridgeway-an-historical-romance-of-t:
Scian Dubh, a pen name, wrote Ridgeway in 1868, a romance of the Fenian raid on Canada. Fenians were Irish patriots who sought to free Ireland by striking at British rule in North America. The novel follows their march, their hopes, and their clash with Canadian troops at Ridgeway. Its preface sets seven hundred years of Irish woe as the spur for the raid.

The tale blends battle scenes with pleas for Irish freedom, casting the raiders as brave men wronged by long rule. It reads as both a war story and a piece of Irish national feeling, raw and earnest. A reader gets a rare, partisan view of a failed 1866 raid, told by a voice close to the cause, not by cool hindsight.
9487-a-fair-barbarian:
Frances Hodgson Burnett, later famed for The Secret Garden, wrote A Fair Barbarian in 1881, a comedy of manners. Octavia Bassett, a bright young woman from Nevada, bursts upon the staid English town of Slowbridge. Slowbridge, unused to shocks, reels at her free ways, her wealth, and her talk of shares and mines. Lady Theobald, Lucia, and Lord Lansdowne circle her as the town gossips.

Chapters follow croquet, garden parties, calls, and a slight indiscretion, as Octavia tests English rules with American candor. Burnett keeps the tone light, but the clash cuts deep: new money meets old form. A reader gets a witty, early Burnett romance, and a comic view of two worlds learning to live together.
9489-michael-o-halloran:
Gene Stratton-Porter wrote Michael O'Halloran in 1915, a novel of a newsboy hero in a city alley. Mickey, a quick, brave lad of Sunrise Alley, fights for fair pay and for a small brother in his care. Chapters bear names like Happy Home in Sunrise Alley, Moccasins and Lady Slippers, and The Song of a Bird. Stratton-Porter, famed for nature tales, sets city grit beside woodland grace.

As Mickey meets Nancy and Peter, an orphans' home, and a hermit thrush, his pluck wins friends and a better life. The Wheel of Life and Mickey's Miracle mark his rise from alley scraps to hope. A reader gets a warm, old-style tale of a boy's grit, with nature lore and a firm belief in kind hearts.
966-maid-marian:
Thomas Love Peacock wrote this comic romance of Maid Marian, opening at Rubygill Abbey. An abbot in his alb stands at the altar with his plump, sleek, rosy friars, to marry the beautiful Matilda Fitzwater, daughter of a baron. Robin Hood's men break in, and Matilda becomes Marian of the greenwood.

Peacock retells the Robin Hood legend with wit and satire, mocking monks, lords, and law, while praising love and liberty in Sherwood. His prose is urbane, his songs are gay, and his Robin is a gentleman outlaw. The book charms readers who like the legend told with a smile, and with a poet's eye for fun.
9664-an-amiable-charlatan:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote An Amiable Charlatan, a light novel of rogues, gamblers, and high society. The tale opens at Stephano's, moves to a coup in a gambling den, and follows the wooing of Eve. Mr. Bundercombe, a genial rogue, winks, loves, and schemes through parties at the Milan and the Alhambra. An exposure and a broken partnership test his charm.

Later chapters free Louis, teach Lord Porthening a lesson, and close with a shorn lamb's fate. Oppenheim writes with easy wit and a fondness for likable scoundrels. A reader gets a breezy Edwardian rogue tale, full of clubs, wagers, and amused villainy.
9749-the-highwayman:
H. C. Bailey wrote The Highwayman, a romance of Queen Anne's England, in chapters of wit and adventure. Harry, the complete hero, moves through the house of Waverton, a gentleman's purse, and a world of miracles. Miss Lambourne looks sideways, an uncle angers, and Captain McBean takes horse. Queen Anne dies, revelations follow, and virtue proves its own reward.

Bailey writes with polished, playful prose, favoring talk, duel, and disguise. The highwayman's road crosses love, debt, and honor in turn. A reader gets a charming historical romance, light yet sharp, from a master of period wit.
9791-harrigan:
Max Brand wrote Harrigan in 1918, a western tale of a red-headed man marked by a police captain's eye. The captain, proud after raiding two opium dens, points Harrigan out in a crowd. Harrigan, hat stuffed in a back pocket, walks through light that sets his hair afire like a danger signal. Brand, famed for western yarns, opens with a manhunt's tension.

The novel follows Harrigan through crowds, dens, and desert trails, as law and outlaw trade wits. Brand writes with swift, pulpy energy. A reader gets a classic Max Brand western, full of red hair, danger signals, and a hero the law cannot quite catch.
986-master-and-man:
Leo Tolstoy wrote this tale of master and man, translated by Louise and Aylmer Maude. It happened in the seventies, in winter, on the day after St. Nicholas's Day, when Vasili Andreevich Brekhunov, a second-guild merchant and church elder, sets out with his servant Nikita through a blizzard on business.

The storm traps master and servant in the snow, and Brekhunov, who has lived for gain, must choose between self and the man he has used. Tolstoy tells the choice with stark, moral power, as the snow closes in. Master and Man is a late Tolstoy masterpiece, short, severe, and profoundly moving.
9879-the-amateur-gentleman:
Jeffery Farnol's novel opens with Barnabas, a strong young countryman, knocking his father down in a quarrel and then setting out for London. He means to remake himself as a gentleman, though he starts with little more than muscle, good manners, and nerve.

In town Barnabas buys books, learns how to bow, meets a lady of quality, and settles disputes with his fists as often as with words. Farnol tells the tale in a warm, old-fashioned voice, and the fun lies in watching a rough diamond learn polish without losing his honesty.
9936-woman-s-institute-library-of-cooker:
Volume two of the Woman's Institute Library of Cookery, from the Woman's Institute of Domestic Arts and Sciences, teaches the dairy and garden staples of the early twentieth-century kitchen. It opens with milk in the diet, its composition, grades, and preserved forms, then moves to butter and cheese.

Later sections take up eggs and vegetables, with rules for choosing, keeping, and cooking each one well. Written as a correspondence-school text, it explains why foods behave as they do, not just how to cook them. Home cooks get a solid, practical grounding in the ingredients behind most family meals.
9938-woman-s-institute-library-of-cooker:
Volume four of the Woman's Institute cookery course covers the lighter and sweeter side of the table: salads and sandwiches, cold and frozen desserts, cakes, cookies, puddings, pastries, and pies. Each section begins with principles, such as what makes a salad suit a meal, before giving methods.

The book explains ingredients and their uses, from salad greens to pastry dough, in the plain teaching style of the Institute's lessons. Cooks learn to judge, mix, and finish dishes rather than merely copy recipes. It is a useful window on American home cooking in the age before electric refrigeration changed the kitchen.
995-ballads-of-a-bohemian:
Robert W. Service wrote these ballads of a bohemian life, opening with a prelude and a first book called Spring. My Garret, Julot the Apache, L'Escargot d'Or, and It Is Later Than You Think follow, with Noctambule, Insomnia, Moon Song, and The Sewing-Girl in turn. Paris, its cafés and garrets, forms the scene.

Service, author of The Spell of the Yukon, writes here of artists, lovers, and night owls, with his usual vigour and rhyme. The ballads mix gaiety with melancholy, as bohemian youth fades into memory. The book suits readers who enjoy Service's rollicking verse, transplanted from the Yukon to the Latin Quarter.
9975-paris-war-days-diary-of-an-american:
Charles Inman Barnard, Paris correspondent of the New York Tribune, kept this diary of war days in the French capital. Barnard, a Harvard man and knight of the Legion of Honor, led the foreign press association in Paris and chaired the Harvard Club there.

His diary records the city under war: its streets, its leaders, and its people, with Ambassador Myron T. Herrick as frontispiece. Barnard writes as a working journalist, close to events and quick to note mood. Readers get Paris in wartime through American eyes, day by day, without hindsight.
a-certain-rich-man: William Allen White tells the story of a certain rich man in this American novel. Its many chapters follow wealth, business, and the changing life of a town and its people. The hero's fortune shapes his family, his neighbors, and his own sense of duty. White writes a broad portrait of American success and its costs.
a-classification-and-subject-index-for-c: Melvil Dewey presents his classification and subject index for arranging library books and pamphlets. Developed early in 1873 after study of hundreds of books and visits to over fifty American libraries, the plan orders knowledge for easy finding. Dewey believed libraries would serve readers better under a clear and uniform system. This early work grew into the decimal system that still bears his name.
a-fair-barbarian: Frances Hodgson Burnett presents a fair barbarian in Miss Octavia Bassett. The American girl arrives at Slowbridge, where shares, white muslin, croquet, and garden parties mark her progress. Lady Theobald, Lucia, and Lord Lansdowne watch her lively manners with surprise. Burnett writes a comic novel of American freshness meeting English society.
a-good-samaritan: Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews tells a good Samaritan story of kindness repaid. Its illustrations show a man chuckling over a telephone charge and praising his best friend Recky. Billy and his friend stand at the center of a tale of generosity. Andrews writes a warm short story of neighborly help.
a-jacobite-exile-being-the-adventures-of: George Alfred Henty tells of a Jacobite exile, a young Englishman in the service of Charles the Twelfth of Sweden. Chapters follow a spy in the household, denunciation, rescue, and service in Sweden. Narva, prison, exchange, and the passage of the Dwina mark his adventures. Henty writes a boys adventure of war, loyalty, and exile.
a-man-and-a-woman: Stanley Waterloo tells of a man and a woman growing up with the country. Chapters move from close to nature and boy, bird, and snake through grim visaged war and the spearing of Alfred. Fiction made fact, new forces at work, and a building fence mark later life. Waterloo writes a frontier novel of love, work, and conscience.
a-man-s-woman: Frank Norris writes a man's woman, a novel completed in March 1899. The story opens at four in the morning in a tent where all are asleep. A man lies ill, conscious the day before, asking what his chances were. Norris writes of strength ebbing away and of love tested by hardship.
a-mountain-woman:
Elia Wilkinson Peattie gathers tales of the American West, most first printed in magazines such as Harper's Weekly and the Cosmopolitan, as her foreword notes. The title story opens with a letter from Colorado: the writer has married a mountain woman, a remnant, he says, of the heroic ages. Eight tales follow, including Jim Lancy's Waterloo and The Three Johns.

Her people are miners, ranch families, schoolteachers, and wanderers in Colorado, Michigan, and the gulches. Peattie writes women who endure weather, loss, and rough men without losing warmth or humor. The tales mix dialect, landscape, and sentiment in the regional style her day loved, and they keep a clear eye on frontier hardship.
a-new-voyage-to-carolina-containing-the-:
John Lawson, surveyor-general of North Carolina, published his voyage account in the early seventeen hundreds, and the title page promises an exact description and natural history of the country. The first part reports his journal of a thousand miles traveled through several nations of Indians. Lawson writes as an explorer who walked the ground himself.

He describes rivers, soil, plants, beasts, and fish, then the customs, dress, food, wars, and beliefs of the native peoples he met. The second part gives the present state of the colony, its towns, trade, and prospects for settlers. Lawson's plain, curious record remains a key source for the early Carolina backcountry and its peoples.
a-peep-into-toorkisthan: Rollo Gillespie Burslem, a captain in the Thirteenth Prince Albert's Light Infantry, offers this brief account of Toorkisthan, published in 1846. The book presents a soldier's view of a Central Asian land then little described for English readers, in period spelling kept intact by the transcription. Its chapters carry the reader through a frontier region of towns, routes, and peoples at the edge of empire.
a-people-s-man:
A People's Man is a 1914 political novel by E Phillips Oppenheim, who called himself the prince of storytellers. Oppenheim wrote some one hundred fifty novels, mainly of suspense and international intrigue. He was among the earliest writers of modern spy fiction and founded the rogue male school of adventure thrillers, and this book turns his hand to politics at home.

As its title signals, the story follows a man of the people through the world of Westminster power. Ambition, loyalty, and public pressure collide in the Edwardian political scene. The novel shows Oppenheim applying his thriller pace to Parliament and party struggle, rather than to the foreign intrigue of his better-known tales.
a-poor-wise-man:
Mary Roberts Rinehart opens in a steel city seen from the railway, blackened walls and river mist under a gray, smoke-laden sky. Through its gates come hopeful workers and men who would destroy their dreams. After the Great War, the city simmers with strikes, radicals, and fear.

Fifty-two chapters follow a rich steel family, its rebellious daughter, and Willy Cameron, the poor wise man of the title, a clerk whose plain decency steadies everyone he touches. Rinehart mixes romance with a serious look at labor unrest and revolutionary plots in America. Known for mysteries, she here writes a novel of ideas about class, loyalty, and the country's future.
a-summary-history-of-the-palazzo-dandolo: This anonymous summary history tells how the Palazzo Dandolo in Venice became the Royal Hotel Danieli, in a pamphlet printed at Venice in 1896. In 1805 the second floor, fronting the Riva degli Schiavoni, was bought by Dal Niel, surnamed Danieli, from members of the Michiel and Bernardo families. Converted into a hotel under his own name, it was kept worthily by Danieli, his daughter Alfonsina, his granddaughter Giuseppina Roux, and finally Genovesi and Campi.
a-tour-through-some-parts-of-france-swit: Richard Boyle Bernard tours France, Switzerland, Savoy, Germany, and Belgium during the summer and autumn of 1814, dedicating the account to the Prince Regent. His dedication congratulates the Regent on glorious events that restored universal peace to England and made the era ever memorable in history. Printed at London in 1815, the tour records countries just emerging from war, seen by a member of Parliament travelling in the first season of peace.
a-trip-abroad-an-account-of-a-journey-to: Don Carlos Janes describes a journey to Palestine and Egypt in this 1905 trip abroad, to the earthly Canaan and the land of the ancient Pharaohs. The preface hopes the book may be interesting and instructive, with a geography chapter to be studied with a good map and a historic sketch as an outline of events. A final chapter gives American readers a better understanding of churches of Christ in Great Britain.
adrift-on-an-ice-pan: Wilfred Thomason Grenfell recounts a drift on a broken sheet of sea ice off the Labrador coast, where a small party faces cold, hunger, and open water. The narrative follows their efforts to stay alive, signal for help, and reach shore, giving a plain account of danger and endurance in the far north. Its spare style keeps the focus on the ice, the weather, and the choices made hour by hour.
adventures-in-the-land-of-canaan:
Robert Lee Berry says in his foreword that his book comes out of his heart and is meant for the hearts of others. Some of it was learned by long and bitter experience. His introductory chapter explains the plan: Israel's story, from bondage in Egypt to conquering Canaan, is a type of the Christian's path from sin to entire sanctification.

Thirteen chapters follow that path as a pilgrimage. They cover getting ready to enter, crossing the Jordan, and a memorial stone. They explore Canaan by faith. They fight Giant Accuser, Giant Mistake, and Giant Doubt. They enter the dungeon of Giant Discourager. The wine of prayer and the pilgrims of the victorious life close the course. Berry writes holiness teaching as allegory, in Bunyan's long shadow.
an-algonquin-maiden-a-romance-of-the-ear: Graeme Mercer Adam and A. Ethelwyn Wetherald tell a romance of the early days of Upper Canada in An Algonquin Maiden. The story joins a Native heroine's fate to the settlers' world, in the manner of Canadian historical romance. Dedicated to a life spent in varied service of his country, the book blends love, frontier life, and national feeling.
an-ambitious-man: Ella Wheeler Wilcox writes An Ambitious Man, a novel of a man whose drive for success tests love, friendship, and honour. Published in London by Gay and Hancock, the story follows ambition from hope to cost. Wilcox, best known as a poet, brings a moralist's eye to the price of getting on in the world.
an-amiable-charlatan: An Amiable Charlatan is a 1916 novel by E Phillips Oppenheim, the English master of suspense and international intrigue. By this date Oppenheim was a major popular author, midway through a career of some one hundred fifty novels. The story centers on its title figure, a charming rogue whose schemes drive the tale, in the light, plot-led style that made Oppenheim a household name for thriller readers of his era.
an-historical-journal-of-the-transaction: John Hunter keeps an historical journal of transactions at Port Jackson and Norfolk Island, with discoveries made in New South Wales and the southern ocean since an earlier publication. The journal records the young colony's daily business, voyages, and encounters. Hunter, a naval officer and governor, writes with first-hand authority on early Australia.
an-iceland-fisherman:
Pierre Loti writes of the Breton fishermen who sail each year to fish off Iceland, in M. Jules Cambon's translation. A long prefatory essay praises Loti's power to carry readers into far lands with simple art. The novel itself divides between the icy sea and the Breton land, as its part titles state.

On the Iceland grounds the men work through fog and storm while the women wait at home in Brittany. A first love grows between a fisherman and a girl of his village, shadowed by orders for foreign service and the sea's long record of taking men. Loti keeps the plot spare and the feeling deep, and the ending is among the saddest in French fiction.
another-study-of-woman:
Honoré de Balzac sets his tale at a Paris ball, in a translation by Ellen Marriage and Clara Bell. When the glittering party thins out, a smaller circle stays behind for the real talk of the night. There the company falls to discussing women, marriage, and love, and one guest tells a story to prove his point.

The frame lets Balzac stage a contest of wits among fashionable men and women, each with a theory and a past. A tale within the tale, of a woman's sacrifice and a husband's blindness, gives the talk its weight. The piece shows Balzac the observer of salons at his most polished and ironic.
arbor-day-leaves-a-complete-programme-fo: Nathaniel Hillyer Egleston assembles readings, recitations, songs, and general guidance for school Arbor Day observance. The programme suits teachers and school officers planning a shared day of tree planting and civic pride. Short pieces alternate with music so a class can mix speaking, singing, and outdoor work.
