Its appeal lies in its ready order of service, not in new science about trees. The book captures a time when schools taught care for nature through public ritual.
arms-and-the-man:
George Bernard Shaw calls his play a pleasant one and sets it in Bulgaria during and after the war with Serbia. The introduction in this edition marvels, with some irony, at orthodox critics who found Shaw ignorant of dramatic art while audiences kept coming. In a young lady's bedroom, a fleeing enemy officer climbs in through the window, more armed with chocolates than with cartridges.

Raina, the romantic heroine, hides the fugitive and slowly trades her heroic ideals for the plain truth he tells about soldiering. Her dashing fiancé Sergius and the practical servant Louka complete the upset of every romance. Three acts of wit carry Shaw's case: war is work, not glory, and sense beats swagger.
arms-and-the-woman: Harold MacGrath tells a romance that opens in a walled garden bright with roses, poppies, and lilacs in May. A young man of twenty two meets a girl whose brown hair and calm eyes stop him in his tracks. The tale then follows love, pride, and danger as the pair test each other and the world around them. MacGrath writes in a lush, old style romance mode, with feeling carried by scene and speech.
b09-luther-freedom-christian:
On the Freedom of a Christian, also called Concerning Christian Liberty, is Martin Luther's gentle tract of 1520. Where his other works of that year attack, this one consoles and teaches. It sets out his core claim: a person is made right with God by faith alone, not by works.

Luther holds two truths in tension through the tract. A Christian is a free lord of all, subject to none, and yet a ready servant of all, subject to everyone. Faith frees the soul; love then spends that freedom on the neighbor. The short work became the best known plain statement of Reformation teaching. Its calm tone still wins first-time readers.
ballads-of-a-bohemian:
Robert W Service organized Ballads of a Bohemian by seasons, spring through winter, following a poet in a Paris garret. The contents promise My Garret, The Sewing-Girl, The Absinthe Drinkers, and the death of Marie Toro, mixed with program pieces like The Philistine and the Bohemian. Service had swapped his Yukon gold rush for Montmartre.

The poems sing of models, pencil sellers, domestic tragedies, and gods in the gutter, in the swinging meters that made Service famous. A cozy middle passage, wife sewing and kettle purring, shows his gift for the sentimental scene. Readers who know only the Yukon ballads will find the same storyteller here, working Paris streets instead of frozen trails.
baree-son-of-kazan:
James Oliver Curwood's Baree, Son of Kazan is the third of his animal books, after Kazan and The Grizzly King. His preface answers hundreds of letters from readers of wild life. Americans, he confesses, have gone after nature with a gun, himself with twenty-seven of them. He has learned to know animals as they actually live.

Baree, Kazan's son by a wild she-wolf, is born in the northern forest. The pup's world is hunger, cold, and the law of claw and fang. A lynx, an owl, and a trapper's cabin shape his first year. Curwood refuses to humanize his hero, letting fact carry the romance. The story follows Baree toward his father's old haunts and man's uneasy friendship. It remains a favourite among readers of true-to-life animal tales.
ben-blair-the-story-of-a-plainsman:
Will Lillibridge published this western novel with McClurg in 1905, and the Burt reprint lists six editions within sixteen months. Ben Blair grows up on the Box R Ranch in rude border-land, schooled by desolation and the sanity of the wild. A frontispiece catches the love story's wound: Florence touches his arm and pleads forgiveness, admitting she cannot say she loves him.

Ranch life hardens into violence in the middle chapters. Everything moves like clockwork in the dark as a captive with tied hands is set on a bare-backed pony. A running noose fashioned from a lariat slips over his neck while the great bull-necked leader, Mick Kennedy, holds the crowd. Lillibridge writes the plains as moral weather: endurance, lynch law, and a heroine from the East who must learn what the soil does to seed.
bond-contract-1895-rothschild-morgan:
The House Ways and Means group sent this report to the full House on February 13, 1895. It is House Report No. 1824 of the 53rd Congress. Its theme is the great bond deal that saved the gold store of the United States that year.

The report prints the bond pact in full, with the terms the syndicate took. That group acted for N. M. Rothschild and Sons of London and for J. P. Morgan and Co. of New York. The deal is a core record of how the house lent to states at the top level.
britannica-1911-aarssens-francis-van:
Francis van Aarssens receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Aarssens, a diplomat of the United Provinces, caught the eye of Oldenbarneveldt, who sent him at twenty-six as agent to the court of France. Work on the twelve years' truce of 1606 raised him further.

France's displeasure cost him his post in 1616, and gratitude turned to hate. Aarssens sat in the packed court that sent his old patron to death in 1619, a stain the entry does not hide. Maurice and Frederick Henry of Orange then took his counsel on foreign affairs. Embassies to Venice, Germany, and England proved his finesse. Richelieu ranked him among the three greatest politicians of his time, the entry reports.
britannica-1911-abbas-tuman: Abbas-Tuman is the subject of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry names a spa in Russian Transcaucasia, in the government of Tiflis. It stands in a cauldron-shaped valley, south-west of the Borzhom railway station and east of Batum, in a picturesque setting. Hot sulphur baths are its draw, with waters running over ninety degrees Fahrenheit. An astronomical observatory stands at 4,240 feet near by. Place, waters, and one science outpost fill the whole brief notice in the gazetteer manner of the 1911 volumes.
britannica-1911-abbott-lyman:
Lyman Abbott receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abbott, son of Jacob Abbott, was born at Roxbury in 1835, trained for law, then turned to theology. Plymouth Church in Brooklyn took him as Henry Ward Beecher's successor in 1888.

Editing ran beside preaching: Harper's Magazine, the Illustrated Christian Weekly, and the Christian Union, renamed The Outlook, which he led from 1881. Social reform and a liberal, near-unitarian theology mark both journal and books. Titles run from Jesus of Nazareth to Industrial Problems and The Rights of Man. Work for the Freedman's Commission filled his early ministry years. He resigned the Plymouth pulpit in 1898 and wrote on. The entry lists his books through 1907.
britannica-1911-abd-ar-rahman:
Abd-ar-Rahman names five Omayyad princes in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, amirs and caliphs of Cordova. Two stand out for great capacity, the entry holds. The first, founder of the Spanish branch, fled the Abbasid overthrow of his house as a youth of twenty.

Desert refuge, a slain brother, and a prophecy of restored fortune mark his flight to Mauritania. Landing at Almuñecar in 755, he beat Amir Yusef outside Cordova in 756, a green turban bound on a spear for his banner. Order forced on Arab and Berber rebels filled his reign, with rebel heads sent salted to the eastern caliph. The second prince brings the Martyrs of Cordova. The third, greatest of the line, reigned half a century from 912.
britannica-1911-abdur-rahman-khan:
Abdur Rahman Khan receives a long life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abdur Rahman, amir of Afghanistan, was grandson of Dost Mahomed, founder of the Barakzai line. Five years of war among Dost's sons after 1863 schooled the young prince in resource and daring.

Kabul taken in 1866, defeat in 1869, and eleven years of exile under Russian shelter at Samarkand followed. Shere Ali's death reopened the game in 1879. Lord Lytton offered terms: British troops out, subsidy and arms in, foreign affairs guided by British advice. The durbar of July 1880 named him amir. Kandahar came in 1881 after Ayub Khan's brief seizure. Griffin's portrait of the man, shrewd, frank, and courteous, heads the rule that followed.
britannica-1911-abersychan: Abersychan is the subject of a short town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, read here inside a shared chunk of text. The entry names an urban district in Monmouthshire's northern division, north-west of Newport, served by three railways. Its people numbered 17,768 in 1901. The town lies in the narrow upper valley of the Afon Lwyd. Coal and iron country of Glamorgan and Monmouth edges it on the east. Mines and ironworks employ its large working population, the entry states. Wild, mountainous country surrounds the settlement.
britannica-1911-acadian:
Acadian, in geology, names a series of rocks identified by Sir J. W. Dawson in 1867. The Britannica entry describes black, red, and green shales and slates with dark grey limestones. They are well developed at St John in New Brunswick, at Avalon in eastern Newfoundland, and at Braintree in eastern Massachusetts.

Age and fossils fix their place. These rocks belong to the Middle Cambrian period and carry a Paradoxides fauna, fossils of a trilobite genus used to date such beds. Geologists correlated them with limestone beds in Tennessee, Alabama, central Nevada, and British Columbia. The entry points readers to the Cambrian System article and to Dawson's own Acadian Geology for the fuller argument.
britannica-1911-adamnan:
Adamnan (about 624-704) was an Irish saint and historian. He was born at Raphoe in Donegal. In 679 he became abbot of Iona. He was ninth in succession from St Columba. A mission took him to Northumberland's court in 686. King Aldfrith received him there at that time. The visit converted him to Roman Easter rules. Roman tonsure practice persuaded him as well. He tried to enforce both changes at Iona. The monks refused, and the attempt failed.

Writing gives him his lasting place. His Life of St Columba abounds in fabulous matter. It remains of great interest and value nonetheless. His De Locis Sanctis describes the holy places. A shipwrecked French bishop supplied its information. Arculf had been entertained at Iona after his wreck.
britannica-1911-albion-michigan:
Albion, a city of Calhoun county in Michigan, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Kalamazoo river, twenty-one miles west of Jackson, and grew from 3,763 people in 1890 to 5,833 in 1910. Two railways and an inter-urban electric line serve it. The city holds a public park and a public library.

Factories cluster in Albion's west, making flour, farm implements, windmills, gasoline engines, harness, and patent medicines. On a commanding site in the east stands Albion College, Methodist Episcopal and co-educational. It embraced a liberal arts college, a preparatory department, a conservatory of music, and schools of art, oratory, teaching, and commerce. The college began as Spring Arbor Seminary in 1835, moved to Albion under a new charter, opened there in 1843, and took its present name in 1861.
britannica-1911-alcazar-de-san-juan:
Alcázar de San Juan grew around a rail junction in La Mancha, where lines from Madrid toward Manzanares and Albacete meet. The town, in Ciudad Real province, counted 11,499 people in 1900. Wine from Estremadura and Andalusia passed through in a busy transit trade, while local soda and alkali went into soap. Gunpowder, chocolate, and inlaid daggers were also made there.

A Moorish castle, al-kasr, gave Alcázar its name; knights of St John later held the fort. Some link the town to Roman Alce, taken by Gracchus in 180 B.C. Townsfolk claim Cervantes as their own, a claim that cannot stand. Yet Don Quixote's world lies close by: El Toboso, home of Dulcinea, and Argamasilla de Alba, said by tradition to be the knight's birthplace.
britannica-1911-alcman:
Alcman, also called Alcmaeon, began Doric lyric song and stands first in the Alexandrian list of Greece's nine lyric poets. He bloomed in the later half of the seventh century B.C. By birth he was a Lydian of Sardis. He came to Sparta as a slave and lived in the house of Agesidas.

Agesidas set him free. His fine command of Greek shows he must have reached Sparta very young. With the Messenian wars done, Sparta could turn to the arts of peace, and Alcman filled that space. He wrote parthenia, songs for maidens, plus hymns, paeans, marching songs, and love songs, a kind he was held to have brought into being. His love of good living shows too, a warm Asian streak that sits oddly in plain Sparta. Little of his work lasts, though a good chunk of a Parthenion came to light on an Egyptian papyrus in 1855.
britannica-1911-alderman:
Alderman is a title with old roots: it comes from the Anglo-Saxon ealdorman, a join of eald, old, and man, and it points to an office of rank and worth. Today the name fits members of town bodies and county councils in England and Wales, and men of like post in Ireland and the United States.

In Anglo-Saxon times earls, lords of shires, and other great folk bore the title. An alderman of all England stood where the chief justice later stood. A county alderman ranked between earl and sheriff and, beside the bishop in court, declared the common law. Scotland knows no alderman at all; bailies hold that rank there. London keeps its old frame, untouched by borough reform, with a court of twenty-six aldermen. Twenty-five of them are picked for life by the free men of their wards.
britannica-1911-alloxan:
Alloxan, also called mesoxalyl urea, is a chemical compound obtained by oxidising uric acid. Cold nitric acid acting on uric acid produces it, along with urea. The entry gives its formula and describes how it crystallises from water in colourless rhombic prisms, holding four molecules of water of crystallisation and showing a strongly acid reaction.

What makes alloxan useful is its place at the start of many preparations. Zinc and hydrochloric acid convert it into alloxantin, hydroxylamine gives a nitroso compound, and baryta water gives alloxanic acid. Hot nitric acid oxidises it further to parabanic acid, while hot potash breaks it down into urea and mesoxalic acid. Methyl and dimethyl forms are also noted, the dimethyl form coming from oxidation of caffeine.
britannica-1911-annan:
Annan is a burgh of Dumfriesshire, Scotland. It stands on the river Annan. The river mouth lies nearly two miles away. Dumfries is fifteen miles by railway. Red sandstone builds most of the town. Its academy educated Thomas Carlyle as a pupil. A stone bridge of 1824 crosses the river. A railway viaduct crosses the Solway Firth nearby. That viaduct stretches a mile and a third.

The Harbour Trust improved shipping in 1897. Vessels of 300 tons approach the town. Cotton and rope manufactures lead local industry. Bacon-curing, distilling, and tanning also operate. Shipbuilding and sandstone quarrying add employment. Nursery gardening and salmon fishing continue too. Roman remains dot the neighbourhood. The Bruces and Baliols figure in its history. Edward Irving was a native of Annan. Population in 1901 was 5,805.
britannica-1911-arcadius-grammarian:
Arcadius of Antioch was a Greek grammarian. He flourished in the second century A.D. Suidas records his works. Treatises on orthography came from him. A treatise on syntax also bears his name. His onomaticon was a vocabulary work. Suidas called it a wonderful production. An epitome circulates under his name too, though. That epitome summarises Herodian on prosody.

The attribution of that epitome is wrong. Theodosius of Alexandria probably wrote it. A grammarian named Aristodemus is another candidate. The epitome covers nineteen of twenty books. A sixteenth-century forger supplied the twentieth book. The work is meagre and carelessly assembled. It remains valuable despite those flaws. It preserves the original work's order. Reconstruction of Herodian rests on it trustworthily. Barker edited the text in 1823. Schmidt's edition followed in 1860.
britannica-1911-avonian:
Avonian, in geology, is the name Dr A. Vaughan proposed in 1905 for rocks of Lower Carboniferous age in the Avon gorge at Bristol. The stage covers much the same ground and fossil zones as the older French and Belgian term Dinantian, the entry explains.

Its substages, though, rest on local conditions and a different reading of the zonal fossils, so they do not match the French and Belgian divisions exactly. The upper Avonian, called Kidwellian, is well shown near Kidwelly in Carmarthenshire. The lower substage, Clevedonian, is well displayed near Clevedon in Somerset. A table in the entry sets Avonian zones beside the Dinantian ones, and readers are sent to Vaughan's and Sibley's papers on the Avon gorge and Mendip limestone.
britannica-1911-ayub-khan:
Ayub Khan (1855- ), an Afghan prince, was son of Shere Ali, former amir of Afghanistan, and cousin of the amir Abdur Rahman. Little is recorded of him under his father. After the British expelled Shere Ali from Kabul and the amir died in 1879, Ayub seized Herat.

In 1880 Ayub marched on Kandahar and beat General Burrows at Maiwand, one of the few pitched battles an Asian leader has won over a European-led army. His triumph collapsed weeks later when Roberts, after the famous march from Kabul, crushed him outside Kandahar. Later tries in 1881 and 1887 also failed, and Ayub ended as a state prisoner in India, having surrendered to the British agent at Meshed.
britannica-1911-azan:
Azan, Arabic for announcement, is the call to public prayer proclaimed by the muezzin, the mosque crier, twice daily across Muslim lands. In small mosques he stands at the door or side of the building; in large ones, up in the minaret, facing Mecca with fingertips in his ears.

The call, in translation, cries God is most great. It testifies that there is no God but God. It says that Mahomet is his apostle. Then it summons hearers to prayer and to salvation. At morning it adds that prayer is better than sleep. Listeners must answer each phrase in set words, and all must pause: street crowds stand still, work stops, sleepers sit up. Legend traces the call's fixing to a follower's dream, after trumpet and bell were weighed and passed over.
britannica-1911-azerbaijan:
Azerbaijan, in ancient writers Atropatene, is the north-western and most important province of Persia. Russian lands bound it across the Aras river. The Caspian Sea lies to the east, Kurdistan to the south, and Asiatic Turkey to the west. Its people, one and a half to two millions, mix Persians, Turks, Kurds, Syrians, and Armenians.

Rolling hills open into wide plains under high mountains: Sahand near the centre at 12,000 feet, and Savelan in the east at 15,792 feet. Rivers drain to the Caspian or to Lake Urmia, whose western shore is the province's richest part. Orchards yield fine fruits, dried in quantity for export to Russia, and a prized polished marble, lead, copper, and sulphur add to its wealth. Forests alone are lacking.
britannica-1911-bach-johann-sebastian:
Bach, Johann Sebastian (1685-1750), was a German composer born into a Thuringian family that shaped music history for nearly two hundred years. The family genealogy, drawn up by Bach himself, traces it to Veit Bach, a baker and miller who played the zither among his mill-wheels.

Orphaned at ten, the boy was raised at Ohrdruf by his elder brother Johann Christoph, the organist who taught him music. The long entry follows the clan first: uncles and cousins ranked among Europe's best musicians though barely known beyond their towns, so that in Erfurt musicians were simply called Bachs. It then traces Sebastian's own life and work in detail, the heir of a united family's art kept pure, the entry argues, by its very narrowness.
britannica-1911-bachian:
Bachian, in Dutch Batjan, is one of the Molucca Islands in the Dutch East Indies, lying west of Halmahera's southern peninsula in the Molucca Sea. With its small neighbour islands it covers 914 square miles, two mountainous parts joined by a low isthmus that slight sinking would drown.

Partly volcanic, with hot springs and coal, the island rises at Mount Labua to 6,950 feet. Rich woods yield sago, cocoa-nuts, and cloves native to the soil. Bachian is famous as the easternmost home of any monkey kind, a black ape shared with Celebes, and it swarms with birds and insects. Its 13,000 coastal people are all newcomers or their descendants: Portuguese Christians, Malays, Papuans, Chinese, and Arabs among them.
britannica-1911-badakshan:
Badakshan, including Wakhan, is a province on Afghanistan's north-east frontier, touching Russian territory. Its borders were fixed by the Anglo-Russian agreement of 1873. That agreement gave Badakshan and Wakhan wholly to the amir of Kabul. It bounded them by the left bank of the Oxus river.

The Hindu Kush crest forms its southern wall. Passes at Khawak and Dorah link it to inner valleys. The Oxus runs along the north. So the province stretches in a bottle shape into the Pamirs. Much of the interior was still unexplored when the entry was written. Old small states like Roshan and Shignan once reached the Oxus bank before the settlement redrew the line. Geography and boundary politics fill most of this long account.
britannica-1911-bailey-nathan:
Bailey, Nathan, or Nathaniel (d. 1742), was an English word scholar and dictionary maker whose Dictionarium Britannicum, dated 1730 and thought published in 1721, boasted itself a more complete universal etymological English dictionary than any before it. The claim, the entry says, was largely fair.

Bailey's book marked a great improvement on all earlier attempts and formed the basis of Dr Johnson's great dictionary, the most famous in English. A Seventh-day Baptist from 1691, Bailey kept a school at Stepney near London and wrote the Dictionarium Domesticum and other teaching works besides. He died on 27 June 1742. Johnson's fame has overshadowed him, but the ground Johnson built on was Bailey's.
britannica-1911-bajocian:
Bajocian, in geology, names rocks of Middle Jurassic age. D'Orbigny proposed the term in 1849. The rocks show well near Bayeux in Calvados. British geologists call the stage the Inferior Oolite. It matches parts of German classifications too. Fossil ammonites split it into zones.

The zones descend from the Parkinsonia zone downward. Each zone takes a marker fossil's name. Most Bajocian rocks in Europe are limestones. Many are oolitic, built of tiny round grains. At Bayeux they are iron-rich oolites. Coral limestone caps crinoid limestone in the Jura. Poitou has dolomitic beds with chert nodules. Clay from the beds serves potters near Wareham. Matching rocks range worldwide. The entry traces them across Africa and Asia. The Americas and Australasia hold them too.
britannica-1911-bake-jan:
Bake, Jan (1787-1864), was a Dutch scholar and critic. He was born at Leiden in 1787. Leiden University made him a professor in 1817. His chair covered Greek and Roman literature. He held it until 1854. He died at Leiden in 1864.

Bake's first work treated Posidonius of Rhodes. That study appeared in 1810. He edited Cleomedes on the heavens in 1820. His Bibliotheca Critica Nova ran from 1825. It continued until 1831. The Scholica Hypomnemata followed for decades. Those essays dealt mainly with Cicero. The Attic orators shared the attention. He edited Cicero's Laws and Orator too. Apsines and Longinus also came from his hand. His pupil wrote his biography in Dutch. It appeared the year after his death.
britannica-1911-balayan:
Balayan was a town and port of entry in Batangas province, on the island of Luzon in the Philippines. It stands at the head of the Gulf of Balayan, about 55 miles south of Manila. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its population in 1903 as 8,493.

Two nearby towns, Calatagan and Tuy, were annexed to it in October 1903. The entry describes a healthy climate and rich volcanic soil growing rice, sugar cane, cacao, coffee, pepper, and cotton. Horses and cattle are raised for market, and the fisheries matter. The local language is Tagalog. The entry is short and factual, setting out the town's place, size, and products in a few lines.
britannica-1911-balbi-adrian:
Adrian Balbi (1782–1848) was an Italian geographer born at Venice. His 1808 survey of the political geography of the world won him a teaching chair at Murano. He later taught physics at Fermo, then worked in the customs office at Venice.

A stay in Portugal led to his statistical essay on that kingdom, printed at Paris in 1822. The 1911 Britannica entry lists his Atlas ethnographique du globe of 1826, which grouped peoples by their languages, and his Abrégé de Géographie of 1832, soon translated across Europe. Balbi died at Padua in 1848. His son Eugenio followed the same field at Pavia.
britannica-1911-balbriggan:
Balbriggan was a market town and seaport in County Dublin, Ireland, about 21 miles north of Dublin on the Great Northern railway. Its population in 1901 was 2,236. The harbour dries at low tide but holds 14 feet of water at high spring tides.

Two piers shelter the port, and a railway viaduct of eleven arches crosses the harbour. The 1911 Britannica entry stresses the town's cotton and hosiery works, founded by Baron Hamilton in 1761. Its hose, sold under the town's own name, was widely known. Grain trade, sea fishing, and summer visitors round out the picture.
britannica-1911-ball-john-irish-politici:
John Ball (1818–1889) was an Irish politician, naturalist, and Alpine traveller, born at Dublin on 20 August 1818. Schooled at Oscott and at Christ's College, Cambridge, he showed an early bent for natural science, above all botany. Travel in Switzerland fed papers on plants and on Swiss glaciers in scientific journals.

Poor-law work came first, then Parliament: he won the county of Carlow in 1852 as a Liberal. Palmerston marked his ability, and Ball served two years as under-secretary for the colonies, where he backed science, the Palliser expedition in Canada, and Hooker's study of colonial floras. The 1911 Britannica entry follows both sides of his career.
britannica-1911-balue-jean:
Jean Balue (about 1421–1491) was a French cardinal and a minister of Louis XI, born of very humble parentage at Angle in Poitou. Backed first by the bishop of Poitiers, he became vicar-general at Angers in 1461. His energy, cunning, and gift for intrigue won the king, who made him his almoner.

Balue rose fast: bishop of Évreux in 1465, first of the great council, and cardinal in 1468, despite a loose life. Then he plotted with Charles the Bold against his own master. The letters were caught, and in April 1469 he went to prison for eleven years. The 1911 Britannica entry ends with his release, papal favour at Rome, and death at Ancona in 1491.
britannica-1911-bamian:
Bamian was a once renowned city of Afghanistan, about 80 miles north-west of Kabul. Its remains lie in a valley of the Hazara country, on the main road from Kabul toward Turkestan, at the northern foot of the Koh-i-Baba range. Passes on the Kabul side rise above 11,000 feet, and the valley floor sits at about 8,500 feet.

Cliffs line the valley for six or seven miles, pierced by countless ancient cave dwellings, some still lived in, while towers crown the heights above. The 1911 Britannica entry describes mounds and wall remains marking the old city, and ruins on a lone rock in the valley read as its acropolis. The valley was surveyed in 1885 during the Russo-Afghan Boundary Commission.
britannica-1911-ban:
Ban is an old word from a Teutonic root meaning to proclaim or announce, with the Latin form bannum. In the laws of the Franks and kindred tribes it had three main uses. It could mean a proclamation itself, the fine paid for disobeying one, or the district over which a lord's proclamations ran.

From the first use grew the second, as wrongdoing became tied to breaking a ban. Feudal lords from the king down used such bans to order amends, and a man who refused lost all protection: he was outlawed. The 1911 Britannica entry goes on to later French uses, where ban could name the summons of men to arms and the body so called out.
britannica-1911-baner-johan:
Johan Banér (1596–1641) was a Swedish soldier of the Thirty Years' War, born at Djursholm Castle on 23 June 1596. He entered the Swedish army and served with distinction against Russia and Poland, reaching high rank by 1630, when Gustavus Adolphus landed in Germany. At the first battle of Breitenfeld he led the right wing of the Swedish horse.

Banér helped take Augsburg and Munich and fought at the Lech and Donauwörth, and he was wounded at the Alte Veste. Left in command in the west, he later entered Bohemia as field-marshal with 16,000 men and marched on Prague with the Saxons. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his recovery of the Swedish cause after the disaster at Nördlingen.
britannica-1911-bart-jean:
Jean Bart (1651–1702), a French naval commander born in Dunkirk, the son of a fisherman, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. He served as a young man in the Dutch navy, then entered French service when war broke out between Louis XIV and Holland in 1672. In the Mediterranean he won great distinction while holding only an irregular commission, since his low birth then blocked a regular naval command.

Results forced the door open. Bart rose quickly, becoming a lieutenant in 1679 and then climbing to captain and admiral. The Peace of Ryswick ended his active service. The entry stresses the many stories told of his courage and blunt manners, and calls the untrained sailor the popular hero of the French naval service. Dunkirk honoured him after death with a statue and a public square bearing his name. Richer's life of Bart heads the sources.
britannica-1911-bartan:
Bartan, more correctly Bartin, a town in the vilayet of Kastamuni in Asiatic Turkey, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It keeps the name of the ancient village Parthenia. The town stands near the mouth of the Bartan-su, the ancient Parthenius, once part of the boundary between Bithynia and Paphlagonia. Old explanations of that river name, including tales of the maiden Artemis hunting on its banks, are noted in the entry.

Town and trade take up the rest. Bartan, the seat of a local governor called a kaïmakam, is built on two low limestone hills, and its streets are paved with limestone blocks. Boxwood grown nearby was prized. Black Sea coasting steamers called at the port, and trade with Constantinople was considerable, though a bar blocking the harbour held it back. The population given, from Cuinet, is 8677.
britannica-1911-bartizan:
Bartizan is a term from castle building defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. According to the New English Dictionary cited there, the word comes through a Scottish corruption of bratticing or brattishing, from the Old French bretesche, meaning a battlemented parapet. The term apparently entered English through the writings of Sir Walter Scott, whose historical novels spread many such old words to general readers of his day.

The thing itself is a small defensive turret. A bartizan sticks out from the angle of a wall or tower, resting on corbels, the projecting stones that support it. From inside, a warder could shelter behind its battlements and still see around the corner of the building, watching ground that the flat wall face left hidden. Bartizans were generally fitted with oylets or arrow-slits, small openings through which defenders could shoot or observe while staying under cover.
britannica-1911-bashan:
Bashan is a biblical region east of the Jordan treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its borders are called ill defined, but it lay north of Gilead, toward the Jordan's source. The name enters Hebrew history with the wanderings of Israel, when King Og of Bashan met the tribes at Edrei and was defeated and killed there. That story is treated with open doubt, Og's giant size and huge bedstead in Deuteronomy being called suggestive of legend.

Later references are firmer ground. Bashan was allotted to the eastern half of the tribe of Manasseh, and Golan in Bashan became a city of refuge. Under Solomon its region of Argob, with sixty walled cities, formed part of an official's district. Hazael of Syria later took the country from Israel under Jehu. Poetic and prophetic books remember Bashan for its noted products.
britannica-1911-battishill-jonathan:
Jonathan Battishill (1738–1801) was an English composer of church music, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry calls him one of the best English church composers of the 1700s. Until 1764 he wrote chiefly for the theatre: songs slipped into plays, pantomime music, and an opera made with Michael Arne, the son of Thomas Arne. His later work left the stage for other forms.

Glees and grief shape the short life. Battishill's later pieces are chiefly glees, part-songs for a small group of voices, and church music for services. In 1763 he wed a singer at Covent Garden theatre, where he himself played the harpsichord, the keyboard instrument of the day. She gave up her profession when she married. Her death in 1777 so crushed him, the entry says, that he composed no more at all. The silence lasted the rest of his life.
britannica-1911-bauan:
Bauan, or Baun, is a town of the province of Batangas, on the island of Luzon in the Philippines, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands at the head of Batangas Bay, about fifty-four miles south of Manila. Its people numbered 39,094 in 1903. A railway to join the town with Manila was being built in 1908. The town has a fine church, and the language spoken there is Tagalog.

Home weaving fills the entry's trade lines. Bauan is known for sinamay, or hemp cloth, dyed and woven by the women in their homes. Mats and hats of palm fibre, fans, bamboo baskets, and cotton fish-nets are also woven in the town. Fishing in the bay is called excellent. Hogs and horses are raised for the Manila market, and the land round the town is rich, growing cacao, indigo, oranges, sugar-cane, corn, and rice.
britannica-1911-baur-ferdinand-christian:
Ferdinand Christian Baur (1792–1860), the leader of the Tübingen school of theology, is the subject of a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. Born at Schmiden near Cannstatt, he was trained at Blaubeuren and at the university of Tübingen. Philosophy worked on him early: Schelling and, most of all, Schleiermacher shaped his mind. In 1826 he was called to a chair at Tübingen, with which his great works are bound up.

History handled by philosophy is his mark. Baur treated the early church as a field of clashing ideas, above all in his Paulus, a study of the apostle Paul, his life, letters, and teaching. His work on the so-called Pastoral Epistles, questioning who wrote them and when, is listed among his key writings. The Tübingen school he led made the critical study of Christian origins a matter of hard evidence and clear stages.
britannica-1911-bemberg-herman:
Herman Bemberg (born 1861) was a French composer born at Buenos Aires to French parents. He studied at the Paris Conservatoire under Massenet, and Massenet’s mark, with Gounod’s, shows strongly in his music. Songs and piano pieces made up much of his output.

Bemberg’s larger works include the cantata La Mort de Jeanne d’Arc, from 1886. The comic opera Le Baiser de Suzon followed in 1888. His grand opera Elaine was staged at Covent Garden in 1892. Among his songs, the dramatic recitative Ballade du Désespéré is singled out as well known. The entry is a short career note: training, influences, and the handful of works by which he was known.
britannica-1911-benedict-of-alignan:
Benedict of Alignan (died 1268) was a Benedictine churchman who became abbot of Notre Dame de la Grasse in 1224. Five years later he was made bishop of Marseilles. Twice, in 1239 and again in 1260, he travelled to the Holy Land on church business.

In the Holy Land Benedict helped the Templars build the great castle of Safet, and he later wrote an account of its building, De constructione Castri Saphet. He also founded a new order, the Brothers of the Virgin, which the council of Lyons suppressed in 1274, after his death. A letter to Pope Innocent IV survives among his writings, and he died a Franciscan.
britannica-1911-berekhiah-naqdan:
Berekhiah Naqdan was a Jewish fabulist, the writer of a collection of Fox Fables in Hebrew. His second name tells his trade: a naqdan is a punctuator, one who adds the vowel points to the biblical text. Grammar, then, was his craft as much as story-telling.

Berekhiah also wrote an ethical treatise, a book on right living, and made various translations. When he lived is disputed. Most authorities put him in the thirteenth century, but J. Jacobs identified him with Benedictus le Puncteur, an English Jew of the twelfth. The entry is short, and that open question of date and country is a large part of what it leaves the reader.
britannica-1911-bergler-stephan:
Stephan Bergler was a German classical scholar born about 1680 at Kronstadt in Transylvania; even his death date is unsure. Leipzig trained him, and Amsterdam set him editing Homer and the Onomasticon of Julius Pollux for the publisher Wetzstein. At Hamburg he helped Fabricius with the Bibliotheca Graeca and an edition of Sextus Empiricus.

Bergler ended as secretary to Alexander Mavrocordato, prince of Walachia, at Bucharest, whose work On Duties he had translated years before. In the prince’s library he found the lost opening of Eusebius’s Demonstratio Evangelica. Wild living and a cynical temper made him enemies everywhere. He edited the first printed Genesius and an Alciphron with seventy-five new letters before dying at Bucharest, or, some say, Constantinople.
britannica-1911-bertaut-jean:
Jean Bertaut (1552–1611) was a French poet born at Caen. Boileau's famous couplet pairs him with Desportes as poets made cautious by Ronsard's fall. Bertaut wrote light verse on court life in Desportes' manner. His verse was more fantastic and full of conceits than his master's. He entered the church early in life. He had a share in the conversion of Henry IV.

That royal link secured his career, the 1911 Britannica entry shows. He became king's secretary, almoner to Marie de' Medici, and abbot of Aulnay. In 1606 he rose to bishop of Sées. He then stopped writing the light verse he excelled in. His later poems on public events are judged dull and lifeless. He died at Sées in June 1611.
britannica-1911-binan:
Binan is a town in the province of La Laguna, on Luzon in the Philippine Islands. It stands on the west shore of Laguna de Bay, about 20 miles south-south-east of Manila. Its population in 1903 was 9,563. A wide and very fertile plain surrounds the town. That plain yields very large crops of rice every year. It also grows a great variety of tropical fruits. Boats carry the produce to a ready market in Manila.

The language of the town is Tagalog, the 1911 Britannica entry notes at its close. The entry is a compact gazetteer note of a few lines. It gives the shore position, the distance from the capital, and the census figure. Rice, fruit, and the Manila boat trade carry the whole account. No church, official, or event is named in the text. The plain's fertility is the town's defining fact in this record.
britannica-1911-black-jeremiah-sullivan:
Jeremiah Sullivan Black (1810–1883) was an American lawyer who rose to the highest legal offices under President Buchanan. Born in Somerset County, Pennsylvania, he taught himself law and was admitted to the bar before he came of age. He served on the supreme court of Pennsylvania from 1851 to 1857, as chief justice for part of that time.

In 1857 Black became attorney-general of the United States, and he fought the fraudulent California land claims covering a vast area. From December 1860 to March 1861 he was secretary of state. The entry stresses that he denied any right of secession and urged that Fort Sumter be held and supplied. After 1861 he returned to private practice and argued major cases.
britannica-1911-blackburn-jonathan:
Jonathan Blackburn (about 1700–about 1765) was an American portrait painter who worked in Boston. He seems to have been a painter's son, born in Connecticut, and he kept a Boston studio from about 1750 to 1765. Many leading Boston families sat for him.

Families named include the Apthorps, Amorys, Bulfinches, Lowells, Saltonstalls, Winthrops, and Otises. A few of his portraits are held by the public library at Lexington and by the Massachusetts Historical Society, but most stayed in private hands, chiefly in Boston. John Singleton Copley learned painting in his studio. The entry adds the story that Blackburn left Boston at last through envy of his pupil's greater success.
britannica-1911-boie-heinrich-christian:
Heinrich Christian Boie (1744–1806) was a German editor whose taste helped start other poets writing. Born at Meldorf in Schleswig-Holstein, then under Denmark, he studied law at Jena and moved to Göttingen in 1769. There he became a leader of the young poets' circle called the Hain or Dichterbund.

His own verse was modest, but his wide reading, fine taste, and sound judgment made him a spur to better writers. With F. W. Gotter he founded the Göttingen Musenalmanach in 1770 and edited it for five years. In 1776 he helped launch Das deutsche Museum, which became a leading literary journal of the day. He ended his career as an administrator in Holstein, from 1781.
britannica-1911-boucher-jonathan:
Jonathan Boucher (1738–1804) was an English clergyman and language scholar who spent the American years of his career in Virginia and Maryland. Born at Blencogo in Cumberland, he went to Virginia about 1754 as a private tutor in planter families. Among his pupils was John Parke Custis, George Washington's stepson, and a long friendship with Washington began.

Ordained in London in 1762, he sailed back and held parishes in Virginia and at Annapolis until 1775. He was famed as a preacher and respected by colonial scholars, and he fought the Maryland vestry act that cut pastors' powers and pay. Though he felt sympathy for the colonies, he denounced resistance to the Stamp Act and stayed loyal, a stance that ended his American ministry when the struggle came.
britannica-1911-boucicaut-jean:
Jean le Meingre, called Boucicaut (about 1366–1421), was a marshal of France driven by one desire, to fight the Turks. His father, of the same name and nickname, had also been a marshal. The son soldiered young in Normandy, Flanders, and Prussia, stood out at Roosebeke in 1382, campaigned in Spain, and journeyed to the Holy Land.

In 1396 he marched to Hungary's defence and shared the Christian disaster at Nicopolis, barely escaping death and spending months as the sultan's captive. Ransomed, he led an army in 1399 to aid the emperor Manuel II and cleared the Turks from before Constantinople. In 1401, instead of returning east, he was sent to Genoa, then under French dominion, where he restored order and made the occupation real. Later pages follow his governorship and final captivity.
britannica-1911-boufflers-stanislas-jean:
Stanislas Jean, chevalier de Boufflers (1737–1815), was a French soldier, colonial governor, and witty man of letters. Born near Nancy, son of the marquis de Boufflers, he was raised at the court of Lunéville, where his mother was the mistress of King Stanislas. Six months of study for the priesthood at Saint Sulpice gave him time to launch a story, Aline, reine de Golconde, that became hugely popular.

He never took vows. Joining the Knights of Malta let him follow arms while keeping a church benefice, and by 1784 he was a maréchal de camp. In 1785 he went to West Africa as governor of Senegal. He governed well, did what he could to soften the slave trade, and worked to open the colony's resources. His departure in 1787 was felt as a calamity by colonists and Africans alike.
britannica-1911-bredael-jan-frans-van:
Jan Frans van Bredael (1683–1750) was a Flemish painter from Antwerp, son of the artist Alexander van Bredael, who died in 1720. His skill lay in copying the manner of Wouverman and Breughel so closely that even experts could mistake his copies for the originals. That talent made copies, not new subjects, the core of his name.

Work in England paid so well that he could retire home after a few years with a comfortable sum saved. The earl of Derwentwater stood among his chief patrons. The entry also sorts out his painter kin, notably Pieter van Bredael (1622–1719) and Jozef (1688–1739). Notes that the family was once wrongly called simply Breda, a name seen on a signature at Amsterdam.
britannica-1911-bridge-of-allan:
Bridge of Allan is a small Scottish burgh in Stirlingshire with 3240 people in 1901, set on the Allan, a left-hand branch stream of the Forth. It lies 3 miles north of Stirling, reached by the Caledonian railway and by tram. Wooded slopes, shelter from the Ochil hills and fine scenery shape its character.

Health seekers made its name, above all in winter and spring, and a pump-room serves visitors taking the waters. Chief buildings are a hydropathic house and the Macfarlane museum of fine art and natural history, while local work covers bleaching, dyeing and paper-making. The Strathallan Gathering nearby ranks as the most popular sports meeting in mid-Scotland, and Airthrey Castle in its park with a lake adjoins the town to the south-east.
britannica-1911-brindaban:
Brindaban is a town of British India in the Muttra district of the United Provinces, on the right bank of the Jumna, 6 miles north of Muttra. It held 22,717 people in 1901. Pilgrimage, not trade, gives the town its pull, and the entry spends its short space on shrines and sacred water.

Brindaban ranks among the most loved pilgrim places in India through its tie to the cult of Krishna as a shepherd. Bathing stairs, tanks and wells serve the crowds, and handsome temples crowd the town. Finest of them is Govind Deva, a cross-shaped vaulted building of red sandstone dated to 1590. The town itself was founded earlier in that same century, so shrine and settlement grew up within a few decades of each other.
britannica-1911-broekhuizen-jan-van:
Jan van Broekhuizen (1649–1707), in Latin Janus Broukhusius, was a Dutch classical scholar and poet born at Amsterdam on 20 November 1649. His father died while he was very young and he was placed with an apothecary for several years. Disliking that work, he entered the army and in 1674 sailed to America in Admiral de Ruyter's fleet, returning the same year.

At the Utrecht garrison in 1678 he befriended the celebrated Graevius, but a duel left him under sentence of death by Dutch law; Graevius wrote to Nicholas Heinsius, who won his pardon. He later captained a company at Amsterdam, and after the peace of Ryswick in 1697 retired on a pension near Amsterdam to classical and literary study. His Dutch poems, modelled on Pieter Hooft, first appeared in 1677, while his classical fame rests on editions of Propertius and other Latin authors.
britannica-1911-buck-bean:
Buck-bean, also called bog-bean, is a bog plant of the north. Its Latin name is Menyanthes trifoliata. It belongs to the gentian family. This short 1911 Britannica entry describes its form and uses. The plant has a creeping stem. Its large leaves grow in an alternate pattern. Each leaf carries three leaflets. Its flowers grow in spikes and are white or pink.

The plant's stout stem has a bitter taste. It has tonic properties, good for strengthening the body. It also works as a febrifuge, a remedy against fever. The species is widely spread through the north temperate zone. The entry is a single short paragraph in the original. It gives the plant's family, shape, flowers and drug value. It adds the range of the species, and nothing further.
britannica-1911-buckland-francis-trevely:
Francis Trevelyan Buckland (1826–1880) was an English zoologist. He was the son of Dean William Buckland, the geologist. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career. He was born at Oxford on 17 December 1826. He was educated at Winchester and Christ Church. He took his degree in 1848. Then he turned to medicine in London. He became house-surgeon at St George's hospital in 1852.

Anatomy work led Buckland into zoology. From 1856 he wrote on natural history for the Field. He wrote above all on fish. In 1866 he started the journal Land and Water. In 1867 he became government inspector of fisheries. His travels in that post spread interest in fish culture. His books include Fish Hatching, in 1863. His Curiosities of Natural History ran to four volumes. He died on 19 December 1880.
britannica-1911-capstan:
A capstan is a machine for hauling cables on ship and dock. This 1911 Britannica article describes it and its history. It heaves in or lets out cables and hawsers. It differs from a windlass in one key point. Its winding axis stands vertical, not horizontal. The word came into English in the 14th century. It came through French or Spanish seamen of the Crusades.

Early capstans were simple wooden machines. An iron spindle ran through them, and men worked them with bars. Heavier cables brought new problems at anchor. Holding, checking and veering the cable grew hard. Cable-holders were then fitted to meet the strain. One was tested in H.M.S. Newcastle in 1870 and proved effective. By 1876 the gear drove a windlass by messenger chain. The article follows such gear into the great iron ships. It explains brakes and chains.
britannica-1911-cardigan:
Cardigan is a seaport and market town of Wales. Its Welsh name is Aberteifi. It is the county town of Cardiganshire. It stands on the right bank of the river Teifi. The river mouth lies about 3 miles below the town. Its population in 1901 was 3511. This 1911 Britannica entry describes the town and its past.

An ancient stone bridge joins Cardigan to its suburb. Bridgend stands on the southern, Pembroke bank of the Teifi. A Great Western branch line ends at the town. A bar at the estuary limits the shipping trade. Brick-works and foundries employ people in the town. Its market serves a large agricultural district well. Two bastions of the ancient castle still survive. Part of a drum tower stands inside Castle Green house. The Priory church of St Mary keeps an early Perpendicular chancel. Its east window holds fragments of ancient stained glass.
britannica-1911-carolus-duran:
Carolus-Duran is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the French painter Charles Auguste Émile Durand (1837–  ), born at Lille on the 4th of July 1837. He trained at the Lille Academy, moved to Paris, and in 1861 travelled to Italy and Spain, where he studied Velázquez with special care. His subject picture “Murdered,” shown in 1866, brought an early success and now hangs in the Lille museum.

Fame came to him as a portrait painter and as head of a leading Paris atelier, where many artists of the next generation trained. His “Lady with the Glove” of 1869, a portrait of his wife, was bought for the Luxembourg. He became a commander of the Legion of Honour in 1889 and joined the Académie des Beaux-Arts in 1904. The next year he took charge of the French academy at Rome. The entry keeps the focus on his standing as portraitist and teacher.
britannica-1911-carver-jonathan:
Jonathan Carver (c. 1725–1780) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an American traveller. He was probably born in Canterbury, Connecticut. He worked first as a shoemaker. He then served with the provincial forces in the French and Indian wars. After the peace of 1763 he planned to explore Britain's new territory in the north west. He set out in 1766. His route ran by Mackinac and the Fox and Wisconsin rivers to the Mississippi.

Carver viewed the Falls of St Anthony. He lived for a time among the Indians. From them he received a grant of 100 square miles between the Mississippi and St Croix rivers. He went to England in 1769 but failed to interest the board of trade. In 1778 a narrative under his name appeared in London. It sold at once and was translated into three languages. Readers long accepted it as a truthful record.
britannica-1911-cavalier-jean:
Jean Cavalier (1681–1740) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the famous chief of the Camisards. He was born at Mas Roux, a hamlet near Anduze in the Gard. His father was a peasant whom persecution had forced into the Roman Catholic church. His mother raised him in secret in the Protestant faith. He worked as a shepherd, then as a baker's apprentice.

Threats over his religion drove Cavalier to Geneva for the year 1701. He returned to the Cévennes on the eve of the Camisard revolt. That revolt began with the murder of the Abbé du Chayla in July 1702. Within months Cavalier led the rebels. Marshal Villars praised him as bold in attack and prudent in retreat. For two years he held the generals of Louis XIV in check. The entry stresses his strict discipline and his gift as an orator.
britannica-1911-cheboygan:
Cheboygan is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a city in Michigan, the county seat of Cheboygan county. It stands on South Channel, between Lakes Michigan and Huron, at the mouth of the Cheboygan river. Its population in 1910 was 6859. Two railways serve it, and steamboats run to Chicago, Milwaukee, Detroit, and other lake ports. A ferry links it with Mackinac. Small boats ply the “Inland Route” to Crooked Lake for much of the year.

The city is the trade centre of a fertile farming region. It has lumber mills, tanneries, paper mills, and boiler works. The water works are owned and run by the city. The place was settled in 1846 under the name Duncan. It was then called Inverness, and finally Cheboygan. It was incorporated as a village in 1871 and chartered as a city in 1889. The entry gives a lake port built on lumber, farming, and water transport.
britannica-1911-chellian:
Chellian is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the name given by G. de Mortillet to the first epoch of the Quaternary period. It is the age when the earliest human remains can be found. The word comes from the French town of Chelles. The climate of the epoch was warm and humid. Fig trees and laurels grew wild in it.

The animals of the age mark it out. They include the Elephas antiquus, the rhinoceros, the cave bear, and the hippopotamus. Man existed, and he belonged to the Neanderthal type. His tools were flints chipped into leaf shaped forms and held in the hand. The entry lists beds held to match the Chellian in age. They include the drift beds of St Acheul near Amiens, of Menchecourt near Abbeville, and of Hoxne in Suffolk.
britannica-1911-chillan:
Chillán is a city and capital of the province of Ñuble, in the southern part of central Chile, 246 miles by rail south-south-west of Santiago. Its people numbered 28,738 in 1895 and an official estimate put them at 36,382 in 1902. The entry calls it one of the most active commercial cities of central Chile. Rich farming and grazing country surrounds it on all sides.

Ruiz de Gambôa founded Chillán in 1594, and its present site was chosen in 1836, with the old site, Chillán Viejo, kept as a suburb. Hot sulphur springs found in 1795 lie about 45 miles east-south-east, issuing at over 135 degrees from the flanks of a volcano 7,000 feet up. The Nevado de Chillán, 9,528 feet high, erupted in 1861 after about two centuries of rest. That eruption caused great destruction before it ceased in 1863.
britannica-1911-chimesyan:
Chimesyan, or Tsimshian, are a tribe of North American Indians, now some 3,000 in number, living around the mouth of the Skeena river in British Columbia. They also live on the islands near that coast, the entry adds. A powerfully built people, they tattoo their bodies for ornament. Rings in noses and ears and labrets, plugs worn in the lip, are part of their dress as described here.

Skill in fishing gives the tribe its living, and the entry stresses that skill directly. They live in large communal houses, housing many people under one roof together. Society is divided into clans, so kin groups order daily life and standing. Distinct social orders also divide the people, setting rank apart from clan in the brief scheme this notice offers.
britannica-1911-chusan:
Chusan is the principal island of a group off the eastern coast of China, in the province of Cheh-kiang, at 30 degrees north and 122 degrees east. It runs north-west to south-east, with a circumference of 51 miles and a breadth from six to ten miles. Hill and dale diversify it, and many small streams water it well. Most of the surface can be cultivated, and nineteen twentieths of the people work in farming.

Rice is favoured wherever it can be reared, with millet, wheat, sweet potatoes, yams, tea and cotton also grown. The capital Tinghai, holding about 40,000 of an estimated 250,000 islanders, stands by a landlocked harbour of four to eight fathoms. Salt works, fisheries, coarse cotton goods and silver wares support trade beyond the farms. British forces took the island in 1840 and 1841, held it till 1846 and occupied it again in 1860.
britannica-1911-clackmannan:
Clackmannan is the county town of Clackmannanshire, Scotland, with 1,505 people, lying near the north bank of the Forth two miles east of Alloa. Two stations on the North British railway serve the small town. The parish church tower, standing on a commanding eminence, is a conspicuous landmark for the district. Clackmannan Tower is now a picturesque ruin, though it once played an important part in Scottish history.

That tower was the seat of a lineal descendant of the Bruce family after the failure of the male line. The old market cross still exists, and beside it stands the stone that gives the town its name, from the Gaelic clach, a stone, and Manann, the district. A large spinning mill and coalpits give a modern touch against the quaint old-world aspect. Kennet House, seat of Lord Balfour of Burleigh, lies a mile south-east.
britannica-1911-clichtove-josse-van:
Clichtove, Josse van (d. 1543) was a Belgian theologian, educated at Louvain and at Paris under Jacques Lefèbvre d'Etaples. He became librarian of the Sorbonne and tutor to the nephews of Jacques d'Amboise, bishop of Clermont and abbot of Cluny. In 1519 he was elected bishop of Tournai, his first see. In 1521 he was translated from Tournai to the see of Chartres, where he remained until his death.

Fame rests on his standing as a distinguished antagonist of Martin Luther, against whom he wrote a good deal. When Cardinal Duprat convened the Synod of Paris in 1528 to discuss the new religion, Clichtove was summoned to that assembly. His task was to collect and summarise the objections to Lutheran doctrine for the synod. That work appeared as his Compendium veritatum against Lutheran assertions at Paris in 1529, and he died at Chartres on 22 September 1543.
britannica-1911-clouet-jean:
Clouet, Jean (d. c. 1541) was a French miniature painter, generally known as Janet, first noted at the French court in 1516, the second year of Francis I. A deed of gift of his escheated estate shows he was not actually a Frenchman and was never naturalised. He is supposed to have been a native of the Low Countries, his real name perhaps Clowet. As groom of the chamber he drew a stipend rising from 180 to 240 livres.

He lived years at Tours, married a jeweller's daughter there, and by 1529 both were settled in Paris. No work in existence has been proved to be his, the entry states plainly. He certainly painted Oronce Finé in 1530, a portrait now known only by a print. A large number of the portrait drawings at Chantilly and the Bibliothèque Nationale are generally believed to be his.
britannica-1911-coloman:
Coloman (1070–1116) was king of Hungary, son of King Geza by a Greek concubine. King Ladislaus meant the book-loving youth for the church. He named him for the see of Eger. Coloman had no taste for that life. With help from friends he fled to Poland. On Ladislaus's death in 1095 he came back and seized the crown.

His younger brother Almos, born in wedlock, would not yield. He stayed a rebel in act or in heart for years. The emperor Henry V took his side and invaded Hungary in 1108, but failed. Coloman made peace and gave back the lost estates. Five years later fear for his infant heir moved him to cruelty. He shut Almos and his son Béla in a monastery and had them blinded. Yet the entry calls him a good king and a wise ruler in the main.
britannica-1911-copan:
Copán is an ancient ruined city of western Honduras, near the Guatemalan frontier. It stands on the right bank of the Río Copán, a branch of the Motagua river. Its rich carved stone buildings rank among the most famed monuments of Mayan civilization. The entry sends readers to the Central America archaeology piece for a full account of those works.

One more thread ties the ruin to later war. Some hold the city to be the same as the Indian stronghold stormed by the Spaniards in 1530. Hernando de Chaves led that attack, after a heroic stand by its defenders. The city has given its name to the department in which it sits. The hosted entry is short and keeps to place, fame and that one point of debate.
britannica-1911-crispin-and-crispinian:
Crispin and Crispinian are the patron saints of shoemakers, kept on 25 October. The entry warns that their story is largely legend, with no trace of it before the 700s. They are said to have been brothers of a noble Roman family. Giving up their property, they travelled to Soissons and lived by shoemaking. Their work there won many converts to Christianity.

The emperor Maximian condemned them to death, but the tale has them survive every ordeal set by the prefect Rictiovarus. At last they were beheaded, in about 287 to 300. Their remains rested at Soissons, and parts later moved to Osnabrück and to Rome. Shoemakers' guilds long kept their feast with processions and merry-making across France and Britain. In England the day gained fresh weight as the anniversary of the battle of Agincourt.
britannica-1911-crittenden-john-jordan:
John Jordan Crittenden (1787–1863) was an American statesman born at Versailles, Kentucky, on 10 September 1787. He graduated at William and Mary in 1807 and took up law in his home state. He served in the Kentucky House, twice in the United States Senate, and as governor of Kentucky from 1848 to 1850. Twice he served as attorney-general of the United States, under Harrison and Tyler, then under Fillmore.

Crittenden stood as the South's foremost champion of the Union in his later Senate years. He opposed the Kansas-Nebraska Bill and backed the Bell and Everett ticket in 1860. In 1860 and 1861 he pressed the compromise measures that bear his name, without success. When war came he worked to keep Kentucky in the Union and sat in the House from 1861 to 1863. He died at Frankfort on 26 July 1863, and the entry adds short lives of his soldier sons George Bibb and Thomas Leonidas.
britannica-1911-cruveilhier-jean:
Jean Cruveilhier (1791–1874) was a French anatomist born at Limoges in 1791. He was educated at the university of Paris. In 1825 he became professor of anatomy there. In 1836 he took the newly founded chair of pathological anatomy, as its first occupant. He died at Jussac in 1874. His career joins the teaching of normal anatomy with the founding of a new branch of the subject.

Cruveilhier's chief works map that double career. His Anatomie descriptive appeared from 1834 to 1836. His Anatomie pathologique du corps humain, issued from 1829 to 1842, carried many coloured plates. A general treatise on pathological anatomy ran from 1849 to 1864. He also wrote on the anatomy of the nervous system of man, in 1845. A fresh descriptive anatomy followed in 1851. The list shows a life given to atlases and treatises.
britannica-1911-cullinan:
Cullinan is a town of the Transvaal, 36 miles by rail east by north of Pretoria. It grew up round the Premier diamond mine and dates from 1903. T. Cullinan, who bought the ground the mine stands on, gave it his name. In January 1905 the largest diamond on record was found there. It weighed 3,025 and three-quarter carats before cutting. No stone found before it matched its size.

In 1907 the Transvaal government presented the great diamond to Edward VII. It was then cut into two stones. One, of 516 and a half carats, and one of 309 carats, were meant to grace the sceptre and crown of England. The chippings from the cutting yielded several smaller diamonds as well. Mine, town, and record stone make the whole of the short entry. For the stones themselves it sends readers to the article on the diamond.
britannica-1911-damghan:
Damghan is a town of Persia in the province of Semnan va Damghan, 216 miles from Teheran on the high road to Khorasan. It stands 3,770 feet above the sea, and its people number about 10,000. Post and telegraph offices serve it. A great export trade runs in pistachios and almonds. Its almonds are the thin-shelled kind called Kaghazi, paper almonds, famed across the country.

Damghan was a weighty city in the middle ages, but little of that age survives. A ruined mosque with massive columns and fine wood carving, and two minarets of the 1000s, are the chief remains. South and west of the town stretch the ruins of Hecatompylos for many miles. The Afghans destroyed Damghan in 1723. On a height in the west of the city stands a ruined citadel holding the house of birth, where Fath Ali Shah was born in 1772.
britannica-1911-dardistan:
Dardistan is a purely conventional name that scientists give to a tract on the north-west frontier of India. No modern race calls itself Dards and no country bears the name, though people on the right bank of the Indus apply it to those on the left. In scientific use it covers Chitral, Yasin, the Gilgit valley, Hunza and Nagar, the Astor valley, and the Indus valley down to Batera.

The so-called Dard races appear in Pliny and Ptolemy and are thought to be an Aryan people who climbed the Indus valley from the Punjab plains. They reached as far north as Chitral, where they drove out the Khos. Their traces survive in the Khoswar, Burishki and Shina tongues spoken in the Gilgit agency.
carolinian: Sabatini set this tale in the southern colonies during America's revolt. A young hero faces love and war in old Carolina. The tale moves fast. The archive keeps the book open to all who seek it. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-dund: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Dundrennan describes a Cistercian house in Kirkcudbrightshire, founded in 1142 by King David the First and Fergus, Lord of Galloway, for monks from Rievaulx. Its name means 'fort of thorn-bushes', and the house commands a view over the Solway Firth. Queen Mary fled there after Langside, spending her final night on Scottish soil before sailing from Port Mary. The abbey passed to the Crown in 1587, was annexed to Stirling's chapel in 1621, and was long quarried for stone before repairs began in 1842.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-mar:
Alexander Martin Sullivan was an Irish politician, lawyer, and journalist, born at Bantry in 1830 and dead at Dublin in October 1884. He drifted into journalism in 1850, becoming the Nation's assistant editor in 1855 and then its editor and proprietor. From 1861 to 1884, with his elder brother T. D. Sullivan, he made the Nation a potent force for Irish nationality, and he also issued the Weekly News and Zozimus.

Sullivan entered Parliament in 1874 as member for Louth and later for Meath, was called to the Irish bar in 1876, and became Queen's Counsel in 1881. As a Dublin Corporation member he secured the site for the Grattan Monument, giving £400 subscribed by admirers while he was jailed for a political offence in 1868. He defended Patrick O'Donnell in his last great case in November 1883, wrote The Story of Ireland and New Ireland, and laboured as a temperance reformer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-dioce:
The early history of Sodor and Man is obscure. The Scandinavian diocese covered Man and the western isles of Scotland, the Southern Hebrides. It took the name Sodor, or southern isles, against Nordr, the Orkneys and Shetland, for the northern isles. Man may have joined Sodor under Magnus Barefoot, in 1098, having earlier stood as a distinct see dependent on Dublin.

When Man became head of a kingdom under Norway, Eugenius III placed the diocese under Nidaros, or Trondhjem, in 1152, and Anastasius IV confirmed the arrangement in 1154. Man stayed under Drontheim until 1458, when Calixtus III moved it to York. Norway's rule ended in 1266, Scotland held the island till 1334, and England followed. Henry IV gave the island to the Stanleys, who held the patronage of the bishoprics, though the bishops never became spiritual lords of Parliament. The last Catholic bishop, Thomas Stanley, appointed under Mary, was recognized until 1568.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrew-forema:
Andrew Foreman, Scottish prelate of border family, was born at Hatton near Berwick-on-Tweed and died in 1522. His talents marked him out for promotion. Through King James IV's influence, he soon became a prothonotary Apostolic and took on important missions. The king sent him in 1497 with two envoys to conclude the truce of Aytoun with Henry VII, and later empowered him to negotiate James's marriage to Henry's daughter Margaret.

By 1502 Foreman was Bishop of Moray, exempt from Saint Andrews' jurisdiction despite the primate's protest. As ambassador to Henry VIII in 1509, he sought peace for a new crusade. Julius II intended him for the cardinalate, but Leo X made him Archbishop of Saint Andrews and legate a latere in 1514, with Dunfermline Abbey. His eight years as primate brought vigorous administration, the restoration of Dunkeld and Dunblane, and a synod showing zeal for clergy reform, learning, and solemn services.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angelica-kauf:
Angelica Kauffman, painter, was born at Coire in Switzerland in 1741 and died at Rome in 1807. Her father Johann Joseph, a mediocre painter, taught her colours early. Before twelve she was summoned to Como by Bishop Nevroni to paint his portrait. Francis III of Este became her protector. Cardinal Roth commissioned his portrait.

She showed aptitude for music, but friends urged her in vain to give up painting. After Parma and Florence, she reached Rome in 1763 for Winckelmann's perspective courses. Meeting English noblemen at Venice, she moved to London in 1766. Her pictures include The Mother of the Gracchi. The Royal Academy elected her an original member. Deceived in 1767 by a stranger posing as Count de Horn, whom she married, she separated. After his death in 1781 she married Antonio Zucchi, settling at Rome, where her salon welcomed Goethe. Sentimentalism helped her vogue, but her works have since declined for weak drawing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ardbraccan:
Ardbraccan, Hill of Braccan or Brecan, is the site of an old abbey, now a parish and village in County Meath, three miles west of Navan. Its abbey was founded and ruled by St. Brecan, grandson of Carthan Finn, first Christian ruler of Thomond, and son of Eochaidh Balldearg, whom Patrick baptized. Brecan, credited with prophecy, died early in the sixth century by Petrie's dating, or after 650 by Ware's, and was buried at Templebrecan in the Great Isle of Arran.

Petrie transcribed his tombstone inscription, found early in the 19th century. The Martyrology of Donegal calls Brecan bishop of Ardbraccan, but the see's founder was St. Ultan, who followed him as abbot. Ultan, famed for charity to children, wrote lives of Brigid and Patrick and died in 657, and his successor Tirechan compiled Acts of Patrick from Ultan's own lips. Ardbraccan was often pillaged between the ninth and twelfth centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-audran:
Audran was the family name of four generations of French artists from Paris and Lyons, counting eight noted engravers and two painters. Their work spans the 1600s and 1700s. Some of their plates rank among the finest work of the burin, the engraver's cutting tool. Charles Audran, born in Paris in 1594, studied in Rome, engraved in pure line, and left more than two hundred plates, including portraits and copies after Titian and the Carracci.

His brother Claude the First taught engraving at Lyons and fathered three sons, of whom Gerard became the family's most famous artist. Later Audrans kept the trade alive into the 1700s. Among them were Germain, Claude the Second, and Benoit the Younger, the last of real artistic weight. Prosper Gabriel, a grandson of Jean, gave up art for law and became professor of Hebrew at the College de France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aurelian:
Aurelian, in full Lucius Domitius Aurelianus, was Roman Emperor from 270 to 275, born near Sirmium in Pannonia in 214 of humble parents. He entered the army at twenty, rose fast through ability and bodily strength, and was proclaimed emperor by the army at Sirmium on Claudius's death. He became sole master when his rival Quintillus, the Senate's candidate, took his own life. The empire he took up was split three ways.

Gaul and Britain stood under a Gallo-Roman empire, the East under Palmyra, and Rome itself held only Italy, Africa, and a few provinces. Invaders pressed the Danube, the treasury was empty, and the coinage was ruined. Backed only by the Danube army, Aurelian restored the frontiers, rebuilt unity, and reformed the state in under five years. He was slain before he could enforce a persecution edict, and the martyr acts tied to his reign are judged unauthentic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auxentius-of-:
Auxentius of Milan was a native of Cappadocia, ordained priest in 343 by Gregory, Alexandria's intruded bishop. After Dionysius of Milan was banished in 355, Arian intrigue made Auxentius bishop of the see, though he did not know Latin. Leading Western bishops tried in vain to bring him to accept the Nicene Creed, the orthodox statement of Christ's divinity. In 359 he made many Illyricum bishops sign the Rimini creed, a compromise formula.

St Hilary of Poitiers publicly accused him at Milan in 364, and a disputation held by Emperor Valentinian's order convicted him of error. His submission was only apparent, and he stayed strong enough to force Hilary's departure from Milan. Though St Athanasius got Pope Damasus to condemn him at a Roman synod in 369, Auxentius kept his see until his death in 374. St Ambrose succeeded him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethany-beyon:
Bethany beyond the Jordan, the place of Jesus's baptism in John's Gospel, is the subject of this textual entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. John 1:28 locates the baptism at Bethany across the Jordan, but a celebrated variant reads Bethabara instead. Most ancient manuscripts of weight support Bethany, a reading approved by Lachmann, Tischendorf, and Westcott-Hort.

Other old manuscripts, the Syriac versions, and Fathers such as Origen, Jerome, Eusebius, and Chrysostom support Bethabara. Origen's commentary argues for the second name. The entry weighs manuscripts and Fathers to settle a single place-name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-betharan: Betharan was an Amorite city east of the Jordan, in its valley plain, some twelve miles from Jericho. Rebuilt by the tribe of Gad, it was later fortified by Herod Antipas, who renamed it Livias for the wife of Augustus, and Josephus calls it Julias. Burnt at Jerusalem's fall, it was restored by Christians and became a bishopric.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethsan:
Bethsan, or Beth Shean, meaning place of rest, was a city within Issachar assigned to Manasseh, profiled in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Later called Scythopolis, it survives as the village of Beisan, three miles west of the Jordan. Its strength kept the Israelites from taking it at the conquest, and it likely stayed Canaanite when the Philistines hung Saul's body on its walls.

Under Solomon it became the centre of an administrative district, and about the third century BC it took its Greek name. The entry follows a strong city from Canaanite holdout to Hellenistic town, with a name that changed with each master.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boetius-egan:
Boetius Egan, Archbishop of Tuam, led Irish Catholics from penal-era hardship toward the relief of the 1790s. Born near Tuam in 1734 to a once-wealthy Galway family, he trained for the priesthood at the Irish College of Bordeaux. He returned to minister in Ireland, became Bishop of Achonry in 1785, and Archbishop of Tuam two years later.

He welcomed the Catholic Relief Act of 1793 with gratitude to George III. He served as a trustee when Maynooth College opened in 1795. One of his last acts signed an address to Lord Camden condemning revolutionary associations, praising the king as the best of kings. He died near Tuam in 1798.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-dolma:
Charles Dolman was a publisher and bookseller born at Monmouth in 1807 and dead at Paris in 1863. The only son of a Monmouth surgeon and Mary Frances Booker, daughter of a London Catholic publisher, he was educated at St. Gregory's, Downside, near Bath. He gave it up when the Bookers, publishers into whose family his father had married, invited him to London.

When Joseph Booker died in 1837, Dolman kept the firm going with his aunt Mary Booker and cousin Thomas Booker. The firm became Booker and Dolman in 1840 and finally continued under his name alone. His periodical career began in 1838 with a new series of The Catholic Magazine. His many attempts to lift the Catholic press to a higher standard came to nothing. Disheartened and ill, he withdrew to Paris and died there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-patri:
An entry on Charles Patrick Meehan, an Irish priest, historian, and translator who spent his life in Dublin parish work and historical writing. Born in Dublin in 1812 to parents from Ballymahon, County Longford, he was sent to the Irish College at Rome. Ordained in 1834, he came home soon after Catholic Emancipation lifted legal penalties on Catholics. After a posting at Rathdrum in Wicklow, he moved to Sts. Michael and John's parish, staying there until his death in 1890.

Meehan wrote histories of the O'Tooles of Powerscourt, the Confederation of Kilkenny, and the Geraldines, and a study of the fate of the Earls of Tyrone and Tyrconnell. He translated Manzoni's tale of a nun, a Latin life of Bishop Kirwan, and an Italian history of Dominican painters. Most of his books went through several revised editions, and he also wrote graceful verse and tales for the young.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-mus:
An entry on the Christian Museum of the Lateran, founded by Pius the Ninth in 1854 in the Lateran palace built by Sixtus the Fifth. Gregory the Sixteenth had founded a profane Lateran museum in 1843 and mooted a Christian collection. Nothing of consequence happened until Pius entrusted the work to Father Marchi and Giovanni Battista de Rossi. Marchi took sculpture, De Rossi took inscriptions, and a third section held copies of catacomb frescoes.

Much material came from the Vatican Library hall set apart by Benedict the Fourteenth in 1750 and from the Capitoline Museum. More came from convents, chapels, sacristies, and private collections, with plaster casts where originals could not move.
