Patrick John Ryan was sixth Bishop and second Archbishop of Philadelphia, born at Thurles in County Tipperary on 20 February 1831 and dead at Philadelphia on 11 February 1911. Schooled by Thurles Christian Brothers, he entered Naughton's Dublin school at twelve for classical studies. In 1844, still a pupil, he headed a student delegation addressing Daniel O'Connell in Richmond prison, and the Liberator praised the young speaker and foretold a bright future.

Adopted for Saint Louis by Archbishop Kenrick in 1847, he studied at Carlow, finished in 1852, and, too young for priesthood, sailed with Patrick Feehan to teach at Carondelet seminary. Kenrick let the young deacon preach often in the cathedral, where his eloquence drew crowds of all denominations. Later pages follow his Saint Louis years, his Philadelphia archbishopric, and his work for schools, churches, and clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrizius-wit:
Patrizius Wittman was a Catholic journalist born at Ellwangen in Wuerttemberg on 4 January 1818 and dead at Munich on 3 October 1883. Son of stonemason Johann Wittmann, he won free scholarships at Ehingen and Tuebingen's Wilhelmsstift through school standing. At Tuebingen from 1838 to 1840 he studied theology and philosophy, won three prizes, and passed a brilliant examination.

Strict orthodoxy clashed with prevailing liberal currents, and he was dismissed from the Wilhelmsstift. Through Riffel of Giessen he joined Augsburg's Sion journal under Herbst, and Doellinger prompted his Glory of the Church in Her Missions Since the Schism of 1841, warmly received. Taking his philosophy doctorate in 1841, he settled at Augsburg, edited Sion as chief, grew its circulation, and laboured there over thirty years after marrying the wealthy widow Caroline Munding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-perpignan:
Perpignan was a French diocese formed from the ancient see of Elne, French Cerdagne, and fragments of Alet and Narbonne. Joined to Carcassonne in 1802, it gained its own bishop again under the Concordat of 1817, seated at Perpignan, where Elne's bishops had lived since 1601. Elne itself had shifted allegiance often, from Narbonne to Rome to Tarragona and back.

Its bishops run from Dominus, named in 571, through Renaissance cardinals like Sforza, Borgia, and Doria to Olympe Gerbet in the nineteenth century. The entry admires Elne's eleventh-century cathedral and cloister, notes Roussillon's late medieval slave deeds under Roman law, and honours the diocese's martyrs: Vincent of Collioure and the virgins Eulalia and Julia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-john-su:
Peter John Sullivan was an Irish-born American soldier, lawyer, and diplomat, born at Cork in 1821. His parents carried him to Philadelphia at two, and he studied at the University of Pennsylvania. He won a major's commission for merit in the Mexican War, then served as an official stenographer of the United States Senate. In 1848 he settled at Cincinnati and joined the bar.

There he stood out as an opponent of the Know-Nothing movement. In the Civil War he helped raise several volunteer regiments and led the 48th Ohio as colonel, winning a brevet brigadier-generalship in March 1865. Soon after he became United States minister to Colombia, holding the post until 1869, then returned to his Cincinnati law practice. He died there in 1883.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-henry-:
Philip Henry Sheridan was a Union general of the Civil War, born at Albany in 1831. His family joined Ohio's Catholic pioneers at Somerset, and he entered West Point in 1848, graduating in 1853. Service in Texas and Oregon against Indian troubles won him credit before the war made him Halleck's chief quartermaster, then colonel of the Second Michigan Cavalry in May 1862. Brigadier-general followed in July.

Commanding the Army of the Potomac's cavalry from April 1864, he became one of Grant's chief reliances against Lee in Virginia. His famous ride from Winchester to Cedar Creek on 19 October 1864 turned a Union retreat into complete victory over Early, and Grant called him one of the ablest of generals. A regular major-generalship followed that November, and his 1865 raids cut Lee's supply lines. He died at Nonquitt in 1888.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-the-ar:
Philip the Arabian was Roman emperor from 244 to 249, son of an Arab sheikh, born at Bosra. He rose through the army to high office, and when Gordian III's able father-in-law Timesitheus died in 243, the boy emperor named Philip his successor. By starving the troops of provisions Philip turned them against Gordian, had him secretly executed, then deified him and raised his monument to fool the Senate.

He gave up Timesitheus's Persian gains, pulled troops from Dacia, Raetia, and Britain to guard Italy, and beat the Carpi on the Danube, earning the name Carpicus Maximus on coins. Kin given high office abused it, his seven-year-old son became co-ruler, and Rome's thousandth birthday was celebrated in April 248. Rival emperors rose, Decius marched on Italy, and Philip and his son were killed near Verona in 249.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-politian:
Politian, born Angelo Ambrosini at Montepulciano in 1454, was an Italian humanist and master of Greek and Latin letters. He went to Florence at ten and studied under Landino, Argyropoulos, Callistus, and Ficino. In 1477 he became tutor to the children of Lorenzo the Magnificent and joined Lorenzo's academy with Ficino, Pico della Mirandola, and Barbarus.

From 1480 he taught Greek and Latin literature at Florence, counting Grocyn, Linacre, and Reuchlin among his pupils. At eighteen he translated five books of the Iliad and won the name Homericus juvenis. His Miscellanea of 1489 treated scholarly puzzles from Greek breathings to the spelling of Virgil, and his care for manuscripts helped fix the texts of many Latin authors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-popayan:
Popayán is a Colombian archdiocese covering the whole department of Cauca and parts of Nariño and Valle. Since the decree of July 1910 its bounds run from the Diocese of Cali in the north and west to Pasto in the south and Garzón in the east. The diocese was established by Paul III in September 1546, though the see was not erected until September 1547.

Its first bishop, Juan del Valle, performed the erection ceremony by apostolic delegation at Aranda del Duero in Spain. Popayán served as suffragan to Lima until 1573, then to Bogotá, and became an archdiocese in June 1900 with Pasto, Garzón, and Cali as suffragans. Among its bishops, Agustín de la Coruña suffered banishment defending the Indians, and Carlos Bermúdez restored the seminary while defending church rights.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-joan:
Pope Joan names a fabled woman pope, first heard of around the middle of the thirteenth century. Jean de Mailly, a Dominican chronicler, tells the earliest version, which Etienne de Bourbon took into his Seven Gifts of the Holy Ghost. There the supposed popess belongs about 1100, still without a name.

The tale has a gifted woman donning men's dress, rising to Curia notary, then cardinal, then pope. Out riding one day, she bore a son, whereupon the crowd tied her to a horse's tail, dragged her through the streets, stoned her, and buried her on the spot. Martin of Troppau's chronicle gives a second version, setting her after Leo IV as John of Mainz, with a reign of two years, seven months, and four days.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-saint-fa:
Fabian was pope from 236 to 250. Eusebius tells the strange story of his election. After Anterus died, Fabian had come to Rome from his farm. While illustrious names were weighed, a dove landed on his head. The crowd recalled the Spirit descending on the Saviour and chose him with joyous unanimity.

His fourteen years brought a lull in persecution. Little else is known. The Liber Pontificalis says he split Rome into seven districts, each under a deacon, and set seven subdeacons to gather martyrs' trial records. Tradition credits him with the four minor orders and work in the catacombs. He moved Pope Pontianus's body from Sardinia to the Catacomb of Callistus. He is also said to have sent seven bishops as missionaries to Gaul in 245, among them Denys of Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-ponti:
Pontian was made pope on 21 July 230 and reigned until 235. The Liber Pontificalis calls him a Roman, son of Calpurnius. With him begins the brief third-century chronicle of Roman bishops that the Liberian list later used, giving more exact data. The Hippolytus schism ran through his reign, but toward its end the schismatics reconciled with Rome's bishop.

After Alexandria condemned Origen in 231 or 232, a Roman synod under Pontian concurred. In 235 Maximinus the Thracian opened a persecution aimed at church heads. Pontian and Hippolytus were banished to unhealthy Sardinia. To allow a new election, Pontian resigned on 28 September 235, and Anteros succeeded him. Hippolytus, banished with him, soon reconciled with Rome, ending his schism. How long Pontian endured Sardinia's mines is unknown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-vital:
Vitalian reigned from 657 to 672 and died on 27 January 672. Nothing is known of his life before the papacy. The Liber Pontificalis calls him a native of Segni, son of Anastasius. After Eugene I died in June 657, Vitalian was elected and enthroned on 30 July. Like his predecessor, he pursued friendly ties with Constantinople and an end to the Monothelite controversy.

He sent letters announcing his elevation to Constans II and Patriarch Peter, who leaned to Monothelitism. The emperor confirmed Rome's privileges and sent St Peter a gold-covered Gospel codex set with gems. Peter answered vaguely, seeming to agree, and intercourse resumed on that mutual reserve. Vitalian's name entered Byzantium's diptychs. In England he backed Rome's Easter and tonsure at Whitby, where Oswy chose Roman practice. After his death, the Monothelite patriarch Theodore struck his name from the diptychs, and the Sixth Council of 681 restored it when Monothelitism was suppressed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prudentius-ma:
Prudentius Maran, learned Benedictine of the Maurist congregation, was born at Sézanne in the Marne on 14 October 1683. He died at Paris on 2 April 1762. After schooling in the humanities at Paris, he took the Benedictine habit at Saint Faron near Meaux in January 1703. He went on studying at Saint Denis. Sent to Saint Germain-des-Prés, he worked with his confrère Touttée on an edition of Saint Cyril of Jerusalem.

Trouble came in 1734, when Cardinal Bissy had him removed from Saint Germain-des-Prés. Bissy suspected Maran of holding his brethren back from accepting the Bull Unigenitus. After a year at Orbais and a stay at Saint Martin de Pontoise, he moved in 1737 to Blancs-Manteaux. There he spent the rest of his life. His wide knowledge of theology and the Church Fathers marks the scholarly works listed at the entry's close.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-publican:
In the Gospels, a publican is a member or servant of the Roman companies that farmed the taxes. This encyclopedia entry traces the word from the publicanus of the Vulgate. From republican times Rome spared itself the trouble of gathering provincial taxes directly. It auctioned each province's taxes in a lump sum, and the highest bidder won the right to wring that sum from the province. The system invited rapacious exactions, and abuses were often intolerable.

Jews who profited by serving foreign rulers in this way drew their countrymen's execration, sharpened by hatred of Roman supremacy. In Gospel stories publicans appear as a class habitually coupled with sinners, the very picture of collaboration. Yet the twelve apostles include Levi, also called Matthew the Publican. Maas, Dietrich and Thibault supply the entry's sources on the tax companies and Roman customs houses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-publius-aeliu:
Publius Aelius Hadrian, Emperor of the Romans, was born at Rome on 24 January 76 and died on 10 July 138. He reigned from 118 to 138, having married Julia Sabina, his cousin and ward and Trajan's grand-niece. He gave up Armenia, Mesopotamia and Assyria, lands his predecessor had hoped to hold after conquering the Parthians, and bent his efforts to developing the Province of Arabia.

Favours to the Senate, including the remission of fifteen years of tax arrears, strengthened his standing, and imperial power under him reached heights never seen before. A conspiracy by distinguished officers on a campaign in Moesia was crushed, its four ringleaders executed. Later pages follow his travels. They tell of his favourite Antinous, drowned in the Nile in 130 and then deified. They also tell of the Jewish revolt of 132, after he planted the colony Aelia Capitolina on Jerusalem's ruins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-verst:
Richard Verstegan, born Rowlands, was a Catholic publisher and antiquary who worked from exile in Antwerp. Born in London about 1548 to a family from Guelderland, he entered Christ Church, Oxford, in 1565 under the name Rowlands. As a Catholic he could not take a degree, so he returned to Antwerp and resumed his family name.

His first major book, a 1583 illustrated account of Catholic martyrdoms in England, was seized and destroyed in France after the English ambassador called it a libel on Elizabeth. Arrested and nearly extradited, he was freed through Cardinal Allen and the papal nuncio. From Antwerp he issued Catholic devotional manuals and primers, acted as a correspondence agent for Allen and the Jesuits, and wrote political tracts. His later antiquarian work, A Restitution of Decayed Intelligence, traced English customs and words to Anglo-Saxon roots. He died at Antwerp in 1636.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-fabyan:
Robert Fabyan was a London clothier and alderman whose chronicle remains a key source for the city's history. He died on 28 February 1513. A member of the Drapers' Company, he held several responsible civic posts but resigned his aldermanship in 1502, probably to escape the heavy costs of the mayoralty.

Fabyan ranks among the city chroniclers, writers chiefly concerned with municipal life, yet he first tried joining London's story to the nation's. His Concordance of Histories runs from Brutus to the death of Richard III, yet his attempt to harmonize earlier chroniclers shows little art or judgment. The work's value lies chiefly in its London material. Its second edition of 1533 adds pithy notes on municipal affairs under Henry VII, thought to abridge a lost chronicle of that reign. The best edition is Ellis's of 1811.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roch-amboise-:
Roch-Ambroise-Auguste Bebian was a pioneer in the education of the deaf in France. Born at Pointe-a-Pitre in Guadeloupe in 1789, he was sent to France under the care of the Abbe Sicard, famed educator of the deaf. Sicard placed him with the Abbe Jauffret. After the Lycee Charlemagne in Paris, Bebian gave himself to studying deaf education. He followed Sicard's courses and attended to Laurent Clerc, later of Hartford.

As prefect of studies at the Paris institution, he sought the signs best fitted to express deaf pupils' ideas. His Essai sur les sourds-muets of 1817, Mimographie of 1822, and Manuel of 1827 set the principles used at Paris. After leaving the school he wrote, refused schools at St Petersburg and New York, and founded an institution in Montparnasse. He directed Rouen's school, then returned to Guadeloupe, where he founded a school for black children. He died there in 1839.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roger-william:
Roger William Vaughan, known as Bede, was the second Archbishop of Sydney. Born at Courtfield in Herefordshire in 1834, second son of Colonel John Vaughan, he was the younger brother of Cardinal Vaughan of Westminster. Delicate in health, he was schooled at home under his saintly mother until seventeen, then went to Downside and became a Benedictine. After his novitiate he studied at St Paul Outside the Walls in Rome from 1855 and was ordained in 1859.

Back at Downside he ran the mission, taught philosophy from 1861, and served as cathedral prior at Belmont from 1862 to 1872. Chosen coadjutor to Archbishop Polding of Sydney in 1872, he was consecrated at Liverpool and sailed for Australia. On Polding's death in 1877 he succeeded as archbishop. He founded Catholic schools, pressed primary education, and opened his completed cathedral. He lived as simply as a monk and died suddenly in Lancashire in 1883 while visiting England for his health.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacristan:
A sacristan looks after the sacristy, the church, and all in them. In old times doorkeepers did much of this work, later mansionarii and treasurers. Gregory IX's Decretals call it an honoured post tied to a benefice. Nowadays he is chosen or paid.

Church rules said that in cathedrals the sacristan should be a priest. It lists work for the sacristy, Eucharist, font, oils, relics, and church decor. It also covers prep for rites, bell ringing, and order in church. The under-sacristan, or custos, helped him, under the archdeacon, with much the same work. Now the post is hardly ever tied to a benefice but is usually paid. Trent wished clerics to hold such posts, but in most churches laymen do much of this work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-john-la:
Saint John Lateran is the oldest of Rome's four patriarchal basilicas, standing where the palace of the Laterani family stood. Plautius Lateranus, consul designate under Nero, was accused of conspiracy and his goods confiscated. Traces of the palace appear in the walls and in a hall found within the basilica. The palace passed to Constantine through his wife Fausta, giving it the name Domus Fausta, and Constantine gave it to the Church by 311.

A council against the Donatists met within its walls in 313, and it was the centre of Christian life, the popes' residence and the city's cathedral. It holds the cathedral rank, with the title of mother and head of all churches of the city and the world. The first church there was probably an adapted palace hall rather than a new building. It was dedicated to the Saviour, with the dedication to Saint John coming later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-lawrenc:
Lawrence Justinian, bishop and first patriarch of Venice, was born in 1381 into the Giustiniani, a Venetian patrician family counting several saints. He died on 8 January 1456. His pious mother planted a devout life in him young. In 1400, at about nineteen, he entered the monastery of the Augustinian Canons Regular on the island of Alga near Venice.

Ordained in 1406, he soon became prior and then general of the congregation, gave it its constitution, and spread it so widely that he counts as its founder. Raised to the bishopric of Castello in 1433, he restored churches, set up parishes in Venice, and reformed the canons, while giving all he could raise to the poor. In 1451 Nicholas V joined Castello to the patriarchate of Grado and moved the see to Venice, naming Lawrence its first patriarch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-loman:
Loman, bishop of Trim in Ireland and nephew of Saint Patrick, was the first man Patrick placed over an Irish see, in the year 433. He had converted Fortchern, prince of Trim and grandson of Laeghaire, king of Meath, together with Fortchern's father Foidilmid, and Trim was given to him as his see.

Some say he was already a bishop before reaching Ireland, but this seems unlikely, since he would not accept Trim unless Patrick came to ratify the gift. The Tripartite Life and Tirechan state plainly that he was only a simple priest whom Patrick consecrated for Trim. He did not long survive his promotion, and after visiting his brother Broccaid in Connacht, he resigned the see to Fortchern with Patrick's permission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-ninian:
Ninian, bishop and confessor who died about 432, counts as the first preacher of Christianity to the southern Picts of Scotland. Almost everything known about him comes from a short passage in Bede's church history, which calls him a Briton trained at Rome. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia builds on that passage and tests the fuller tales that came later.

Bede places his see at Candida Casa, the White House, named for a stone church he built in honour of Martin of Tours, a rarity among the Britons. A twelfth-century Life by Aelred adds much detail, claiming older sources, but the entry shows how little of it can be checked. Readers meet a shadowy founder whose stone church and mission to the Picts outlived the man himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saints-kieran:
Kieran is a name shared by many Irish saints, and this entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia sorts them out. Most celebrated is Kieran of Clonmacnoise, treated under that place, but Kieran of Seir-Kieran and Kieran of Disert-Kieran stand next in fame. The note serves as a guide to a crowded calendar, not a single biography.

Seir-Kieran's founder, active through much of the fifth century from about 450, also founded the see of Ossory and is honoured in England, Brittany, Wales, and Scotland on 5 March. Disert-Kieran's Kieran, called the Devout by Irish annalists, wrote a Life of Patrick and died in 775, kept on 14 June. Two lesser Kierans follow, of Clonsost on 30 April and son of Colga on 19 May.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-severian:
Severian, Bishop of Gabala in Syria, flourished in the fourth and fifth centuries and was known as a good preacher and writer of biblical commentaries and sermons. Nothing survives about his life before his consecration. This entry remembers him chiefly for the regrettable part he played in the deposition and banishment of Saint John Chrysostom. Drawn to Constantinople about 400 by the success of his fellow Syrian Antiochus, he won hearers despite a strong Syrian accent.

Chrysostom invited him to preach and, leaving for Asia in 401, made him his deputy for liturgical functions. Severian used the absence to quarrel openly with Serapion, the archdeacon and administrator. Swayed by personal interest amid the strained relations between Chrysostom and Empress Eudoxia, he sided against Chrysostom and helped bring about his fall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-dominic-c:
Dominic Corrigan, physician born in Dublin in 1802, died there in 1880, won distinction for original observations in heart disease, with a special pulse type named after him. Son of a poor shopkeeper, he was schooled at Maynooth. Drawn to medicine by the attending physician, he took his medical degree at Edinburgh in 1825.

Back in Dublin he became physician to Jervis Street Hospital, then holding only six medical beds. Over four years he recast teaching on aortic valve disease. His paper on permanent patency of the aortic valves appeared in Edinburgh's Medical and Surgical Journal in April 1832. A gifted teacher, he won a London diploma in 1842 and a Dublin honorary doctorate in 1849. His work in the famine fever years made him famous, and Trousseau proposed calling aortic heart disease Corrigan's disease.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-th:
The Sisters of the Good Samaritan, Tertiaries Regular of Saint Benedict, began at Sydney, Australia, on 2 February 1857. A second community followed at Windsor in 1859, and foundations multiplied until the Archdiocese of Sydney alone counted 21 houses with 202 members, and all Australia 29 communities.

Houses followed at Gawler in 1902, Northcote in 1904, and South Yarra, with boarding and day schools in Port Augusta, Rockhampton, and Cooktown. At Tempe, Arncliffe, the sisters established Saint Magdalen's Retreat, a home for penitent women of all creeds, supported by voluntary gifts and the inmates' labour. About 130 women lived there in 1909, encouraged to remain at least two years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-son-of-man:
Son of Man is a phrase with a long biblical career. This entry follows it from Hebrew poetry to the Gospels. In the Old Testament it serves as a poetic synonym for man, or for ideal man. God addresses the prophet Ezekiel by it more than ninety times. That usage is found elsewhere only once, in Daniel.

Daniel's night vision of one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven gave the phrase its apocalyptic weight. The entry shows how the New Testament takes it up as Christ's own chosen self-designation. Tracing each occurrence, it explains why a humble-sounding title became one of the richest names in Christian speech.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-adamnan-eu:
St. Adamnan, also called Eunan, was abbot of Iona, born at Drumhome in County Donegal about 624 and dead at Iona in 704. This entry follows a boy schooled by Columban monks at home who became a novice at Iona in 650, rose to the abbacy in 679. And presided over all Columban houses in Ireland.

Three long visits to Ireland marked his rule, one remembered for winning acceptance of the Roman date of Easter. And on his third, in 697, he stood at the Synod of Tara when the Cain Adamnain, his canon, was adopted, freeing women and children from being killed or captured in war. The entry also notes his possible rule of Mayo, and his memory remains inseparable from Iona.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-aileran:
St. Aileran, generally known as Sapiens, the Wise, was one of the most distinguished teachers at Clonard in seventh-century Ireland. This entry places him at the great school through the fame of St. Finian and his disciples, rector of that celebrated seat of learning about 650. And dead of the Yellow Plague, his death recorded in the Annals of Ulster on 29 December 664.

As a classical scholar he had almost no rival in his day, and his command of Origen, Philo, Jerome, and Augustine marks him as a master of Latin and Greek. Colgan credits him with many works, including a Fourth Life of St. Patrick and lives of Brigid and Fechin, while the Latin-Irish Litany is scarcely doubted as his, and the entry presents a scholar-saint of the Irish golden age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-alban:
St. Alban was the first martyr of Britain, suffering about 304, and this entry retells the account known since Bede's Ecclesiastical History. A pagan living at Verulamium, now St. Albans in Hertfordshire, he sheltered a cleric fleeing persecution, and after some days, moved by his guest's example, received baptism himself.

When the governor's men came to search the house, Alban put on his guest's cloak and gave himself up in his place, was dragged before the judge, scourged. And, refusing to deny his faith, condemned to death. On the road to execution he held back a river's waters so the party crossed dry-shod. And a fountain sprang on the hilltop, wonders the entry reports as Bede told them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-aphian:
St. Aphian, or Apian, was an illustrious martyr under Emperor Maximian, about 306. This entry follows a youth of only eighteen who entered the temple at Caesarea while the prefect Urbanus offered sacrifice. Seizing the outstretched hand that presented the incense, he reproached the magistrate for idolatry. Guards fell on him furiously, tortured him cruelly, and flung him into a dungeon.

On the following day the prefect had him torn with iron claws, beaten with clubs, and burned over a slow fire. Then he was sent back to confinement. After three days he was taken from prison again and cast into the sea, stones tied to his feet. Eusebius, who saw it, declares that an earthquake shook the city at that moment, and the sea flung his corpse onto the shore.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-brendan:
St. Brendan of Ardfert and Clonfert — Brendan the Voyager, as he is also known — was born in 484 in Ciarraighe Luachra, near present-day Tralee in County Kerry, Ireland. He died at Enachduin, now Annaghdown, in 577. This entry follows a boy baptized at Tubrid near Ardfert by Bishop Erc. For five years St. Ita, the Brigid of Munster, educated him; St. Erc finished his studies and ordained him priest in 512.

Between 512 and 530 Brendan set up monastic cells at Ardfert and at Shanakeel, or Baalynevinoorach, below Brandon Hill. From there he sailed on his famous voyage to the Land of Delight. The old Irish calendars mark a special feast for the Egressio familiae S. Brendani on 22 March. In his litany from the close of the eighth century, St. Aengus the Culdee invokes the sixty who accompanied Brendan on his quest for the Land of Promise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-brogan:
St. Brogan flourished in the sixth or seventh century, and this entry follows a name borne by several persons in repute for holiness. The name is written Brogan, Broccan, Bracan, and even Bearchan and Bearchanus. Two of those persons are commemorated in the Irish Martyrology of Aengus, whose early date, about 800, is now generally admitted. There, under 8 July, we read that Brocan the scribe gained a noble triumph without any fall.

Under 17 September we read that Brocan of Ross Tuirc thou shouldst declare. Colgan seems inclined to identify both persons as the author of an Irish hymn upon St. Brigid. The Aengus glosses and the Martyrology of Gorman, while seemingly treating them as distinct, prove the matter admits of no certainty. Some modern hagiographers regard the Brogan of 8 July as the amanuensis and possibly the nephew of St. Patrick, styling him bishop and locating him at Ross Tuirc.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-cajetan:
St. Cajetan, or Gaetano, was founder of the Theatines, born in October 1480 at Vicenza in Venetian territory. He died at Naples in 1547. This entry follows a boy raised by a pious mother, studious and exemplary in youth. He took his law doctorate at Padua in his twenty-fourth year. In 1506 he became a prothonotary apostolic at Rome in Julius II's court.

He took an important share in reconciling the Republic of Venice with that pontiff. On Julius's death in 1523 he withdrew from court. Shortly after, he is credited with founding the Oratory of Divine Love, an association of pious priests and prelates that spread to other Italian towns. Though remarkable for intense love of God, he did not reach the priesthood till 1516. Recalled to Vicenza in 1517 by his mother's death, he founded a hospital for incurables there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-conan:
St. Conan, bishop of the Isle of Man, died in January 684. This Irish missionary was also known as Mochonna. This entry follows a man easily confused with St. Conindrius — said to have been a disciple of St. Patrick who lived to a very advanced age, dying 17 November 560. The Bollandists count Conan among Man's early bishops, and Colgan recounts his life and labours.

Unfortunately, fifth- and sixth-century Isle of Man history is very obscure, and definite facts are hard to get at. Yet Conan, or Mochonna, also called Bishop of Inis-Patrick, left a clear mark of his zeal for souls in Manxland. Some authorities give his death date as 26 January, but Colgan, quoting the ancient Irish martyrologies, gives 13 January, the day Conan's feast is observed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-corbinian:
Freising in Bavaria had him as bishop, and Chatres near Melun in France was where he was born, about 680. He died 8 September 730, the date also kept as his feast; 20 November marks his translation, and a bear is his emblem. Of his early years, nothing survives in the record. Waldekiso, his father, had died before his birth, and after his mother Corbiniana died, he withdrew to a solitary life at the Saint-Germain church in Chatres.

With some disciples he went to Rome in 716, or 709 by another reckoning. There he was consecrated bishop and given the pallium, then sent to preach, with great success near his former home. In 723, or 716, he visited Rome again, meaning to resign. The pope refused to hear his request. Heading home, Corbinian reached Mais in Tyrol, where Duke Grimoald's messengers induced him to go to Bavaria and settle at Freising.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-cyprian:
St. Cyprian was bishop of Toulon, born at Marseilles in 476. He died 3 October 546. This entry follows the favourite pupil of St. Caesarius of Arles, by whom he was trained. In 506 Caesarius ordained him to the diaconate, and in 516 consecrated him as Bishop of Toulon. Cyprian was apparently present at the 524 synod of Arles, and at a number of councils in following years.

At every one of these assemblies he proved a vigorous opponent of Semipelagianism. Soon after Caesarius's death in 543, Cyprian wrote a two-book life of his great teacher. The Abbess Caesaria the Younger, who had headed the Arles convent since 529, moved him to the undertaking. The life ranks among the sixth century's most valuable biographical remains. Firminus and Viventius, bishops and friends of Caesarius, aided Cyprian, as well as the priest Messianus and the deacon Stephen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-donnan:
Several seventh-century saints named Donnan blur into one another, and this entry patiently pulls their threads apart. Its main figure, abbot of Eigg, was a friend and disciple of Columba who followed him from Ireland to Scotland late in the sixth century. Seeking solitude, he settled with companions on Eigg, then used only to graze the queen's sheep. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 weighs Irish annals against the Bollandists and later scholars.

Ordered slain for the intrusion, Donnan's company was found by the queen's agents at Mass on Easter eve. Asked to wait until the sacrifice ended, they were then killed. The entry also notes Donnan of Auchterless, treated by some as a separate man, and argues the two were likely one. Readers get a martyrdom story wrapped in honest doubt about names and dates.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-drostan:
Drostan, a Scottish abbot of about the year 600, is known only through two sources that do not quite agree, and this entry says so plainly. Born to the royal house of the Scoti, son of Cosgrach, he was handed young to Columba, who trained him and gave him the monastic habit. He travelled with Columba to Aberdour in Buchan, where a Pictish ruler granted the site of Deir. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 draws on the Breviarium Aberdonense and the ninth-century Book of Deir.

When Columba returned to Iona, Drostan stayed as abbot of the new house. Years later he succeeded the abbot of Dalquhongale, then gave up office for deeper solitude as a hermit at Glenesk. The entry's charm lies in its gaps: a life pieced from two old books, with the seams left visible.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-dunstan:
Dunstan, archbishop and one of Anglo-Saxon England's greatest saints, lived at the hinge between hermit holiness and high politics. Born near Glastonbury, he lived as a hermit in a tiny cell against the old church of St. Mary, studying, crafting, and playing his harp. There the late legend puts the devil's face in his smith's tongs. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 follows him from that cell to the king's council.

His clash with King Eadwig at the coronation feast of 956 cost him his property and drove him into exile in Flanders. Under Edgar he returned to shape sixteen prosperous years, crowning the king at Bath in 973 and settling church disputes through the Witan. He died on 19 May, still the people's favourite saint until Thomas Becket overshadowed him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-elo-colman:
Colman Elo, famed in Irish hagiology, founded two monastic houses and is counted bishop of Connor. Born about 555 at Glenelly in present County Tyrone, he studied under his maternal uncle Columcille. That saint obtained for him the site now called Lynally, giving him the name Colman Elo, or Colmanellus. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Lynally to 26 September 611, his feast day.

Styled coarb, or successor, of MacNisse, he is regarded as bishop of Connor. He later founded the Abbey of Muckamore, where he served as first abbot. Also known as Colman Macusailni, he links the Columban circle to the church of northeast Ireland. The entry is brief, but it fixes a founder, two houses, and a lineage of teaching passed from uncle to nephew.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-elzear-of-:
Elzear of Sabran, a Provençal nobleman, lived a married life of deliberate chastity and public service. Born in 1285 at Saint-Jean de Robians, he was trained in piety and learning by his uncle, abbot of St. Victor at Marseilles. At Charles II of Naples' wish he married Delphine of Glandèves, respected her wish to live a virgin, and joined the Third Order of St. Francis. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Paris to 27 September 1323.

At twenty he moved to Puy-Michel for solitude and set household rules that made his home a model of Christian virtue. After his father's death in 1309 he won over scornful Italian subjects by kindness, helped expel Emperor Henry VII from Rome, and later tutored Duke Charles of Naples. With Delphine he vowed chastity, joining prayer, mortification, and charity to high office.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ernan:
Ernan is a name shared by many Irish saints, and this entry untangles four of them from a crowd of twenty-five. Its first Ernan, son of Eogan and nephew of Columba, died about 640 and kept a monastery at Druim-Tomma in Donegal. Fishing the River Finn on the night Columba died, he saw the sky blaze and a pillar of fire rise eastward like the noonday sun. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 takes the vision from Adamnan, who heard it from Ernan himself.

O'Hanlon's count explains the confusion: Acts of different Ernans blended together over time. Writers even mistook this Ernan for Ernan of Hinba, Columba's uncle. The entry commemorates him on 1 January in the Martyrology of Tallaght. Readers get both a vivid death-night vision and a warning about how saints' lives merge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-finan:
Finan, second bishop of Lindisfarne until 661, built in timber and reed while converting kings and founding abbeys. An Irish monk trained at Iona, he was chosen by Columban monks to succeed Aidan, who ruled from 635 to 651. Bede calls him an able ruler. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 9 February 661.

He raised a cathedral in Irish fashion, hewn oak roofed with reeds, dedicated to St. Peter. His zeal founded St. Mary's at the Tyne's mouth, Gilling on the spot where Oswin was murdered, and great Whitby, Streanaeshalch. He converted Peada of the Middle Angles with all his nobles and thanes, giving him four priests, including Diuma, consecrated bishop of Middle Angles and Mercia. The Aberdeen breviary praises his venerable life and eloquent teaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-flavian:
Flavian, bishop of Constantinople until August 449, fell to court intrigue before he fell to a council's violence. A presbyter and sacristan famed for holiness, he succeeded Proclus against the wishes of Chrysaphius, eunuch minister of Theodosius II. The minister demanded rich gifts disguised as blessed bread at his appointment, and Flavian's refusal to spend church treasure on the emperor earned lasting enmity. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Hypaepa in Lydia to August 449.

Pulcheria championed him, while Chrysaphius won Empress Eudocia, and early plots to disgrace him failed. A council of bishops then gave his enemies their opening, in the doctrinal storms of the age. The entry follows a bishop caught between palace factions and theological war, dying in exile after his see was torn from him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-foillan:
Foillan, Irish missionary of the seventh century, is pictured with a crown at his feet for despising worldly honour. Brother of Ultan and of Fursey, famed preacher to Irish, Anglo-Saxons, and Franks, he followed Fursey into exile when invaders ravaged Ireland. At Burgh Castle in Suffolk, built between 634 and 650, Fursey left the monastery in Foillan's care when solitude called again. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 follows Foillan through war and wandering.

About 650 Fursey, now among the Franks, visited his brother once more. Then war between Penda of Mercia and Ana of East Anglia broke the community: Ana fled, and the monastery at Cnoberesburg suffered. The entry breaks off mid-disaster, but its shape is clear: a brother holding a house together while kingdoms fought around it, honour refused, service kept.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-fulcran:
Fulcran, bishop of Lodève from 949 to 1006, rebuilt his diocese's churches and hospitals with tireless care. Born to a distinguished family, he consecrated himself early to the Church, lived purely from youth, and became priest. When Bishop Theoderich died in 949, Fulcran was chosen successor despite his unwillingness and consecrated by Narbonne's archbishop on 4 February. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 13 February 1006.

He laboured to conserve moral life among clergy and religious, rebuilt many churches and convents, including the cathedral of St. Genesius and the Holy Redeemer church with its Benedictine house. Poor and sick drew his special care, and he founded hospitals and endowed existing ones. The entry's source is Bernard Guidonis, himself later bishop of Lodève, writing a predecessor's life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-capis:
John Capistran, Franciscan preacher and former governor of Perugia, turned prison reflection into a friar's life. Born at Capistrano in 1385, his father had come to Naples with Louis of Anjou and was thought French, though some say German. His father dying early, his mother educated him, first at home, then in law at Perugia under the eminent Pietro de Ubaldis. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 23 October 1456.

In 1412 Ladislaus of Naples made him governor of Perugia, where he set himself against civic corruption and bribery. War with the Malatesta in 1416 sent him as ambassador to propose peace, but they cast him into prison. There he began to think seriously about his soul, and a dream of Francis warning him to enter the order decided him. He had married a wealthy wife, whose story the entry leaves at that turning point, as governor became friar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-kilian:
Kilian, apostle of Franconia, was murdered for telling a duke his marriage was unlawful. Born about 640 to noble parents, probably in Ireland, though some say Scotland, he was famed from youth for piety and study. The later Passio makes him a monk, and Trithemius calls him monk, even abbot, of Iona, though that cannot be proved. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 8 July, probably 689.

The older Passio, trusted here, says he was raised to bishop's rank before leaving home. As a travelling bishop without fixed diocese, in Irish custom, he reached Würzburg, then held by the pagan duke Gozbert. After gaining missionary faculties from Pope Conon at Rome, he preached there and won Gozbert's promise to leave Geilana, his brother's widow. In the duke's absence Geilana had Kilian and two companions secretly murdered and buried with vessels, vestments, and writings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-maccathbad: MacCathbad Colman, famed in Irish hagiology, was bishop of Kilroot, a minor see later joined to Connor's diocese. Distinguished by the name MacCathbad, which gave Kilmackevat in County Antrim its name, he lived as a contemporary of Ailbe. His feast falls on 16 October, as it has from time immemorial. The entry is among the briefest in the slice, yet it fixes his see, his namesake place, and his feast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-maelruan:
Maelruan, founder and first abbot of Tallaght, gave a hidden Culdee scholar an honoured place and co-wrote his rule. Nothing is known of him before Tallaght's foundation in 769, on land Donnchadh, king of Leinster, gave for a church dedicated to St. Michael. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 follows Aengus the Culdee to his door.

Aengus came during Maelruan's abbacy, concealing his name and serving for a time at mere manual work. His identity emerged through help he gave a backward scholar. Maelruan sought him at once, gently reproaching him, and gave him a place of honour among them. The two saints jointly authored the Rule of the Célidhé Dé, preserved in the Royal Irish Academy's library. O'Curry describes its minute rules for prayers, preaching, conversation, confession, communion, ablutions, fasting, abstinence, and relaxation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-peter-dami:
Peter Damian, cardinal bishop of Ostia and Doctor of the Church, rose from a swineherd's hardship to reform the eleventh-century papacy. Born at Ravenna in 1007, youngest of a large noble but poor family, he was ill-treated by an elder brother until another brother, the archpriest Damian, took him away to school. Grateful, Peter added Damian's name to his own.

He became a famous teacher at Parma and Ravenna, then prior of Fonte-Avellana, where he spread the discipline and founded daughter hermitages. As a papal reformer beside Hildebrand, he attacked simony and clerical vice in the Liber Gomorrhianus and defended the validity of simoniacal ordinations. He died at Faenza on 21 February 1072, a fierce and learned monk at the heart of reform.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ronan:
Ronan is not one saint but twelve, and this hagiographical entry sorts the most celebrated Irish bearers of the name. The Martyrology of Donegal commemorates a dozen Ronans. The piece picks out the chief figures. Ronan of Ulster, brother of Carnech, died in 535. Ronan son of Berach, first abbot of Drumshallon, died in 665.

Ronan Fionn serves as patron of Lan Ronan in Iveagh, honoured on 22 May. Ronan of Iona argued for the Roman Easter against Finan of Lindisfarne, and Whitby in 664 upheld his view. Ronan of Lismore succeeded Carthage, with Munster churches in his honour. The entry offers a compact guide through a tangle of shared names, feasts, and places.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ruadhan:
Ruadhan, one of the twelve Apostles of Erin, founded the monastery of Lorrha in Tipperary. He studied under Finian of Clonard and died at Lorrha on 5 April 584. His embassy to King Dermot at Tara in 556 grew into the romance of the Cursing of Tara, though the king kept living at Tara until 564.

The entry corrects the late legend that Tara's halls stood deserted after 564, noting a feast held there in 697. Ruadhan's bell survives in the British Museum, and his feast is kept on his death's anniversary. Short as it is, the piece blends monastic foundation, royal diplomacy, and the unravelling of a famous Irish legend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-sebastian:
Sebastian, a Roman martyr, is proved by little more than his burial on the Via Appia, yet art made him famous. The chronologer of 354 records his grave there, and Ambrose states he came from Milan, where he was already venerated. Acts from the early fifth century, wrongly ascribed to Ambrose, call him an officer of the imperial guard who secretly aided Christians.

Discovered in 286, he was handed to Mauretanian archers, pierced with arrows, healed by the widow Irene, and finally clubbed to death. The entry calls these stories unhistorical and unworthy of belief. A mosaic of about 682 shows a bearded man in court dress with no arrow. Renaissance art invented the arrow-pierced youth. A basilica rose over his grave in 367.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-senan:
Senan, bishop and founder of Scattery Island, planted churches across Munster before settling on the Shannon estuary. Born at Magh Lacha near Kilrush about 488 to Erean and Comgella, his birth was prophetically announced by Patrick. He studied under Abbot Cassidan and finished under Naul at Kilmanagh in Kilkenny.

He began mission work with a church near Enniscorthy in 510 or 512, then visited Menevia, Rome, and Tours, returning to Ireland in 520. He founded churches at Inniscarra, Inisluinghe, Deer Island, Inismore, and Mutton Island. Settling at Iniscathay, or Scattery Island, he drew visits from Ciaran and Brendan. The island became an abbey and a bishopric, with Senan as first bishop. He died on 1 March 560.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ternan:
Ternan, bishop of the Picts, worked in a sixth century whose chronology no writer has reconciled. Some say Palladius consecrated him in 440. Others say he was a monk of Culross in Fife, a house founded by Serf, tutor of Kentigern. The Picts were not converted until about 570 by Columba, and Serf died in 583, so a contemporary of Serf fits the evidence best.

The Aberdeen Martyrology mentions a Gospel of Matthew belonging to Ternan, enshrined in a metal cumdach covered with silver and gold after the Irish fashion. He is commemorated on 12 June and must not be confused with Trumwine. The entry is a model of honest uncertainty, giving the reader conflicting dates rather than a smoothed life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ultan-of-a:
Ultan of Ardbraccan, abbot-bishop and scholar, fed and taught thousands of poor Irish students. Maternal uncle of Brigid, he collected a life of that great saint for his pupil Brogan Cloen of Rostuirc in Ossory. His relation to Brigid seems to demand an extraordinary longevity of one hundred and eighty years, since his death is not chronicled until 657, but Windisch explains the puzzle away.

The Irish Annals call him of the royal race of O'Connor, and he succeeded Breccan as abbot-bishop of Ardbraccan about 570. O'Clery's Irish Calendar records that he taught and fed poor students by the thousand from every part of Ireland. His writings include lives of Patrick and Brigid, and his Latin hymn to Brigid, Christus in nostra insula, entered the Solesmes chant books. He died on 4 September, probably in 657.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-wolstan:
Wolstan, Benedictine bishop of Worcester, served his diocese through the Norman Conquest without losing his see. Born at Long Itchington about 1008, he was schooled at the great monasteries of Evesham and Peterborough. He fought down youthful temptations, entered Bishop Brithege's service, and was ordained priest about 1038.

Refusing preferment, he became a novice at Worcester priory and rose to cathedral prior, edifying all by charity, holiness, and strict observance. When Aldred moved to York in 1062, two Roman cardinals who had lodged at Worcester during Lent recommended Wolstan to King Edward. Consecrated on 8 September 1062, he visited, preached, and confirmed without ceasing, rebuilding his cathedral in simple Saxon style and planting churches everywhere. He died at Worcester on 19 January 1095.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stanislaus-an:
Stanislaus and John Kozmian, two Polish brothers, fought in the insurrection of 1831 and then served Poland in exile. Stanislaus settled in England, studied its institutions, and laboured to make England and Poland know each other. John lived in France, spread Catholic ideas, and after his wife's death became a priest.

Later John went to Posen, edited the Posen Review, and became the hub of religious and political life there. Stanislaus helped him, went back to Posen, and headed the Society of Friends of Science. Both men were fervent Catholics, skilled reformers, bold politicians, and thinkers of rare power. Stanislaus, born in 1811 and dead in 1885, spent thirty years translating Shakespeare into Polish, unfinished at his death, beside Byron, Moore, Southey, Shelley, Cowper, and Campbell.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-moyla:
Stephen Moylan, an Irish-born American patriot, served Washington as aide and commissary general. Born in Ireland in 1734, he was schooled there, lived for a time in England, and travelled on the Continent before emigrating to Philadelphia. He backed the patriot cause on the Revolution's eve and rushed to join the Continental Army outside Boston in 1775.

His zeal and business acumen won John Dickinson's notice, and Dickinson placed him in the commissariat. Washington, struck by his dignity and military manner, made him an aide-de-camp in March 1776. Restless for wider action, he was chosen by Congress on Washington's recommendation in June 1776 as Commissary General of the Continental Army. Resigning that October for direct combat, he raised a troop of light dragoons and served through the war. He died at Philadelphia on 11 April 1811.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-abdon-and:
Abdon and Sennan were Persian martyrs put to death under the emperor Decius about 250, and this entry weighs what can be trusted about them. Their veneration reaches back to the third century, yet their Acts, mostly written before the ninth century, mix invention with fact about their journey to Rome and their torments.

According to those Acts, the subdeacon Quirinus buried their bodies, which were later moved under Constantine to the Pontian cemetery near Rome. A seventh-century fresco on their supposed sarcophagus shows them receiving crowns from Christ. Florence and Soissons both claim their remains, though the Bollandists judge that they rest in Rome. Their feast falls on 30 July.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-cosmas-an:
Cosmas and Damian were twin physicians of early Christian Arabia. They healed the sick without charge and died as martyrs, probably in 287. This entry follows them from their practice at Aegea on the Gulf of Iskanderun, where free treatment won them the Greek name anargyroi, the silverless ones.

Their healing brought many to the faith. Arrested in the Diocletian persecution, they survived water, fire, and the cross unharmed in legend before the sword beheaded them with their three brothers. Justinian rebuilt their church at Constantinople after a cure he credited to them. Felix IV raised their Roman church, and they remain patrons of doctors and surgeons. Their feast is 27 September.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-crispin-a:
Crispin and Crispinian were beheaded in 285 or 286. They are the patron saints of shoemakers, and this entry retells their legend with a critical eye. Romans of high birth turned missionaries in Gaul, the brothers settled at Soissons and earned their bread making shoes, as Paul had done.

Their surplus went to the poor. Hauled before Maximian, they refused threats and bribes. They endured the rack, the cutting of thongs from their flesh, and awls under their nails. Then they survived drowning with millstones round their necks, and a great fire. Beheaded at last, they left relics at Soissons and Osnabrück. Their feast, 25 October, still marks the shoemaker's calendar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-cronan:
Several Irish saints share the name Cronan, and this entry sorts them out one by one. Chief among them is Cronan Mochua, founder of Balla in Connacht. Educated at Bangor under Comgall, he died in 637 after a life crowded with reported miracles.

Next stands Cronan of Roscrea, abbot and patron, who founded his abbey about 610 and set up a famous school. Most vivid is the tale of his monk Dimma, ordered to copy the four Gospels in a single day. Dimma wrote on while the sun shone for forty days and nights, never noticing the time. Shorter notices cover other Cronans, their feast days, and the sees their foundations later joined.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-eoghan:
Five or more Irish saints answer to the name Eoghan. This entry untangles their identities and feast days. Foremost is Eoghan of Ardstraw, a Leinster man who ruled Kilnamanagh abbey for fifteen years. He settled in the Mourne valley about 576 and was consecrated first bishop of Ardstraw around 581.

St Kevin of Glendalough studied under him. His name, latinized as Eugenius, survives in Tir Eoghain, Tyrone, where he remains patron of the see of Derry. Shorter notices follow Eoghan of Cloncullen, a bishop named only in martyrologies, Eoghan the Sage, and Eoghan of Cranfield, whose identity may hide behind a scribe's slip for Ernan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-fintan:
Two Irish saints named Fintan anchor this entry. Fintan of Clonenagh, born about 524, studied under Columba of Terryglass, then settled in the Slieve Bloom Mountains in 550. Disciples gathered round his oratory, he wrote them a rule, and his austerities won him the title Father of the Irish Monks.

Fintan Munnu of Taghmon, who died in 636, founded his abbey in Wexford in 599. He is best known for defending the Irish way of fixing Easter, dissenting at the synods of Magh Lene in 630 and Magh Ailbe. His stone cross, called St Munn's, still stands in the village churchyard, and his feast is 21 October.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-mark-and-:
Mark and Marcellian, twin brothers, were martyred at Rome under Diocletian, most likely in 286. This entry draws on the ancient Acts of Sebastian, legendary in part yet very old. Jailed for their faith, the brothers were visited by their parents Tranquillinus and Martia, still pagans, who begged them to save their lives by returning to the gods.

Sebastian, himself soon to die, slipped into the prison and urged the brothers to stand firm. His words held them fast and converted their parents and friends on the spot. Brought before a judge who could not shake them, they were condemned and buried on the Via Ardeatina. Their bodies later moved to the church of Cosmas and Damian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-primus-an:
Primus and Felician suffered martyrdom about 304, in the Diocletian persecution. The Martyrologium Hieronymianum lists them under 9 June, buried at the fourteenth milestone of the Via Nomentana near Nomentum. That notice comes from a fourth-century catalogue of Roman martyrs, and the pair were evidently natives of Nomentum.

In 648 Pope Theodore moved their bones to the Roman church of San Stefano, placing them under an altar raised in their honour, where they remain. Their feast is still kept on 9 June, and the entry closes with the early sources that preserve their names.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-processus:
Processus and Martinian are Roman martyrs whose dates are unknown. The Martyrologium Hieronymianum gives their names under 2 July, and a Berne manuscript adds their burial place at the second milestone of the Via Aurelia. Old catalogues of martyr graves agree, and public veneration in Rome reaches back to the fourth century, perhaps the third.

A legend makes them keepers of the prison where Peter and Paul were held, though no one can show how that identification arose. Pope Paschal I moved their bones to a chapel in old St Peter's, and they still rest under their altar in the right transept of the present basilica. Their feast is 2 July.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-timotheus:
Timotheus and Symphorian share a feast on 22 August, and this entry pairs their stories. Timotheus came from Antioch to Rome under Pope Melchiades, preached for fifteen months, and lodged with Sylvester, later pope. The city prefect Tarquinus Perpenna jailed him, tortured him, and beheaded him in 311, and a Christian woman named Theon buried him in her garden.

Symphorian of Autun, beheaded while still young under Marcus Aurelius, walked to execution on 22 August 178 while his mother Augusta cheered him on. Bishop Euphronius later built a church and monastery over his grave. He remains patron of Autun, and his cult spread early through Frankish lands, with Tours a favoured centre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sudan:
The Vicariate Apostolic of Sudan, also called Central Africa, covered a vast region. It took in the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, Egypt south of Assuan, French land from Fezzan to the tenth parallel, parts of Adamaua and Sokoto by Lake Chad, and the Nile Province of Uganda. Gregory XVI erected it on 3 April 1846, and the Austrian emperor took it under his protection in 1851.

From 1883 to 1898 the Mahdi's rising shut the mission out of its own territory, and priests worked from Egypt until Anglo-Egyptian forces overthrew the Khalifa in September 1898. Work resumed in 1899 among southern peoples such as the Dinka, Nuer, and Jur, while the Muslim north held only immigrant Catholics. The vicariate counted 3,000 Catholics, 1,030 catechumens, and 35 priests under Vicar Apostolic Francis Xavier Geyer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tatian:
Tatian was a second-century apologist born in Assyria and trained in Greek philosophy. He travelled widely as a young man. Disgusted by pagan philosophers' greed, he scorned their teachings. Repelled by pagan grossness and drawn by Christian holiness and Scripture's simplicity, he converted about 150. In Rome he heard Justin, though Justin did not convert him. While Justin lived, Tatian stayed orthodox.

About 172 he apostatized, joined the Encratite Gnostics, and returned east. His death is unknown. Only two works survive. The Oratio ad Graecos defends Christianity, first expounding the faith against Greek philosophy, then proving its high antiquity. Its tone is bitter and denunciatory. The Diatessaron harmonizes the four Gospels into one continuous narrative. Scholars still dispute whether its original language was Syriac or Greek.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tertullian:
Tertullian, Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus, was an ecclesiastical writer of the second and third centuries. Born probably about 160 at Carthage, he was a centurion's son in proconsular service. An advocate, he knew Roman law's procedure and terms closely, though his identity with a Pandects jurist is doubtful. He knew Greek as well as Latin and wrote lost Greek works. A pagan until middle life, he shared pagan prejudices and pleasures.

His conversion came no later than 197 and may have come earlier. He embraced the faith with impetuous ardour and became a priest of Carthage. Monceaux holds his earlier writings came as a layman, putting ordination about 200. His extant works run from the apologetics of 197 to an attack on a bishop probably Pope Callistus after 218. After 206 he joined the Montanists, separated from the Church about 211 or 213, then left the Montanists and founded his own sect. Augustine later reconciled its remnant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-jordan:
Palestine's great river, dropping 3,133 feet from source to outlet, is mapped here from Hermon to the Dead Sea. Three headstreams join below Banias: the Hasbani from Hasbeya, the Leddan rising at Tell el Qadi, ancient Laïs-Dan, and the Banias, glory of what was Caesarea Philippi. Five and a half miles on, the united stream enters Lake Huleh, likely the waters of Merom.

Clear and swift between Huleh and the Lake of Tiberias, the river widens past twenty yards in places and deepens near seventeen feet. Jisr Benat Yaqub bridges Damascus to Galilee, and near Bethsaida Julias the Jordan enters the Sea of Genesareth. Biblical crossings and baptisms give the geography its sacred weight.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-monastic-:
Three limestone islands guarding Galway Bay form the setting here, above all Aran Mor, nine miles long and little more than one wide. Bluish-grey stone hard as marble covers it, bare in places and thinly soiled in others. It feeds over three thousand islanders, who add the stormy sea's harvest to arid fields and cling to their home in good times and bad.

From about 500 to 800 Aran ranked as a famed centre of sanctity and learning. Holy men came from across Ireland to study the science of the saints in this remote western school. Saint Enda's arrival crowns the story, after Firbolg remnants held the isles. Churches, cells, and scholars trace a monastic world carved from rock and prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-priory-of:
An Argyllshire priory on Loch Etive's sheltered shore gives this entry its place, one of only three Scottish houses of the Order of Vallis Caulium, or Valley of Cabbages. Duncan Mackoul, or McDougall, founded it about 1230 for Mary and John the Baptist, as with every house of the order. Its name joins Chattan, a companion of Columba, to ard, meaning promontory.

Local tradition puts a chapel on the spot centuries before the monks built priory and church, beneath Ben Cruachan's bulk. Before the dissolution of religious houses it joined the Cistercians, and at the Reformation its lands passed to a Campbell family whose descendants still own the place. Church and domestic fragments remain in use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-ring-of-f:
Gold on a new pope's finger, showing Peter fishing from a boat, is the ring described in this brief entry. Earliest mention comes in a letter of Clement IV, written in 1265 to his nephew Peter Grossi. Popes then sealed private letters with the seal of the Fisherman, while public documents bore leaden bulls attached.

From the fifteenth century the ring sealed papal Briefs, a class of official documents. Cardinal camerlengo places it on the finger of each newly elected pope, with the reigning pope's name around Peter's image. Destruction at a pope's death, a custom the entry notes, guards the seal against misuse after the pontificate ends.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-vatican:
Palace, gardens, chapels, art, and government of the Vatican fill this vast entry under sixteen heads, from introduction and architectural history to legal position. Grouping like subjects together, regardless of palace location, beats a purely topographical march, the entry argues. Territory on the Tiber's right bank between Monte Mario and Gianicolo, known to antiquity as Ager Vaticanus, marshy and low-lying, opens the tale.

Palace description, gardens, chapels, residence, art treasury, scientific institute, state halls and staircases, administrative, juridical, and hygienic boards, policing, business centre, and polyglot press follow in turn. For readers seeking the Vatican whole, it is the encyclopedia's grandest single survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thegan:
Chronicler of Louis the Pious, Thegan, who died about 850, is a shadowy figure sketched here from letters and verses. Certainty extends only to his post as assistant Bishop of Trier and his warm friendship with Walafrid Strabo. Whether he matches Theganbert, provost of Saint Cassius at Bonn who enshrined Chrysanthus and Daria at Münstereifel, cannot be positively settled.

His Vita Ludovici imperatoris, an unsatisfactory narrative in scanty annals, begins with Arnulf of Metz, traces Louis's brothers' vicissitudes, and details the reign from 814 to 835. Later narrative likely comes from another hand, and Strabo supplied an introduction. Partisan throughout, it exalts Louis while harshly judging Lothair and bishops, above all Ebo of Reims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-canon-:
Thomas Flanagan, an English priest and historian of Irish descent, was born in 1814 and died at Kidderminster in 1865. Educated at Sedgley Park School, he entered Oscott at eighteen and was ordained in 1842, becoming one of the first students of the new college buildings. President Wiseman kept him on as professor, where he met many Oxford converts.

Flanagan's bent was historical: in 1847 he published a small manual of British and Irish history packed with statistical tables, and served as prefect of studies until 1850. He then became vice-president and president of Sedgley Park School and one of the first canons of the Birmingham diocese. His methodical mind suited the careful, table-driven history he favoured.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-dongan:
Thomas Dongan, second Earl of Limerick, was born in County Kildare in 1634 and died in London in 1715. A Stuart loyalist, he served in an Irish regiment under Turenne in France, rising to colonel, then returned to England and held the governorship of Tangiers. In 1682 the Duke of York chose him to govern New York, then bankrupt and restless.

Dongan called the province's first representative assembly in October 1683, which passed a Charter of Liberties giving the colony a share in lawmaking. He set up a post office in 1685, granted charters to New York and Albany in 1686, and planned a Jesuit college in the city. His charters shaped New York government for generations, the city's lasting 135 years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-dorman:
Thomas Dorman, an English theologian who died at Tournai in the 1570s, gave up fellowship and fortune rather than conform to the new religion. Born at Berkhamstead, he studied at Winchester and New College, Oxford, where Thomas Harding took an interest in him. Under Mary he became a fellow of All Souls and took a civil law degree in 1558.

After Elizabeth's accession he left England for Antwerp and Louvain, took a doctorate at Douai, and crossed pens with the Anglican divines Jewel and Nowell. In 1569 he joined Allen's new English College at Douai, helping it with his service and his money. He died holding a benefice at Tournai, a scholar in exile.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-o-haga:
Thomas O'Hagan, first Baron of Tullyhogue, was born at Belfast in 1812 and died in 1885. Called to the Irish bar in 1836, he edited the Newry Examiner from 1838 to 1841 and won distinction defending Charles Gavan Duffy in 1842. He took silk in 1849, became a bencher of King's Inn in 1859, and served as Solicitor General for Ireland in 1860 and Attorney General the next year.

He sat as member for Tralee from 1863 to 1865, then became a judge of Common Pleas. In 1868 he became Lord Chancellor of Ireland, the first Catholic to hold the office since James II's reign. Created Baron of Tullyhogue in 1870, he served again as chancellor under Gladstone from 1880 until resigning in November 1881.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-titian:
Titian, or Tiziano Vecelli, was the greatest of Venetian painters, born at Pieve di Cadore and dying at Venice in 1577. He claimed in 1571 to be over ninety-five, which would set his birth in 1477, but modern study puts it about 1487, making him between eighty-five and ninety at death. That younger age fits the fresh power of his late works far better.

Brought to Venice at ten, he learned from the mosaicist Sebastiano Zuccato, then entered the aged Giovanni Bellini's studio and formed a close friendship with Giorgione. He soon outshone them in colour and in the joy of life his pictures breathe. His art joined calm, harmony and serenity with a magic of colouring that led some to call him the most complete of all painters. His early masterpieces include Sacred and Profane Love and the Three Ages, poems in paint.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tommaso-de-vi:
Tommaso de Vio, called Cajetan, was a Dominican cardinal, philosopher, theologian and biblical scholar, born at Gaeta in 1469 and dying at Rome in 1534. Baptized Giacomo, he entered the Dominicans before sixteen against his parents' will, and amazed teachers at Naples, Bologna and Padua. He took the chair of metaphysics at Padua, fought Scotists and Averroists, and wrote De Ente et Essentia, counted his most subtle work.

At Ferrara in 1494 he defended theses before Pico della Mirandola with such success that students carried him in triumph to the master general. Made master of sacred theology, he expounded Thomas's Summa at Brescia and Pavia. As papal legate he met Luther in 1518, and Protestants admit his moderation, though neither pleading nor learning won the monk's submission. Later he advised Clement VII and was seized in the sack of Rome in 1527.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-torlogh-o-car:
Torlogh O'Carolan, usually called the last of the Irish bards, was born in County Meath in 1670 and died at Ballyfarnon in 1737. Smallpox blinded him in youth. Descended from an old family, he won fame as a harper, and his career marks the merging of the old Gaelic roles of bard and harper into one.

He composed probably over two hundred poems, lively and Pindaric in manner, mostly for patrons and ladies of the old county families who welcomed him as a guest. His verses twist their metre to fit his airs, and few fall into regular stanzas. His Ode to Whiskey ranks among the finest drinking songs in any tongue, and Moore borrowed many of his planxties, or tunes, for his Melodies. His harp survives at Clonalis, Roscommon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trajan:
Trajan, emperor of Rome from 98 to 117, was born at Italica in Spain in 53 and adopted by Nerva in 97. Stately and majestic in bearing, with a powerful will and a chivalrous kindness, he ranks among the ablest emperors. He won wide lands for the empire and planted civilization in the provinces by founding towns.

He secured the Rhine frontier and built much of the boundary wall from Danube to Rhine. He fought two Dacian wars in 101 to 102 and 105 to 107, turning Decebalus's kingdom into a province. Syria's governor won Arabia Petraea, and Trajan himself entered Armenia in the Parthian war of 114 to 117. At home he enlarged Ancona's harbour, built roads and harbours, and raised Trajan's Forum in Rome, whose column still tells his Dacian victories.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tucuman:
A diocese, suffragan to Buenos Aires, erected from Salta on 15 February 1897, covering the province of Tucumán in north-west Argentina across 8,926 square miles. Its first and present bishop is Pablo Padilla y Barcena, born at Jujuy in 1848, transferred from Salta in January 1898.

The episcopal city, founded in 1565 by Diego de Villaruel, gained a Jesuit college in 1586 and replaced Santiago del Estero as provincial capital in 1680. Belgrano's Argentines defeated the Spanish there in 1812, and Independence Hall, where delegates proclaimed the Río de la Plata provinces free on 9 July 1816, remains its most notable monument.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-turkestan:
A survey of Central Asia in its Chinese and Russian divisions, opening with the empire of Djagatai, second son of Jenghiz Khan, who died in 1227. His lands stretched from Mávará-un-Nahr between the Syr Daria and the Amu Daria to Ferghana, Badakhshan and Chinese Turkestan. His capital was Almaliq in the Ili Valley.

In the fourteenth century the empire split into Transoxiana and Moghulistan. In 1759 the Emperor K'ien Lung subjugated the lands north and south of the T'ienshan, appointing a military governor in 1762. After rebellion and treaty strife with Russia, settled at St. Petersburg in 1881, the territory was organized in 1878 as Sin-Kiang, the New Dominion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Perpignan's university was founded on 20 March 1349 by Peter IV of Aragon, who had conquered the town in 1344 and reunited the Kingdom of Majorca to his lands. Perpignan had been that kingdom's capital, and the new university for civil and canon law and other arts and sciences compensated the city for its lost power. The charter praised the deep learning of Perpignan's professors.

The antipope Clement VII confirmed the foundation by a bull of 28 November 1379, and the university later called him its father and founder. In 1381 John I, son of Peter IV, let the city build the university near the royal castle. The entry follows the school's spread of learning in Perpignan, its faculties, and its later fortunes under French rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valerian:
Valerian, Publius Aurelius Licinius Valerianus, ruled as Roman emperor from 253 to 260. Of distinguished family, he had already held several offices when the army proclaimed him emperor at Rhaetia in 253. Weak and irresolute, his talents fell short of the age's troubles, and his son and co-ruler Gallienus likewise lacked force. Christian tradition blames him for the persecution under Decius, though kindly disposed to Christians at first.

Driven by a hostile court party led by the general Macrianus, who sought gain from internal strife, Valerian acted. He issued a rescript in 257, in mild language, barring Christians from assemblies and from entering their burial catacombs. Later edicts struck harder at clergy and property. The entry follows his Persian campaign, his capture, and his death in captivity, a tragic end for an emperor of good will.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-good:
John Goodman was a priest and martyr born in the Diocese of Bangor, Wales, in 1590, who died in 1642. Schooled at Oxford and ordained a Protestant minister, he abandoned heresy and crossed to Paris, where Mr Richard Ireland received him into the church. Admitted to Douai College on 12 February 1621, he studied there until 1624, when he moved to St Omer hoping to join the Society of Jesus.

Seeing that path was not his vocation, he took ordination as a secular priest and left for the English mission. He worked with unremitting zeal for years, was twice seized and twice freed. A prisoner once more in 1642, he was tried and condemned to death, but the queen's intercession won a reprieve. When that mercy angered Parliament, Goodman begged that he might be sacrificed to calm popular feeling. Instead he was left to languish in Newgate, where hardship ended his life on Good Friday 1642.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-william-d:
William Dean was a Yorkshire priest executed at Mile End, London, in August 1588, the year of the Spanish Armada. He studied at Reims and was ordained at Soissons in December 1581, together with martyrs George Haydock and Robert Nutter, on the very day news of Campion's death reached the college. His first Mass followed in January, and he left for England at once.

Banished with other priests in 1585 and put ashore in Normandy under threat of death if he returned, he promptly resumed his work in England. Rearrested, he was condemned for his priesthood in August 1588 and was the first to suffer on new gallows at Mile End, erected, it was said, at Leicester's prompting. With him suffered layman Henry Webley, who had sheltered him. At his death Dean tried to address the crowd, but men in the cart stopped his mouth violently.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-william-f:
William Freeman was a priest executed at Warwick in August 1595. Born at Manthorp near York about 1558, he took his degree at Magdalen College, Oxford, in 1581 and lived some years in London. Witnessing the martyrdom of Edward Stransham in 1586 moved him deeply. He left England and was ordained at Reims in 1587.

Returning in 1589, he worked for six years on the Warwickshire borders, in a circle that included contemporaries and friends of Shakespeare. In January 1595 a commission searched the Stratford house where he tutored a boy, and Freeman was arrested. He spent seven months in prison, denied his priesthood, yet refused friendly offers of escape, not wishing to lose his chance of martyrdom. Betrayed by a fellow prisoner, he was sentenced as a seminary priest and suffered a traitor's death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-edw:
Edward Morgan was a Welsh priest executed at Tyburn in April 1642. Born at Bettisfield in Flintshire, he studied at St-Omer and at the English colleges in Rome, Valladolid. Madrid, briefly became a Jesuit novice in 1609, and was ordained at Salamanca before being sent to England in 1621.

He laboured in his native country and was imprisoned in Flintshire in 1629 for refusing the oath of allegiance. About 1632 the Star Chamber condemned him to have his ears nailed to the pillory for accusing certain judges of treason. He was then held in the Fleet Prison in London for years. Condemned at the Old Bailey on St George's Day 1642 for being a priest, he was executed three days later, in a final scene recorded, apparently, by an eyewitness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vespasian:
Vespasian, Titus Flavius Vespasianus, was the Roman emperor who founded the Flavian dynasty, born at Reate in AD 9 and dying there in 79. His father was a prosperous tax collector and moneylender, his mother's brother a senator. The young man entered public service, serving as quaestor in the Levant, commanding the Second Legion in southern Britain, and reaching consular rank in 51.

A poor courtier who reportedly fell asleep while Nero recited his own poems in Greece. He was nevertheless chosen to lead the war against the Jews after brutal governors, above all Gessius Florus, drove them to revolt.
