He derived the equations needed to allow for turning solar panels. A step by step procedure follows from those equations. Designers of the modular station could then size their control systems.
new-version-of-les-contes-d-hoffmann-the:
Jacques Offenbach's opera Les Contes d'Hoffmann appears here in a new version, with a book by Jules Barbier. Charles Alfred Byrne made the new English version. Steinway and Sons issued it in New York in 1907. The opera was first given in America at the Manhattan Opera House, under Oscar Hammerstein.

The title page promises an original and novel first act, with other large changes. Both English and French texts are printed in this edition, errors and all, per a transcriber's note. The cast list opens with Hoffmann himself. Counselor Lindorf, Coppelius, and Dapertutto stand among his foes. Singers and readers could follow the whole opera in two tongues.
nobody-s-man:
E. Phillips Oppenheim published Nobody's Man in 1921, a tale of politics and rest. Andrew Tallente, a great statesman, steps off a quaint little train in a Devonshire hamlet among hills. A tall, ungainly man waits on the flower decked platform with an unpleasant smile. The meeting, Tallente sees at once, is no accident.

Miller greets him with a challenge about statesmen needing to leave the treadmill. Oppenheim sets the two men side by side in sharp contrast. Tallente bears heritage, education, and natural culture in his manner. Miller, a postman's son from a small Scotch town, mimics social gifts he lacks. Old rivalry walks off the platform with them.
note-on-the-resemblances-and-differences:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote this note on the brains of men and apes for Charles Darwin's Descent of Man. It stands there at the end of chapter seven, closing part one. Huxley takes up a fight then about fifteen years old. The question was how far ape and human brains truly differ in structure.

Some had claimed, again and again, that all ape brains lack certain parts. The parts named were the posterior lobes, the posterior cornu, and the hippocampus minor. Those parts are plain in man, they said, and missing in apes. Huxley answers that all three are as well developed in apes as in men. All primates but lemurs, he says, share them.
noto-an-unexplored-corner-of-japan:
Percival Lowell wrote Noto as an account of a corner of Japan he calls unexplored. A letter to Basil Hall Chamberlain opens the book. Lowell asks Chamberlain to be his best man in the matter before the world. The fancy took me to go to Noto, he begins, calling it love at first sight on a Tokyo map.

Contents trace the road: the Usui Pass, Zenkoji, and a new cornice road. The Etchiu delta, the Arayama Pass, and an inland sea follow. Snow, a genial inkyo, a passport, and a basha carriage all get chapters. Down the Tenriu river and to the sea close the trip. Lowell travels for the love of the place.
observations-of-a-retired-veteran:
Henry C. Tinsley, editor of the Vindicator at Staunton, Virginia, wrote his Observations of a Retired Veteran under the pen name P. Boyzy. An introduction explains that the essays ran at intervals over years in that weekly paper. Tinsley had laid down his arms at the close of the War between the States, it says.

The essays mix winning humor with pathos, the introduction claims. Shrewd, homely wit joins a deep knowledge of the human heart. Political journalism took most of Tinsley's strength until his last illness. These pieces were his outlet for a courageous, hopeful philosophy. To cover pain with a jest, and preach love without cant, was his gospel.
occasional-thoughts-in-reference-to-a-ve:
Damaris, Lady Masham, wrote this discourse on Christian life. It was printed in London in 1705. The preface says the papers waited two years before publication. Friends urged her to share them for wider use. The subject is how people learn virtue.

Masham argues that good principles need early habits. Neither one alone can form a good life, she says. She blames loose education for much vice and sadness. Parents must teach with steady care, she urges. The work links family training to happiness here and hereafter. Her calm tone suits the private, thoughtful form of the work.
on-being-human:
Woodrow Wilson wrote this literary essay before his presidency. It first appeared in the Atlantic Monthly in 1897. Wilson held doctoral and honorary degrees at that time. The essay is divided into six numbered parts. It asks what makes a book truly worth reading.

Wilson quotes Bagehot on the knack of human style. He says readers seek companionship, not mere instruction. Good books widen the reader's world of men and affairs. He warns against tearing texts apart for grammar drills. Leave the text whole, he urges, and read it alive. The essay shows Wilson as a thoughtful man of letters.
on-some-fossil-remains-of-man:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote this essay on early human fossils. He studies skulls from Engis and the Neanderthal valley. Sir Charles Lyell had checked their geology with care. The Engis skull lay with mammoth and rhinoceros bones. That link gave it very great age, Huxley argues.

Huxley asks if fossils bridge the gap between man and apes. He finds man a well defined group among primates. No living form links man to the next family, he says. Fossils might narrow that gap, but evidence stays thin. It shows Victorian science weighing human antiquity.
one-young-man:
John Ernest Hodder-Williams edited this true war story in 1917. Hodder and Stoughton published it in London that year. The subtitle calls it the simple, true story of a clerk. He enlisted in 1914 and fought on the Western Front. He served nearly two years before the Somme.

The clerk was severely wounded at the Battle of the Somme. He was then on his way back to his desk. The book is dedicated to Sir George Williams. Williams founded the Y.M.C.A. and was the editor's uncle. Chapter one introduces the young man to readers. Chapter two follows him as he joins the army.
our-friend-the-charlatan:
George Gissing's novel Our Friend the Charlatan opens at Alverholme Vicarage, where the Reverend Philip Lashmar waits for a breakfast that is never served to time. Lashmar is in his sixty-seventh year: thin, round-shouldered, and bearded like Darwin. The resemblance pleases him. He lives in ceaseless mild indignation against the age. A newspaper article as depressing as he could have wished privately pleases him too.

His troubles are also financial. The income of his living shrinks with the agricultural depression, his glebe yields less each year, and his small private fortune is nearly spent on charities he refuses to stint. Gissing, the great novelist of genteel poverty, builds the book on such a man: broad-minded in private, contemptuous in public, and worried over everything.
our-mr-wrenn-the-romantic-adventures-of-:
Sinclair Lewis's first novel, Our Mr. Wrenn, appeared in 1914 with the subtitle The Romantic Adventures of a Gentle Man. Its chapter titles track the hero's escape from loneliness. He walks with Miss Theresa, then starts for the Land of Elsewhere. He finds quaint English flavor and encounters the intellectuals. He goes a-gipsying, buys an orange tie, and at last discovers America.

Chapter one explains the loneliness. Mr. Wrenn trots down Fourteenth Street past a dozen movie shows. He wants only the ticket-taker's cordial nod at the Nickelorion. His furnished room is empty, and his daytime job is tedious. Lewis would later anatomize American small towns and Babbitts; here, gently, he begins with one clerk's hunger to be noticed.
paine-rights-of-man:
Thomas Paine published Rights of Man in two parts, 1791 and 1792, as his answer to Edmund Burke's attack on the French Revolution. Paine had already stirred America with Common Sense. Now he defended the revolution in France and the natural rights of ordinary people.

Part one argues that rights belong to all men by nature, and that governments rest on the people's consent alone. Part two goes further, sketching tax cuts, old-age pensions, and aid for the poor, all paid for by trimming courts and armies. The book sold hugely among working readers and rattled the British state. Paine was tried for sedition in his absence.
paris-war-days-diary-of-an-american: Charles Inman Barnard's Paris War Days is the diary of an American. Barnard was the New York Tribune's Paris correspondent. Harvard gave him his law degree, and France made him a Knight of the Legion of Honor. He dedicated the diary to Ogden Mills Reid. It memorializes Reid's father Whitelaw, the Tribune's late editor. The hosted sample shows the title pages and illustrations list only. Ambassador Herrick fronts it. A wrecked German shop and the American Ambulance Hospital appear. No diary entry itself appears in the sample.
paula-the-waldensian:
Eva Lecomte wrote Paula the Waldensian for young readers, and this English version was adapted and translated from a Spanish one. Lecomte lived at Villar-Pellice in France, among the hills of the Waldensian valleys. Her preface introduces Paula as a simple country girl, tender-hearted and forgetful of self, who loved God with all her heart.

The Waldensians were an old Alpine people who kept their faith through centuries of persecution. Paula's story shows that faith in a young life. Lecomte compares her to a clear brook slipping between flowered banks, and says she conquered by love.
peeps-at-many-lands-japan: A hosted sample showing only the front matter of Peeps at Many Lands: Japan, the title page and contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names John Finnemore as author and Ella Du Cane as the artist of twelve full-page colour illustrations. The contents cover the land of the rising sun, boys and girls in Japan, life in the house, a Japanese day. Games follow, and the feast of dolls and the feast of flags.
personal-experience-of-a-physician: Hosted here, the sample shows only the front matter of Personal Experience of a Physician, the title page and contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names John Ellis, M.D., and promises an appeal to the medical and clerical professions, with an appendix reviewing Christ and the temperance question. The contents move from his personal medical experience to chapters urging physicians to examine homoeopathy, warning of dangers in allopathic treatment, and turning to his religious experience.
peter-pan:
J. M. Barrie's Peter Pan, in the Peter and Wendy text of 1911, begins with a law of childhood: all children, except one, grow up. Wendy Darling learns at two years old, over a flower given to her mother, that she must grow up too. Two, Barrie says, is the beginning of the end.

The contents promise Peter breaking through, the shadow, the flight, and the island come true. In Neverland wait the mermaids' lagoon, the home under the ground, and Captain Hook's pirate ship. The final chapter, When Wendy Grew Up, gives the story its famous ache: Peter alone stays a child.
pierre-and-jean:
Guy de Maupassant's novel Pierre and Jean, read here in Clara Bell's English translation, follows two brothers in the Roland family. It opens on a fishing party at sea, where old Roland grumbles over his line while his wife dozes beside their guest, Madame Rosemilly.

Pierre and Jean sit to port and starboard, each holding a line twisted round his finger, laughing at their father's temper. That easy family scene sets up the contrast between the brothers that drives the book. Maupassant builds the story in nine chapters, watching how money, suspicion, and family feeling can split two sons of the same house.
poems-by-walt-whitman:
Walt Whitman's poems reach English readers here in a selection made and edited by William Michael Rossetti, the Pre-Raphaelite critic who championed Whitman in Britain. Rossetti's letter to William Bell Scott explains his debt: Scott gave him the original quarto Leaves of Grass soon after its first appearance in 1855. When few Britons had read it and most who did found only matter for ridicule. Rossetti read eagerly and found power beyond any praise.

Quotations from Michelangelo, Swedenborg, Carlyle, and Robespierre stand at the front as a guard of honor for a poet England had mocked. The selection itself draws on Leaves of Grass, giving British readers a manageable Whitman, chosen by one of his earliest and most serious admirers. The edition marks the moment American poetry forced its way into English respect.
quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-madame:
Quotes and Images from the Memoirs of Madame de Montespan selects from the recollections of Louis XIV's famous mistress, set in alphabetical order by David Widger. Montespan writes of the court that made and unmade her, armed, as one entry says, with beauty and sarcasm.

The death-in-life of a convent opens the extracts. Ambition puts a thick bandage over the eyes. Things are always sold at a loss when they must be sold at a set moment. A woman happy with a man who takes her husband's place sketches her own story. "Hate me, but fear me" sums up the pride that runs through the selection.
raffles-further-adventures-of-the-amateu:
Raffles: Further Adventures of the Amateur Cracksman, by E. W. Hornung, continues the tales of the gentleman thief, narrated by his friend and accomplice. The contents list eight stories, among them No Sinecure, A Jubilee Present, The Fate of Faustina, To Catch a Thief, and The Knees of the Gods.

No Sinecure opens with a telegram that reached the narrator in a Holloway attic on May 11, 1897, pointing him to a Daily Mail advertisement. The sender is his rich relative, a knighted specialist who had lately cast him off as a disgrace. The advertisement seeks a male nurse and constant attendant for an elderly gentleman, offering a liberal salary to a university or public-school man.
redburn-his-first-voyage-being-the-sailo:
Herman Melville cast this sea tale as the confessions of Wellingborough Redburn, a son of a gentleman in the merchant navy. Chapter headings tell the story before it starts: his taste for the sea was born and bred in him. He leaves home, sells his fowling piece, and buys his sea wardrobe in town.

Aboard ship he is set to cleaning the pig-pen and slushing the topmast, joins the larboard watch, and turns sea-sick and forlorn. Shipmates such as Jackson, the cook, and the steward fill his days, with a narrow escape and fog work as bell-toller. Ireland comes in sight at last, then Liverpool, its docks, emigrant ships, and dead-house.
reproduction-of-copyrighted-works-by-edu:
Circular 21 of the United States Copyright Office gives basic facts on copying copyrighted works in schools and libraries. The Office states at the start that it cannot give legal advice or opinions on what is allowed. What it offers instead is the text of the law and the record behind it.

The booklet's contents list the exclusive rights section and the fair use section of the copyright law, each with excerpts from the House report. A statement of intent on classroom copying follows. The circular also points readers to the Register's 1983 report on library reproduction, with its seven appendixes of hearings and comments.
rhymes-of-a-red-cross-man:
Robert W. Service, the British-born Canadian poet of The Spell of the Yukon, turned to war in these rhymes, transcribed from a New York edition of 1916. He dedicates the book to the memory of his brother, Lieutenant Albert Service of the Canadian Infantry. Albert Service was killed in action in France in August 1916.

The contents name The Call, The Fool, and The Volunteer first, then The Convalescent and The Man from Athabaska. The Red Retreat, The Haggis of Private McPhee, and The Odyssey of 'Erbert 'Iggins mix battle with barrack humour. A Song of the Sandbags, On the Wire, and Bill's Grave close the list shown, in verse close to the men's own speech.
ridgeway-an-historical-romance-of-the-fe:
Scian Dubh published this historical romance of the Fenian invasion of Canada in 1868, under a motto from Moore: on our side is virtue and Erin. Its introduction is a fiery brief for Irish nationality. Seven hundred years of famine, fire, and sword under English rule, it says, tested the children of Ireland as no other people were tested.

Confiscation, exile, and death were their portion, the introduction argues, yet the crimson ore of their patriotism still flashes. The heart of Brien of the Cow Tax beats in them still, yearning for another Clontarf. Against that background the romance treats the Fenian raid and the battle ground at Ridgeway.
robert-moffat-the-missionary-hero-of-kur:
David J. Deane wrote this life of Robert Moffat, the missionary hero of Kuruman, here in a fifth edition and twenty-fifth thousand from Fleming H. Revell. Deane had also written lives of John Wicliffe and Martin Luther. His preface argues that Moffat's record can never lose interest while noble deeds still stir the heart.

The preface promises dangers faced and overcome: the king of beasts on the African plain, and time spent with chiefs whose warriors' spears had slain thousands. Sickness, hunger, thirst, and years of disappointment stand in the story too. Deane hopes Moffat's strong faith and quiet courage will stir readers, and the young above all, to perseverance.
romano-lavo-lil-word-book-of-the-romany-:
George Borrow compiled this word-book of the Romany, or English Gypsy language, in an edition from John Murray of London dated 1905. Its title promises specimens of Gypsy poetry and an account of certain gypsyries, or places Gypsies inhabit. Things relating to Gypsy life in England fill out the book's scope.

A verse at the front asks, in Romany and then in English, can you speak the Roman tongue and play the fiddle. Borrow states that the vocabulary had existed in manuscript for many years. He had made such word-lists in several countries: his Spanish Gypsy vocabulary appeared in 1841, and a Transylvanian one, made at Kolosvár in 1844, stayed unpublished.
satan:
Lewis Sperry Chafer published Satan in 1909, with a short foreword by C. I. Scofield. Twelve chapters trace a single figure across time. Early chapters cover Satan's career, past ages, and the present age. Later chapters turn to his followers, his aims and tactics, and a coming figure called the Man of Sin.

The closing chapters warn of a grave omission and present-day schemes, then address where believers stand now and how they prevail. In the foreword Scofield urges ministers and church workers in particular to take up the book. He argues that grasping Satan's real power is central to grasping the present age and the struggle each believer faces. The foreword also praises the book as firmly grounded in scripture.
schnitzler-bertha-garlan:
A respectable young widow feels the pull of the bohemian life, and the lover, she left behind. Schnitzler's Bertha Garlan, from 1901 and presented here in English, follows that temptation through a few charged days. A trip to Vienna reopens everything Bertha Garlan thought she had settled in her provincial widowhood.

Schnitzler dissects her inner life with his famous psychological precision, letting thoughts ripple under polite surfaces. Music, memory, and erotic longing mix in her private reckoning. The novella was pioneering work in stream-of-consciousness fiction, before the method had a name. Its portrait of desire against duty stays subtle to the last page. Few writers have entered a woman's daydream with such tact and accuracy.
science-in-the-kitchen-a-scientific-trea:
Mrs. E. E. Kellogg published Science in the Kitchen in 1893, drawing on her work running two cookery schools. She led the Sanitarium school at Battle Creek and the Bay View Assembly school, and she chaired Michigan's food work for the World's Fair. Her book joins food science to daily practice in the kitchen.

Kellogg explains what food substances are and how they act in the body, then turns those lessons into rules for healthful cooking. Many original recipes show the rules at work in dishes she calls tasty and wholesome. Her preface notes that schools of cookery were spreading across the United States, yet most taught clever dish making and skipped the science of diet. Her own Battle Creek classes, tied to an experimental kitchen, ran nearly all year.
selected-official-documents-of-the-south:
Hugh Williams and Frederick Charles Hicks, both of the Library of Congress, edited this set of state papers from the South African Republic and Great Britain. The editors aimed to show, through records, the causes of the war then gripping South Africa. A preface notes keen American interest in the fight.

Williams and Hicks note that the papers sat buried in huge library sources most readers could never reach. They chose a full, linked series while cutting bulk where they could. Students and citizens could thus read the claims, notes, and terms on both sides and judge the quarrel from the record itself.
semmelweis-open-letters-1861-german:
Ignaz Semmelweis fought for hand disinfection in two open letters printed in German in 1861. He addressed them to Hofrath Siebold and Hofrath Scanzoni, two leading doctors who doubted him. Semmelweis had shown that chlorine hand washing cut childbed fever deaths sharply. Vienna's clinics had resisted his finding for years.

The letters lay out his data and his fury in full. They form the primary record of his fight, in his own words. No public domain English translation exists, so the German text stands as a documentary edition. Readers with German meet the scandal of his rejection directly. Medicine now honors what his peers refused.
sermons-to-the-natural-man:
William G. T. Shedd published these sermons with Charles Scribner in New York in 1871. Shedd had written on Christian doctrine, preaching, and the philosophy of history. A solemn preface says the title states the aim: the purpose is to lay open the natural heart.

Shedd holds that law must cut before the gospel can heal, and that his age errs toward softness, not severity. He preaches sin in depth so conscience wakes to its own state. Redemption gets less space than diagnosis here, by design: Shedd saw waking sinners as the preacher's first and hardest present task.
she-and-allan:
H. Rider Haggard first published this African adventure in 1921, joining his immortal queen, called She, with hunter Allan Quatermain. A note in Quatermain's name fronts the tale. Sixteen chapters follow, their heads given as bare numbers in this copy's contents.

Haggard had built both figures across earlier books: the white queen who rules a lost realm, and the plain hunter who tells the tale. Their meeting promises magic, peril, and old African lore. Readers who know either line of tales get a crossing of paths that fans of Haggard had long wished to see staged in full.
showell-s-dictionary-of-birmingham-a-his:
Thos. T. Harman compiled this alphabetical history and guide to Birmingham for the proprietors Walter Showell and Sons. Harman had written a local book of dates and notes before this larger work. Cornish Brothers published it in New Street, with printing by J. G. Hammond and Company.

Thousands of dates and references cover churches, chapels, clubs, schools, parks, theatres, and halls. Friendly societies, charities, colleges, trades, and factories all find entries. Worthy townsmen, population counts, rates, and marks of growth round out the record. Local readers get a full civic portrait of a great factory town in one thick reference.
slippy-mcgee-sometimes-known-as-the-butt: Marie Conway Oemler wrote Slippy McGee, Sometimes Known as the Butterfly Man, printed by the Century Co. at New York. The copyright is 1917, and the title page lists new printings through February 1920. Oemler gives the book to Elizabeth and Alan Oemler. The contents open in Appleboro, then bring Slippy McGee to town, meet the neighbors, and pass under the head Underwings before Kerry enters.
some-mooted-questions-in-reinforced-conc:
Edward Godfrey, a member of the American Society of Civil Engineers, attacks set rules of his trade in Some Mooted Questions in Reinforced Concrete Design. The paper, No. 1169 in the society's Transactions, drew printed replies from seventeen named men, Joseph Wright, S. Bent Russell, and J. R. Worcester among them. Godfrey closes the list by answering his critics in turn.

Godfrey opens with the old art of blood-letting. Doctors once had firm rules for when and where to bleed a sick man, and those rules are now dropped. If they were sound, he asks, why were they left behind? His aim is to show that concrete men hold rules no more sound. Sharp attack, he argues, does good when it kills error, and no reform was ever won without it.
statesman:
Plato's Statesman comes in Benjamin Jowett's English. A first note gives a survey of its thought. Later talks of Plato join two themes in one, the note marks. The Sophist and Statesman show that habit most of all. Their talk serves in part as a show of method. Likenesses come from far off to light the main theme. Stage power falls in the later work as well.

The persons in such talks wake little care. Side paths tend to bury the main claim. The sure Socrates stands withdrawn from view. Plato now fights the sophistry of the schools. That sophistry is making reason itself unworkable. It drives him back toward common sense in his thought. A stress on right sorting marks the late work. Words must not stand in the place of things. Yet the bright ideal is not snuffed out. He still seeks a city of wise kings.
stories-by-foreign-authors-italian:
Italian, in the Stories by Foreign Authors set, was printed at New York in 1898. It holds two tales by Edmondo de Amicis, A Great Day and College Friends. Fogazzaro's Pereat Rochus and D'Annunzio's San Pantaleone follow. Castelnuovo's It Snows closes the set. Edith Wharton made the English version of A Great Day.

That tale visits a Catholic family near Florence as the Italian army readies its march on Rome. The parents and their grown daughters dread the move and call it the wrong way to take the city, recalling how things stood in forty-eight. Faith, family feeling, and a nation being remade press on each other through the set.
stories-by-foreign-authors-polish-greek-:
One mixed set in Stories by Foreign Authors joins five tales. It holds Sienkiewicz's Lighthouse Keeper of Aspinwall and Bikelas's Plain Sister. Maeterlinck's Massacre of the Innocents and Lemonnier's Saint Nicholas Eve follow. Jokai's In Love with the Czarina closes the set.

Sienkiewicz's tale, in Jeremiah Curtin's English version, starts when the lighthouse keeper at Aspinwall, near Panama, vanishes in a storm, his boat gone from its rocky niche. The post must be filled fast, since ships bound between New York and Panama thread sandbars and fog by that light. Four nations' storytellers share the small volume.
stories-by-foreign-authors-russian:
Russian, in the Stories by Foreign Authors set, printed at New York in 1898, holds Mumu by Ivan Turgenev, The Shot by Alexander Poushkin, St. John's Eve by Nikolai Vasilievitch Gogol, and An Old Acquaintance by Lyof N. Tolstoi. Constance Garnett made the English version of Mumu.

Turgenev's tale opens in a gray Moscow house where a widow keeps a large household of serfs. Among them stands Gerasim, a porter of huge build, deaf and dumb from birth, brought from his village hut and famed for paying his dues on time. Duels, folk terror, and old soldiers fill out a short shelf of Russian masters.
stories-by-foreign-authors-scandinavian:
Scandinavian, in the Stories by Foreign Authors set, holds tales by six writers. Bjornson gives The Father and The Railroad and the Churchyard. Aho, Goldschmidt, Kielland, and Bremer complete the set. R. B. Anderson made the English version of The Father.

Bjornson's opening tale names Thord Overaas. He is the richest and most weighty man of his parish. He comes to the priest's study to have his son baptized. He names the boy Finn, after his father. Plain farms, parish pride, and family duty give these northern tales their quiet force.
stories-of-red-hanrahan:
W. B. Yeats wrote the Stories of Red Hanrahan, tales of a wandering Irish poet and hedge schoolmaster. The contents list Red Hanrahan, The Twisting of the Rope, Hanrahan and Cathleen the Daughter of Houlihan, Red Hanrahan's Curse, Hanrahan's Vision, and The Death of Hanrahan.

Yeats thanks Lady Gregory, who helped him rewrite the tales in the fine country speech of Kiltartan, close to how the people who remember Hanrahan still talk. The first tale opens on Samhain Eve in a barn, where village men sit by the fire and Hanrahan comes in with a message in hand. Magic, music, and longing follow him on the road.
study-of-a-woman:
Honore de Balzac's Study of a Woman, in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's English version, is dedicated to the Marquis Jean-Charles di Negro. The tale takes as its subject the Marquise de Listomere, a young woman raised in the spirit of the Restoration.

Balzac sketches her as a living image of her day. She fasts and takes the sacrament. She goes to balls and operas in fine dress. She holds Church and world together under one motto. That motto is legality. Married seven years to a deputy who waits for a peerage, she stays strictly virtuous, from policy and perhaps from inclination. Balzac warns that women of thirty-six often find they have been dupes of social laws, and watches for her moment of change.
sweet-cicely-or-josiah-allen-as-a-politi:
Marietta Holley, writing as Josiah Allen's Wife, published Sweet Cicely, or Josiah Allen as a Politician, here in its eighth edition, with illustrations. She dedicates the book to the sad-eyed mothers who, like Cicely, look across the cradle of their boys into the great world of temptation and danger.

The preface is a dialogue. Josiah asks his wife a pointed question. Why had she said she loved sweet Cicely best of all her thought-children? She answers that she said it to tell the truth. Plainer still, she said it to keep from lying. Holley's dialect humor carries serious causes, temperance first among them, as Josiah blunders into politics and his wife comments on drink, votes, and village folly.
t-mann-tristan:
A tubercular writer and a Wagner-drunk dilettante circle each other at a Swiss sanatorium in Mann's novella Tristan, given here in German. Art against bourgeois life plays out as tragicomedy of manners around the frail Frau Kloeterjahn. Her husband's healthy world of business has no idea what is happening under its nose.

Mann rehearses, in comic form, themes The Magic Mountain would later treat at epic length. Music becomes both seduction and diagnosis among the patients. The wit here is Mann's sharpest early vintage, cutting in every direction at once. Spinell's triumph and humiliation arrive in the same gesture. The story remains a perfect small specimen of his early art.
tales-of-old-japan:
Lord Redesdale, once second secretary at the British post in Japan, published Tales of Old Japan in an 1910 printing, with the work first issued in 1871. Pictures drawn and cut on wood by Japanese artists fill the book, and the contents mix true tales, love tales, and fairy tales.

Named tales include The Forty-Seven Ronins, Kazuma's Revenge, and The Tongue-Cut Sparrow. A note explains that Redesdale spent years in Japan with the British legation and kept a deep love of its ways. Readers get an early English guide to Japanese lore, codes of honor, and folk tales, still read as a key source.
tallqvist-maqlu-1895-german:
Knut Tallqvist, a Finnish scholar of Assyria, published his edition of the Maqlû series at Helsingfors in 1895. Maqlû means 'Burning,' and the series is the great Assyrian rite against witchcraft. Tallqvist worked from clay tablets held by the British Museum, adding a German translation.

The rite runs through the night, burning clay figures of the witch while gods are called on to break her spells. Tallqvist's edition was the first full printing of the series. It is still the standard public source for Maqlû, since no free English version of the whole series exists.
th-barrel-organ:
Edwin Waugh wrote Th' Barrel Organ, a Lancashire dialect sketch printed at Manchester by John Heywood and in London by Simkin, Marshall and Co. Waugh tells the tale in the broad speech of the moor country.

The narrator sets out from Haslingden town-end with old Rondle o' th' Nab, called Sceawter, a moor-end farmer and cattle dealer. Rondle tells of a cross-eyed cat grown fat by catching two mice at one go, then gives road directions over the moor. Singers are due at his house that night. Readers get Waugh's famed ear for Lancashire talk, humor, and moorland ways, in a tale where the road talk is half the joy.
the-alaskan: James Oliver Curwood wrote The Alaskan, billed as a novel of the North, with art by Walt Louderback. Curwood gives the book, in a note signed at Owosso, Michigan, on August 1, 1923, to the strong-hearted folk of Alaska, a new empire then rising in the North. Chapters are numbered one through twenty-seven with no titles given.
the-amateur-cracksman:
E. W. Hornung's story set, dated 1898 in its heading, brings together eight tales about Raffles, a polished thief who moves in fine rooms. The contents list names pieces such as The Ides of March, A Costume Piece, Gentlemen and Players, Wilful Murder, and The Gift of the Emperor.

In the first tale the narrator returns late at night to Raffles's rooms at the Albany. Baccarat counters, empty glasses, and ash-trays still crowd the table after his loss. He pushes in without ceremony and begs a hearing from a man he hardly knows, though he once served him as a school fag.
the-amateur-gentleman: Front matter and a long contents list open Jeffery Farnol's The Amateur Gentleman, with pictures by Herman Pfeifer; Farnol is also billed as author of The Broad Highway. The book is dedicated to his father. Chapter titles trace young Barnabas as he knocks down his father and sets out for London Town. He buys a prized book from a pedler and meets a lady of quality. He also learns rules for bowing. Silk purses, a fateful lace handkerchief, and a torn bottle-green coat fill out the promised fare.
the-american:
Henry James published The American in 1877, a novel in twenty-six chapters. It opens on a bright May day in 1868 inside the Louvre in Paris. A gentleman lounges at ease on the great round divan in the Salon Carré, head thrown back and legs stretched out.

He gazes up at Murillo's moon-borne Madonna, plainly pleased with his own comfort. James sets a relaxed American ease against the old art of Europe in this first scene. The divan itself, the narrator notes, has since been removed, to the regret of weak-kneed art lovers who once rested there.
the-ancestral-footstep-fragment-outlines:
Nathaniel Hawthorne left The Ancestral Footstep as outlines of an English romance, printed here as an appendix alongside The Dolliver Romance, Fanshawe, and Septimius Felton. An opening note traces how the piece grew. While living in England, Hawthorne planned a romance set in that country, then set the plan aside.

A new idea took its place: a fanciful search for a way to live forever on earth. That idea grew into Septimius Felton and, later, the unfinished Dolliver Romance. The note calls the whole chain a family history of one story. Papers tied to the dropped English scheme still remained after Septimius Felton appeared, and these outlines are among them.
the-beasts-of-tarzan:
Edgar Rice Burroughs dedicated his Tarzan book to Joan Burroughs and opened it with a kidnapping. In Paris, D'Arnot tells John Clayton, Lord Greystoke, that Nikolas Rokoff has escaped from a French military prison. Neither police nor staff agents know how it was done.

Rokoff, Tarzan's arch-enemy, had been sentenced for life on the ape-man's testimony. Contents promise marooning, beasts at bay, a panther named Sheeta, a man called Mugambi, and a dance of death. Later chapters name a Swede, an escape, a trip down the Ugambi, and a return to jungle island and the law of the jungle.
the-bells-of-san-juan:
Jackson Gregory published a novel with Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1919, illustrated by Frank Tenney Johnson. Gregory is named for Judith of Blue Lake Ranch and Man to Man. A frontispiece shows a rider reining in his horse and staring at a woman in surprise.

A foreword about bells leads into chapters where bells ring and a sheriff of San Juan appears. Later headings name a man's boots, a banker's home, darkness in a patio, and a ride through the night. A home of cliff-dwellers and Jim Galloway's game promise western danger and intrigue in the opening list.
the-booming-of-acre-hill-and-other-remin: John Kendrick Bangs wrote The Booming of Acre Hill, put out in 1902 in New York and London with art by C. Dana Gibson. A note says the tales first ran in The Ladies Home Journal, The Woman's Home Companion, and Harper's own sheets. The list names eight tales. They start with the title tale and The Strange Misadventures of an Organ. The Plot That Failed and The Base Ingratitude of Barkis, M.D. come next. The Valor of Brinley and Wilkins close the set.
the-business-of-being-a-woman: Ida M. Tarbell wrote The Business of Being a Woman, put out in New York by the Macmillan Company in 1921. Tarbell was an associate editor of the American Magazine. The chapters shown are five. They are The Uneasy Woman, On the Imitation of Man, and The Business of Being a Woman. The Socialization of the Home and The Woman and Her Raiment complete the list. The book is given to two people named by initials alone, E.I.T. and C.C.T.
the-complete-plays-of-gilbert-and-sulliv: William S. Gilbert and Sir Arthur Sullivan made fourteen operas together between 1871 and 1896, and this volume gathers their plays. Only a contents list is present here, naming The Gondoliers, The Grand Duke, H.M.S. Pinafore, Iolanthe, The Mikado, and The Pirates of Penzance, each divided into two acts.Readers must take the book on its title page alone.
the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-part-: Part 1 of the complete works of Artemus Ward, the pen name of Charles Farrar Browne, opens a seven-part Project Gutenberg series. Only the Gutenberg header is present here, with its standard copyright warnings and donation notes. The header names this first part as number one of the series.What the book holds past its front matter stays untold here.

Part 6 of Charles Farrar Browne's Artemus Ward works carries a record title that breaks off after its first letters, hiding the part's theme. A Project Gutenberg header stands in place of the text, with the usual copyright warnings. That is all a reader gets here, so the part's pieces cannot be described.
the-constitution-of-the-united-states-of: Senate Document No. 170 of the 82nd Congress prints the United States Constitution with notes on cases ruled by the Supreme Court up to June 30, 1952. The Legislative Reference Service of the Library of Congress prepared it, with Edward S. Corwin as editor, and the Government Printing Office issued it in Washington in 1953 at a price of six dollars and twenty-five cents. Senate Joint Resolution 69, calling for a fresh edition of the 1938 annotated constitution, follows the title page. Only the front matter is present here.
the-coral-island-a-tale-of-the-pacific-o: R. M. Ballantyne's The Coral Island, a tale of the Pacific Ocean, opens with a preface signed Ralph Rover. Rover says he was a boy when he lived the adventures, and offers the book to boys for facts, pleasure, profit, and amusement. Boys or men who love to be gloomy, he warns, should shut it and put it away. The contents list chapters on his life, a dreadful storm, the island, a shark fight, diving, boat building, and a monster wave. Only the preface and contents are present here.
the-deserted-woman:
Honore de Balzac's The Deserted Woman, translated by Ellen Marriage, carries a dedication to the Duchesse d'Abrantes dated Paris, August 1835. In the early spring of 1822, Paris doctors sent a young man to Lower Normandy to recover from an inflammatory complaint brought on by overstudy, or perhaps by excess of another kind.

The fat lands of Bessin offered rest, light diet, bracing air, and freedom from excitement. Baron Gaston de Nueil settled at Bayeux, six miles from the sea, among retired relatives who treated a new arrival as a godsend. Within a few evenings in his cousin's house and in Mme. de Sainte-Severe's circle, he knew the whole town. Balzac then walks through its stock figures, starting with the family of incontestable, ancient nobility, unknown fifty leagues away, whose head is a determined sportsman with no manners.
the-desired-woman:
Will N. Harben, author of Dixie Hart and Pole Baker, opens The Desired Woman inside an Atlanta bank on a June morning. Clerks and accountants bend over ponderous ledgers on high stools minutes before the opening hour. Locomotive bells clang outside, and cabs, drays, and trucks rumble past the gray-stone building near the old passenger depot.

Jarvis Saunders, of the firm of Mostyn, Saunders and Company, bankers and brokers, comes in, hangs up his straw hat, and asks Wright, the paying-teller, what this is about Mostyn feeling badly. Wright, sponging his fat fingers as he counts currency. He is surprised the news has got out: Mostyn cautioned them all to say nothing, being a queer, sensitive man about his health and business. Saunders explains he met Dr. Loyd on the corner.
the-doctrine-and-practice-of-yoga-includ:
Swami Mukerji, a yogi of the South India Order, sets out yoga's doctrine and practice in lessons dated 1922. His front notes warn that no sentence is wasted, that the lessons pair with his books on the soul's force, and that no swift miracles should be hoped for. The first lesson takes up focus and thought control.

Students are told their lives are their own to shape. Desire, held firm, draws means and people by a law of attraction, he teaches. Drills for body and will, notes on Maya, guru worship, and will-force fill the course.
the-earlier-work-of-titian:
Claude Phillips, keeper of the Wallace Collection, wrote The Earlier Work of Titian, dated 1897, as one of the Portfolio art monographs. Its plate list names Flora as frontispiece, Sacred and Profane Love from the Borghese Gallery, a Virgin and Child from the Louvre, and The Young Man with a Glove. Two more works appear in colour plates.

Phillips traces the young Titian in Venice, from Giorgione's shadow to his own bold hand. Short text and many plates suit the student and the gallery-goer. The book helped fix the list of Titian's early works.
the-evolution-of-man:
Ernst Haeckel's The Evolution of Man, a popular scientific study rendered by Joseph McCabe from the fifth enlarged edition, was issued at London in 1912 for the Rationalist Press Association. Contents run from the fundamental law of organic evolution through older and modern embryology, phylogeny, the ovum and amoeba, conception, and the gastraea theory.

Later chapters claim man's vertebrate kinship and trace the germ layers. Haeckel held that each creature's growth replays its line's long past. McCabe's plain version spread that claim to a wide public. Plates and a glossary aid the general reader.
the-fall-of-the-moghul-empire-of-hindust: Only the old Project Gutenberg header is present here, before the book itself begins. It names The Fall of the Moghul Empire of Hindustan by H. G. Keene, and gives the book's release data from September 1998. No title page, contents list, or chapter text appears in these opening pages, so nothing about the history inside can be judged from the front pages alone.
the-first-man:
Eugene O'Neill wrote The First Man as a play in four acts. The cast centers on Curtis Jayson, his wife Martha, his banker father, his brothers and sisters, and his friend Mark Sheffield.

The acts move through the Jayson house in set steps. They start in the living room on a fall day. They move to Curtis's study the next morning. They end after a spring night at three in the morning. O'Neill sets a clash in that house. A man wants a free life of study and travel. His family wants heirs and a fixed place. Birth, death, and pride press on them all.
the-first-white-man-of-the-west-life-and:
Timothy Flint wrote this life of Colonel Daniel Boone, The First White Man of the West, printed in 1856. Verse on Boone's first view of Kentucky stands at the front.

The contents start with Boone's birth, school pranks, first hunts, and a brush with a panther. The family moves to North Carolina, and Boone grows into a hunter famed for fire hunting by night. A near-fatal blunder in that sport and his marriage close the first chapter's list. Flint, an early western writer, shaped Boone into the model of the backwoods pathfinder for a wide young readership.
the-foreigner-a-tale-of-saskatchewan:
Ralph Connor wrote The Foreigner as a tale of Saskatchewan, signed from Winnipeg in 1909 with a preface on the making of Canada. Many breeds, he says, are being made into one people there.

The contents open with a city on the plain where East meets West, then turn to the marriage of Anka, an unbidden guest, and the grip of British law. Kalman finds a mine and fights for it in the later chapters. Connor pleads for fair dealing and kind faith to bind Saxon, Slav, Celt, and Gaul into one Canadian people, and his tale tests that plea in love and law.
the-foundations-of-japan: The Foundations of Japan is present here only in front matter. Two pictures show life in a farm school. A list gives the author's past books on the Far East and on farming. The title page then begins. It gives the book's ground in a few lines. The notes were made on journeys of six thousand miles through the rural districts. The author's name does not stand in what can be read here. No chapter text is present. So the book's findings cannot be judged from the front pages alone.
the-going-of-the-white-swan:
Gilbert Parker wrote The Going of the White Swan. D. Appleton and Company printed it in New York in 1912. Earlier copyrights are dated 1895 and 1898. The tale opens in a northern cabin. A hurt child lies under a wolfskin robe. He asks his father why his mother does not come back.

The father shakes his head. He fumbles with the robe and says nothing. The child insists she would come if she knew he was hurt. The father nods, then turns to the door. He acts as if he still waits and hopes. A picture caption shows a priest in the tale. The priest says: No, no — this! The spare opening sets a story of loss and faith. It is also a story of a child's longing in the far north.
the-golden-mean:
The Golden Mean gives the golden ratio to one million digits. The ratio is written as (1 plus the square root of 5) over 2. A short head note gives the basis. It rests on a square root of 5 by Robert Nemiroff and Jerry Bonnell. No author, story, or argument is present. The work is the number itself, printed out in full.

The digits begin 1.6180339887498948482045868343656381177203091798057. They run on, block after block. They show no repeat and no end in sight. Such a list serves math readers. They need the constant to great depth for tests of machines. They need it for checks of methods. They need it for study of the ratio in geometry, growth, and art. Its value lies in its length and exactness.
the-goldfish-being-the-confessions-af-a-: Arthur Train edited The Goldfish. Its subtitle is Being the Confessions of a Successful Man. The book is dated 1921. Only front matter is present here: the title page, a contents list, and two quotes. The contents split the confessions into Myself, My Friends, My Children, My Mind, My Morals, and My Future. A line likens the rich to goldfish in a bowl: they can look out dimly, but cannot get out. A quote from William James calls the fear of poverty the worst moral disease of the age.
the-great-prince-shan:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote The Great Prince Shan. It is dated 1922. Chapter I opens in the card room of the St. Philip's Club. Prince Karschoff looks through a cloud of tobacco smoke. The room is spacious but almost deserted. He calls it a club for diplomats and gentlemen. Yet, he says, a decent rubber of bridge seems impossible to get.

Sir Daniel Harker answers him. Harker is a retired plenipotentiary to one of the smaller Powers. He has concluded that the club's reason for being is passing. There is no diplomacy nowadays, he says. Every man who pays his taxes is a gentleman. The Honourable Nigel Kingley is told to ransack the club for a fourth. The idle talk of three men in a fading club opens the tale. Behind it stand the new powers of the postwar world.
the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-dicti:
This record is the F to G section of Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary. The C. and G. Merriam Company published the version of 1913 at Springfield, Massachusetts. Noah Porter directed the work. The section begins on page 535 with the letter F. F is defined as the sixth letter of the English alphabet, and a nonvocal consonant. Its form came from the Latin, which took it from the Greek digamma, and that from the Phoenician.

The entries give pronunciation, derivation, and senses in the Merriam manner. Fa is the fourth tone in solmization. Fabaceous means having the nature of a bean. Fabian means cautious and dilatory, after the Roman general Fabius Maximus. His policy of delays and cautions foiled Hannibal. Fable is a feigned story meant to instruct or amuse. The section serves readers who need exact meanings and word histories from F into G.

This record is the M to N section of Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary. The C. and G. Merriam Company published the version of 1913 at Springfield, Massachusetts. Noah Porter directed the work. The section opens with the letter M. M is defined as the thirteenth letter of the English alphabet, and a vocal consonant. From its formation, it is called the labio-nasal consonant. Its form came from the Greek, through the Latin, and behind that the Phoenician and the Egyptian.

The entry gives M's further uses. As a numeral, M stands for one thousand, in English and in Latin. In printing, an em is a square quadrat, the unit for measuring type. In law, an M was a brand for a manslaughter convict admitted to benefit of clergy. The entries that follow run in the same full manner, for words from M into N.
the-henchman:
Mark Lee Luther wrote The Henchman. The Macmillan Company published it in New York in 1902. The copyright is dated 1901. Luther is named as the author of The Favor of Princes. A note before book one addresses knowing readers, who will spot the Tuscarora Stories from western New York history. Luther adapted them from Judge Arad Thomas's county history.

Chapter one opens with old geography lessons for children. Italy was likened to a boot in those lessons. France was likened to a coffee-pot. New York state figured as a couchant lion. Its head was thrust high in the North Country. Luther uses the playful image to place his tale.
the-highwayman: H. C. Bailey wrote The Highwayman. The contents list nineteen chapters. Early titles include The Complete Hero and The House of Waverton. Later titles include A Man of Many Worlds. One chapter is called A Gentleman's Purse. Another is called The World's a Miracle. Later titles include Harry Is Not Grateful. The list ends with Alison Finds Friends. No text past the front matter is present here. The novel itself does not appear.
the-hillman:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote The Hillman, copyright 1917 by Little, Brown, and Company. He is named as the author of The Kingdom of the Blind and Mr. Grex of Monte Carlo, and a frontispiece by George Avison is noted. Chapter one opens with Louise leaning back among the cushions of a motionless car.

Louise feels self-engrossed yet pleasantly apart from the troubles of the moment. Her eyes travel past a dim hillside of wall-enclosed fields, up to leaning clouds and unseen heights lost in mist. Oppenheim begins with stillness, wealth, and distance from the world below, before the calm of the scene is set to break.
the-home-of-the-blizzard-being-the-story:
Sir Douglas Mawson, D.Sc., B.E., wrote The Home of the Blizzard, the story of the Australasian Antarctic Expedition, 1911-1914. The title page promises maps and 260 illustrations by Dr. E. A. Wilson and other members of the expedition, plus plates in facsimile from Wilson's sketches. An author's preface states the object of the book.

Mawson aims to give one linked, plain account of the expedition for general readers, while granting that any such account falls short of the endeavor. Lasting reputation, he says, rests on the scientific volumes to come. History of Antarctic exploration is kept to a minimum, reports from sledging leaders were cut for balance, and a glossary helps readers with the terms.
the-hoosier-schoolmaster-a-story-of-back:
Edward Eggleston wrote The Hoosier Schoolmaster, subtitled a story of backwoods life in Indiana, dated 1871. A revised library edition carries an introduction and notes on the district by the author, character sketches by F. Opper, and other illustrations by W. E. B. Starkweather. Eggleston inscribes the edition to the memory of James Russell Lowell.

A preface to the library edition, called the history of a story, explains the occasion. Eggleston dates the writing and printing to the autumn of 1871. That made the book about twenty-one years old at the new edition. The publishers mean to mark its coming of age, and Eggleston uses the chance to revise the text and tell how the book began.
the-hunted-woman:
James Oliver Curwood wrote this northern adventure. His earlier novel Kazan is named on the title page. Frank B. Hoffman drew the illustrations. Curwood dedicated the book to his wife. He added their comrades of the trail. It appeared in 1915. Chapter I follows a woman in a pearl-gray veil. She has ridden eighteen hours into the mountains. A rushing crowd surrounds her. A voice behind her calls it the horde.

The illustrations list promises her story's shape. One caption quotes a man drawn north by a grave, not gold. Another shows a woman beside a huge brown bear. A third gives a tunnel sealing shut. Forty-five minutes of air remain in that scene. Curwood frames the gold-rush migration grandly. Such crowds made the flesh-and-blood foundation of nations. One frightened, watchful woman rides inside it.
the-institutes-of-justinian:
J. B. Moyle, barrister of Lincoln's Inn and fellow of New College, Oxford, translated Justinian's Institutes into English; the copy here is the fifth edition of 1913. The work opens with the emperor's own prologue, addressed to the youth desirous of studying the law. Justinian declares that majesty should carry laws as proudly as arms. Rome's ruler should be as careful in justice as in triumph over his foes.

He recounts the codification: inconsistencies removed from the sacred constitutions, the immense volumes of older jurisprudence crossed like a mid-ocean, and Tribonian, Theophilus, and Dorotheus commissioned to compose the Institutes. Where students once waited four years to read the constitutions, beginners may now learn their first lessons in law directly from the emperor's mouth. Moyle's translation keeps that proud voice intact for English law students.
the-iron-woman:
Margaret Deland wrote this novel. She dedicated it to Lorin Deland on August 12, 1911. He was her patient, ruthless, inspiring critic, she says. A text from Ezekiel fronts the book. It names fulness of bread and abundance of idleness as sin. Chapter I opens years earlier in an orchard. Elizabeth Ferguson has climbed an apple-tree there. She commands three children to climb up and play house. Her white-stockinged legs swing recklessly above them.

Her threat is gentle and frightening at once. She is afraid, perhaps, maybe, she will get mad. A giggle and a dimple soften nothing. All three children know what Elizabeth mad means. Nannie Maitland answers helplessly, as she always does. Deland begins with a child tyrant of charm and will. That child grows toward the iron woman of the title.
the-koran-al-qur-an:
George Sale's English Koran was made from the original Arabic. Notes from the most approved commentators explain it. A preliminary discourse opens the work. Sale dedicates it to John, Lord Carteret. He expects to need an apology. Founders of states and givers of laws are usually honored, he writes. Arabia's lawgiver has fared very differently at their hands. All who deny his divine mission treat him so. Christians especially do.

Sale argues the Arab conquests cannot alone explain the hatred. Calamity charges apply to all conquerors alike. The difference is that Mohammed gave a new religion. Sale's version was the first English Koran made directly from Arabic. It held the field for two centuries. Its long preliminary discourse made it a work of scholarship too. Scripture and scholarship stand together in it.
the-last-man:
Mary Shelley wrote this vast tale of the last man on earth in 1826. She had by then lost her husband and most of her dear kin and friends. The book is the first great work of its kind, the tale of the end of mankind.

A plague spreads year by year through the world and leaves Lionel Verney alone at last. He roams a Rome of tombs and writes his tale for no reader who may come. The book founds the whole line of tales of the end of the world in print.
the-later-works-of-titian: Claude Phillips, keeper of the Wallace Collection, published his study of Titian later paintings in 1898. Only the title page and list of illustrations are present here, naming copper plates of a self portrait, La Bella, Titian daughter Lavinia, and the Cornaro family. Sepia plates and text images from galleries in Florence, Berlin, London, and Paris also appear in the list. The critical text on the Venetian painter late style does not appear in this record.
the-leopard-woman: Stewart Edward White published his African adventure novel in 1916, illustrated by W. H. D. Koerner. Only the title page and contents are present here, listing thirty-two chapters on a march, a rhinoceros, a stranger, a water hole, thirst, an ivory stockade, a murder, and a trial. Kingozi and a woman called the Leopard Woman drive the later chapter titles. The safari narrative itself cannot be seen in this record beyond those chapter headings.
the-life-and-opinions-of-tristram-shandy:
Laurence Sterne presents his comic novel through a dedication to the Right Honourable Mr. Pitt. He writes from a retired thatched house in a far corner of the kingdom. Mirth, he says, forms his defense against ill health and the other evils of life.

Sterne begs Pitt to carry the book into the country and hopes it may win a smile or ease a moment of pain. That playful plea sets the tone for Tristram own wandering account of his life and opinions. Digression, jokes, and family oddity rule a novel famous for refusing a straight line.
the-life-of-john-bunyan:
Edmund Venables wrote his life of John Bunyan for an 1888 Walter Scott edition. Chapter one places Bunyan birth at Elstow in Bedfordshire late in 1628, with baptism on the last day of November. His book, Venables says, likely leads all English books in editions, readers, and translations.

The birth year also brought the Petition of Right and a growing struggle between Charles I and Parliament. Venables sets a tinker preacher life against civil war politics and church pressure. Grace Abounding and The Pilgrim Progress grew from that pressure, and the life traces both faith and jail time.
the-little-red-chimney-being-the-love-st: Mary Finley Leonard wrote The Little Red Chimney, subtitled The Love Story of a Candy Man, published by Duffield and Company in 1914 with silhouette pictures by Katharine Gassaway. What is present stops at the title page and part of the contents; the story itself does not appear. The chapter summaries are playful. The curtain rises on the Candy Wagon. The Candy Man walks abroad in citizen's clothes and is mistaken for a man of wealth. The Little Red Chimney appears on the horizon without a clue to its importance.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-1:
Volume ten of Suetonius's Lives, in the Thomson translation revised by T. Forester, turns to Titus Flavius Vespasianus Augustus. Suetonius says the empire, long unsettled after its last three rulers rebelled and died violently, was restored to peace by the Flavian family. That family was obscure and boasted no ancestral honors, yet he adds that the public had no cause to regret its rise.

He traces the line to Titus Flavius Petro of Reate, who fled the battle of Pharsalia and later collected money at public auctions. Petro's son Sabinus never served as a soldier and instead farmed the tax of the fortieth penny in Asia. An emperor from tax collectors and auction rooms makes the volume a study in unlikely origins.

Domitian, the last of the Twelve Caesars, closes Suetonius's set in volume twelve, in Alexander Thomson's translation revised by T. Forester. He was born on October 24 at a place called the Pomegranate in Rome, in a house he later turned into a temple of the Flavian family. Suetonius reports hostile stories about his youth: great want, no silver plate of his own, and shameful bargains alleged by his enemies.

During the war with Vitellius, Domitian fled into the Capitol with his uncle Sabinus. When the temple burned, he hid all night with the sacristan, then escaped across the Tiber disguised as a worshipper of Isis among her priests. Suetonius mixes documented danger with scandal, inviting readers to judge which parts deserve belief.
the-lookout-man: B. M. Bower's The Lookout Man was published by Little, Brown of Boston in August 1917, with a frontispiece by H. Weston Taylor. Only the title pages, a list of Bower's novels, and the start of the contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The chapters include Some Time!, Thanks for the Car, and To the Feather River Country and Freedom. They hint at a car and an escape into Sierra country. Bower's listed books include Good Indian and The Heritage of the Sioux.
the-magician:
W. Somerset Maugham's The Magician, dated 1908, is printed together with a fragment of his autobiography. In that fragment Maugham recalls qualifying as a doctor at St Thomas's Hospital in 1897 after five years of study. While still a student he had published a novel, Liza of Lambeth, which caused a mild sensation. On its strength he rashly abandoned doctoring to earn his living as a writer, and set out for Spain, spending the best part of a year in Seville.

He amused himself hugely and wrote a bad novel, he admits. Back in London he shared a small flat near Victoria Station and spent six years writing novels and plays that mostly failed. One play, A Man of Honour, at last reached the Stage Society. Sixteen chapters of The Magician follow, but the fragment itself is the candid draw here.
the-make-believe-man:
Richard Harding Davis's The Make-Believe Man is told by a twenty-five-year-old stenographer at Joyce and Carboy's, woollen manufacturers, who has always wished for adventures that avoid him. His friend Kinney, a clerk a year older, sits next to him at work and rooms at the same boarding-house. Adventures find Kinney constantly: he helps people down fire-escapes, befriends noblemen and actors, and is pursued by beautiful women in taxicabs calling for assistance.

The narrator, raised in the pretty harbor of Fairport, studies law at night hoping to reach the bar. For vacation he plans to seek adventures at last, and Kinney arranges that they go together, pointing out that no better guide exists. The narrator half suspects Kinney invents his exploits, and the trip is set up as a test of the make-believe man.
the-making-of-an-american:
Jacob A. Riis, author of How the Other Half Lives, wrote The Making of an American as his autobiography. A note to the reader, dated from Richmond Hill, New York, in October 1901, explains that the papers first appeared in The Outlook, with parts in The Churchman and The Century Magazine. To readers asking whether the stories are made up, Riis answers that they are not, and that he is glad to have lived every part of it.

The contents begin the arc in chapter titles: The Meeting on the Long Bridge and I Land in New York and Take a Hand in the Game. I Go to War at Last, Working and Wandering, and I Go into Business Headlong follow. A chapter in which he becomes an editor and receives his first love letter closes the list. Readers get a reporter's life told as an American success story.
the-man:
Bram Stoker, author of Dracula, wrote The Man, shown here in the 1897 Robert Hayes edition from London. A short opening called Fore-Glimpse sets a young man and a young girl on a low tombstone in an old churchyard. Through a hawthorn tree they overhear two children talking, and one child's sentence stops them cold: "I would rather be an angel than God!" They sit as still as mice to listen.

Stoker pauses over the scene like a painter. The low, square-towered church has long mullioned windows and yellow-grey stone roughened with lichens. Tombstones tilt in all directions, gnarled yews line the back, and laburnum, lilac, hawthorn, and meadowsweet mingle their sweetness over a lazy stream in June sunlight. The foreglimpse promises a story seeded by a child's remark about ambition and heaven.
the-martyrdom-of-man:
Winwood Reade published The Martyrdom of Man in 1872, a sweeping work shaped by his travels and his religious skepticism. An opening note gives his life in brief: born near Crieff in 1838, nephew of the novelist Charles Reade, and educated at Oxford. He traveled in Africa in 1862, returned in 1868, and later reported the Ashanti War for The Times.

Reade's own preface explains that a London merchant, Andrew Swanzy, financed his second African journey and left him free to choose his route. He spent two years traveling, in 1868 to 1870, studying religion and morality among the peoples he met. The note also traces his other books, from Savage Africa to The Outcast, a novel about persecution for unbelief. Readers meet a Victorian explorer whose field experience fed a bold, questioning history of mankind.
the-master-christian:
Marie Corelli's novel The Master-Christian carries a dedication to all churches who quarrel in the name of Christ. Corelli, author of Thelma and Ardath, opens her story in Rouen as the Angelus bells ring at sunset. Market women cross themselves on the road home, and a bargeman on the Seine mutters a prayer from habit. Schoolchildren hesitate over whether the old formula still belongs in their modern, secular schooling.

A visitor gives the evening its charge: a cardinal-archbishop famed for purity of heart has come to Rouen that day. His own diocese regards him almost as a saint. Corelli sets the scene amid grey towers, river light, and a France that has pushed God out of its national institutions. Readers enter a tale about living faith set against church quarrels and public unbelief. Corelli's Rouen glows while her questions sharpen.
the-measure-of-a-man: Amelia E. Barr published The Measure of a Man with D. Appleton and Company in 1915, with illustrations by Frank T. Merrill. Only the title page, the dedication, and the opening contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. Barr dedicated the book, with sincere esteem, to Mrs. Arthur Roberts of Evanston, Illinois. The contents begin with The Great Sea Waters and The People of the Story, then turn to love venturing in, brothers, a hearth fire, and love's young dream.
the-middle-class-gentleman:
Moliere's comedy-ballet The Middle Class Gentleman, in a translation by Philip Dwight Jones, was first presented at Chambord for the king's entertainment in October 1670. Jones also produced the text. The cast centers on Monsieur Jourdain, a bourgeois, with his wife, their daughter Lucile, and her suitor Cleonte. A count, Dorante, and a marchioness, Dorimene, supply the aristocracy Jourdain longs to join. Masters of music, dancing, fencing, and philosophy crowd the household staff.

Act One opens in Jourdain's Paris house, where the Music Master's pupil sits composing a serenade Jourdain has ordered. The Music Master and Dancing Master settle their performers on either side of the stage to wait for their patron. Their patience frames the joke of the whole play: artists, tutors, and tradesmen all live off one rich man's vanity. Readers meet the machinery of flattery assembled before its victim even enters.
the-miracle-man: Frank L. Packard published The Miracle Man with Grosset and Dunlap of New York in 1914. Only the title page, a dedication 'to nearly everybody,' and the opening contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. The contents open with The Roost, then promise A New Cult, a character called Needley, and the Patriarch. Later chapters bring the Patriarch's grand niece, a pilgrimage, and the miracle itself, with the bait nibbled along the way.
the-motor-maids-in-fair-japan:
Katherine Stokes's The Motor Maids in Fair Japan, dated 1913, is present here only in title page and contents, so the Japanese tour does not appear. Stokes is billed as author of The Motor Maids' School Days, The Motor Maids by Palm and Pine, and The Motor Maids Across the Continent, among other volumes in the series.

Eighteen chapters are listed. Off for Japan opens the book, followed by Tea in the Garden and Shopping in Jinrikshas, the hand-pulled carts of Japan. Cherry blossoms, a birthday party, a theatre party, and a letter that came though it was never sent fill the middle headings. The Ancient City of Sleep, The Storm King, and The Magnet and the Silver Churn close the list.
the-naturewoman:
Upton Sinclair's play The Naturewoman opens with a cast list and a plan of its four acts. Oceana, the Naturewoman herself, heads the characters. Around her stands the Masterson family of Beacon Street, Boston: Mrs. Sophronia Masterson, her husband Dr. Quincy Masterson, their son Freddy, and their daughters Ethel and the married Letitia Selden. Remson, a butler, completes the household.

Act I is set in the Masterson drawing room on a winter afternoon, and Act II in the same room the next day. Act III moves to a portion of the parlour used as a stage that evening, while Act IV shifts to Henry Selden's camp in the White Mountains a week later. The curtain rises on Ethel, a frail girl of sixteen, opening a framed photograph and crying Oceana's name in rapture.
the-new-frontiers-of-freedom-from-the-al:
E. Alexander Powell's The New Frontiers of Freedom, subtitled From the Alps to the Aegean, was published in New York by Charles Scribner's Sons in April 1920. Only a list of Powell's books, title page, dedication, and the heading of an acknowledgment are present here, so the travel narrative does not appear. A caption shows the Queen of Rumania telling Major Powell how much she enjoys being a queen.

Powell's earlier war books head the list printed on the facing page: Fighting in Flanders, The Road to Glory, Vive la France! and Italy at War. The volume is dedicated to Major J. Stanley Moore of the Department of State, called a real and lifelong friend. The acknowledgment begins by citing the disturbed conditions prevailing across most of the region.
the-night-horseman:
Max Brand's The Night Horseman, dated 1920, is present here only in a series list, title page, and contents, so the western itself does not appear. The facing list names three Brand books in the set: The Untamed, Trailin', and The Night Horseman itself. Eighteen chapters are listed, each with a short title.

The Scholar opens the book, followed by Words and Bullets and The Doctor Rides. The Chain, The Waiting, and The Mission Starts build toward Jerry Strann and The Gift-Horse. Battle Light, a chapter titled Sweet Adeline, The Buzzard, and Music for Old Nick fill the middle list. Buck Makes His Get-Away and Doctor Byrne Analyses close what is shown.
the-patrician: John Galsworthy wrote the novel The Patrician, dated 1911 in the header. Only the contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The chapters are numbered without titles. Part I alone runs to eighteen numbered chapters in the list shown. Nothing in the pages present names the characters or the setting. The record offers only the book's bare frame, the plan of a long first part with no word of its people or places.
the-perpetuation-of-living-beings-heredi:
Thomas Henry Huxley lectured on The Perpetuation of Living Beings, hereditary transmission, and variation. He begins by setting aside the origin of life, on which, he says, we know nothing historically or experimentally. The question for the night is narrower: given living forms, how are they reproduced, perpetuated, and modified?

On that question our knowledge is large. Huxley divides perpetuation into asexual and sexual kinds. Gardeners know the first from cuttings: a geranium cutting, given light, warmth, and nourishment, grows into a plant with all its parent's properties. Sexual perpetuation, by the action of two individuals, is far more common among animals. The lecture lays out heredity in plain terms.
the-pharisee-and-the-publican:
The Pharisee and the Publican appears here in the 1845 Thomas Nelson edition of the Works of the Puritan Divines (Bunyan). The text opens with the parable from Luke, chapter eighteen. Two men went up into the temple to pray. The Pharisee thanked God he was not as other men. The publican smote his breast and asked for mercy.

Bunyan first recalls the earlier parable of the unjust judge and the widow. That parable teaches men to pray and not faint. If urging moved an unjust judge, he argues, God's people will prevail with a loving Father all the more. He then turns to his text with two aims. He means to convict the proud Pharisee. He also means to raise up the cast-down publican.
the-poor-gentleman:
Hendrik Conscience's The Poor Gentleman, translated expressly for this American edition, closes a series of tales about women in positions of trial. The preface explains the design. In The Village Innkeeper the heroine is torn between propriety and foolish ambition for high life. In The Conscript the heroine of humble life shows uncorrupted virtue and courage against authority. Here the heroine comes from the educated classes of Conscience's own countrymen.

The tale's hero, the perplexed De Vlierbeck, is praised as a character who engraves himself on the memory. The French critic Pontmartin is quoted calling these simple stories pearls set in Flemish gold. At not more than a hundred and fifty pages, the book is credited with a photographic minuteness of detail. That detail never loses motion or picturesque effect. The preface withholds plot summary on purpose, so as not to anticipate the author.
the-return-of-tarzan:
Edgar Rice Burroughs lists twenty-six chapters for Tarzan's return. The list opens with an affair on a liner. Paris streets and a countess's explanation follow. A duel and a desert fight come next. A wreck leads back to the primitive. Treasure vaults of Opar close the contents. Chapter one opens aboard ship instead. The Countess de Coude murmurs admiration under her breath.

Her husband asks what is magnificent. She covers a flush with a quick excuse. She was only recalling wit, she claims. Shipboard manners hide jungle loyalties in the exchange. The contents promise a wide arc for Tarzan. He will pass from drawing rooms to apes. Waziri warriors and a city of gold await him.
the-revolt-of-man:
Walter Besant explains in a preface dated December 1896 that his satire first appeared anonymously fourteen years earlier and stood ignored for six weeks until a strong review drew readers. Many editions followed, and he thanks two ladies who heard chapters read aloud during a summer holiday.

Their key advice shaped the ending: keep the revolt bloodless rather than closing with a real battle. Contents then open in Park Lane with an earl, a chancellor, and a great duchess. The preface alone tells readers to expect a role-reversal comedy handled with wit rather than violence.
the-river-war-an-account-of-the-reconque:
Winston S. Churchill recounts the reconquest of the Sudan. A 1902 edition carries his account here. Contents run from the Mahdi's rebellion onward. A Dervish empire and years of preparation follow. Firket and the Dongola recovery mark the advance. A desert railway transforms the campaign's supply lines. Abu Hamed and Berber fall in sequence.

The Atbara battle and the grand advance follow. Operations of the first of September precede Omdurman. The city's fall and the Fashoda incident come next. The Khalifa's end closes the contents list. Only the title page is present on these pages. The contents list and a campaign map appear with it. The campaign narrative itself does not appear here.
the-riverman:
Stewart Edward White sets his logging novel in 1872. A river bend above a pond holds the scene. A dam ends the pond at its lower reach. A two-story mill stands on the flat below it. Stump-dotted clearing surrounds the mill on every side. Dense forest covers all the land beyond it. Hardwoods crowd the bottom-lands along the stream. Their branches spray out in first spring green.

White pine and hemlock crown the higher lands behind. Norway pine and spruce stand sturdy among them there. Wind riffles the pond in fan-shaped cat's-paws overhead. Wavelets lap against a barrier of floating logs below. More logs carpet the inlet as far as sight reaches. A man could walk down that river like a highway. White builds a working river world before its rivermen.
the-rover-boys-on-the-great-lakes-or-the:
The fifth Rover Boys volume, The Rover Boys on the Great Lakes, is introduced by Arthur M. Winfield, identified as Edward Stratemeyer. He admits he first planned only three or four volumes. Reader demand kept extending the line. A frontispiece shows a blaze revealing a mass of lumber on turbulent waters.

The tale moves Dick, Tom and Sam from Putnam Hall to a pleasure tour of the Great Lakes. On Lake Erie they meet an old enemy. He schemes to kidnap Dick after the boy falls overboard from his yacht in a storm. The subtitle points to the secret of the island cave.
the-scarlet-gown-being-verses-by-a-st-an:
The Scarlet Gown gathers verses by a St. Andrews man. No name is given for the poet. The edition transcribed here was published in 1891. Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton and Company issued it in London. An epigraph from Andrew Lang calls St. Andrews a haunted town. Lang names its college of the scarlet gown and its northern sea.

The first poem, The Voice That Sings, asks who can hear a voice across the night. It carries echoes of long forgotten days and things. Faded eyes brim over at the sound, the poem says. The next piece, The Best Pipe, turns comic. The speaker rejects a cutty clay pipe, however fervently praised. A twelvemonth smoked, it smells of rank decay, he complains. He asks instead for a finely seasoned briar.
the-second-story-man:
Upton Sinclair's play The Second-Story Man has three characters. Jim Faraday is the second-story man of the title. Harvey Austin is a lawyer, and Helen Austin is his wife. The scene is the library of the Austin home. The time is two in the morning. Stage directions show a luxuriously furnished room. A lamp stands on a central table, and a cabinet of curios fills one corner.

At rise, the room is dark except for firelight. Sounds of breaking wood come from the window. Jim enters through it, a roughly dressed young fellow with a patch over one eye.
